# Plasmon-mediated pairing and dynamical screening

Understand collective charge modes, dielectric screening and pairing proposals without confusing a measured plasmon with proof of its superconducting role.

## Scope

Plasmon-mediated pairing is a proposal in which the frequency-dependent screening of Coulomb interactions contributes to a superconducting pairing kernel. A plasmon is a collective charge oscillation; it is not an exciton, a static charge-density wave or an acoustic phonon. Observing a charge mode establishes something available to couple to electrons, not the cause of their superconductivity.

Takada's early electron-gas calculation used weak coupling and a plasmon-pole approximation to examine dimensionality. Akashi and Arita later developed a dynamical superconducting density-functional kernel and predicted cooperative phonon–plasmon enhancement for compressed fcc lithium. These are calculations under specified approximations, not experimental isolation of a universal pairing mechanism. Only their publisher abstracts have been checked here. [R1](#ref-source-aa923c1f369b97dc) [R5](#ref-source-9f1dd3c6cc7b89c4)

## Mathematical assumptions

In a homogeneous scalar description, the screened interaction is $W(q,z)=V_q/\epsilon(q,z)$. Crystals and interfaces can require dielectric matrices and wavefunction matrix elements. A longitudinal collective mode is associated with a pole of the response; with damping its frequency is complex. A zero of $\operatorname{Re}\epsilon$ on the real axis is not a complete mode definition. The measured loss function $-\operatorname{Im}\epsilon^{-1}$ also contains line-shape information.

An independent Drude illustration normalizes the background dielectric constant to one and assumes plasma frequency $\omega_p$ and damping rate $\gamma$:

$$\epsilon(z)=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{z(z+i\gamma)},\qquad z_\pm=-\frac{i\gamma}{2}\pm\sqrt{\omega_p^2-\frac{\gamma^2}{4}}.$$

Direct complex substitution and numerical loss maximization were checked for four damping ratios. At $\gamma/\omega_p=0.5$, the positive real-part zero is approximately $0.866\omega_p$, the real part of the pole is $0.96825\omega_p$, and the loss maximum is $0.96877\omega_p$. They are different quantities. For stronger damping a loss maximum can remain even without a real-axis dielectric zero; it does not guarantee a long-lived excitation.

With damping set to zero and imaginary frequency $i\nu$, the same illustration gives

$$\frac{W(i\nu)}{V}=1-\frac{\omega_p^2}{\nu^2+\omega_p^2}=\frac{\nu^2}{\nu^2+\omega_p^2}.$$

Five direct evaluations are nonnegative despite the negative retarded term in the decomposition. Removing the instantaneous term would change the model. This long-wavelength expression must not be substituted for finite-momentum static screening. Whether a frequency-dependent interaction supports pairing requires the full gap equation, normal self-energy and a defensible treatment of high-energy states; the sign of one separated term is insufficient.

Geometry also changes the modes. For two identical ideal electron sheets separated by $d$, with no tunneling and a hydrodynamic density response, diagonalizing the Coulomb layer matrix gives

$$\omega_\pm^2=Cq\left(1\pm e^{-qd}\right),\qquad C=\frac{2\pi n_{2D}e^2}{\kappa m}.$$

Here $q$ is the in-plane wavevector magnitude, $\kappa$ the background permittivity and Gaussian electrostatic units are used. In the $qd\ll1$ limit, the in-phase mode scales as $\sqrt{2Cq}$ and the out-of-phase mode as $q\sqrt{Cd}$. Four direct matrix checks recover these limits. The illustration omits tunneling, finite thickness, carrier pressure and the particle–hole continuum. A linear branch in this ideal model neither guarantees weak Landau damping nor describes every layered crystal.

A separate lossless ionic-screening illustration uses $\epsilon_{\mathrm{tot}}/\epsilon_\infty=(\omega_L^2-z^2)/(\omega_T^2-z^2)-\omega_e^2/z^2$, where $\omega_L>\omega_T>0$ describe one polar oscillator and $\omega_e$ is the electronic plasma scale screened only by $\epsilon_\infty$. Its squared mode frequencies satisfy $x^2-(\omega_L^2+\omega_e^2)x+\omega_e^2\omega_T^2=0$. Direct root searches agree with the quadratic roots for five normalized examples. At low electronic plasma scale the lower branch approaches $\omega_e\omega_T/\omega_L$; at high scale it approaches $\omega_T$. This demonstrates hybridization, not a calculated material transition temperature.

## Experimental criteria

Measure the charge response over the momentum and energy window relevant to the electrons, including linewidths, polarization, dielectric surroundings and calibration. Optical measurements near zero momentum and finite-momentum scattering constrain different parts of the problem. A pairing attribution additionally needs a screened interaction consistent with the band structure, normal response and superconducting observations on comparable samples.

Hepting and colleagues' 2018 electron-doped cuprate study used polarization and momentum dependence to identify collective charge excitations with out-of-plane dispersion. Its publisher abstract supports the mode assignment; this entry has not independently reanalyzed its spectra or extracted a pairing interaction from them. [R3](#ref-source-e960d0fed8eb7d7f)

Their 2022 published SLCO study reports Cu-edge RIXS at 20 K with about 40 meV energy resolution and an approximately 120 meV plasmon gap. Near $|H|\le0.005$ reciprocal lattice units, overlap with a phonon prevents unambiguous peak fitting; these points were excluded from the model fit. The authors describe an acousticlike but gapped branch and interpret its dispersion using a layered model with interlayer hopping. The measurement temperature and mode gap are not superconducting transition temperatures or direct pairing evidence. [R4](#ref-source-06e9bd0e34513767)

The earlier manuscript's selected equations and the final publisher abstract were checked; full final-version comparison is still pending. The study is not a theorem excluding all plasmon mechanisms. [R6](#ref-source-87b23717bc50e3a9)

Nor does a high collective-mode energy justify applying a phonon adiabatic approximation unchanged. Electronic scales, coupling strength, vertex corrections and competing fluctuations need explicit treatment. No independent calculation in this article solves a superconducting instability or certifies a material mechanism.

articles.body:
## Scope

Resonating valence bond, or RVB, denotes a family of correlated-state constructions built from quantum superpositions of singlet bonds. Anderson's 1987 proposal connected singlets in a correlated insulator to superconductivity after doping. It is a theoretical route, not a diagnosis obtained merely by finding a superconductor near an insulator. The original article's indexed abstract was checked; its complete argument remains outside this source review. [R1](#ref-source-5a6026d6455bf7a0)

RVB is not synonymous with a particular quantum spin liquid, a universal pairing boson or a directly measurable order parameter. A chosen wavefunction, projection and treatment of emergent gauge dynamics determine its physical predictions. The Lee–Nagaosa–Wen formulation distinguishes the redundancy used to represent electrons from the low-energy gauge structure of a state. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

## Mathematical assumptions

A singlet on ordered sites $i,j$ is $|s_{ij}\rangle=(|\uparrow_i\downarrow_j\rangle-|\downarrow_i\uparrow_j\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Different products of such bonds need not be orthogonal. An independent four-spin illustration takes $A=|s_{12}s_{34}\rangle$ and $B=|s_{14}s_{23}\rangle$, with the stated orientation fixing their relative sign. Direct expansion gives $\langle A|B\rangle=-1/2$, so the normalized superposition is $(A-B)/\sqrt3$, not $(A-B)/\sqrt2$.

For the periodic four-site spin Hamiltonian $H=J\sum_{i=1}^4\mathbf S_i\cdot\mathbf S_{i+1}$ with $J>0$, direct action on this superposition gives energy $-2J$ and zero eigenvector residual. An equal incoherent mixture of the two bond coverings has energy $-3J/2$. The difference demonstrates quantum interference in a specified finite spin problem. Neither result establishes bulk topological order or superconductivity: this model has no mobile charge degrees of freedom.

To distinguish a strong-coupling approximation from an exact scale, consider a two-site, one-orbital Hubbard model with two electrons, hopping $t$ and repulsion $U>0$. Exact diagonalization of its six-state sector gives a singlet–triplet splitting

$$J_{\mathrm{dimer}}=\frac{\sqrt{U^2+16t^2}-U}{2}\simeq\frac{4t^2}{U}\quad(U\gg|t|).$$

Four independent matrix calculations agree with the exact expression. At $U/|t|=4$, the leading expression overestimates the splitting by about 20.7%; at 32 the error is about 0.39%. The local exchange scale and its expansion do not by themselves predict a pairing temperature in a doped lattice. Multiorbital charge-transfer materials require additional assumptions before using this one-band reduction.

A projected-electron construction writes $c_{i\sigma}=b_i^\dagger f_{i\sigma}$ with $b_i^\dagger b_i+\sum_\sigma f_{i\sigma}^\dagger f_{i\sigma}=1$. It represents the reduced local Hilbert space containing an empty site and two singly occupied spin states. Under the internal redundancy $f_i\to e^{i\theta_i}f_i$, $b_i\to e^{i\theta_i}b_i$, the electron remains invariant. A spinon pair alone changes phase; the accompanying charge factor cancels it. Three explicit phase checks confirm this cancellation. A gauge-fixed factorization into spin and charge averages is an approximation, not separate observation of either factor. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

An independent Gaussian response illustration minimizes

$$F(a,A)=\frac{\rho_b}{2}(A-a)^2+\frac{\rho_f}{2}a^2,\qquad \rho_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\rho_b\rho_f}{\rho_b+\rho_f}.$$

Here $A$ is a normalized external field, $a$ an internal field, and nonnegative coefficients describe two sectors within this quadratic model. Four direct minimizations agree with the expression. A finite $\rho_f$ does not provide charged stiffness when $\rho_b=0$. This is a restricted response illustration: non-Gaussian and compact gauge fluctuations are absent, and it is not a universal experimental law.

## Experimental criteria

Establish the insulating state's magnetic and structural properties before naming it a spin liquid. Vaknin and colleagues' neutron-diffraction study of undoped La2CuO4-y reports magnetic superlattice evidence for antiferromagnetism. That parent-state observation must be retained alongside the historical RVB proposal. A measured superconducting gap symmetry may constrain candidate states without uniquely selecting their microscopic explanation. [R7](#ref-source-9dda11fbf0c41f73)

Lefebvre and colleagues mapped kappa-(ET)2Cu[N(CN)2]Cl using helium pressure, proton NMR and ac susceptibility. The selected manuscript uses a 0.5 T field for NMR and no static field for the susceptibility measurement; it restricts hydrostatic sweeps to conditions above helium solidification. The authors report inhomogeneous phase coexistence but do not resolve whether it is macroscopic or mesoscopic. These conditions belong to kappa-Cl and cannot be transferred to a different organic salt. [R3](#ref-source-2cc5358d54a65217)

For kappa-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3, Shimizu and colleagues' abstract reports no NMR indication of long-range order down to 32 mK, despite a susceptibility-derived exchange scale around 250 K. Neither number is a superconducting transition temperature. Kurosaki and colleagues separately studied its pressure-dependent NMR and resistivity phase diagram. The existence of neighboring superconductivity does not identify the insulating state's excitations as its pairing mechanism. Those two sources remain abstract-scoped here. [R4](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R5](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c)

## Limits and disputes

Pustogow and colleagues' 2023 strain-transport study favors a low-entropy, spin-gapped valence-bond-solid interpretation of the organic candidate's 6 K anomaly. The 140 nm crystal is coupled to a PET substrate; quoted hydrostatic-equivalent pressures are inferred by comparison with transport data. The paper acknowledges that a gapped chiral spin liquid is not ruled out without a discriminating experiment. It also assigns sharp resistance jumps to mounting-related microcracks. A transport anomaly or phase-diagram shape alone must not be promoted to an unambiguous microscopic spin-state determination. [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

The Lee–Nagaosa–Wen review itself notes an experimental mismatch in the doping dependence of the Gaussian U(1) prediction for the temperature slope of superfluid density. Thus the simple response construction above has an explicit historical limitation. Naming a redundant representation U(1), SU(2) or Z2 is not sufficient to establish the corresponding emergent low-energy phase. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

Pseudogaps, Fermi arcs, singlet correlations and d-wave pairing each admit more than one theoretical description. Test a specified RVB state against physical correlation functions, charge stiffness, spectral weight, symmetry and disorder responses. Treating all these observations as interchangeable proof would remove the very distinctions needed to compare mechanisms. Full final-version, data and material-specific calculations remain open.

## Discovery implications

Track a controlled doping or bandwidth path with independently established magnetic, structural and superconducting observables. Distinguish tuning the filling from changing hopping, disorder or lattice geometry. Preserve the local constraints of a theoretical model and calculate gauge-invariant observables before assigning a material interpretation. A finite singlet-energy gain is a useful model check, not an experimentally verified route to high-temperature superconductivity.

## Related topics

Compare [quantum spin liquids](/scwiki/spin-liquids-and-superconductivity), [spin fluctuations](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), [superconducting gap](/scwiki/superconducting-gap) and [charge fluctuations](/scwiki/charge-fluctuation-pairing).

The local exchange scale and its expansion do not by themselves predict a pairing temperature in a doped lattice. Multiorbital charge-transfer materials require additional assumptions before using this one-band reduction.

A projected-electron construction writes $c_{i\sigma}=b_i^\dagger f_{i\sigma}$ with $b_i^\dagger b_i+\sum_\sigma f_{i\sigma}^\dagger f_{i\sigma}=1$. It represents the reduced local Hilbert space containing an empty site and two singly occupied spin states. Under the internal redundancy $f_i\to e^{i\theta_i}f_i$, $b_i\to e^{i\theta_i}b_i$, the electron remains invariant. A spinon pair alone changes phase; the accompanying charge factor cancels it. Three explicit phase checks confirm this cancellation. A gauge-fixed factorization into spin and charge averages is an approximation, not separate observation of either factor. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

An independent Gaussian response illustration minimizes

$$F(a,A)=\frac{\rho_b}{2}(A-a)^2+\frac{\rho_f}{2}a^2,\qquad \rho_{\mathrm{eff}}=\frac{\rho_b\rho_f}{\rho_b+\rho_f}.$$

Here $A$ is a normalized external field, $a$ an internal field, and nonnegative coefficients describe two sectors within this quadratic model. Four direct minimizations agree with the expression. A finite $\rho_f$ does not provide charged stiffness when $\rho_b=0$. This is a restricted response illustration: non-Gaussian and compact gauge fluctuations are absent, and it is not a universal experimental law.

## Experimental criteria

Establish the insulating state's magnetic and structural properties before naming it a spin liquid. Vaknin and colleagues' neutron-diffraction study of undoped La2CuO4-y reports magnetic superlattice evidence for antiferromagnetism. That parent-state observation must be retained alongside the historical RVB proposal. A measured superconducting gap symmetry may constrain candidate states without uniquely selecting their microscopic explanation. [R7](#ref-source-9dda11fbf0c41f73)

Lefebvre and colleagues mapped kappa-(ET)2Cu[N(CN)2]Cl using helium pressure, proton NMR and ac susceptibility. The selected manuscript uses a 0.5 T field for NMR and no static field for the susceptibility measurement; it restricts hydrostatic sweeps to conditions above helium solidification. The authors report inhomogeneous phase coexistence but do not resolve whether it is macroscopic or mesoscopic. These conditions belong to kappa-Cl and cannot be transferred to a different organic salt. [R3](#ref-source-2cc5358d54a65217)

For kappa-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3, Shimizu and colleagues' abstract reports no NMR indication of long-range order down to 32 mK, despite a susceptibility-derived exchange scale around 250 K. Neither number is a superconducting transition temperature. Kurosaki and colleagues separately studied its pressure-dependent NMR and resistivity phase diagram. The existence of neighboring superconductivity does not identify the insulating state's excitations as its pairing mechanism. Those two sources remain abstract-scoped here. [R4](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R5](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c)

## Limits and disputes

Pustogow and colleagues' 2023 strain-transport study favors a low-entropy, spin-gapped valence-bond-solid interpretation of the organic candidate's 6 K anomaly. The 140 nm crystal is coupled to a PET substrate; quoted hydrostatic-equivalent pressures are inferred by comparison with transport data. The paper acknowledges that a gapped chiral spin liquid is not ruled out without a discriminating experiment. It also assigns sharp resistance jumps to mounting-related microcracks. A transport anomaly or phase-diagram shape alone must not be promoted to an unambiguous microscopic spin-state determination. [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

The Lee–Nagaosa–Wen review itself notes an experimental mismatch in the doping dependence of the Gaussian U(1) prediction for the temperature slope of superfluid density. Thus the simple response construction above has an explicit historical limitation. Naming a redundant representation U(1), SU(2) or Z2 is not sufficient to establish the corresponding emergent low-energy phase. [R2](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

Pseudogaps, Fermi arcs, singlet correlations and d-wave pairing each admit more than one theoretical description. Test a specified RVB state against physical correlation functions, charge stiffness, spectral weight, symmetry and disorder responses. Treating all these observations as interchangeable proof would remove the very distinctions needed to compare mechanisms. Full final-version, data and material-specific calculations remain open.

## Discovery implications

Track a controlled doping or bandwidth path with independently established magnetic, structural and superconducting observables. Distinguish tuning the filling from changing hopping, disorder or lattice geometry. Preserve the local constraints of a theoretical model and calculate gauge-invariant observables before assigning a material interpretation. A finite singlet-energy gain is a useful model check, not an experimentally verified route to high-temperature superconductivity.

### scwiki-b9-claim-scope-1

Resonating valence bond, or RVB, denotes a family of correlated-state constructions built from quantum superpositions of singlet bonds. Anderson's 1987 proposal connected singlets in a correlated insulator to superconductivity after doping. ### scwiki-b9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

A singlet on ordered sites $i,j$ is $|s_{ij}\rangle=(|\uparrow_i\downarrow_j\rangle-|\downarrow_i\uparrow_j\rangle)/\sqrt2$. Different products of such bonds need not be orthogonal. Direct expansion gives $\langle A|B\rangle=-1/2$, so the normalized superposition is $(A-B)/\sqrt3$, not $(A-B)/\sqrt2$.

Neither result establishes bulk topological order or superconductivity: this model has no mobile charge degrees of freedom.

claims.statement: An isotropic, sign-preserving spin-singlet gap is the conventional s-wave reference. Three questions must nevertheless be separated: whether quasiparticles are fully gapped, how the order parameter transforms under crystal symmetry, and whether it changes sign between parts of the Fermi surface. A full gap answers the first question within the measurement's resolution; it does not settle the other two.

articles.body:
## Scope

An isotropic, sign-preserving spin-singlet gap is the conventional s-wave reference. Three questions must nevertheless be separated: whether quasiparticles are fully gapped, how the order parameter transforms under crystal symmetry, and whether it changes sign between parts of the Fermi surface. A full gap answers the first question within the measurement's resolution; it does not settle the other two. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

For a centrosymmetric tetragonal crystal, A1g denotes the fully symmetric even-parity representation. It permits a constant gap but also higher harmonics and accidental nodes. In another crystal, use that crystal's representation labels. In multiband systems, fully open gaps can have opposite signs on different sheets; see the separate s± entry. Identifying an s-wave state also does not, by itself, identify its microscopic pairing interaction. [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

## Mathematical assumptions

The equilibrium, single-band, isotropic, constant-density-of-states weak-coupling BCS model gives $2\Delta(0)/(k_BT_c)\simeq3.528$ and $\Delta C/(\gamma T_c)\simeq1.426$, with $\gamma$ the normal electronic heat-capacity coefficient. These are limiting benchmarks, not mandatory ratios for every s-wave material. The existing independent gap and entropy checks establish these model limits; strong coupling, multiband structure and anisotropy require their own calculation. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

To illustrate symmetry without fitting a material, take a circular Fermi surface centered at the tetragonal zone center and $\Delta(\phi)=\Psi f(\phi)$, where

$$f(\phi)=1+r\cos(4\phi).$$

Rotations by $\pi/2$, reflections and inversion leave this function unchanged. For $|r|<1$ it is positive everywhere; at $|r|=1$ four zeros touch the Fermi surface without sign reversal; for $|r|>1$ there are eight sign-changing nodes. Their presence changes with a parameter rather than being required by A1g symmetry. This global fourfold example is distinct from Mishra and colleagues' local twofold harmonic on a selected off-center pocket. [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

For clean weak-coupling separable pairing with uniform angular density-of-states weight, the illustrative heat-capacity jump is

$$\frac{\Delta C}{\gamma T_c}=\frac{12}{7\zeta(3)}\frac{\langle f^2\rangle^2}{\langle f^4\rangle},\qquad \langle f^2\rangle=1+\frac{r^2}{2},\quad \langle f^4\rangle=1+3r^2+\frac{3r^4}{8}.$$

Independent angular sums and a thermal-kernel quadrature verify five cases. At $r=0.6$ the gap remains nodeless, while the jump is about $0.933$ rather than $1.426$. This shows why applying the isotropic ratio as a symmetry test can fail. It is a clean separable-model result, not a disorder simulation or a measured sample value. The cited BCS paper provides the underlying mean-field context; the angular calculation is our independent illustration. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

For a real symmetric normal Hamiltonian $h$ and an imposed uniform real gap, the block matrix $\mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta I\\\Delta I&-h\end{pmatrix}$ has energies $\pm\sqrt{\epsilon_n^2+\Delta^2}$. Six small-matrix checks confirm this relation with different scalar site potentials. It does not prove an unchanged self-consistent $T_c$: the normal eigenvalues, density of states and pairing matrix elements can change. Anderson's argument pairs exact time-reversed states; it is not a blanket guarantee against all chemical disorder, localization or magnetic scattering. [R2](#ref-source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b)

## Experimental criteria

A magnitude-sensitive quasiparticle spectrum cannot generally determine an interband sign. Six independent-band, broadened-DOS comparisons give identical spectra after reversing one band's gap sign. This deliberately excludes interband scattering and coherent phase-sensitive tunneling. Measurements sensitive to phase or sign need their own geometry and matrix-element analysis. Low-temperature activation alone also cannot distinguish an isotropic gap from a smaller nonzero gap minimum. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

Hebel and Slichter's aluminum experiment used field cycling: nuclear spins relaxed in the superconducting state but were read out in the normal state. Its 0.94–4.2 K interval is a measurement range, not a range of transition temperatures. Nuclear relaxation tests a response with coherence effects; observing or missing a peak alone does not measure relative signs between bands. Only the original abstract has been checked here. [R4](#ref-source-99644bb2badd2d56)

Nagamatsu and colleagues' MgB2 report separates a zero-field four-probe resistance onset at 39 K from its 38 K end point, alongside magnetic measurements at 10 Oe. [R5](#ref-source-fade6558e7eafb2b)

Choi and colleagues subsequently calculated distinct band-dependent gaps using anisotropic electron–phonon theory. The discovery experiment and the gap calculation answer different questions; neither justifies assigning one fixed gap value to every MgB2 sample. The corrected Choi DOI is nature00898. [R6](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221)

For lanthanum superhydrides, Somayazulu's sample A had room-temperature pressures of 188 GPa before and 196 GPa after cycling; pressure at the resistance change was not directly measured. The published account distinguishes four-probe data from contact-sensitive pseudo-four-probe configurations and mixed phases. Drozdov's later study reports additional field and isotope evidence, defines $T_c$ by resistance onset, and states that magnetization of its small samples remained unresolved. Neither transport report is a phase-sensitive measurement of gap sign. [R8](#ref-source-77b774e18b0f50c7) [R9](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

## Limits and disputes

Mishra and colleagues show node lifting in a model with weak pointlike scatterers treated in the Born approximation. Their single-sheet calculation can suppress $T_c$ too strongly; additional bands change that balance, while interband scattering cannot generally be discarded. This supports a conditional explanation of activated behavior after disorder, not the rule that disorder always preserves or improves s-wave superconductivity. [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

The ideal isotope value $\alpha=-d\ln T_c/d\ln M=1/2$ assumes a harmonic phonon scale and otherwise mass-independent model parameters. Sulfur-hydride isotope observations support phonon involvement within their experimental context. For lanthanum hydrides, the published methods discuss different hydride/deuteride phase mixtures and zero-point/anharmonic stability effects. Matching pressure, phase and preparation is therefore essential before interpreting a mass derivative. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R7](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434) [R9](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

## Discovery implications

Combine thermodynamics, spectroscopy, magnetic response and controlled perturbations. Keep disorder-induced carrier or structural changes separate from elastic scattering, and distinguish small gaps from true nodes within a stated temperature window. Track superconducting evidence, symmetry, relative phase and pairing interaction as separate conclusions. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R2](#ref-source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b) [R3](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9) [R9](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

## Related topics

Read [BCS theory](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), [Eliashberg theory](/scwiki/eliashberg-strong-coupling), [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [energy gaps](/scwiki/superconducting-gap).

Track superconducting evidence, symmetry, relative phase and pairing interaction as separate conclusions. ### scwiki-c1-claim-scope-1

An isotropic, sign-preserving spin-singlet gap is the conventional s-wave reference. Three questions must nevertheless be separated: whether quasiparticles are fully gapped, how the order parameter transforms under crystal symmetry, and whether it changes sign between parts of the Fermi surface. A full gap answers the first question within the measurement's resolution; it does not settle the other two.

### scwiki-c1-claim-mathematical-assumptions-8

For a real symmetric normal Hamiltonian $h$ and an imposed uniform real gap, the block matrix $\mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta I\\\Delta I&-h\end{pmatrix}$ has energies $\pm\sqrt{\epsilon_n^2+\Delta^2}$. ### scwiki-c1-claim-experimental-criteria-1

A magnitude-sensitive quasiparticle spectrum cannot generally determine an interband sign. Six independent-band, broadened-DOS comparisons give identical spectra after reversing one band's gap sign. ### scwiki-c1-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

Mishra and colleagues show node lifting in a model with weak pointlike scatterers treated in the Born approximation. Their single-sheet calculation can suppress $T_c$ too strongly; additional bands change that balance, while interband scattering cannot generally be discarded. This supports a conditional explanation of activated behavior after disorder, not the rule that disorder always preserves or improves s-wave superconductivity.

claims.statement: A superconducting node is a zero of the quasiparticle excitation energy. In a simple weak-pairing single-band description it lies where the normal-state Fermi surface intersects a zero of the gap. A point, a line, a small but finite minimum and an extended Bogoliubov Fermi surface are different possibilities. In multiband systems, inspect the full Bogoliubov spectrum rather than only one scalar gap. Nodal dimension, symmetry protection and the pairing representation are separate questions.

claims.statement: A low-temperature power law constrains low-energy excitations within a measured window; it is not a unique symmetry label. The dispersion near a node, probe weighting, disorder, nonlocal response, multiple gaps and backgrounds can change the observed dependence. A fit should state its lowest temperature and energy resolution, and compare with alternatives before assigning a representation.

claims.statement: For $m$ linearly dispersing directions transverse to a nodal manifold, an ideal spectrum $E^2=\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_i^2q_i^2$ has phase volume below E proportional to $E^m$, hence density of states $N(E)\propto E^{m-1}$. A three-dimensional line node has two such directions; an isolated linear point has three. Independent cross-section integrations recover these powers. A point with $E^2=q_z^2+(q_x^2+q_y^2)^2$ instead has volume proportional to $E^2$ and a linear density of states. This explicit quadratic-dispersion example shows why the same density-of-states exponent need not imply the same nodal dimension. Velocities, units and degeneracies set the prefactors; these examples use dimensionless coordinates.

claims.statement: With a temperature-independent low-energy density of states $N(E)=AE^p$ and $k_B=1$, the positive-energy quasiparticle contribution satisfies $C(T)=\int_0^\infty N(E)E^2 e^{E/T}/[T^2(1+e^{E/T})^2]dE\propto T^{p+1}$. Direct energy integrals and numerical derivatives of internal energy agree for $p=0,1,2$. Thus ideal linear line nodes give $C\propto T^2$, whereas ideal linear point nodes in three dimensions give $C\propto T^3$. These are electronic contributions in the stated regime, not the total measured heat capacity. Two hard-gap toy densities also show increasing suppression as temperature falls below the gap; they do not model a BCS coherence peak or an actual sample.

claims.statement: On an imposed circular Fermi surface, $\Delta_s(\theta)=s_0+s_4\cos4\theta$ can have zeros while retaining fully symmetric character. For real amplitudes with $s_4\ne0$, $|s_0/s_4|<1$ gives eight zeros, equality gives four merged quadratic zeros, and a larger ratio gives none. In contrast, $\Delta_d=\cos2\theta+\eta\cos6\theta$ retains diagonal zeros for the tested small real $\eta$ values in the B1g sector. Seven numerical root checks verify these examples. Changing a model harmonic ratio is not a calculation of how irradiation changes a real gap; a disorder self-energy and gap equation are needed for that connection.

claims.statement: Agterberg, Brydon and Timm's even-parity multiband model supplies another caution. With its inversion and particle-hole symmetries, the Hamiltonian can be transformed to an antisymmetric form with real Pfaffian P and $\det H=P^2$. Opposite signs of P enclose protected zero-energy surfaces. For the specified pure-quintet example, $P=(\epsilon_+\epsilon_-)^2+4\Delta_0^2(\epsilon_+\epsilon_-+c_{xz}^2+c_{yz}^2)$. Five independent eight-dimensional Hamiltonian determinants match this expression, including a change of sign between two nearby momenta. This tests the named model identity. It does not show that every multiband or time-reversal-breaking superconductor has such a surface, nor establish a material's energetic stability.

articles.body:
## Scope

A superconducting node is a zero of the quasiparticle excitation energy. In a simple weak-pairing single-band description it lies where the normal-state Fermi surface intersects a zero of the gap. A point, a line, a small but finite minimum and an extended Bogoliubov Fermi surface are different possibilities. In multiband systems, inspect the full Bogoliubov spectrum rather than only one scalar gap. Nodal dimension, symmetry protection and the pairing representation are separate questions. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R8](#ref-source-558057f5efd127fe)

A low-temperature power law constrains low-energy excitations within a measured window; it is not a unique symmetry label. The dispersion near a node, probe weighting, disorder, nonlocal response, multiple gaps and backgrounds can change the observed dependence. A fit should state its lowest temperature and energy resolution, and compare with alternatives before assigning a representation. [R2](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53) [R3](#ref-source-d140b2e83ddf11d9) [R6](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2)

## Mathematical assumptions

For $m$ linearly dispersing directions transverse to a nodal manifold, an ideal spectrum $E^2=\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_i^2q_i^2$ has phase volume below E proportional to $E^m$, hence density of states $N(E)\propto E^{m-1}$. A three-dimensional line node has two such directions; an isolated linear point has three. Independent cross-section integrations recover these powers. A point with $E^2=q_z^2+(q_x^2+q_y^2)^2$ instead has volume proportional to $E^2$ and a linear density of states. This explicit quadratic-dispersion example shows why the same density-of-states exponent need not imply the same nodal dimension. Velocities, units and degeneracies set the prefactors; these examples use dimensionless coordinates. [R3](#ref-source-d140b2e83ddf11d9)

With a temperature-independent low-energy density of states $N(E)=AE^p$ and $k_B=1$, the positive-energy quasiparticle contribution satisfies $C(T)=\int_0^\infty N(E)E^2 e^{E/T}/[T^2(1+e^{E/T})^2]dE\propto T^{p+1}$. Direct energy integrals and numerical derivatives of internal energy agree for $p=0,1,2$. Thus ideal linear line nodes give $C\propto T^2$, whereas ideal linear point nodes in three dimensions give $C\propto T^3$. These are electronic contributions in the stated regime, not the total measured heat capacity. Two hard-gap toy densities also show increasing suppression as temperature falls below the gap; they do not model a BCS coherence peak or an actual sample. [R3](#ref-source-d140b2e83ddf11d9) [R7](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

On an imposed circular Fermi surface, $\Delta_s(\theta)=s_0+s_4\cos4\theta$ can have zeros while retaining fully symmetric character. For real amplitudes with $s_4\ne0$, $|s_0/s_4|<1$ gives eight zeros, equality gives four merged quadratic zeros, and a larger ratio gives none. In contrast, $\Delta_d=\cos2\theta+\eta\cos6\theta$ retains diagonal zeros for the tested small real $\eta$ values in the B1g sector. Seven numerical root checks verify these examples. Changing a model harmonic ratio is not a calculation of how irradiation changes a real gap; a disorder self-energy and gap equation are needed for that connection. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R9](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

Agterberg, Brydon and Timm's even-parity multiband model supplies another caution. With its inversion and particle-hole symmetries, the Hamiltonian can be transformed to an antisymmetric form with real Pfaffian P and $\det H=P^2$. Opposite signs of P enclose protected zero-energy surfaces. For the specified pure-quintet example, $P=(\epsilon_+\epsilon_-)^2+4\Delta_0^2(\epsilon_+\epsilon_-+c_{xz}^2+c_{yz}^2)$. Five independent eight-dimensional Hamiltonian determinants match this expression, including a change of sign between two nearby momenta. This tests the named model identity. It does not show that every multiband or time-reversal-breaking superconductor has such a surface, nor establish a material's energetic stability. [R8](#ref-source-558057f5efd127fe)

## Experimental criteria

Hardy and colleagues measured the penetration-depth change in YBa2Cu3O6.95 using a resonator with a 1.3 K lower operating temperature. The reported strong linear term extended approximately from 3 to 25 K; those are different intervals. The publisher abstract supports a classic nodal constraint, with defects relevant to comparisons, but the full experimental analysis has not been reviewed here. [R2](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53)

Hashimoto and colleagues' P-substituted BaFe2(As0.67P0.33)2 study combined penetration depth and thermal conductivity. The author version describes measurements down to about 0.15 K with a tunnel-diode oscillator and about 1.6 K with a microwave resonator. Its zero-field thermal fit resolves a residual contribution of approximately $25\,\mathrm{mW\,K^{-2}\,m^{-1}}$. The low-temperature penetration-depth upturn was discussed as a small paramagnetic contribution, not silently discarded. These combined observations support line nodes; the measurements do not alone locate every node or uniquely select d-wave over nodal s-wave. [R5](#ref-source-ad52940b1b5c5ecd)

The inherited Reid citation concerns KFe2As2, not P-substituted BaFe2As2. Reid and colleagues compared heat flow along two crystal directions using different samples and measurements down to 50 mK. A 0.05 T field made solder contacts normal; the residual zero-field term was obtained by extrapolation, with thermal fits below 0.3 K. Cross-sample scattering comparisons also used resistivity normalization and assumptions relating resistivity to scattering. The authors favored d-wave from several constraints. That interpretation must retain these conditions and its material identity rather than become an automatic classification of another compound. [R4](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

Mizukami and colleagues irradiated P-substituted BaFe2As2 with 2.5 MeV electrons and followed penetration depth across multiple samples and doses. Selected data show a nodal-like response becoming nearly temperature independent, then developing low-energy excitations again. One irradiated sample was measured to 80 mK; the reported flat response had roughly 1 Å precision. The proposed two-band interpretation removes accidental nodes before an impurity band reaches zero energy: the final gapless response is not simply restored symmetry-enforced nodes. Retain the separate sample batches, partial defect annealing on warming, and assumed interband/intraband scattering ratio. [R6](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2)

Rotating-field heat measurements require a response calculation. Vorontsov and Vekhter's quasi-two-dimensional model includes vortex scattering and finds that the same nodal direction can give a maximum or a minimum depending on temperature and field. The selected calculation neglects Zeeman splitting and uses an approximate vortex-state treatment; its illustrated reversal scale is not universal. Reading every fourfold minimum as a node would discard precisely the physics that changes the sign. [R7](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

## Limits and disputes

“Universal” residual heat transport refers to a specified low-temperature, low-frequency scattering regime. Durst and Lee distinguish thermal transport from electrical and spin responses, whose corrections differ; an impurity-independent formula cannot be transferred indiscriminately across all probes or multiband materials. Likewise, a symmetry-enforced zero is robust only while the protecting symmetry, relevant Fermi-surface crossing and phase remain applicable. Strong perturbations may change the phase or electronic structure. [R3](#ref-source-d140b2e83ddf11d9) [R9](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

Topology requires an appropriate invariant and protecting symmetries, with any surface prediction tied to surface orientation and the projected bulk nodes. Schnyder and Ryu's time-reversal-symmetric noncentrosymmetric model links nodal-line topology to surface flat bands, distinct from a fully gapped bulk classification. A tunneling feature, a normal-state Weyl band or the word “topological” in a gap-evolution title is not sufficient to establish superconducting Weyl nodes. The cited abstract is checked here; its full surface calculation remains open. [R10](#ref-source-082f6af19b62ce2b)

## Discovery implications

Store the lowest measured temperature, fit interval, residual background, field orientation, contact protocol, dose history and sample identity with each observation. Separate the measured response, inferred low-energy spectrum and proposed representation. Our numerical examples test fixed spectra, roots and a named Pfaffian identity, not the complete experiments. Full scientific acceptance, complete source-version comparisons, raw-data reconstruction and disorder/vortex self-consistency remain open. [R4](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff) [R5](#ref-source-ad52940b1b5c5ecd) [R6](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2) [R7](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

## Related topics

Continue with [s-wave pairing](/scwiki/s-wave), [d-wave pairing](/scwiki/d-wave), [singlet and triplet classification](/scwiki/singlet-and-triplet-pairing) and [topological superconductivity](/scwiki/topological-superconductivity).

The publisher abstract supports a classic nodal constraint, with defects relevant to comparisons, but the full experimental analysis has not been reviewed here. [R2](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53)

Hashimoto and colleagues' P-substituted BaFe2(As0.67P0.33)2 study combined penetration depth and thermal conductivity. The author version describes measurements down to about 0.15 K with a tunnel-diode oscillator and about 1.6 K with a microwave resonator. Its zero-field thermal fit resolves a residual contribution of approximately $25\,\mathrm{mW\,K^{-2}\,m^{-1}}$. The low-temperature penetration-depth upturn was discussed as a small paramagnetic contribution, not silently discarded. These combined observations support line nodes; the measurements do not alone locate every node or uniquely select d-wave over nodal s-wave. [R5](#ref-source-ad52940b1b5c5ecd)

The inherited Reid citation concerns KFe2As2, not P-substituted BaFe2As2. Reid and colleagues compared heat flow along two crystal directions using different samples and measurements down to 50 mK. A 0.05 T field made solder contacts normal; the residual zero-field term was obtained by extrapolation, with thermal fits below 0.3 K. Cross-sample scattering comparisons also used resistivity normalization and assumptions relating resistivity to scattering. The authors favored d-wave from several constraints. That interpretation must retain these conditions and its material identity rather than become an automatic classification of another compound. [R4](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

Mizukami and colleagues irradiated P-substituted BaFe2As2 with 2.5 MeV electrons and followed penetration depth across multiple samples and doses. Selected data show a nodal-like response becoming nearly temperature independent, then developing low-energy excitations again. One irradiated sample was measured to 80 mK; the reported flat response had roughly 1 Å precision. The proposed two-band interpretation removes accidental nodes before an impurity band reaches zero energy: the final gapless response is not simply restored symmetry-enforced nodes. Retain the separate sample batches, partial defect annealing on warming, and assumed interband/intraband scattering ratio. [R6](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2)

Rotating-field heat measurements require a response calculation. Vorontsov and Vekhter's quasi-two-dimensional model includes vortex scattering and finds that the same nodal direction can give a maximum or a minimum depending on temperature and field. The selected calculation neglects Zeeman splitting and uses an approximate vortex-state treatment; its illustrated reversal scale is not universal. Reading every fourfold minimum as a node would discard precisely the physics that changes the sign. [R7](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

## Limits and disputes

“Universal” residual heat transport refers to a specified low-temperature, low-frequency scattering regime. Durst and Lee distinguish thermal transport from electrical and spin responses, whose corrections differ; an impurity-independent formula cannot be transferred indiscriminately across all probes or multiband materials. Likewise, a symmetry-enforced zero is robust only while the protecting symmetry, relevant Fermi-surface crossing and phase remain applicable. Strong perturbations may change the phase or electronic structure. [R3](#ref-source-d140b2e83ddf11d9) [R9](#ref-source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9)

Topology requires an appropriate invariant and protecting symmetries, with any surface prediction tied to surface orientation and the projected bulk nodes. Schnyder and Ryu's time-reversal-symmetric noncentrosymmetric model links nodal-line topology to surface flat bands, distinct from a fully gapped bulk classification. A tunneling feature, a normal-state Weyl band or the word “topological” in a gap-evolution title is not sufficient to establish superconducting Weyl nodes. The cited abstract is checked here; its full surface calculation remains open. [R10](#ref-source-082f6af19b62ce2b)

## Discovery implications

Store the lowest measured temperature, fit interval, residual background, field orientation, contact protocol, dose history and sample identity with each observation. Separate the measured response, inferred low-energy spectrum and proposed representation. Our numerical examples test fixed spectra, roots and a named Pfaffian identity, not the complete experiments. Full scientific acceptance, complete source-version comparisons, raw-data reconstruction and disorder/vortex self-consistency remain open. ## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-c10-claim-scope-1

A superconducting node is a zero of the quasiparticle excitation energy. In a simple weak-pairing single-band description it lies where the normal-state Fermi surface intersects a zero of the gap. A point, a line, a small but finite minimum and an extended Bogoliubov Fermi surface are different possibilities. In multiband systems, inspect the full Bogoliubov spectrum rather than only one scalar gap. Nodal dimension, symmetry protection and the pairing representation are separate questions.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f, source-558057f5efd127fe.

Conditions: Distinguish scalar gap zeros, full quasiparticle spectrum, nodal dimension and representation.

### scwiki-c10-claim-scope-2

### scwiki-c10-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

For $m$ linearly dispersing directions transverse to a nodal manifold, an ideal spectrum $E^2=\sum_{i=1}^{m}v_i^2q_i^2$ has phase volume below E proportional to $E^m$, hence density of states $N(E)\propto E^{m-1}$. A three-dimensional line node has two such directions; an isolated linear point has three. Independent cross-section integrations recover these powers. A point with $E^2=q_z^2+(q_x^2+q_y^2)^2$ instead has volume proportional to $E^2$ and a linear density of states. This explicit quadratic-dispersion example shows why the same density-of-states exponent need not imply the same nodal dimension. Velocities, units and degeneracies set the prefactors; these examples use dimensionless coordinates.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-d140b2e83ddf11d9.

Conditions: Fixed dimensionless spectra/amplitudes, explicit Fermi surface and symmetry sector. No material fit, disorder/vortex self-consistency or stability calculation.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and independent finite examples; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-c10-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

With a temperature-independent low-energy density of states $N(E)=AE^p$ and $k_B=1$, the positive-energy quasiparticle contribution satisfies $C(T)=\int_0^\infty N(E)E^2 e^{E/T}/[T^2(1+e^{E/T})^2]dE\propto T^{p+1}$. Direct energy integrals and numerical derivatives of internal energy agree for $p=0,1,2$. Thus ideal linear line nodes give $C\propto T^2$, whereas ideal linear point nodes in three dimensions give $C\propto T^3$. These are electronic contributions in the stated regime, not the total measured heat capacity. Two hard-gap toy densities also show increasing suppression as temperature falls below the gap; they do not model a BCS coherence peak or an actual sample.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-d140b2e83ddf11d9, source-6c82ca23c0fda096.

Conditions: Fixed dimensionless spectra/amplitudes, explicit Fermi surface and symmetry sector. No material fit, disorder/vortex self-consistency or stability calculation.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and independent finite examples; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-c10-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

On an imposed circular Fermi surface, $\Delta_s(\theta)=s_0+s_4\cos4\theta$ can have zeros while retaining fully symmetric character. For real amplitudes with $s_4\ne0$, $|s_0/s_4|<1$ gives eight zeros, equality gives four merged quadratic zeros, and a larger ratio gives none. In contrast, $\Delta_d=\cos2\theta+\eta\cos6\theta$ retains diagonal zeros for the tested small real $\eta$ values in the B1g sector. Seven numerical root checks verify these examples. Changing a model harmonic ratio is not a calculation of how irradiation changes a real gap; a disorder self-energy and gap equation are needed for that connection.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f, source-fcdf63980c7fb4f9.

Conditions: Fixed dimensionless spectra/amplitudes, explicit Fermi surface and symmetry sector. No material fit, disorder/vortex self-consistency or stability calculation.

### scwiki-c10-claim-mathematical-assumptions-4

Agterberg, Brydon and Timm's even-parity multiband model supplies another caution. With its inversion and particle-hole symmetries, the Hamiltonian can be transformed to an antisymmetric form with real Pfaffian P and $\det H=P^2$. Opposite signs of P enclose protected zero-energy surfaces. For the specified pure-quintet example, $P=(\epsilon_+\epsilon_-)^2+4\Delta_0^2(\epsilon_+\epsilon_-+c_{xz}^2+c_{yz}^2)$. Five independent eight-dimensional Hamiltonian determinants match this expression, including a change of sign between two nearby momenta. This tests the named model identity. It does not show that every multiband or time-reversal-breaking superconductor has such a surface, nor establish a material's energetic stability.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-558057f5efd127fe.

articles.body:
## Scope

The label s± describes relative sign reversal between superconducting gaps on relevant Fermi-surface sheets. In common tetragonal iron-based models it belongs to the fully symmetric $A_{1g}$ representation, even when different pockets carry opposite signs. A nodeless excitation gap therefore does not establish sign-preserving pairing. Identify the actual bands and crystal symmetry: the original hole–electron-pocket picture is a model for particular systems, not an inventory that every iron-based compound must share. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R10](#ref-source-b934eb95c4cbf8c6)

## Mathematical assumptions

A two-pocket illustration takes $\Delta_h=+\Delta_1$ and $\Delta_e=-\Delta_2$, with positive magnitudes. Repulsive interband pair transfer can favor this relative phase in a linearized pairing equation. Its eigenfunction depends on the interaction matrix, orbital weights and Fermi surface; the sign pattern alone does not uniquely identify the microscopic mediator. The [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing) article gives an independently checked common-cutoff model and its limits. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

For real singlet gaps, a simplified spin pair-creation coherence factor is $C=\tfrac12[1-(\xi_k\xi_{k+q}+\Delta_k\Delta_{k+q})/(E_kE_{k+q})]$, with $E_k=\sqrt{\xi_k^2+\Delta_k^2}$. At two Fermi-surface points it is zero for equal signs and one for opposite signs. An independent 450-case check verifies the bounds and these limits, while reversing a gap sign leaves the quasiparticle energy unchanged. This is one factor in a response function, not a complete neutron intensity or a guarantee of a resonance. [R7](#ref-source-5717dacf7df85626)

An illustrative circular-sheet gap $\Delta(\theta)=\Delta_0[1+r\cos(4\theta)]$ retains fourfold rotations and reflections. It is fully open for $|r|<1$, touches zero at four angles for $|r|=1$, and has eight simple zeros for $|r|>1$. The zeros in this example are accidental and can disappear without changing representation. The check covers 2,520 symmetry cases and seven anisotropy controls; it is not a fitted KFe2As2 gap or a proof that all observed nodes are accidental. [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R6](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

Kuroki and colleagues published an erratum correcting an orbital-to-band transformation error in the original gap plot. The corrected diagonal band gap is fully open for the displayed parameter set, while strong anisotropy and parameter-dependent nodal or d-wave competition remain. The correction does not make every $A_{1g}$ solution nodeless. Its one-page text has been checked, but its original figure and the full five-orbital calculation have not been independently reproduced here. [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R6](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

## Experimental criteria

Christianson and colleagues studied polycrystalline K-doped Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2, correcting the pinned draft's Co-doped attribution. Their MERLIN neutron measurements used several incident energies and a vanadium intensity standard. The 7 K and 50 K comparison shows a superconductivity-related feature near 14 meV and a momentum-transfer magnitude near 1.15 inverse angstroms. These are measurement temperatures and excitation scales, not separate superconducting transitions. The paper reports a 38 K susceptibility transition, whose exact operational threshold is not assigned here. [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3)

Figure 4 integrates momenta from 1.0 to 1.3 inverse angstroms and energies from 12.5 to 17.5 meV. The resonance contribution fades near the transition while the plotted background remains finite; the entire intensity does not fall to zero. The authors allow a possible small phonon contribution. Their phase-sensitive interpretation combines a coherence-factor model with separate gap information, rather than directly measuring an isolated gap sign. Sample-matched continuum thresholds and normal-state backgrounds matter when testing that inference. [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R7](#ref-source-5717dacf7df85626)

Maier and Scalapino's two-orbital RPA–BCS calculation illustrates why orbital matrix elements and the momentum being probed matter. The model qualitatively captures Fermi-surface shapes but acknowledges imperfect velocities. Different singlet gaps produce different responses, and triplet spin components require different coherence factors. A missing or enhanced peak cannot be interpreted from gap signs alone without the accessible scattering channels, interaction model and broadening. This selected check does not reproduce a material's complete susceptibility. [R7](#ref-source-5717dacf7df85626)

Hanaguri and colleagues inferred sign reversal from field-dependent STM interference in Fe(Se,Te), not pure FeSe. A subsequent preprint comment by Mazin and Singh argued for Bragg peaks and a possible surface reconstruction instead. Their proposed surface magnetic order was a hypothesis, not an independently observed feature of those samples. The existence of a Fourier peak does not by itself settle whether it is a lattice, interference or mixed contribution. [R4](#ref-source-3ee65ce8fc5080da) [R8](#ref-source-7b146cbf6ec35c32)

The authors' preprint reply separates broad conductance-ratio features near the gap scale from sharp Bragg-like components. Its Figure 1 compares 0 T and 10 T linecuts against topographic peaks; a sharp field-enhanced component persists above the gap range, while the broad component has a different energy dependence. This is an explicit experimental response to the critique. Both documents remain labelled as preprints here, and their exchange does not substitute for a full raw-map or scattering-matrix reanalysis. [R9](#ref-source-b6cd1a68d7c03084)

## Corrected nodal example

Reid and colleagues' 2012 thermal-conductivity study concerns KFe2As2, not P-substituted Ba122. Its residual heat-transport evidence and cross-sample comparison support nodes, with the authors arguing for d-wave pairing. The selected accepted-manuscript check preserves the separate directional samples and low-temperature extrapolation. A citation making that argument cannot be repurposed as evidence for accidental nodes in another material. [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

Later work makes the distinction between nodal evidence and symmetry assignment especially clear. Wu and colleagues' 2024 laser-ARPES study of KFe2As2 maps gap nodes and argues for nodal s± pairing, including hole pockets around the zone corners. That publisher-abstract check identifies a competing interpretation, not a completed resolution of the disagreement. Gap magnitude and node location constrain a model; neither alone directly measures the relative phase or establishes a universal pairing glue. [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff) [R10](#ref-source-b934eb95c4cbf8c6)

## Limits and disputes

FeSe, electron-only interfaces, strongly hole-doped endpoints and nickelate proposals must retain their own electronic structure and evidence. Disorder sensitivity can also involve carrier, structural and magnetic changes, so suppressing a transition is not a unique gap-sign test. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including original STM methods, supplementary controls, raw spectra and final-version comparisons. The neutron, QPI and thermal observations constrain different claims; none should be silently promoted to an unconditional family-wide phase verdict. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R4](#ref-source-3ee65ce8fc5080da) [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff) [R10](#ref-source-b934eb95c4cbf8c6)

## Discovery implications

State which sheets should change sign and what result would reject that assignment. Use measured electronic structure, distinguish magnitude from phase, and compare independent probes on matched compositions and conditions. For a proposed phase-sensitive junction, explain which bands the interface couples to. For neutron and QPI interpretations, preserve the normal-state background, scattering selection and competing models. A useful evidence record makes those assumptions searchable together with the claim. [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R4](#ref-source-3ee65ce8fc5080da) [R7](#ref-source-5717dacf7df85626) [R9](#ref-source-b6cd1a68d7c03084)

## Related topics

Continue with [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), [gap nodes](/scwiki/superconducting-node-structure), [iron-based superconductors](/scwiki/iron-based-superconductors), [quasiparticle interference](/scwiki/quasiparticle-interference), and [nickelate materials](/scwiki/nickelates).

# s± pairing: a sign change between Fermi surfaces

The [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing) article gives an independently checked common-cutoff model and its limits. [R1](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31)

For real singlet gaps, a simplified spin pair-creation coherence factor is $C=\tfrac12[1-(\xi_k\xi_{k+q}+\Delta_k\Delta_{k+q})/(E_kE_{k+q})]$, with $E_k=\sqrt{\xi_k^2+\Delta_k^2}$. At two Fermi-surface points it is zero for equal signs and one for opposite signs. An independent 450-case check verifies the bounds and these limits, while reversing a gap sign leaves the quasiparticle energy unchanged. This is one factor in a response function, not a complete neutron intensity or a guarantee of a resonance. [R7](#ref-source-5717dacf7df85626)

An illustrative circular-sheet gap $\Delta(\theta)=\Delta_0[1+r\cos(4\theta)]$ retains fourfold rotations and reflections. It is fully open for $|r|<1$, touches zero at four angles for $|r|=1$, and has eight simple zeros for $|r|>1$. The zeros in this example are accidental and can disappear without changing representation. The check covers 2,520 symmetry cases and seven anisotropy controls; it is not a fitted KFe2As2 gap or a proof that all observed nodes are accidental. [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R6](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

Kuroki and colleagues published an erratum correcting an orbital-to-band transformation error in the original gap plot. The corrected diagonal band gap is fully open for the displayed parameter set, while strong anisotropy and parameter-dependent nodal or d-wave competition remain. The correction does not make every $A_{1g}$ solution nodeless. Its one-page text has been checked, but its original figure and the full five-orbital calculation have not been independently reproduced here. [R2](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R6](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

## Experimental criteria

Christianson and colleagues studied polycrystalline K-doped Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2, correcting the pinned draft's Co-doped attribution. Their MERLIN neutron measurements used several incident energies and a vanadium intensity standard. The 7 K and 50 K comparison shows a superconductivity-related feature near 14 meV and a momentum-transfer magnitude near 1.15 inverse angstroms. These are measurement temperatures and excitation scales, not separate superconducting transitions. The paper reports a 38 K susceptibility transition, whose exact operational threshold is not assigned here. [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3)

Figure 4 integrates momenta from 1.0 to 1.3 inverse angstroms and energies from 12.5 to 17.5 meV. The resonance contribution fades near the transition while the plotted background remains finite; the entire intensity does not fall to zero. The authors allow a possible small phonon contribution. Their phase-sensitive interpretation combines a coherence-factor model with separate gap information, rather than directly measuring an isolated gap sign. Sample-matched continuum thresholds and normal-state backgrounds matter when testing that inference. [R3](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R7](#ref-source-5717dacf7df85626)

Maier and Scalapino's two-orbital RPA–BCS calculation illustrates why orbital matrix elements and the momentum being probed matter. The model qualitatively captures Fermi-surface shapes but acknowledges imperfect velocities. Different singlet gaps produce different responses, and triplet spin components require different coherence factors. A missing or enhanced peak cannot be interpreted from gap signs alone without the accessible scattering channels, interaction model and broadening. This selected check does not reproduce a material's complete susceptibility. [R7](#ref-source-5717dacf7df85626)

Hanaguri and colleagues inferred sign reversal from field-dependent STM interference in Fe(Se,Te), not pure FeSe. A subsequent preprint comment by Mazin and Singh argued for Bragg peaks and a possible surface reconstruction instead. Their proposed surface magnetic order was a hypothesis, not an independently observed feature of those samples. The existence of a Fourier peak does not by itself settle whether it is a lattice, interference or mixed contribution. [R4](#ref-source-3ee65ce8fc5080da) [R8](#ref-source-7b146cbf6ec35c32)

The authors' preprint reply separates broad conductance-ratio features near the gap scale from sharp Bragg-like components. Its Figure 1 compares 0 T and 10 T linecuts against topographic peaks; a sharp field-enhanced component persists above the gap range, while the broad component has a different energy dependence. This is an explicit experimental response to the critique. Both documents remain labelled as preprints here, and their exchange does not substitute for a full raw-map or scattering-matrix reanalysis. [R9](#ref-source-b6cd1a68d7c03084)

## Corrected nodal example

Reid and colleagues' 2012 thermal-conductivity study concerns KFe2As2, not P-substituted Ba122. Its residual heat-transport evidence and cross-sample comparison support nodes, with the authors arguing for d-wave pairing. The selected accepted-manuscript check preserves the separate directional samples and low-temperature extrapolation. A citation making that argument cannot be repurposed as evidence for accidental nodes in another material. [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff)

Later work makes the distinction between nodal evidence and symmetry assignment especially clear. Wu and colleagues' 2024 laser-ARPES study of KFe2As2 maps gap nodes and argues for nodal s± pairing, including hole pockets around the zone corners. That publisher-abstract check identifies a competing interpretation, not a completed resolution of the disagreement. Gap magnitude and node location constrain a model; neither alone directly measures the relative phase or establishes a universal pairing glue. [R5](#ref-source-8a117f38b78526ff) [R10](#ref-source-b934eb95c4cbf8c6)

## Limits and disputes

FeSe, electron-only interfaces, strongly hole-doped endpoints and nickelate proposals must retain their own electronic structure and evidence. Disorder sensitivity can also involve carrier, structural and magnetic changes, so suppressing a transition is not a unique gap-sign test. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including original STM methods, supplementary controls, raw spectra and final-version comparisons. The neutron, QPI and thermal observations constrain different claims; none should be silently promoted to an unconditional family-wide phase verdict. State which sheets should change sign and what result would reject that assignment. Use measured electronic structure, distinguish magnitude from phase, and compare independent probes on matched compositions and conditions. For a proposed phase-sensitive junction, explain which bands the interface couples to. For neutron and QPI interpretations, preserve the normal-state background, scattering selection and competing models. A useful evidence record makes those assumptions searchable together with the claim. articles.body:
## Scope

For the tetragonal point group D4h, the familiar $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state belongs to B1g: a quarter turn changes its sign, while inversion preserves it. This entry separates symmetry, low-energy excitations and phase-sensitive evidence. A node or a small gap alone does not identify B1g, and identifying B1g does not uniquely determine the interaction that produced pairing. The cuprate evidence combines complementary measurements rather than a single universal diagnostic. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

The usual even-parity spin-singlet description assumes a centrosymmetric setting with the appropriate spin or pseudospin pairing structure. Orthorhombicity, multiple bands and additional broken symmetries require the actual crystal symmetry to be used. A label inherited from an ideal square lattice is not a substitute for that analysis. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

## Mathematical assumptions

An illustrative lattice harmonic, with lattice spacing set to one, is $\Delta(\mathbf k)=\Delta_0[\cos k_x-\cos k_y]/2$. Direct rotation, diagonal-reflection and inversion checks establish its B1g transformation. Its diagonal zero lines produce quasiparticle nodes only where they intersect the Fermi surface. A circular contour centered at the zone center intersects them; hypothetical small pockets around $(\pi,0)$ and $(0,\pi)$ do not. The latter have opposite gap signs while each pocket remains fully gapped. These checks establish a geometric possibility, not a band structure for a particular cuprate. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

On a circular Fermi surface, $f(\phi)=\cos2\phi$ has four zeros. A real admixture $f=\cos2\phi+s$ shifts the four nodes for $|s|<1$, gives two touching zeros at $|s|=1$, and removes them for $|s|>1$. Such a mixture is not pure B1g in a tetragonal crystal; orthorhombic symmetry can permit the corresponding real components to mix. The complex illustrative mixture $\cos2\phi+is$ instead has minimum magnitude $|s|$ and, when both components are nonzero, breaks time reversal. Five direct checks distinguish these cases. They do not demonstrate that any material selects the mixture. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

Near one simple node, take $E(\mathbf q)=\sqrt{(v_Fq_1)^2+(v_\Delta q_2)^2}$ in units $\hbar=k_B=1$. The ellipse of states below $E$ has area $\pi E^2/(v_Fv_\Delta)$; dividing by $(2\pi)^2$ and differentiating gives a positive-energy density of states $g(E)=E/(2\pi v_Fv_\Delta)$ for this one declared branch. Polygon-area checks verify six cases. For a linear density $g(E)=aE$, a converged thermal integral gives $C=(9\zeta(3)/2)aT^2$. Spin, node and band multiplicities must be supplied consistently. This clean local model illustrates a power law; disorder, finite temperature windows and different nodal dispersions change its applicability. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

For a separate illustration of phase frustration, consider a zero-field, single-junction loop with a built-in $\pi$ phase shift. Writing $f=\Phi/\Phi_0$, $\Phi_0=h/(2e)$ and $\beta=2\pi LI_c/\Phi_0$, with $E_J=\Phi_0 I_c/(2\pi)$, its energy is $U/E_J=2\pi^2f^2/\beta+\cos(2\pi f)$. The stationary condition is $f=\beta\sin(2\pi f)/(2\pi)$. Five energy-minimization checks show a zero-flux minimum for $\beta\leq1$ and paired nonzero minima for $\beta>1$; their magnitude approaches one half only as the inductance parameter grows. A finite loop therefore need not contain exactly half a flux quantum. This is not a reproduction of the extended three-boundary tricrystal geometry used in the experiments below. [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826)

## Experimental criteria

Hardy and colleagues measured changes in penetration depth in YBa2Cu3O6.95 using a 900 MHz resonator. Their abstract reports a linear contribution over approximately 3–25 K, within measurements extending from 1.3 K to the transition. This supports low-energy nodal excitations; the temperature interval is not a reported transition-temperature interval. Only the publisher abstract is checked here, so the full calibration, defect comparison and raw traces remain outside this review. [R2](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53)

Shen and colleagues' 1993 Bi2212 photoemission report finds a large in-plane gap anisotropy compatible with $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Photoemission primarily constrains excitation energies and gap magnitude; it does not directly read the relative order-parameter phase. The pinned chapter's DOI ending in 75.4234 actually identifies a Brillouin-spectroscopy paper and is corrected to 70.1553. Published comments and replies in 1993 and 1994 have been identified but not fully examined; the early ARPES result is not presented as a standalone final symmetry proof. [R3](#ref-source-22f5417afdec3a9f)

The original 1994 tricrystal-ring and 1995 scanning-SQUID papers are retained as historical source pointers. Their identities are checked, but this entry's detailed geometry discussion relies on the explicitly reviewed later author manuscripts, rather than claiming a new full audit of those originals. [R4](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7) [R5](#ref-source-6fe9eb9d2301fe93)

In the 2004 study of Ca-doped Y-123, La-214 and Bi-2212 films, selected crystal orientations create an odd phase frustration for a predominantly $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state. The authors compare opposite vortex polarities and model the pickup-loop response. The La-214 fit allowing flux to vary gives $0.585\pm0.1\,\Phi_0$, compatible with one half within its stated uncertainty. Imaging at 4.2 K is distinct from the samples' transition temperatures. Constraints on a fixed imaginary component depend on resolution; sufficiently small alternating domains are an explicitly discussed caveat. Doping coordinates are estimated using an empirical relation, and grain-boundary doping need not exactly equal bulk doping. [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826)

The 2000 electron-doped study tests NCCO and PCCO films. For NCCO it compares a frustrated tricrystal with two unfrustrated geometries; the controls show little central flux. Sensor height and pickup-loop integration enter the field model. Allowing total flux to vary gives $0.47^{+0.18}_{-0.14}\,\Phi_0$ in the quoted NCCO fit; the authors define the uncertainty using a doubling of best-fit chi-square, not an asserted standard confidence interval. This is sample- and geometry-specific phase evidence. The reported 22–25 K NCCO and 22–23 K PCCO transition ranges are separate from 4.2 K imaging and junction measurements; no single transition criterion is invented for the material table. [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Low-temperature power laws, gap anisotropy and phase-sensitive interference probe different quantities. Interpret them with sample composition, disorder, field, temperature range, surface sensitivity and interface geometry attached. A magnitude-only spectrum cannot distinguish a gap from another function with the same absolute value; this mathematical ambiguity does not imply that every such function is a smooth, physically realizable pairing state. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6) [R3](#ref-source-22f5417afdec3a9f)

Spin-fluctuation calculations provide one route to a sign-changing gap, subject to their input spectrum and approximations. Their agreement with a symmetry assignment does not prove a unique pairing mechanism. High transition temperatures or family membership likewise cannot replace a phase-sensitive measurement of a particular pressure state. [R8](#ref-source-7755cb2d156620a8)

The 2019 oxygen-17 NMR work on Sr2RuO4 constrains earlier order-parameter proposals by observing a Knight-shift reduction. This does not automatically establish B1g pairing. The inherited review distinguishes RF heating, strain and applied-field conditions; a complete current order-parameter survey remains separate work. [R9](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41)

## Discovery implications

For a candidate material, first state its point group and measured Fermi surface. Then ask which experiments constrain node locations, spin response and relative phase, and whether those measurements describe comparable sample states. A useful next experiment should distinguish competing explanations within a specified geometry and resolution. Keep computed pairing preference, observed superconductivity and experimentally constrained symmetry as separate conclusions. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6) [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826) [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Related topics

Read [s-wave symmetry](/scwiki/s-wave), [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [spin-fluctuation pairing](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), and [superconducting gaps](/scwiki/superconducting-gap).
