# d-wave: nodes, crystal symmetry and phase evidence

Connect B1g symmetry to Fermi-surface nodes and distinguish magnitude measurements from controlled phase-sensitive experiments.

## Scope

For the tetragonal point group D4h, the familiar $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state belongs to B1g: a quarter turn changes its sign, while inversion preserves it. This entry separates symmetry, low-energy excitations and phase-sensitive evidence. A node or a small gap alone does not identify B1g, and identifying B1g does not uniquely determine the interaction that produced pairing. The cuprate evidence combines complementary measurements rather than a single universal diagnostic. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

The usual even-parity spin-singlet description assumes a centrosymmetric setting with the appropriate spin or pseudospin pairing structure. Orthorhombicity, multiple bands and additional broken symmetries require the actual crystal symmetry to be used. A label inherited from an ideal square lattice is not a substitute for that analysis. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

## Mathematical assumptions

An illustrative lattice harmonic, with lattice spacing set to one, is $\Delta(\mathbf k)=\Delta_0[\cos k_x-\cos k_y]/2$. Direct rotation, diagonal-reflection and inversion checks establish its B1g transformation. Its diagonal zero lines produce quasiparticle nodes only where they intersect the Fermi surface. A circular contour centered at the zone center intersects them; hypothetical small pockets around $(\pi,0)$ and $(0,\pi)$ do not. The latter have opposite gap signs while each pocket remains fully gapped. These checks establish a geometric possibility, not a band structure for a particular cuprate. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

On a circular Fermi surface, $f(\phi)=\cos2\phi$ has four zeros. A real admixture $f=\cos2\phi+s$ shifts the four nodes for $|s|<1$, gives two touching zeros at $|s|=1$, and removes them for $|s|>1$. Such a mixture is not pure B1g in a tetragonal crystal; orthorhombic symmetry can permit the corresponding real components to mix. The complex illustrative mixture $\cos2\phi+is$ instead has minimum magnitude $|s|$ and, when both components are nonzero, breaks time reversal. Five direct checks distinguish these cases. They do not demonstrate that any material selects the mixture. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

Near one simple node, take $E(\mathbf q)=\sqrt{(v_Fq_1)^2+(v_\Delta q_2)^2}$ in units $\hbar=k_B=1$. The ellipse of states below $E$ has area $\pi E^2/(v_Fv_\Delta)$; dividing by $(2\pi)^2$ and differentiating gives a positive-energy density of states $g(E)=E/(2\pi v_Fv_\Delta)$ for this one declared branch. Polygon-area checks verify six cases. For a linear density $g(E)=aE$, a converged thermal integral gives $C=(9\zeta(3)/2)aT^2$. Spin, node and band multiplicities must be supplied consistently. This clean local model illustrates a power law; disorder, finite temperature windows and different nodal dispersions change its applicability. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6)

For a separate illustration of phase frustration, consider a zero-field, single-junction loop with a built-in $\pi$ phase shift. Writing $f=\Phi/\Phi_0$, $\Phi_0=h/(2e)$ and $\beta=2\pi LI_c/\Phi_0$, with $E_J=\Phi_0 I_c/(2\pi)$, its energy is $U/E_J=2\pi^2f^2/\beta+\cos(2\pi f)$. The stationary condition is $f=\beta\sin(2\pi f)/(2\pi)$. Five energy-minimization checks show a zero-flux minimum for $\beta\leq1$ and paired nonzero minima for $\beta>1$; their magnitude approaches one half only as the inductance parameter grows. A finite loop therefore need not contain exactly half a flux quantum. This is not a reproduction of the extended three-boundary tricrystal geometry used in the experiments below. [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826)

## Experimental criteria

Hardy and colleagues measured changes in penetration depth in YBa2Cu3O6.95 using a 900 MHz resonator. Their abstract reports a linear contribution over approximately 3–25 K, within measurements extending from 1.3 K to the transition. This supports low-energy nodal excitations; the temperature interval is not a reported transition-temperature interval. Only the publisher abstract is checked here, so the full calibration, defect comparison and raw traces remain outside this review. [R2](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53)

Shen and colleagues' 1993 Bi2212 photoemission report finds a large in-plane gap anisotropy compatible with $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Photoemission primarily constrains excitation energies and gap magnitude; it does not directly read the relative order-parameter phase. The pinned chapter's DOI ending in 75.4234 actually identifies a Brillouin-spectroscopy paper and is corrected to 70.1553. Published comments and replies in 1993 and 1994 have been identified but not fully examined; the early ARPES result is not presented as a standalone final symmetry proof. [R3](#ref-source-22f5417afdec3a9f)

The original 1994 tricrystal-ring and 1995 scanning-SQUID papers are retained as historical source pointers. Their identities are checked, but this entry's detailed geometry discussion relies on the explicitly reviewed later author manuscripts, rather than claiming a new full audit of those originals. [R4](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7) [R5](#ref-source-6fe9eb9d2301fe93)

In the 2004 study of Ca-doped Y-123, La-214 and Bi-2212 films, selected crystal orientations create an odd phase frustration for a predominantly $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state. The authors compare opposite vortex polarities and model the pickup-loop response. The La-214 fit allowing flux to vary gives $0.585\pm0.1\,\Phi_0$, compatible with one half within its stated uncertainty. Imaging at 4.2 K is distinct from the samples' transition temperatures. Constraints on a fixed imaginary component depend on resolution; sufficiently small alternating domains are an explicitly discussed caveat. Doping coordinates are estimated using an empirical relation, and grain-boundary doping need not exactly equal bulk doping. [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826)

The 2000 electron-doped study tests NCCO and PCCO films. For NCCO it compares a frustrated tricrystal with two unfrustrated geometries; the controls show little central flux. Sensor height and pickup-loop integration enter the field model. Allowing total flux to vary gives $0.47^{+0.18}_{-0.14}\,\Phi_0$ in the quoted NCCO fit; the authors define the uncertainty using a doubling of best-fit chi-square, not an asserted standard confidence interval. This is sample- and geometry-specific phase evidence. The reported 22–25 K NCCO and 22–23 K PCCO transition ranges are separate from 4.2 K imaging and junction measurements; no single transition criterion is invented for the material table. [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Low-temperature power laws, gap anisotropy and phase-sensitive interference probe different quantities. Interpret them with sample composition, disorder, field, temperature range, surface sensitivity and interface geometry attached. A magnitude-only spectrum cannot distinguish a gap from another function with the same absolute value; this mathematical ambiguity does not imply that every such function is a smooth, physically realizable pairing state. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6) [R3](#ref-source-22f5417afdec3a9f)

Spin-fluctuation calculations provide one route to a sign-changing gap, subject to their input spectrum and approximations. Their agreement with a symmetry assignment does not prove a unique pairing mechanism. High transition temperatures or family membership likewise cannot replace a phase-sensitive measurement of a particular pressure state. [R8](#ref-source-7755cb2d156620a8)

The 2019 oxygen-17 NMR work on Sr2RuO4 constrains earlier order-parameter proposals by observing a Knight-shift reduction. This does not automatically establish B1g pairing. The inherited review distinguishes RF heating, strain and applied-field conditions; a complete current order-parameter survey remains separate work. [R9](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41)

## Discovery implications

For a candidate material, first state its point group and measured Fermi surface. Then ask which experiments constrain node locations, spin response and relative phase, and whether those measurements describe comparable sample states. A useful next experiment should distinguish competing explanations within a specified geometry and resolution. Keep computed pairing preference, observed superconductivity and experimentally constrained symmetry as separate conclusions. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R1](#ref-source-e933e3bbd4beade6) [R6](#ref-source-a9db90b0ffeff826) [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

Read [s-wave symmetry](/scwiki/s-wave), [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [spin-fluctuation pairing](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), and [superconducting gaps](/scwiki/superconducting-gap).

articles.body:
## Scope

In a tetragonal D4h crystal, a single-component $d_{xy}$ gap transforms as B2g. It is distinct from the B1g $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state when both are described using the same crystallographic axes. Both are even under inversion; the usual spin-singlet interpretation assumes the corresponding centrosymmetric spin or pseudospin setting. This entry covers symmetry and tests of a B2g candidate, not a claim that every material with line nodes realizes it. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

No sample in this entry is classified as experimentally established B2g. This describes the present review's evidence, not a proof that no such material exists. A calculated pairing channel, an Fe dxy orbital contribution and an experimentally determined gap representation are three different statements. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

## Mathematical assumptions

With lattice spacing one, an illustrative harmonic is $\Delta(\mathbf k)=\Delta_0\sin k_x\sin k_y$. It changes sign under either axial reflection and under a quarter turn, but is unchanged by inversion or interchange of $k_x$ and $k_y$. These transformations give B2g for the stated axes. Gap zeros lie on axial lines, including their periodic zone-boundary counterparts; quasiparticle nodes require intersections with the Fermi surface. Higher harmonics can add zeros without changing the representation. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

Coordinate conventions matter. For a unit circular contour, $2xy=\sin2\phi$ and $x^2-y^2=\cos2\phi$. Under the passive coordinate change $x'=(x+y)/\sqrt2$, $y'=(-x+y)/\sqrt2$, one finds $x'^2-y'^2=2xy$. The polynomial name changes while the physical pattern relative to the crystal is unchanged. Four direct checks verify this identity. A comparison between Fe–Fe and Fe–As coordinate conventions must therefore include the axes and symmetry operations, rather than matching the word “d-wave” alone. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

On an ideal circular contour with uniform weight, replacing $\cos2\phi$ by $\sin2\phi$ is an angular shift. Four independent broadened-density-of-states integrals coincide for the two gaps; both also have $\langle f^2\rangle=1/2$ and $\langle f^4\rangle=3/8$. Consequently an angularly averaged spectrum or a clean nodal power law can fail to distinguish these orientations. The checks assume identical amplitudes and broadening. Real velocity weights, multiple sheets and selective probes can break this equivalence. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

To isolate what a pairing eigenvalue does, define normalized basis functions $u_s=1$, $u_1=\sqrt2\cos2\phi$, $u_2=\sqrt2\sin2\phi$ and a deliberately separable operator $K(\phi,\phi')=\sum_a\lambda_a u_a(\phi)u_a(\phi')$, integrated with $d\phi'/(2\pi)$. Numerical application confirms the prescribed eigenvalues for three choices: $(0.3,0.4,0.1)$ selects B1g, $(0.3,0.2,0.45)$ selects B2g, and $(0.3,0.4,0.4)$ makes the two d channels degenerate. These couplings were chosen, not inferred from a material. The equality is accidental within this example: D4h does not require its two distinct one-dimensional representations to have equal pairing strength. The calculation illustrates model selection, not an RPA reproduction or a measured transition temperature. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

An orbital basis change must act on both electrons of a pair: $\Delta_{\rm band}(\mathbf k)=U^\dagger(\mathbf k)\Delta_{\rm orbital}(\mathbf k)U^*(-\mathbf k)$. Four real, momentum-independent two-orbital examples change matrix entries while preserving the imposed gap-matrix eigenvalues. This limited check does not replace the full momentum-dependent transformation. Likewise, two electrons in the same dxy orbital contribute the product of the orbital's symmetry characters; an orbital sign squared is positive. The orbital name alone therefore does not assign a B2g momentum dependence to the pair. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462) [R5](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

## Experimental criteria

Momentum-resolved measurements must locate a gap minimum or node relative to measured crystal axes and Fermi sheets. Distinguish insufficient energy resolution from a true zero and compare temperatures within the same superconducting state. Thermodynamic power laws can motivate a nodal hypothesis, but without directional information they do not distinguish B1g from B2g in the circular example above. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Rotating-field measurements also require a response model. Vorontsov and Vekhter calculate a reversal of specific-heat anisotropy with temperature or field while the imposed nodal directions remain fixed. Their quasiclassical treatment includes vortex scattering, a corrugated quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface and impurity scattering; the selected manuscript neglects Zeeman splitting. The authors caution that their spatial-averaging approximation can overestimate vortex scattering at low fields. Thus a heat-capacity minimum is not universally a node locator. Their comparison with CeCoIn5 favors B1g within that analysis; this is not evidence establishing B2g. [R6](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

The thermal weighting itself can be checked without reproducing that calculation. In units $k_B=1$, the factor $w(x)=x^2e^{-x}/(1+e^{-x})^2$, with $x=E/T$, peaks near $2.399$. For a deliberately chosen bounded spectral difference $\delta N(E)=0.1[1-(E/E_*)^2]e^{-(E/E_*)^2}$, five converged integrals of $w(x)\delta N(Tx)$ change sign as temperature increases. The total spectra can remain positive by adding this small difference to a unit background. This illustrates finite-energy weighting; it does not calculate vortices, assign a physical inversion temperature or validate a material symmetry. [R6](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

Phase-sensitive junction tests need a geometry that distinguishes the candidate representations, with calibrated crystal orientations and controls for trapped flux and interfaces. The reviewed electron-doped cuprate tricrystal experiment demonstrates why frustrated and unfrustrated control geometries matter. Its result concerns those samples and the tested $d_{x^2-y^2}$ pattern; it cannot simply be relabeled as a dxy measurement. [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Graser and colleagues explicitly align their orbital basis with nearest-neighbor Fe–Fe directions. In their five-orbital model, the principal competition discussed is anisotropic s-wave versus $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Equation (33) separately defines dxy by its reflection characters, and Figure 13 includes it as a subleading channel for the displayed electron-doped, zero-Hund-coupling case. That calculated ordering depends on parameters; it neither establishes a B2g material nor justifies reading an orbital-weight plot as a gap-symmetry plot. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

Bickers, Scalapino and White provide an early conserving-approximation framework for the two-dimensional Hubbard model. The abstract checked here does not establish a B2g-specific result. Kuroki and colleagues' later five-orbital work must be read with its 2009 erratum: an orbital-to-band transformation error changed the original gap plot. The corrected displayed diagonal band gaps are fully open, while parameter-dependent nodal competition remains. This correction is retained as a required companion citation. [R3](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0) [R4](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R5](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

A complex combination of two d components is a separate state, not the single-component B2g case covered here. Likewise, changing to an orthorhombic or hexagonal crystal requires a new symmetry classification. Do not assume that a familiar polynomial name carries the same representation, enforced zeros or degeneracy into a different point group. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

## Discovery implications

For a proposed dxy candidate, specify the crystal axes, point group, band or orbital basis, and the sample state. Compare competing representations using both directional and phase information, with temperature, field and interface assumptions attached. Keep the present absence of an accepted material record separate from the existence of a theoretical channel. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462) [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Related topics

Read [d-wave phase evidence](/scwiki/d-wave), [s-wave symmetry](/scwiki/s-wave), [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [spin-fluctuation pairing](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), and [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing).

# dxy pairing: B2g symmetry and directional evidence

Distinguish orbital names, coordinate conventions and pairing representations, and test what directional measurements can establish.

## Scope

In a tetragonal D4h crystal, a single-component $d_{xy}$ gap transforms as B2g. It is distinct from the B1g $d_{x^2-y^2}$ state when both are described using the same crystallographic axes. Both are even under inversion; the usual spin-singlet interpretation assumes the corresponding centrosymmetric spin or pseudospin setting. This entry covers symmetry and tests of a B2g candidate, not a claim that every material with line nodes realizes it. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

No sample in this entry is classified as experimentally established B2g. This describes the present review's evidence, not a proof that no such material exists. A calculated pairing channel, an Fe dxy orbital contribution and an experimentally determined gap representation are three different statements. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

## Mathematical assumptions

With lattice spacing one, an illustrative harmonic is $\Delta(\mathbf k)=\Delta_0\sin k_x\sin k_y$. It changes sign under either axial reflection and under a quarter turn, but is unchanged by inversion or interchange of $k_x$ and $k_y$. These transformations give B2g for the stated axes. Gap zeros lie on axial lines, including their periodic zone-boundary counterparts; quasiparticle nodes require intersections with the Fermi surface. Higher harmonics can add zeros without changing the representation. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

Coordinate conventions matter. For a unit circular contour, $2xy=\sin2\phi$ and $x^2-y^2=\cos2\phi$. Under the passive coordinate change $x'=(x+y)/\sqrt2$, $y'=(-x+y)/\sqrt2$, one finds $x'^2-y'^2=2xy$. The polynomial name changes while the physical pattern relative to the crystal is unchanged. Four direct checks verify this identity. A comparison between Fe–Fe and Fe–As coordinate conventions must therefore include the axes and symmetry operations, rather than matching the word “d-wave” alone. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

On an ideal circular contour with uniform weight, replacing $\cos2\phi$ by $\sin2\phi$ is an angular shift. Four independent broadened-density-of-states integrals coincide for the two gaps; both also have $\langle f^2\rangle=1/2$ and $\langle f^4\rangle=3/8$. Consequently an angularly averaged spectrum or a clean nodal power law can fail to distinguish these orientations. The checks assume identical amplitudes and broadening. Real velocity weights, multiple sheets and selective probes can break this equivalence. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

To isolate what a pairing eigenvalue does, define normalized basis functions $u_s=1$, $u_1=\sqrt2\cos2\phi$, $u_2=\sqrt2\sin2\phi$ and a deliberately separable operator $K(\phi,\phi')=\sum_a\lambda_a u_a(\phi)u_a(\phi')$, integrated with $d\phi'/(2\pi)$. Numerical application confirms the prescribed eigenvalues for three choices: $(0.3,0.4,0.1)$ selects B1g, $(0.3,0.2,0.45)$ selects B2g, and $(0.3,0.4,0.4)$ makes the two d channels degenerate. These couplings were chosen, not inferred from a material. The equality is accidental within this example: D4h does not require its two distinct one-dimensional representations to have equal pairing strength. The calculation illustrates model selection, not an RPA reproduction or a measured transition temperature. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

An orbital basis change must act on both electrons of a pair: $\Delta_{\rm band}(\mathbf k)=U^\dagger(\mathbf k)\Delta_{\rm orbital}(\mathbf k)U^*(-\mathbf k)$. Four real, momentum-independent two-orbital examples change matrix entries while preserving the imposed gap-matrix eigenvalues. This limited check does not replace the full momentum-dependent transformation. Likewise, two electrons in the same dxy orbital contribute the product of the orbital's symmetry characters; an orbital sign squared is positive. The orbital name alone therefore does not assign a B2g momentum dependence to the pair. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462) [R5](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

## Experimental criteria

Momentum-resolved measurements must locate a gap minimum or node relative to measured crystal axes and Fermi sheets. Distinguish insufficient energy resolution from a true zero and compare temperatures within the same superconducting state. Thermodynamic power laws can motivate a nodal hypothesis, but without directional information they do not distinguish B1g from B2g in the circular example above. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Rotating-field measurements also require a response model. Vorontsov and Vekhter calculate a reversal of specific-heat anisotropy with temperature or field while the imposed nodal directions remain fixed. Their quasiclassical treatment includes vortex scattering, a corrugated quasi-two-dimensional Fermi surface and impurity scattering; the selected manuscript neglects Zeeman splitting. The authors caution that their spatial-averaging approximation can overestimate vortex scattering at low fields. Thus a heat-capacity minimum is not universally a node locator. Their comparison with CeCoIn5 favors B1g within that analysis; this is not evidence establishing B2g. [R6](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

The thermal weighting itself can be checked without reproducing that calculation. In units $k_B=1$, the factor $w(x)=x^2e^{-x}/(1+e^{-x})^2$, with $x=E/T$, peaks near $2.399$. For a deliberately chosen bounded spectral difference $\delta N(E)=0.1[1-(E/E_*)^2]e^{-(E/E_*)^2}$, five converged integrals of $w(x)\delta N(Tx)$ change sign as temperature increases. The total spectra can remain positive by adding this small difference to a unit background. This illustrates finite-energy weighting; it does not calculate vortices, assign a physical inversion temperature or validate a material symmetry. [R6](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

Phase-sensitive junction tests need a geometry that distinguishes the candidate representations, with calibrated crystal orientations and controls for trapped flux and interfaces. The reviewed electron-doped cuprate tricrystal experiment demonstrates why frustrated and unfrustrated control geometries matter. Its result concerns those samples and the tested $d_{x^2-y^2}$ pattern; it cannot simply be relabeled as a dxy measurement. [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

## Limits and disputes

Graser and colleagues explicitly align their orbital basis with nearest-neighbor Fe–Fe directions. In their five-orbital model, the principal competition discussed is anisotropic s-wave versus $d_{x^2-y^2}$. Equation (33) separately defines dxy by its reflection characters, and Figure 13 includes it as a subleading channel for the displayed electron-doped, zero-Hund-coupling case. That calculated ordering depends on parameters; it neither establishes a B2g material nor justifies reading an orbital-weight plot as a gap-symmetry plot. [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462)

Bickers, Scalapino and White provide an early conserving-approximation framework for the two-dimensional Hubbard model. The abstract checked here does not establish a B2g-specific result. Kuroki and colleagues' later five-orbital work must be read with its 2009 erratum: an orbital-to-band transformation error changed the original gap plot. The corrected displayed diagonal band gaps are fully open, while parameter-dependent nodal competition remains. This correction is retained as a required companion citation. [R3](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0) [R4](#ref-source-f80a18149666bd31) [R5](#ref-source-6570d4401413e026)

A complex combination of two d components is a separate state, not the single-component B2g case covered here. Likewise, changing to an orthorhombic or hexagonal crystal requires a new symmetry classification. Do not assume that a familiar polynomial name carries the same representation, enforced zeros or degeneracy into a different point group. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

## Discovery implications

For a proposed dxy candidate, specify the crystal axes, point group, band or orbital basis, and the sample state. Compare competing representations using both directional and phase information, with temperature, field and interface assumptions attached. Keep the present absence of an accepted material record separate from the existence of a theoretical channel. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-4bdcd96b3b93d462) [R7](#ref-source-7700f02a5390b1cf)

articles.body:
## Scope

p-wave describes orbital structure: angular momentum $l=1$ in a rotationally invariant continuum, or specified odd basis functions in a crystal. It is not a synonym for every odd-parity state. Spin triplet, odd parity, orbital representation and chirality answer different questions. The familiar relation between triplet and odd momentum parity assumes even-frequency pairing with no additional antisymmetric orbital index. Multiorbital and odd-frequency cases require the full exchange symmetry. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Neutral liquid helium-3 provides the established triplet p-wave benchmark through its A and B phases. It does not certify a crystal superconductor by analogy. Sr2RuO4 remains a constrained, unresolved order-parameter problem, while uranium superconductors motivate triplet and odd-parity studies without thereby selecting a p-wave representation. [R4](#ref-source-b4553aaaeacb3c3d) [R6](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41) [R7](#ref-source-c4434644191d0174) [R11](#ref-source-ca6322be2694e430)

## Mathematical assumptions

For an even-frequency, single-band spin basis, write $\Delta(\mathbf k)=i[\mathbf d(\mathbf k)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma]\sigma_y$, so $\Delta_{\uparrow\uparrow}=-d_x+id_y$, $\Delta_{\downarrow\downarrow}=d_x+id_y$ and $\Delta_{\uparrow\downarrow}=\Delta_{\downarrow\uparrow}=d_z$. Odd $\mathbf d(-\mathbf k)=-\mathbf d(\mathbf k)$ makes $\Delta(\mathbf k)=-\Delta^T(-\mathbf k)$, as required by fermionic exchange. In a centrosymmetric spin-orbit-coupled system the analogous pseudospin basis must be defined explicitly; these entries are not automatically laboratory spin populations. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

The identity $\Delta\Delta^\dagger=|\mathbf d|^2I+i(\mathbf d\times\mathbf d^*)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$ gives squared gaps $|\mathbf d|^2\pm|i\mathbf d\times\mathbf d^*|$. A unitary state has vanishing cross product; it need not preserve time reversal. Four complex examples verify the matrix identity and exchange symmetry. Independent diagonalization of 48 imposed-gap Bogoliubov matrices also agrees with $E_\pm^2=\xi^2+|\mathbf d|^2\pm|i\mathbf d\times\mathbf d^*|$. The normal band here is spin-degenerate: this spectrum is not a general formula for a ferromagnetic multiband metal. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

On a unit circular Fermi contour, with gap scale one, compare polar $\mathbf d=(0,0,k_x)$, helical $\mathbf d=(k_x,k_y,0)$ and chiral $\mathbf d=(0,0,k_x+ik_y)$. Polar pairing has two nodes; the other two are fully gapped on this contour. All three are unitary. A global-phase comparison with the time-reversed texture preserves the polar and helical states but distinguishes the two chiral partners. Thus a full gap or unitary pairing alone does not establish broken time reversal. These are imposed examples, not self-consistent material solutions. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Changing the Fermi surface changes the answer. On a sphere the same chiral form has squared gap $k_x^2+k_y^2=\sin^2\theta$ and two polar point nodes, whereas the illustrative BW texture $\mathbf d=(k_x,k_y,k_z)$ has constant squared gap one. Four spherical checks confirm both. Conversely, the nonunitary circular texture $\mathbf d=(k_x,ik_y,0)$ has squared branches $(|k_x|\pm|k_y|)^2$; a complex vector does not by itself imply the fully gapped chiral example above. No topological invariant is calculated here. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R4](#ref-source-b4553aaaeacb3c3d) [R5](#ref-source-24556d6dba4d8cc1)

For a clean unitary model at zero temperature with negligible spin-orbit coupling and a fixed d texture, the ideal diagonal response is $\chi_{ii}/\chi_N=1-\langle|d_i|^2/|\mathbf d|^2\rangle$. Uniform circular averaging gives $(1/2,1/2,1)$ for the helical example; fixed-z chiral pairing gives $(1,1,0)$. Isotropic spherical BW averaging gives $(2/3,2/3,2/3)$. These omit interaction corrections, orbital response and field-driven rotation. They illustrate why a decrease for one field direction alone cannot identify a singlet or an orbital representation. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R4](#ref-source-b4553aaaeacb3c3d) [R7](#ref-source-c4434644191d0174)

## Experimental criteria

The 1972 discovery record needs two steps. Osheroff, Richardson and Lee initially interpreted pressure anomalies in a Pomeranchuk cell as a possible new solid-helium phase. The later NMR paper, also authored by Gully, separated solid and liquid signals using a field gradient and associated the changes with the liquid. Its temperatures below 3 mK came from approximate melting-curve extrapolation. These measurements are historical evidence for new liquid phases, not a standalone determination of the full p-wave order parameter. [R2](#ref-source-017750e49092dcb4) [R3](#ref-source-b4c5ef61b3180334)

Leggett's later review develops the ABM and BW descriptions associated with A and B phases. Its 1976 erratum withdraws a claimed factor-of-two disagreement with Brinkman and Smith near the transition; it does not retract the phase framework. The review abstract and correction text are checked here, while its complete derivations remain outside this scoped review. Helium is neutral and approximately rotationally invariant, so its response cannot be transferred directly to a charged crystal with strong spin-orbit coupling. [R4](#ref-source-b4553aaaeacb3c3d) [R5](#ref-source-24556d6dba4d8cc1)

In Sr2RuO4, Pustogow and colleagues' oxygen-17 NMR work found a reduced spin response after controlling radio-frequency heating. The reviewed author manuscript distinguishes zero-strain measurements at 0.7107 T from strained measurements at 1.9980 T. This challenges the simple fixed-d-vector chiral interpretation used previously; it does not uniquely establish d-wave or invalidate every report of time-reversal breaking. Heating, field direction, strain and the assumed pseudospin response must accompany the inference. [R6](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41)

Matsuki and colleagues' study was published on 9 February 2026; the checked author manuscript is dated December 2025. Comparing one and six crystals exposed stray-field artifacts. They combined single-crystal muon shifts with field-cooled magnetization of that same crystal. For fields along [100], they inferred a spin-shift reduction consistent with singlet-like behavior. The spin-contact extraction was insufficiently accurate at 0.2 T; magnetization stopped at 0.5 K. Their conclusions therefore do not distinguish fully gapped, line-nodal, helical and interorbital states. The reported 0.05 K spectrum is a measurement temperature, not a transition. [R7](#ref-source-c4434644191d0174)

Junction phase tests, directional spin response, thermodynamic gaps and symmetry-breaking probes should constrain the same proposed state under matched sample conditions. A time-reversal-breaking signal alone does not select p-wave over other complex order parameters or establish its microscopic origin. Boundary features require comparison with surface disorder and ordinary bound states, plus an independently specified bulk phase; calling a feature “Majorana-like” is not a pairing-symmetry measurement. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

## Limits and disputes

UGe2, URhGe and UCoGe have original reports connecting superconductivity with ferromagnetism under different pressure and sample conditions. These motivate equal-spin and odd-parity hypotheses, but ferromagnetic coexistence alone does not select a p-wave basis. Their source checks here are abstract-scoped; no new sample transition values or microscopic coexistence maps are extracted. [R8](#ref-source-db2917242488a101) [R9](#ref-source-15aec45a868e9fb9) [R10](#ref-source-a4695ba5bfa789f3)

The UTe2 discovery paper presents triplet-related evidence and a nearly ferromagnetic interpretation without ambient-pressure long-range ferromagnetic order. Its approximately 40 T b-axis critical-field estimate was extrapolated beyond measurements reaching 20 T. Treat that historical inference separately from a directly observed boundary or a settled orbital representation. Strong coupling, spin-orbit coupling, anisotropic orbital limiting and multiple bands must be considered when interpreting unusually large critical fields. [R11](#ref-source-ca6322be2694e430)

Inversion absence permits singlet–triplet mixing; multiple orbitals and spin-orbit coupling further change the bookkeeping. Even in an inversion-symmetric crystal, several odd basis functions can belong to the same representation. A label such as p-wave must state which basis and symmetry operations are meant. A finite collection of supporting observations is not a universal exclusion of all alternatives. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

## Discovery implications

For each candidate, record inversion symmetry, the spin or pseudospin convention, field orientation, sample conditions and competing gap structures. Separate evidence for odd parity from evidence for chirality, nodes and topology. Use the explicit examples above to identify measurements that actually distinguish hypotheses. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open; the local model checks do not determine a material's pairing state. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R6](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41) [R7](#ref-source-c4434644191d0174)

## Related topics

Continue with [ferromagnetic fluctuations](/scwiki/ferromagnetic-fluctuations), [topological superconductivity](/scwiki/topological-superconductivity), [d-wave phase evidence](/scwiki/d-wave), [s-wave symmetry](/scwiki/s-wave), and [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing).

# p-wave pairing: parity, spin and chirality

Separate odd parity, triplet spin structure and chirality, with helium-3 benchmarks and carefully bounded crystal evidence.

## Scope

p-wave describes orbital structure: angular momentum $l=1$ in a rotationally invariant continuum, or specified odd basis functions in a crystal. It is not a synonym for every odd-parity state. Spin triplet, odd parity, orbital representation and chirality answer different questions. The familiar relation between triplet and odd momentum parity assumes even-frequency pairing with no additional antisymmetric orbital index. Multiorbital and odd-frequency cases require the full exchange symmetry. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Neutral liquid helium-3 provides the established triplet p-wave benchmark through its A and B phases. It does not certify a crystal superconductor by analogy. Sr2RuO4 remains a constrained, unresolved order-parameter problem, while uranium superconductors motivate triplet and odd-parity studies without thereby selecting a p-wave representation. [R4](#ref-source-b4553aaaeacb3c3d) [R6](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41) [R7](#ref-source-c4434644191d0174) [R11](#ref-source-ca6322be2694e430)

## Mathematical assumptions

For an even-frequency, single-band spin basis, write $\Delta(\mathbf k)=i[\mathbf d(\mathbf k)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma]\sigma_y$, so $\Delta_{\uparrow\uparrow}=-d_x+id_y$, $\Delta_{\downarrow\downarrow}=d_x+id_y$ and $\Delta_{\uparrow\downarrow}=\Delta_{\downarrow\uparrow}=d_z$. Odd $\mathbf d(-\mathbf k)=-\mathbf d(\mathbf k)$ makes $\Delta(\mathbf k)=-\Delta^T(-\mathbf k)$, as required by fermionic exchange. In a centrosymmetric spin-orbit-coupled system the analogous pseudospin basis must be defined explicitly; these entries are not automatically laboratory spin populations. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

The identity $\Delta\Delta^\dagger=|\mathbf d|^2I+i(\mathbf d\times\mathbf d^*)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$ gives squared gaps $|\mathbf d|^2\pm|i\mathbf d\times\mathbf d^*|$. A unitary state has vanishing cross product; it need not preserve time reversal. Four complex examples verify the matrix identity and exchange symmetry. Independent diagonalization of 48 imposed-gap Bogoliubov matrices also agrees with $E_\pm^2=\xi^2+|\mathbf d|^2\pm|i\mathbf d\times\mathbf d^*|$. The normal band here is spin-degenerate: this spectrum is not a general formula for a ferromagnetic multiband metal. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

On a unit circular Fermi contour, with gap scale one, compare polar $\mathbf d=(0,0,k_x)$, helical $\mathbf d=(k_x,k_y,0)$ and chiral $\mathbf d=(0,0,k_x+ik_y)$. Polar pairing has two nodes; the other two are fully gapped on this contour. All three are unitary. A global-phase comparison with the time-reversed texture preserves the polar and helical states but distinguishes the two chiral partners. Thus a full gap or unitary pairing alone does not establish broken time reversal. These are imposed examples, not self-consistent material solutions. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Changing the Fermi surface changes the answer. On a sphere the same chiral form has squared gap $k_x^2+k_y^2=\sin^2\theta$ and two polar point nodes, whereas the illustrative BW texture $\mathbf d=(k_x,k_y,k_z)$ has constant squared gap one. Four spherical checks confirm both. Conversely, the nonunitary circular texture $\mathbf d=(k_x,ik_y,0)$ has squared branches $(|k_x|\pm|k_y|)^2$; a complex vector does not by itself imply the fully gapped chiral example above. No topological invariant is calculated here. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R4](#ref-source-b4553aaaeacb3c3d) [R5](#ref-source-24556d6dba4d8cc1)

For a clean unitary model at zero temperature with negligible spin-orbit coupling and a fixed d texture, the ideal diagonal response is $\chi_{ii}/\chi_N=1-\langle|d_i|^2/|\mathbf d|^2\rangle$. Uniform circular averaging gives $(1/2,1/2,1)$ for the helical example; fixed-z chiral pairing gives $(1,1,0)$. Isotropic spherical BW averaging gives $(2/3,2/3,2/3)$. These omit interaction corrections, orbital response and field-driven rotation. They illustrate why a decrease for one field direction alone cannot identify a singlet or an orbital representation. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R4](#ref-source-b4553aaaeacb3c3d) [R7](#ref-source-c4434644191d0174)

## Experimental criteria

The 1972 discovery record needs two steps. Osheroff, Richardson and Lee initially interpreted pressure anomalies in a Pomeranchuk cell as a possible new solid-helium phase. The later NMR paper, also authored by Gully, separated solid and liquid signals using a field gradient and associated the changes with the liquid. Its temperatures below 3 mK came from approximate melting-curve extrapolation. These measurements are historical evidence for new liquid phases, not a standalone determination of the full p-wave order parameter. [R2](#ref-source-017750e49092dcb4) [R3](#ref-source-b4c5ef61b3180334)

Leggett's later review develops the ABM and BW descriptions associated with A and B phases. Its 1976 erratum withdraws a claimed factor-of-two disagreement with Brinkman and Smith near the transition; it does not retract the phase framework. The review abstract and correction text are checked here, while its complete derivations remain outside this scoped review. Helium is neutral and approximately rotationally invariant, so its response cannot be transferred directly to a charged crystal with strong spin-orbit coupling. [R4](#ref-source-b4553aaaeacb3c3d) [R5](#ref-source-24556d6dba4d8cc1)

In Sr2RuO4, Pustogow and colleagues' oxygen-17 NMR work found a reduced spin response after controlling radio-frequency heating. The reviewed author manuscript distinguishes zero-strain measurements at 0.7107 T from strained measurements at 1.9980 T. This challenges the simple fixed-d-vector chiral interpretation used previously; it does not uniquely establish d-wave or invalidate every report of time-reversal breaking. Heating, field direction, strain and the assumed pseudospin response must accompany the inference. [R6](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41)

Matsuki and colleagues' study was published on 9 February 2026; the checked author manuscript is dated December 2025. Comparing one and six crystals exposed stray-field artifacts. They combined single-crystal muon shifts with field-cooled magnetization of that same crystal. For fields along [100], they inferred a spin-shift reduction consistent with singlet-like behavior. The spin-contact extraction was insufficiently accurate at 0.2 T; magnetization stopped at 0.5 K. Their conclusions therefore do not distinguish fully gapped, line-nodal, helical and interorbital states. The reported 0.05 K spectrum is a measurement temperature, not a transition. [R7](#ref-source-c4434644191d0174)

Junction phase tests, directional spin response, thermodynamic gaps and symmetry-breaking probes should constrain the same proposed state under matched sample conditions. A time-reversal-breaking signal alone does not select p-wave over other complex order parameters or establish its microscopic origin. Boundary features require comparison with surface disorder and ordinary bound states, plus an independently specified bulk phase; calling a feature “Majorana-like” is not a pairing-symmetry measurement. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

These motivate equal-spin and odd-parity hypotheses, but ferromagnetic coexistence alone does not select a p-wave basis. Inversion absence permits singlet–triplet mixing; multiple orbitals and spin-orbit coupling further change the bookkeeping. Even in an inversion-symmetric crystal, several odd basis functions can belong to the same representation. A label such as p-wave must state which basis and symmetry operations are meant. A finite collection of supporting observations is not a universal exclusion of all alternatives. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open; the local model checks do not determine a material's pairing state. Inversion absence permits singlet–triplet mixing; multiple orbitals and spin-orbit coupling further change the bookkeeping. Even in an inversion-symmetric crystal, several odd basis functions can belong to the same representation. A label such as p-wave must state which basis and symmetry operations are meant. A finite collection of supporting observations is not a universal exclusion of all alternatives.

articles.body:
## Scope

In a rotationally invariant continuum, f-wave means orbital angular momentum $l=3$. A crystal instead classifies a gap by its actual point group, spin or pseudospin structure and basis functions. An odd cubic polynomial, an experimentally inferred node and a particular irreducible representation are different statements. The discussion below assumes even-frequency pairing unless stated otherwise; orbital exchange and spin-orbit coupling must also be included when applying parity arguments to a multiorbital material. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f)

UPt3 is an important test case with competing descriptions of its superconducting phases. The historical E2u framework and a proposed E1u planar state organize different observations, but a candidate label is not a unique experimental determination. UTe2 has a different crystal symmetry and must not inherit UPt3's representation merely because both are uranium compounds. [R2](#ref-source-a329f7df31c7d3e9) [R3](#ref-source-d3edee404071ac81) [R5](#ref-source-34df31af237b76a7) [R7](#ref-source-5ff091aacae25bb0)

## Mathematical assumptions

An illustrative hexagonal E2u orbital doublet is $[k_z(k_x^2-k_y^2),2k_zk_xk_y]$. With a fixed spin vector along z, its equal-amplitude chiral combination is proportional to $k_z(k_x+ik_y)^2$. It is odd under inversion. Under rotation by angle $\alpha$ about z, its orbital factor acquires $e^{2i\alpha}$: the continuum harmonic has $l=3$ but axial projection $m=2$, not $m=3$. Four direct transformation checks and finite-difference Laplacians verify the polynomial identities. In a lattice, continuous angular momentum is only a comparison, not an exact conserved quantum number. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R3](#ref-source-d3edee404071ac81)

On a unit sphere this chiral form has magnitude $|\cos\theta|\sin^2\theta$: an equatorial line zero and quadratic polar zeros. A planar E1u illustration uses two orthogonal spin vectors multiplying $k_x(5k_z^2-1)$ and $k_y(5k_z^2-1)$. Its magnitude is $\sin\theta|5\cos^2\theta-1|$, with polar point zeros and two horizontal zeros at $\cos^2\theta=1/5$. These are model angles, not measured node coordinates. Tsutsumi and colleagues use a related planar construction in their weak-spin-orbit scenario, with field-dependent spin orientation. [R5](#ref-source-34df31af237b76a7)

The constant one in the spherical E1u expressions represents $k_x^2+k_y^2+k_z^2$. Restoring it makes each component a homogeneous harmonic cubic. Yet the lower-order pair $(k_x,k_y)$ transforms as the same orbital doublet under the crystal's in-plane operations. In the chosen planar model, adding amplitude $a(k_x,k_y)$ changes the horizontal-zero condition to $k_z^2=(1-a)/5$. Five examples move or eliminate these zeros while preserving odd parity and the orbital transformation rule. A representation therefore need not fix the positions of every node. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R5](#ref-source-34df31af237b76a7)

The polar zeros have different local phase space. Restricting to small polar caps, count the fraction of a unit sphere with imposed gap below $\epsilon$. Doubling a sufficiently small cutoff approximately doubles this fraction for the quadratic E2u zero, but quadruples it for the linear E1u zero. Eight cap calculations verify these limits. This is a geometric illustration, not a density-of-states or thermal-conductivity calculation; real velocities, impurity scattering and other nodes still contribute to a measured power law. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R5](#ref-source-34df31af237b76a7)

A separate two-component illustration shows how split transitions can arise without determining a material representation. Set $u=|\eta_1|^2$, $v=|\eta_2|^2$ and relative phase $\delta$, with dimensionless free energy $F=(t-1)u+(t-0.8)v+(u^2+v^2)/2+(0.4+0.15\cos2\delta)uv$. When both amplitudes are present, $\delta=\pm\pi/2$ minimizes the phase term. The first onset is $t=1$; the second is $t=(0.8-0.25)/(1-0.25)\simeq0.7333$. Five independent positive-amplitude grid comparisons agree with the analytic minima. These coefficients are chosen, not fitted to UPt3 or UTe2. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-a329f7df31c7d3e9)

## Experimental criteria

The 2002 Joynt–Taillefer review weighs UPt3's phase diagram, nodal responses and magnetic coupling. Its abstract favors E1g or E2u on balance while acknowledging that neither explains all observations. That historical conclusion is not a current universal assignment. Machida and colleagues' later angle-dependent thermal-conductivity study instead interprets the B/C-phase data using E1u. The 2011 author abstract and 2012 journal abstract differ in the stated phase coverage; this entry uses the latter and does not claim a complete version comparison. [R2](#ref-source-a329f7df31c7d3e9) [R4](#ref-source-31577c7cb2ae0ac8)

Schemm and colleagues reported a UPt3 Kerr signal below about 0.46 K, separated from an upper susceptibility onset near 0.55 K. Their 1550 nm optical probe required an estimated local-heating allowance up to 50 mK; bulk heating inferred from mutual inductance was much smaller. Cooling in either sign of a 50 G field and then measuring with the field removed trained the signal's sign. These observations support additional time-reversal breaking in the lower-temperature phase within the experiment's controls; the optical signal alone does not select E2u. The Kerr onset is not the upper superconducting transition. [R3](#ref-source-d3edee404071ac81)

Node assignment requires field direction, heat-current direction, temperature and the response model. A minimum in an angle-dependent signal is not automatically a node: vortex scattering and thermal weighting can reverse anisotropy. Compare multiple axes and independent probes before deciding between equatorial, off-equatorial and vertical zeros. The relative success of one calculation under selected assumptions does not eliminate every competing representation. [R4](#ref-source-31577c7cb2ae0ac8) [R5](#ref-source-34df31af237b76a7) [R9](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

For a null Kerr result, record illumination, surface, residual field, cooldown history and statistical sensitivity. Independent noise and domain signals add in variance, $\sigma_{\rm total}^2=\sigma_{\rm noise}^2+\sigma_{\rm signal}^2$. A small constructed example verifies this identity for uncorrelated sequences. The equation requires its independence assumption; a measured absence of increased scatter is a constraint at finite sensitivity, not proof that all possible microscopic time-reversal breaking is absent. [R8](#ref-source-dd4e897d833ce69c)

## Limits and disputes

Hayes and colleagues reported UTe2 Kerr and calorimetric signatures supporting a multicomponent state. Their low-field warmups were compared with measurements following positive and negative training fields; the interpretation includes domains. Ajeesh and colleagues later found no spontaneous zero-field Kerr signal in four single-transition samples spanning two growth methods. Their heat-pulse procedure repeatedly crossed the transition, and trained signals varied with position and sample. The selected manuscript's optical and susceptibility sample sets are different: one must not attribute the separate double-transition susceptibility sample to the Kerr set. Retain this disagreement and its conditions rather than declaring all UTe2 samples chiral or all possible states excluded. [R7](#ref-source-5ff091aacae25bb0) [R8](#ref-source-dd4e897d833ce69c)

Orthorhombic D2h has one-dimensional ordinary point-group representations, unlike hexagonal E2u. A complex combination of distinct components can still break time reversal if the energetics permit it; multidimensional point-group representations are not a universal prerequisite. Spin degeneracy, orbital structure and accidental near-degeneracy must be specified. UTe2's discovery evidence for unusual spin pairing does not independently choose an f-wave basis or a unique multicomponent state. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R6](#ref-source-ca6322be2694e430) [R7](#ref-source-5ff091aacae25bb0)

The spherical polynomial examples neglect UPt3's real multiband, nonsymmorphic band structure. The Ginzburg–Landau example does not reproduce its field–temperature phase diagram, and no surface-state or bulk-topology calculation is supplied. A change of polynomial order, a broken-symmetry signal or a high critical field cannot replace that missing analysis. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-a329f7df31c7d3e9)

## Discovery implications

Specify the crystal symmetry and basis first. Then test whether one proposed state explains phase splitting, directional nodes, spin response and symmetry-breaking observations under compatible conditions. Preserve null results, competing interpretations and source-version differences alongside positive evidence. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open; the model calculations here constrain language and logic, not the pairing state of a new material. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R3](#ref-source-d3edee404071ac81) [R5](#ref-source-34df31af237b76a7) [R8](#ref-source-dd4e897d833ce69c)

## Related topics

Compare [p-wave spin and chirality](/scwiki/p-wave), [dxy directional evidence](/scwiki/dxy-pairing), [d-wave phase tests](/scwiki/d-wave), [ferromagnetic fluctuations](/scwiki/ferromagnetic-fluctuations), and [topological superconductivity](/scwiki/topological-superconductivity).

sections.markdown:
## Experimental criteria

The 2002 Joynt–Taillefer review weighs UPt3's phase diagram, nodal responses and magnetic coupling. Its abstract favors E1g or E2u on balance while acknowledging that neither explains all observations. That historical conclusion is not a current universal assignment. Machida and colleagues' later angle-dependent thermal-conductivity study instead interprets the B/C-phase data using E1u. The 2011 author abstract and 2012 journal abstract differ in the stated phase coverage; this entry uses the latter and does not claim a complete version comparison. [R2](#ref-source-a329f7df31c7d3e9) [R4](#ref-source-31577c7cb2ae0ac8)

Schemm and colleagues reported a UPt3 Kerr signal below about 0.46 K, separated from an upper susceptibility onset near 0.55 K. Their 1550 nm optical probe required an estimated local-heating allowance up to 50 mK; bulk heating inferred from mutual inductance was much smaller. Cooling in either sign of a 50 G field and then measuring with the field removed trained the signal's sign. These observations support additional time-reversal breaking in the lower-temperature phase within the experiment's controls; the optical signal alone does not select E2u. The Kerr onset is not the upper superconducting transition. [R3](#ref-source-d3edee404071ac81)

Node assignment requires field direction, heat-current direction, temperature and the response model. A minimum in an angle-dependent signal is not automatically a node: vortex scattering and thermal weighting can reverse anisotropy. Compare multiple axes and independent probes before deciding between equatorial, off-equatorial and vertical zeros. The relative success of one calculation under selected assumptions does not eliminate every competing representation. [R4](#ref-source-31577c7cb2ae0ac8) [R5](#ref-source-34df31af237b76a7) [R9](#ref-source-6c82ca23c0fda096)

For a null Kerr result, record illumination, surface, residual field, cooldown history and statistical sensitivity. Independent noise and domain signals add in variance, $\sigma_{\rm total}^2=\sigma_{\rm noise}^2+\sigma_{\rm signal}^2$. A small constructed example verifies this identity for uncorrelated sequences. The equation requires its independence assumption; a measured absence of increased scatter is a constraint at finite sensitivity, not proof that all possible microscopic time-reversal breaking is absent. [R8](#ref-source-dd4e897d833ce69c)

sections.title: Limits and disputes
sections.markdown:
## Limits and disputes

Hayes and colleagues reported UTe2 Kerr and calorimetric signatures supporting a multicomponent state. Their low-field warmups were compared with measurements following positive and negative training fields; the interpretation includes domains. Ajeesh and colleagues later found no spontaneous zero-field Kerr signal in four single-transition samples spanning two growth methods. Their heat-pulse procedure repeatedly crossed the transition, and trained signals varied with position and sample. The selected manuscript's optical and susceptibility sample sets are different: one must not attribute the separate double-transition susceptibility sample to the Kerr set. Retain this disagreement and its conditions rather than declaring all UTe2 samples chiral or all possible states excluded. [R7](#ref-source-5ff091aacae25bb0) [R8](#ref-source-dd4e897d833ce69c)

Orthorhombic D2h has one-dimensional ordinary point-group representations, unlike hexagonal E2u. A complex combination of distinct components can still break time reversal if the energetics permit it; multidimensional point-group representations are not a universal prerequisite. Spin degeneracy, orbital structure and accidental near-degeneracy must be specified. UTe2's discovery evidence for unusual spin pairing does not independently choose an f-wave basis or a unique multicomponent state. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R6](#ref-source-ca6322be2694e430) [R7](#ref-source-5ff091aacae25bb0)

The spherical polynomial examples neglect UPt3's real multiband, nonsymmorphic band structure. The Ginzburg–Landau example does not reproduce its field–temperature phase diagram, and no surface-state or bulk-topology calculation is supplied. A change of polynomial order, a broken-symmetry signal or a high critical field cannot replace that missing analysis. [R1](#ref-source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f) [R2](#ref-source-a329f7df31c7d3e9)

Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open; the model calculations here constrain language and logic, not the pairing state of a new material. ### scwiki-c6-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Schemm and colleagues reported a UPt3 Kerr signal below about 0.46 K, separated from an upper susceptibility onset near 0.55 K. Their 1550 nm optical probe required an estimated local-heating allowance up to 50 mK; bulk heating inferred from mutual inductance was much smaller. Cooling in either sign of a 50 G field and then measuring with the field removed trained the signal's sign. These observations support additional time-reversal breaking in the lower-temperature phase within the experiment's controls; the optical signal alone does not select E2u. The Kerr onset is not the upper superconducting transition.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-d3edee404071ac81.

Conditions: Declared point group and spin/orbital conventions; spherical harmonics,GL coefficients and variance examples are not material fits. Experimental sample/field/heating limits retained.

Verification scope: Named primary passages and independent examples only; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-c6-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Node assignment requires field direction, heat-current direction, temperature and the response model. A minimum in an angle-dependent signal is not automatically a node: vortex scattering and thermal weighting can reverse anisotropy. Compare multiple axes and independent probes before deciding between equatorial, off-equatorial and vertical zeros. The relative success of one calculation under selected assumptions does not eliminate every competing representation.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-31577c7cb2ae0ac8, source-34df31af237b76a7, source-6c82ca23c0fda096.

Conditions: Declared point group and spin/orbital conventions; spherical harmonics,GL coefficients and variance examples are not material fits. Experimental sample/field/heating limits retained.

Verification scope: Named primary passages and independent examples only; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-c6-claim-experimental-criteria-4

For a null Kerr result, record illumination, surface, residual field, cooldown history and statistical sensitivity. Independent noise and domain signals add in variance, $\sigma_{\rm total}^2=\sigma_{\rm noise}^2+\sigma_{\rm signal}^2$. A small constructed example verifies this identity for uncorrelated sequences. The equation requires its independence assumption; a measured absence of increased scatter is a constraint at finite sensitivity, not proof that all possible microscopic time-reversal breaking is absent.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-dd4e897d833ce69c.

Conditions: Declared point group and spin/orbital conventions; spherical harmonics,GL coefficients and variance examples are not material fits. Experimental sample/field/heating limits retained.

Verification scope: Named primary passages and independent examples only; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-c6-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

Hayes and colleagues reported UTe2 Kerr and calorimetric signatures supporting a multicomponent state. Their low-field warmups were compared with measurements following positive and negative training fields; the interpretation includes domains. Ajeesh and colleagues later found no spontaneous zero-field Kerr signal in four single-transition samples spanning two growth methods. Their heat-pulse procedure repeatedly crossed the transition, and trained signals varied with position and sample. The selected manuscript's optical and susceptibility sample sets are different: one must not attribute the separate double-transition susceptibility sample to the Kerr set. Retain this disagreement and its conditions rather than declaring all UTe2 samples chiral or all possible states excluded.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-5ff091aacae25bb0, source-dd4e897d833ce69c.

Conditions: Declared point group and spin/orbital conventions; spherical harmonics,GL coefficients and variance examples are not material fits. Experimental sample/field/heating limits retained.

Verification scope: Named primary passages and independent examples only; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-c6-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

Orthorhombic D2h has one-dimensional ordinary point-group representations, unlike hexagonal E2u. A complex combination of distinct components can still break time reversal if the energetics permit it; multidimensional point-group representations are not a universal prerequisite. Spin degeneracy, orbital structure and accidental near-degeneracy must be specified. UTe2's discovery evidence for unusual spin pairing does not independently choose an f-wave basis or a unique multicomponent state.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f, source-ca6322be2694e430, source-5ff091aacae25bb0.

Conditions: Declared point group and spin/orbital conventions; spherical harmonics,GL coefficients and variance examples are not material fits. Experimental sample/field/heating limits retained.

### scwiki-c6-claim-limits-and-disputes-3

The spherical polynomial examples neglect UPt3's real multiband, nonsymmorphic band structure. The Ginzburg–Landau example does not reproduce its field–temperature phase diagram, and no surface-state or bulk-topology calculation is supplied. A change of polynomial order, a broken-symmetry signal or a high critical field cannot replace that missing analysis.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f, source-a329f7df31c7d3e9.

Conditions: Declared point group and spin/orbital conventions; spherical harmonics,GL coefficients and variance examples are not material fits. Experimental sample/field/heating limits retained.

Specify the crystal symmetry and basis first. Then test whether one proposed state explains phase splitting, directional nodes, spin response and symmetry-breaking observations under compatible conditions. Preserve null results, competing interpretations and source-version differences alongside positive evidence. Full scientific acceptance, complete final-version comparisons and raw-data review remain open; the model calculations here constrain language and logic, not the pairing state of a new material.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-8d1b859d5ffcad9f, source-d3edee404071ac81, source-34df31af237b76a7, source-dd4e897d833ce69c.

articles.body:
## Scope

Chiral pairing describes a superconducting order with a handed orbital structure, such as a complex combination of two directional basis functions. Three questions must remain separate: whether time reversal is broken, whether the pairing is chiral, and whether a specified gapped Hamiltonian has a nonzero topological invariant. A Kerr signal, a complex coefficient or a named lattice does not answer all three. Kallin and Berlinsky's 2016 review is a historical guide; its candidate-material assignments are not current confirmations. [R2](#ref-source-69d33a869fbbb0c6)

Broken time reversal need not mean orbital chirality. For example, frustrated interband pair scattering can favor complex relative phases among otherwise s-wave gaps. Stanev and Tešanović studied this possibility in a three-band model. An illustrative vector of gaps on three inequivalent labelled bands, $(1,e^{2\pi i/3},e^{-2\pi i/3})$, cannot be made equal to its conjugate by one common phase, although each component has no angular winding. This statement assumes only a common U(1) freedom; it is not a stability calculation or a material assignment. [R8](#ref-source-3c7aa9b4c8da3abf)

## Mathematical assumptions

Read and Green distinguish weak- and strong-pairing phases of a two-dimensional spinless complex p-wave model. Their continuum chemical potential is measured relative to the band bottom: its zero marks a gap-closing transition in that model. The broken symmetry alone does not distinguish the two phases. This continuum criterion must not be copied unchanged into a lattice or multiband calculation. [R1](#ref-source-a33c639b7db4f05a)

For an independent lattice illustration, set hopping and pairing scales to one and use $H(\mathbf{k})=\mathbf{h}(\mathbf{k})\cdot\boldsymbol{\tau}$, with $\mathbf{h}=(\sin k_x,\chi\sin k_y,-2\cos k_x-2\cos k_y-\mu)$ and $\chi=\pm1$. In this Nambu convention the off-diagonal gap is $\sin k_x-i\chi\sin k_y$. Define the occupied-band Berry connection as $\mathbf{A}=i\langle u_-|\nabla_{\mathbf{k}}u_-\rangle$. With the orientation $(k_x,k_y)$, the lower-band Chern number for $\chi=1$ is $0,-1,+1,0$ in the intervals separated by $\mu=-4,0,4$. Reversing $\chi$ reverses its sign. [R1](#ref-source-a33c639b7db4f05a) [R2](#ref-source-69d33a869fbbb0c6)

Sixteen calculations compare two mesh sizes, four chemical potentials and both handedness choices. Berry-link phases from explicit occupied eigenvectors agree with independently summed spherical solid angles. Four analytic gap-closing checks identify the excluded critical points; no gapped-band invariant is assigned there. The same complex gap can thus accompany a zero or nonzero Chern number. The calculation fixes the gap by hand and omits self-consistency, realistic bands and disorder. [R1](#ref-source-a33c639b7db4f05a)

A boundary calculation illustrates a different distinction. In Huang, Taylor and Kallin's ideal sharp-edge continuum treatment, occupied bound states and continuum states both contribute to the integrated current. For axial harmonic index $m=1$, their respective values are $1/2$ and $-1/4$ in units $\hbar k_F^2/(4\pi m^*)$ per spin component. For integer $m>1$, each integrated contribution vanishes in this limit despite the chiral edge branches. Independent angular quadrature reproduces the analytic sums for six values of $m$. [R3](#ref-source-25d6a80b561d5ad2)

That cancellation is not a universal absence of current in higher-order chiral pairing. The same paper shows that making the density vary slowly over distances much longer than the coherence length restores a current; lattice effects also matter. A sharp specular boundary, a smooth trap and a disordered multiband surface are different problems. The calculation above does not predict a magnetic-field amplitude for a real sample. [R3](#ref-source-25d6a80b561d5ad2)

## Experimental criteria

Kerr rotation probes an optical response. In the clean Galilean-invariant limit, a spatially uniform electric field couples to center-of-mass motion and the charge Hall response vanishes even for complex pairing. At the single-particle level, the clean one-band current-vertex structure also gives a cancellation; multiband and impurity processes require separate treatment. Optical frequency, refractive response and geometry matter. Neither a null Kerr measurement nor one nonzero angle can be converted directly into a Chern number. [R1](#ref-source-a33c639b7db4f05a) [R2](#ref-source-69d33a869fbbb0c6)

For UPt3, retain Schemm and colleagues' distinction between the Kerr onset near 0.46 K and the upper susceptibility onset near 0.55 K, including optical heating and field-training controls. For Sr2RuO4, Pustogow and colleagues' oxygen NMR response constrains a simple fixed-d-vector interpretation. The later 2026 muon Knight-shift study also has field-dependent extraction and low-temperature magnetization limits. These are complementary constraints, not a license to restore a historically favored chiral p-wave label as settled fact. [R4](#ref-source-d3edee404071ac81) [R5](#ref-source-c7f8b99a795aba41) [R9](#ref-source-c4434644191d0174)

Mielke and colleagues studied KV3Sb5, not the whole AV3Sb5 family interchangeably. Their selected manuscript shows an increased muon relaxation below the charge-order scale near 80 K that remains approximately constant across the superconducting transition near 1.1 K. They explicitly discuss electric-field-gradient contributions and use high-field measurements to support an electronic interpretation. The methods report residual-field compensation better than 30 mG; a 50 G longitudinal field decouples the relaxation. These are charge-order constraints, not a new superconducting chirality onset at 80 K. [R6](#ref-source-484da7abcc165cd3)

Chen and colleagues studied CsV3Sb5 with tunneling and Josephson spectroscopy. Their selected manuscript distinguishes bulk signatures near 2.8 K from a surface transition near 2.3 K, and uses a calibrated 300 mK electron temperature. Spatial gap and conductance modulations motivate their roton-PDW interpretation. The authors explicitly state that roton excitations were not directly observed. A proposed complex vortex–antivortex pattern is therefore an interpretation to test, not a measured uniform chiral d-wave order parameter. [R7](#ref-source-057c43c86174f961)

## Limits and disputes

Local magnitude alone does not resolve handedness: $|\Delta|^2=|\Delta^*|^2$. Four complex spatial examples verify this identity without making a tunneling-response model. A Josephson signal can support superconducting coherence, while determining orbital phase structure requires suitable reference geometry and controls. Fourier peaks, gap-depth maps and zero-bias peaks must retain their individual evidential roles. [R7](#ref-source-057c43c86174f961)

Do not require every time-reversal-breaking state to belong to a two-dimensional crystal representation. Complex combinations of distinct representations or interband phases can behave differently. Likewise, half-quantum vortices can occur in equal-spin-pairing states without establishing orbital chirality. A strain response or vortex signature must be interpreted in the actual symmetry and spin-orbit setting. [R2](#ref-source-69d33a869fbbb0c6) [R8](#ref-source-3c7aa9b4c8da3abf)

The local topology check is a fully gapped two-dimensional model. Nodal three-dimensional superconductors may instead require momentum-resolved invariants; a single integer cannot simply be carried over. Edge spectra, thermal transport, optical response and screened equilibrium charge currents require distinct calculations. Complete scientific acceptance, final-version comparisons, raw-data review and material-specific modelling remain open. [R1](#ref-source-a33c639b7db4f05a) [R2](#ref-source-69d33a869fbbb0c6) [R3](#ref-source-25d6a80b561d5ad2)

## Discovery implications

First identify the transition and its probe. Then specify the order-parameter basis, domain controls, bulk gap and Hamiltonian used for any topology claim. Compare positive and null evidence under compatible conditions, retaining charge-order and superconducting temperature scales separately. A useful discovery target is a state that satisfies these linked tests, not a material selected merely for a complex gap notation or a kagome lattice. [R1](#ref-source-a33c639b7db4f05a) [R4](#ref-source-d3edee404071ac81) [R6](#ref-source-484da7abcc165cd3) [R7](#ref-source-057c43c86174f961)

## Related topics

Continue with [p-wave spin structure](/scwiki/p-wave), [f-wave candidate states](/scwiki/f-wave), [d-wave phase tests](/scwiki/d-wave), [topological superconductivity](/scwiki/topological-superconductivity), and [charge and density-wave pairing](/scwiki/charge-fluctuation-pairing).

Stanev and Tešanović studied this possibility in a three-band model.
