articles.body:
## Scope

Magnetic substitution can change carrier balance, crystal structure, potential scattering, spin-flip scattering and exchange fields at the same time. These effects are distinguishable experimental questions, not mutually exclusive channels. A falling superconducting transition temperature does not uniquely identify magnetic pair breaking, and the presence of a magnetic element does not establish magnetically mediated pairing. Compare actual composition, valence, phase purity and preparation before treating concentration as a single physical control. [R3](#ref-source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b) [R4](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83) [R5](#ref-source-9ff1d5edeb007a39) [R11](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

Dilute paramagnetic impurities, an ordered lattice of rare-earth moments and a concentrated magnetic film require different models. Independent magnetic ions can scatter Cooper pairs, while their ordering, screening and coupling to itinerant states change the relevant timescales and fields. A material that contains both magnetic and superconducting signals may also be spatially inhomogeneous; their coexistence must be tested at the relevant volume and length scale. [R1](#ref-source-daf8f301de81a726) [R2](#ref-source-3a528aeee1b7cf04) [R7](#ref-source-e4fdbfe063c34217) [R8](#ref-source-6666556b639390d7)

## Mathematical assumptions

For dilute, uncorrelated weak magnetic scattering in an isotropic singlet host, define a pair-breaking energy $\Gamma$ through $\ln(T_{c0}/T_c)=\psi[1/2+\Gamma/(2\pi k_BT_c)]-\psi(1/2)$. Here $T_{c0}$ is the corresponding clean-host transition, not necessarily the transition of the unsubstituted parent if substitution also changes its bands or interaction. With $g=\Gamma/(k_BT_{c0})$ and $t=T_c/T_{c0}$, this convention gives $dt/dg=-\pi/4$ initially and $g_c=\pi e^{-\gamma_E}/2\simeq0.882$. Scattering-rate conventions require explicit factors of $\hbar$; neither atomic fraction nor residual resistivity can be inserted directly as $\Gamma$. The equation convention has a scoped review-paper check, while the original AG full text remains unaudited. [R1](#ref-source-daf8f301de81a726) [R2](#ref-source-3a528aeee1b7cf04) [R4](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83)

An independent inversion illustrates the ambiguity. In units with $k_B=1$, prescribe an observed curve $T_c=1-0.6c$, where $c$ is a synthetic dimensionless control. ## Experimental criteria

Sugawara and Eguchi measured transition temperatures and critical fields magnetically in dilute La–Ce and La–Gd alloys. Their original abstract reports deviations from the AG Born-approximation result that depend on the exchange sign, interpreting them as evidence of Kondo effects. It also describes behavior characteristic of inhomogeneous type-II superconductors. This is a historical test of the theory's limits, not permission to assign one universal critical impurity fraction or transition-temperature slope to magnetic substitutions. [R5](#ref-source-9ff1d5edeb007a39)

Anderson's robustness argument for nonmagnetic disorder applies when appropriate time-reversed states, an essentially unchanged pairing interaction and density of states, and extended electronic states remain available. [R3](#ref-source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b) [R4](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83)

Yaron's small-angle neutron study provides a more direct coupling test. The measured vortex lines rotate away from the applied field as temperature falls, and their rocking curves broaden. These observations support microscopic coexistence through interaction between magnetic order and the vortex structure, rather than merely coincident bulk anomalies. [R8](#ref-source-6666556b639390d7)

The geometry matters: the applied field in that experiment was already tilted about 1.6 degrees from the c axis. The additional vortex rotation begins around 4 K and can approach one degree, whereas antiferromagnetic ordering occurs near 6 K. These temperatures should not be equated. Large upper critical fields or field-enhanced resistance drops alone are insufficient. [R9](#ref-source-849f7f4f675464de) [R10](#ref-source-d564bee026e788c7)

Yang's 2026 Sm/Ca/Eu infinite-layer nickelate study involves rare-earth substitution, fixed nominal Ca content and film reduction. [R11](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

## Limits and disputes

The same substitution series may move a clean-host pairing scale, alter scattering and create an exchange contribution. An AG-looking fit cannot separate these without additional constraints. Conversely, a departure from simple AG behavior does not automatically prove unconventional pairing or exchange compensation. Complete scientific acceptance remains open: original AG and several classic full texts, final-version comparisons, calibration details and raw-data reanalysis remain unfinished. The numerical exercises check restricted inference and units, not a complete magnetic-alloy theory. [R1](#ref-source-daf8f301de81a726) [R2](#ref-source-3a528aeee1b7cf04) [R5](#ref-source-9ff1d5edeb007a39) [R7](#ref-source-e4fdbfe063c34217) [R10](#ref-source-d564bee026e788c7) [R11](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

## Discovery implications

Track chemical composition and valence alongside diffraction, magnetic response, transport and thermodynamics. Preserve the distinction between dilute moments, ordered sublattices and possible glassy or inhomogeneous behavior. Keep onset, midpoint, measured-zero, ordering and measurement temperatures separate. For compensation, constrain the electronic exchange field and its uncertainty independently; for coexistence, seek a probe of coupling or spatial overlap. Use those measurements to distinguish explanations before extrapolating a concentration trend to a new material. ## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-d15-claim-scope-1

Magnetic substitution can change carrier balance, crystal structure, potential scattering, spin-flip scattering and exchange fields at the same time. These effects are distinguishable experimental questions, not mutually exclusive channels. A falling superconducting transition temperature does not uniquely identify magnetic pair breaking, and the presence of a magnetic element does not establish magnetically mediated pairing. Compare actual composition, valence, phase purity and preparation before treating concentration as a single physical control.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b, source-23c62b46f5681d83, source-9ff1d5edeb007a39, source-3504ee9027165d0a.

### scwiki-d15-claim-scope-2

Dilute paramagnetic impurities, an ordered lattice of rare-earth moments and a concentrated magnetic film require different models. Independent magnetic ions can scatter Cooper pairs, while their ordering, screening and coupling to itinerant states change the relevant timescales and fields. A material that contains both magnetic and superconducting signals may also be spatially inhomogeneous; their coexistence must be tested at the relevant volume and length scale.

### scwiki-d15-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

For dilute, uncorrelated weak magnetic scattering in an isotropic singlet host, define a pair-breaking energy $\Gamma$ through $\ln(T_{c0}/T_c)=\psi[1/2+\Gamma/(2\pi k_BT_c)]-\psi(1/2)$. Here $T_{c0}$ is the corresponding clean-host transition, not necessarily the transition of the unsubstituted parent if substitution also changes its bands or interaction. With $g=\Gamma/(k_BT_{c0})$ and $t=T_c/T_{c0}$, this convention gives $dt/dg=-\pi/4$ initially and $g_c=\pi e^{-\gamma_E}/2\simeq0.882$. Scattering-rate conventions require explicit factors of $\hbar$; neither atomic fraction nor residual resistivity can be inserted directly as $\Gamma$. The equation convention has a scoped review-paper check, while the original AG full text remains unaudited.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-daf8f301de81a726, source-3a528aeee1b7cf04, source-23c62b46f5681d83.

Conditions: Preserve composition, valence, sample, field direction, probe and temperature type; scattering energy is not nominal concentration.

Verification scope: Named primary passages/figures and restricted inference checks; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-d15-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

An independent inversion illustrates the ambiguity. In units with $k_B=1$, prescribe an observed curve $T_c=1-0.6c$, where $c$ is a synthetic dimensionless control. Both a fixed clean-host scale $T_{c0}=1$ and a changing scale $T_{c0}=1-0.2c$ admit different positive $\Gamma(c)$ values that reproduce the same transitions. Five checked points demonstrate non-uniqueness; they are not alloy fits or concentration calibrations. Additional composition, band, magnetic and scattering measurements are needed to choose between such explanations.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-3a528aeee1b7cf04, source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b, source-23c62b46f5681d83.

### scwiki-d15-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

For a free Eu2+ ion with $S=7/2$ and $g=2$, the saturated moment is $gS\mu_B=7\mu_B$, whereas the Curie effective moment is $g\sqrt{S(S+1)}\mu_B\simeq7.94\mu_B$. Neither specifies the sign or strength of the exchange field acting on conduction electrons. In a collinear compensation illustration, $B_{\mathrm{eff}}=B_{\mathrm{ext}}+B_{\mathrm{ex}}$ and opposite signed contributions can reduce Zeeman splitting. This does not eliminate the orbital action of the applied field. Local-moment size, exchange energy and magnetic induction have different units and roles.

### scwiki-d15-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Sugawara and Eguchi measured transition temperatures and critical fields magnetically in dilute La–Ce and La–Gd alloys. Their original abstract reports deviations from the AG Born-approximation result that depend on the exchange sign, interpreting them as evidence of Kondo effects. It also describes behavior characteristic of inhomogeneous type-II superconductors. This is a historical test of the theory's limits, not permission to assign one universal critical impurity fraction or transition-temperature slope to magnetic substitutions.

### scwiki-d15-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Anderson's robustness argument for nonmagnetic disorder applies when appropriate time-reversed states, an essentially unchanged pairing interaction and density of states, and extended electronic states remain available. It is not immunity to arbitrary chemical substitution. Prozorov's controlled electron-irradiation study of a ruthenium-substituted iron arsenide illustrates why intra- and interband scattering, annealing and sample continuity matter. Nonmagnetic disorder can suppress sign-changing pairing, so comparing magnetic and nonmagnetic substitutions alone does not supply an independent singlet verdict.

### scwiki-d15-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Cava established superconductivity in the LnNi2B2C family, including magnetic rare-earth members. Cho's cited paper then studied single-crystal ErNi2B2C specifically: transport and magnetization show a superconducting transition around 10.5 K, while the magnetic transition lies near 6 K. Its heat-capacity estimate is $5.85\pm0.15$ K. These are distinct probe-specific scales. The paper is not a systematic survey of all rare-earth ions, and changing the rare earth also changes crystal fields, structure and exchange. No universal free-ion-moment ranking follows.

### scwiki-d15-claim-experimental-criteria-4

Yaron's small-angle neutron study provides a more direct coupling test. On a boron-11-enriched ErNi2B2C crystal, superconducting vortex diffraction and magnetic diffraction establish their relative orientations. Figure 1's vortex pattern is measured at 1.6 K and 4 kOe with field near the c axis; the magnetic comparison uses zero field and a different neutron wavelength. The measured vortex lines rotate away from the applied field as temperature falls, and their rocking curves broaden. These observations support microscopic coexistence through interaction between magnetic order and the vortex structure, rather than merely coincident bulk anomalies.

### scwiki-d15-claim-experimental-criteria-5

The geometry matters: the applied field in that experiment was already tilted about 1.6 degrees from the c axis. The additional vortex rotation begins around 4 K and can approach one degree, whereas antiferromagnetic ordering occurs near 6 K. These temperatures should not be equated. The authors also consider long-distance orientation variation as an alternative contribution to rocking-curve broadening; width alone is not a unique measure of microscopic pinning or a demonstration of triplet pairing.

Meul's Eu–Sn molybdenum chalcogenide work reports magnetic-field-induced superconductivity interpreted through exchange compensation. The checked original abstract supports that historical connection, but does not establish every numerical endpoint or the precise alloy composition used in earlier summaries. A compensation claim in another material needs its own signed exchange estimate, local-moment response, angle dependence and orbital constraints. Large upper critical fields or field-enhanced resistance drops alone are insufficient.

### scwiki-d15-claim-experimental-criteria-7

Yang's 2026 Sm/Ca/Eu infinite-layer nickelate study involves rare-earth substitution, fixed nominal Ca content and film reduction. In the checked later author version, SCE0.34 regains zero resistance at 2 K beyond 6.23 T; SCE0.32 does so at 3 K by 13.04 T. SCE0.36 remains superconducting to the 45 T measurement limit at 0.3 K. These are different samples and measurement temperatures, not a single transition curve. Compensation-like and magnetic-fluctuation explanations remain under discussion; neither established uniform ferromagnetism nor triplet pairing follows from the reported reentrance alone.

### scwiki-d15-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

The same substitution series may move a clean-host pairing scale, alter scattering and create an exchange contribution. An AG-looking fit cannot separate these without additional constraints. Conversely, a departure from simple AG behavior does not automatically prove unconventional pairing or exchange compensation. Complete scientific acceptance remains open: original AG and several classic full texts, final-version comparisons, calibration details and raw-data reanalysis remain unfinished. The numerical exercises check restricted inference and units, not a complete magnetic-alloy theory.

### scwiki-d15-claim-discovery-implications-1

Track chemical composition and valence alongside diffraction, magnetic response, transport and thermodynamics. Preserve the distinction between dilute moments, ordered sublattices and possible glassy or inhomogeneous behavior. Keep onset, midpoint, measured-zero, ordering and measurement temperatures separate. For compensation, constrain the electronic exchange field and its uncertainty independently; for coexistence, seek a probe of coupling or spatial overlap. Use those measurements to distinguish explanations before extrapolating a concentration trend to a new material.

claims.statement: For current perpendicular to field, the pinning-force magnitude is $F_p=J_cB$. A common fixed-temperature field shape is $f(h)=h^{1/2}(1-h)^2$, with $h=B/B_{c2}$. It peaks at $h=0.2$ and produces a linear Kramer plot of $J_c^{1/2}B^{1/4}$ only under the model's assumptions. A triangular vortex lattice has $a_\Delta=(4/3)^{1/4}\sqrt{\Phi_0/B}$; the flux-shear expression includes $(1-a_\Delta/d)^{-2}$ for mean grain size $d$. At 12 T and $d=100$ nm, this factor is about 1.36, so neglecting it requires a stated tolerance. Neither the pinning peak nor a fitted Kramer intercept independently identifies the thermodynamic upper critical field.

articles.body:
## Scope

A15 is a crystal-structure family, usually written $A_3B$, with cubic space group $Pm\bar{3}n$ before any distortion. Three orthogonal chains of A atoms help organize its electronic structure. They do not guarantee a high transition temperature: composition, site ordering, phonons and strain all matter. The brittle Nb–Sn A15 phase illustrates why a favorable electronic structure must also survive fabrication and mechanical loading. [R5](#ref-source-29d0a9915f8b6c0e)

Nb3Sn, V3Si and Nb3Ge are distinct examples, not one table of universal constants. Matthias and colleagues reported Nb3Sn near 18 K in 1954. Gavaler's 1973 abstract reports sputtered Nb–Ge films remaining superconducting up to 22.3 K. That historical film result is neither an equilibrium bulk value nor a strict A15 temperature ceiling. “High pressure” in the deposition description refers to sputtering conditions, not a high-pressure superconductivity measurement. [R1](#ref-source-830f887afcf548c4) [R2](#ref-source-82a0df3d764cd0bc)

Near-stoichiometric Nb3Sn is a conventional strong-coupling benchmark, but even its coupling classification depends on composition and how the gap and transition are sampled. Godeke's review discusses interface-gap and inhomogeneity effects that can bias a gap-to-temperature ratio. A full gap is not proof that all samples have the same coupling, and a large upper critical field alone is not evidence for triplet pairing. [R5](#ref-source-29d0a9915f8b6c0e) [R9](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66)

## Mathematical assumptions

For an orbital dirty-limit description, write $B_{c2}=\mu_0H_{c2}$ and $\ln(T/T_c)=\psi(1/2)-\psi[1/2+\hbar D B_{c2}(T)/(2\Phi_0k_BT)]$, where $D$ is an effective diffusion parameter and $\psi$ the digamma function. The Maki–de Gennes form omits Pauli, spin–orbit, strong-coupling and Fermi-surface anisotropy corrections. A useful fit to an inhomogeneous wire does not measure a unique microscopic $D$. Independent numerical roots recover the model ratio $B_{c2}(0)/(T_c|dB_{c2}/dT|_{T_c})=\pi^2e^{-\gamma}/8\simeq0.693$; this is not a universal material relation. [R7](#ref-source-d27a049f764be753)

For current perpendicular to field, the pinning-force magnitude is $F_p=J_cB$. A common fixed-temperature field shape is $f(h)=h^{1/2}(1-h)^2$, with $h=B/B_{c2}$. It peaks at $h=0.2$ and produces a linear Kramer plot of $J_c^{1/2}B^{1/4}$ only under the model's assumptions. A triangular vortex lattice has $a_\Delta=(4/3)^{1/4}\sqrt{\Phi_0/B}$; the flux-shear expression includes $(1-a_\Delta/d)^{-2}$ for mean grain size $d$. At 12 T and $d=100$ nm, this factor is about 1.36, so neglecting it requires a stated tolerance. Neither the pinning peak nor a fitted Kramer intercept independently identifies the thermodynamic upper critical field. [R6](#ref-source-c4b57e9e8e5aa3d7)

A two-component illustrative sum of currents, with imposed critical fields of 20 and 28 T, gives Kramer intercepts of 25.06 and 26.35 T over different finite field windows. This is a numerical counterexample to treating every extrapolated intercept as the largest component field; it is not a fitted wire network. Separately, Godeke's hypothetical uniform-wire comparison holds the prefactor fixed in $J_c=C B_{c2}^{2}h^{1/2}(1-h)^2/B$. Its printed 24.9-to-26.9 T inputs give 2888.01 A/mm² from 2250 A/mm² at 12 T and 4.2 K, versus the paper's 2883 A/mm². The latter lies within input-field rounding bounds. Neither improved value was measured. [R6](#ref-source-c4b57e9e8e5aa3d7) [R7](#ref-source-d27a049f764be753)

## Experimental criteria

Godeke and colleagues measured small-current resistive transitions of filamentary Nb3Sn, using approximately 0.2–0.6 A/mm² and fields up to 30 T. Their 10%, 50% and 90% normal-resistance criteria probe different parts of a broadened transition. At high field, the 99% criterion was extrapolated from the less noisy 10–90% region under a width assumption. The study also retained an unresolved interlaboratory offset of about 4%, treated as approximately ±2% uncertainty. Its highest-quality fractions are not every part of the conductor. [R7](#ref-source-d27a049f764be753)

The B34 wire reacted for 64 hours at 675 °C provides a concrete comparison: transport at a 10 µV/m criterion gave non-Cu $J_c=2250$ A/mm² at 12 T and 4.2 K. The Kramer field was 24.9 T, while the 99% resistive field was 26.9 T at the same temperature. Keep the non-Cu area normalization, voltage criterion and heat treatment attached to those numbers. They are not interchangeable measures of performance. [R7](#ref-source-d27a049f764be753)

Gapud and colleagues studied a floating-zone V3Si single crystal, MP3, with residual-resistivity ratio 47. Their 51V NMR experiment used 6.67 T, where the reported superconducting transition was 12.8 K and the structural transition 21.1 K. Cubic and tetragonal spectra coexisted around the structural transition. The authors found no conclusive cubic-phase spectrum below the zero-field transition scale of 17 K; that is distinct from the 12.8 K transition in the actual NMR field. These observations do not establish that a martensitic transition is necessary for every A15 superconductor. [R8](#ref-source-9fe69d0a6cecbb0c)

## Limits and disputes

Elastic softening, anharmonicity and superconductivity can be correlated without a universal rule that moving closer to structural instability always improves $T_c$. Testardi's papers motivate this coupled problem; they do not remove the need for sample-specific structural and thermodynamic evidence. Changes in composition or disorder can alter several electronic and phonon parameters together. Increasing a density-of-states peak or an estimated coupling constant alone is not a validated optimization strategy. [R3](#ref-source-33f4444a5825b443) [R4](#ref-source-509b869080567558) [R9](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66)

The V3Si NMR assignments depend on orientation, spectral resolution and a model of local electric-field gradients. Absence of a resolved line is not a proof of literally zero phase fraction, and zero-field and finite-field transition temperatures must not be conflated. Similarly, a Nb3Sn resistive onset, a pinning-derived extrapolation and a magnetic transition need their own criteria and uncertainty. Record strain state and mounting as well as nominal composition. [R7](#ref-source-d27a049f764be753) [R8](#ref-source-9fe69d0a6cecbb0c)

A May 2026 doctoral-dissertation preprint explores Cu–Sn routes to Nb3Sn films for microwave dark-matter cavities. Its abstract describes a chosen cavity tested at 50 mK and 9 T, but reports a quality-factor decline in field. Neither the operating temperature nor the maximum applied field is a measured transition temperature or a demonstrated upper critical field. This is an abstract-level research pointer, not a peer-reviewed performance certification. [R10](#ref-source-3633507cd1108d10)

## Discovery implications

Optimize a complete, conditional objective: transition temperature, useful field range, current density, mechanical tolerance and manufacturability. Preserve measured and predicted quantities separately. Compare transition criteria, composition gradients, annealing, strain, grain structure and area normalization before ranking conductors. For a proposed material, check phase stability and the coupling-weighted phonon spectrum; for a working wire or cavity, test the actual operating condition and retain negative results. [R5](#ref-source-29d0a9915f8b6c0e) [R6](#ref-source-c4b57e9e8e5aa3d7) [R9](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66) [R10](#ref-source-3633507cd1108d10)

## Related topics

Continue with [elemental superconductors](/scwiki/elemental-superconductors), [Eliashberg theory](/scwiki/eliashberg-strong-coupling), [s-wave pairing](/scwiki/s-wave), [critical fields](/scwiki/critical-fields) and [critical current](/scwiki/critical-current).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-d2-claim-scope-1

A15 is a crystal-structure family, usually written $A_3B$, with cubic space group $Pm\bar{3}n$ before any distortion. Three orthogonal chains of A atoms help organize its electronic structure. They do not guarantee a high transition temperature: composition, site ordering, phonons and strain all matter. The brittle Nb–Sn A15 phase illustrates why a favorable electronic structure must also survive fabrication and mechanical loading.

### scwiki-d2-claim-scope-2

Nb3Sn, V3Si and Nb3Ge are distinct examples, not one table of universal constants. Matthias and colleagues reported Nb3Sn near 18 K in 1954. Gavaler's 1973 abstract reports sputtered Nb–Ge films remaining superconducting up to 22.3 K. That historical film result is neither an equilibrium bulk value nor a strict A15 temperature ceiling. “High pressure” in the deposition description refers to sputtering conditions, not a high-pressure superconductivity measurement.

### scwiki-d2-claim-scope-3

Near-stoichiometric Nb3Sn is a conventional strong-coupling benchmark, but even its coupling classification depends on composition and how the gap and transition are sampled. Godeke's review discusses interface-gap and inhomogeneity effects that can bias a gap-to-temperature ratio. A full gap is not proof that all samples have the same coupling, and a large upper critical field alone is not evidence for triplet pairing.

### scwiki-d2-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

For an orbital dirty-limit description, write $B_{c2}=\mu_0H_{c2}$ and $\ln(T/T_c)=\psi(1/2)-\psi[1/2+\hbar D B_{c2}(T)/(2\Phi_0k_BT)]$, where $D$ is an effective diffusion parameter and $\psi$ the digamma function. The Maki–de Gennes form omits Pauli, spin–orbit, strong-coupling and Fermi-surface anisotropy corrections. A useful fit to an inhomogeneous wire does not measure a unique microscopic $D$. Independent numerical roots recover the model ratio $B_{c2}(0)/(T_c|dB_{c2}/dT|_{T_c})=\pi^2e^{-\gamma}/8\simeq0.693$; this is not a universal material relation.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-d27a049f764be753.

### scwiki-d2-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

For current perpendicular to field, the pinning-force magnitude is $F_p=J_cB$. A common fixed-temperature field shape is $f(h)=h^{1/2}(1-h)^2$, with $h=B/B_{c2}$. It peaks at $h=0.2$ and produces a linear Kramer plot of $J_c^{1/2}B^{1/4}$ only under the model's assumptions. A triangular vortex lattice has $a_\Delta=(4/3)^{1/4}\sqrt{\Phi_0/B}$; the flux-shear expression includes $(1-a_\Delta/d)^{-2}$ for mean grain size $d$. At 12 T and $d=100$ nm, this factor is about 1.36, so neglecting it requires a stated tolerance. Neither the pinning peak nor a fitted Kramer intercept independently identifies the thermodynamic upper critical field.

### scwiki-d2-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

A two-component illustrative sum of currents, with imposed critical fields of 20 and 28 T, gives Kramer intercepts of 25.06 and 26.35 T over different finite field windows. This is a numerical counterexample to treating every extrapolated intercept as the largest component field; it is not a fitted wire network. Separately, Godeke's hypothetical uniform-wire comparison holds the prefactor fixed in $J_c=C B_{c2}^{2}h^{1/2}(1-h)^2/B$. Its printed 24.9-to-26.9 T inputs give 2888.01 A/mm² from 2250 A/mm² at 12 T and 4.2 K, versus the paper's 2883 A/mm². The latter lies within input-field rounding bounds. Neither improved value was measured.

### scwiki-d2-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Godeke and colleagues measured small-current resistive transitions of filamentary Nb3Sn, using approximately 0.2–0.6 A/mm² and fields up to 30 T. Their 10%, 50% and 90% normal-resistance criteria probe different parts of a broadened transition. At high field, the 99% criterion was extrapolated from the less noisy 10–90% region under a width assumption. The study also retained an unresolved interlaboratory offset of about 4%, treated as approximately ±2% uncertainty. Its highest-quality fractions are not every part of the conductor.

### scwiki-d2-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Gapud and colleagues studied a floating-zone V3Si single crystal, MP3, with residual-resistivity ratio 47. Their 51V NMR experiment used 6.67 T, where the reported superconducting transition was 12.8 K and the structural transition 21.1 K. Cubic and tetragonal spectra coexisted around the structural transition. The authors found no conclusive cubic-phase spectrum below the zero-field transition scale of 17 K; that is distinct from the 12.8 K transition in the actual NMR field. These observations do not establish that a martensitic transition is necessary for every A15 superconductor.

### scwiki-d2-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

Elastic softening, anharmonicity and superconductivity can be correlated without a universal rule that moving closer to structural instability always improves $T_c$. Testardi's papers motivate this coupled problem; they do not remove the need for sample-specific structural and thermodynamic evidence. Changes in composition or disorder can alter several electronic and phonon parameters together. Increasing a density-of-states peak or an estimated coupling constant alone is not a validated optimization strategy.

### scwiki-d2-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

The V3Si NMR assignments depend on orientation, spectral resolution and a model of local electric-field gradients. Absence of a resolved line is not a proof of literally zero phase fraction, and zero-field and finite-field transition temperatures must not be conflated. Similarly, a Nb3Sn resistive onset, a pinning-derived extrapolation and a magnetic transition need their own criteria and uncertainty. Record strain state and mounting as well as nominal composition.

claims.statement: Cuprates contain electronically important CuO2 planes, but layer count, oxygen coordination, charge reservoirs, disorder and doping differ across families. Many parent compounds are correlated antiferromagnetic insulators. Superconductivity, pseudogap behavior and competing orders do not define one universal phase diagram or establish a unique pairing interaction. A schematic dome organizes observations; its coordinates require a material-specific calibration.

claims.statement: Oxygen content is not automatically the hole density in a CuO2 plane. As an explicitly formal ionic exercise for YBa2Cu3O7−δ, assign Y charge +3, Ba +2, O −2, two plane Cu sites charge $2+p$, and one chain site charge $v_c$. Neutrality gives $2(2+p)+v_c=7-2\delta$, or $p=(3-2\delta-v_c)/2$. Ten checked allocations show that the same oxygen count admits different plane/chain charge partitions. This exercise illustrates missing information; it does not measure actual orbital occupation or include ligand-hole covalency.

articles.body:
## Scope

Cuprates contain electronically important CuO2 planes, but layer count, oxygen coordination, charge reservoirs, disorder and doping differ across families. Many parent compounds are correlated antiferromagnetic insulators. Superconductivity, pseudogap behavior and competing orders do not define one universal phase diagram or establish a unique pairing interaction. A schematic dome organizes observations; its coordinates require a material-specific calibration. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

The discovery sequence also needs that specificity. Bednorz and Müller's 1986 original abstract describes three-phase Ba–La–Cu–O polycrystals with a current-dependent resistivity decrease in the 30 K range, interpreted as possible percolative superconductivity. It is not a complete bulk magnetic characterization of a modern, homogeneous composition. [R1](#ref-source-ad4ee05105f93caf)

Wu and colleagues' 1987 discovery studied mixed-phase material with nominal composition Y1.2Ba0.8CuO4−y. It established a reproducible transition above liquid-nitrogen temperature using transport and magnetic measurements, while detailed phase identification remained open. The later Grant study of the principal YBa2Cu3Ox superconducting phase is a separate publication. Do not replace the original sample composition with a retrospectively assigned pure Y123 crystal. [R2](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e) [R9](#ref-source-82098193516b8d9a)

## Mathematical assumptions

Oxygen content is not automatically the hole density in a CuO2 plane. As an explicitly formal ionic exercise for YBa2Cu3O7−δ, assign Y charge +3, Ba +2, O −2, two plane Cu sites charge $2+p$, and one chain site charge $v_c$. Neutrality gives $2(2+p)+v_c=7-2\delta$, or $p=(3-2\delta-v_c)/2$. Ten checked allocations show that the same oxygen count admits different plane/chain charge partitions. This exercise illustrates missing information; it does not measure actual orbital occupation or include ligand-hole covalency. [R8](#ref-source-e24ef58054ac9b71)

Liang, Bonn and Hardy's author manuscript explicitly distinguishes chain oxygen ordering from total oxygen content. Its empirical dome, $T_c/T_{c,\max}=1-82.6(p-0.16)^2$, has two inverse branches away from its peak. Five independent algebra controls confirm that a single transition temperature cannot choose underdoping versus overdoping. The authors also discuss deviations near one-eighth doping, so treating this relation as a universal carrier-density measurement is unjustified. [R8](#ref-source-e24ef58054ac9b71)

The familiar square-lattice expression $\Delta(\mathbf{k})\propto\cos k_x-\cos k_y$ illustrates a d-wave sign structure. Its symmetry does not supply a gap magnitude, a material's exact Fermi surface or a pairing mediator. Orthorhombicity, disorder and the measurement geometry must remain part of a material-specific interpretation. See the dedicated [d-wave pairing](/scwiki/d-wave) and [gap-node](/scwiki/superconducting-node-structure) pages for the model boundaries. [R5](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7) [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed)

## Experimental criteria

Wu's selected final text distinguishes a resistive deviation at 93 K, a sharp drop beginning at 92 K, zero resistance at 80 K and a diamagnetic onset at 91 K. The diamagnetic signal at 4.2 K was compared with a similarly sized lead sample; that relative signal is not an independently corrected superconducting volume fraction. Its 80–180 T upper-critical-field estimate is an extrapolation, whereas the reported field measurements reached 5.7 T. Preserve these criteria and scales separately. [R2](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e)

A later doping-calibration experiment used a different operational criterion: Liang and colleagues chose the midpoint of the field-cooled magnetic transition with 1 Oe along the c axis. Their lattice parameter was measured by room-temperature diffraction. Temperature, field direction, oxygen ordering and the selected calibration therefore belong with the inferred doping, rather than being discarded after assigning a number to a phase diagram. Only the named author-version passages and figure have been checked here. [R8](#ref-source-e24ef58054ac9b71)

Phase-sensitive and magnitude-sensitive probes answer different questions. Tsuei and colleagues' original abstract reports scanning-SQUID measurements of tricrystal rings at 4.2 K, providing a phase-sensitive constraint. Hardy and colleagues' penetration-depth abstract describes a low-temperature linear term in YBa2Cu3O6.95, constraining low-energy excitations. Neither abstract alone verifies all junction assumptions, sample comparisons or raw traces; combine complementary evidence without turning a nodal observation into an unconditional mechanism verdict. [R5](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7) [R10](#ref-source-b7bc48c845a47b53)

## Pressure and recovered samples

Schilling's historical Hg-based report concerns superconductivity above 130 K at ambient pressure. Gao's original abstract reports resistive measurements under quasihydrostatic pressure up to 45 GPa and a maximum of 164 K for the three-layer member. The often-quoted 31 GPa point and its onset-versus-zero criterion have not been re-extracted from the full original in this review. The comparison record therefore leaves the exact pressure unknown; a study's maximum applied pressure is not the pressure of every reported transition. [R3](#ref-source-d95477ebe515f481) [R4](#ref-source-6d09a24a26a15997)

The 2026 pressure-quench report now has a selected primary-text and author-figure check inherited from the [pressure-quench](/scwiki/pressure-quenching) page. Sample S4, released from 18.9 GPa at 4.2 K, showed an ambient-pressure resistive onset of 151 K on warming and 150 K on cooling. This is a reported onset in a recovered metastable sample, not a zero-resistance criterion or an equilibrium ambient-pressure phase. [R7](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

The magnetic onset near 140 K came from retrieved sample S2, not the S4 transport sample. The estimated shielding at 70 K, the separate cold-storage protocol, and an unreproduced broad 172 K anomaly are distinct observations. The latter has no accepted transition-temperature value in this catalogue. Complete final supplementary comparison, raw-data reanalysis and independent replication remain open. [R7](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

## Limits and disputes

A charge-density modulation does not alone establish a pair-density wave; a linear resistivity does not alone determine a scattering time. Pseudogap, magnetic and charge correlations constrain theories without selecting one unique glue. Oxygen rearrangement and pressure history can alter more than carrier concentration, so a changed transition temperature does not by itself identify the causal variable. Complete scientific acceptance remains open for this article and the associated materials. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed) [R7](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb) [R8](#ref-source-e24ef58054ac9b71)

## Discovery implications

Compare matched compositions, preparation histories and criteria. Record what each probe measures, what a model infers and what alternative explanation survives. A mechanism proposal should connect an interaction to a symmetry prediction and a falsifiable material trend. For recovered samples, add decompression temperature, storage and subsequent measurement history before comparing them with equilibrium materials. The site preserves those conditions in searchable records and section exports. [R6](#ref-source-6c1991333d4a6fed) [R7](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

## Related topics

Continue with [magnetic evidence](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [hydrostatic pressure](/scwiki/pressure-tuning), [phase-sensitive tests](/scwiki/vortex-topological-charge), [spin-liquid and RVB proposals](/scwiki/spin-liquids-and-superconductivity), and [Planckian transport](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-d3-claim-scope-1

Cuprates contain electronically important CuO2 planes, but layer count, oxygen coordination, charge reservoirs, disorder and doping differ across families. Many parent compounds are correlated antiferromagnetic insulators. Superconductivity, pseudogap behavior and competing orders do not define one universal phase diagram or establish a unique pairing interaction. A schematic dome organizes observations; its coordinates require a material-specific calibration.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-6c1991333d4a6fed.

Conditions: Composition, oxygen order, plane/chain allocation, probe criterion, pressure and recovered-sample history remain distinct.

Verification scope: Named selected final/author passages or original abstracts, and bounded independent algebra; complete scientific acceptance open.

### scwiki-d3-claim-scope-2

The discovery sequence also needs that specificity. Bednorz and Müller's 1986 original abstract describes three-phase Ba–La–Cu–O polycrystals with a current-dependent resistivity decrease in the 30 K range, interpreted as possible percolative superconductivity. It is not a complete bulk magnetic characterization of a modern, homogeneous composition.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-ad4ee05105f93caf.

Conditions: Composition, oxygen order, plane/chain allocation, probe criterion, pressure and recovered-sample history remain distinct.

### scwiki-d3-claim-scope-3

Wu and colleagues' 1987 discovery studied mixed-phase material with nominal composition Y1.2Ba0.8CuO4−y. It established a reproducible transition above liquid-nitrogen temperature using transport and magnetic measurements, while detailed phase identification remained open. The later Grant study of the principal YBa2Cu3Ox superconducting phase is a separate publication. Do not replace the original sample composition with a retrospectively assigned pure Y123 crystal.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-9350a30b2eabe27e, source-82098193516b8d9a.

Conditions: Composition, oxygen order, plane/chain allocation, probe criterion, pressure and recovered-sample history remain distinct.

Verification scope: Named selected final/author passages or original abstracts, and bounded independent algebra; complete scientific acceptance open.

### scwiki-d3-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

Oxygen content is not automatically the hole density in a CuO2 plane. As an explicitly formal ionic exercise for YBa2Cu3O7−δ, assign Y charge +3, Ba +2, O −2, two plane Cu sites charge $2+p$, and one chain site charge $v_c$. Neutrality gives $2(2+p)+v_c=7-2\delta$, or $p=(3-2\delta-v_c)/2$. Ten checked allocations show that the same oxygen count admits different plane/chain charge partitions. This exercise illustrates missing information; it does not measure actual orbital occupation or include ligand-hole covalency.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-e24ef58054ac9b71.

Conditions: Composition, oxygen order, plane/chain allocation, probe criterion, pressure and recovered-sample history remain distinct.

Verification scope: Named selected final/author passages or original abstracts, and bounded independent algebra; complete scientific acceptance open.

### scwiki-d3-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

Liang, Bonn and Hardy's author manuscript explicitly distinguishes chain oxygen ordering from total oxygen content. Its empirical dome, $T_c/T_{c,\max}=1-82.6(p-0.16)^2$, has two inverse branches away from its peak. Five independent algebra controls confirm that a single transition temperature cannot choose underdoping versus overdoping. The authors also discuss deviations near one-eighth doping, so treating this relation as a universal carrier-density measurement is unjustified.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-e24ef58054ac9b71.

Conditions: Composition, oxygen order, plane/chain allocation, probe criterion, pressure and recovered-sample history remain distinct.

Verification scope: Named selected final/author passages or original abstracts, and bounded independent algebra; complete scientific acceptance open.

### scwiki-d3-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

The familiar square-lattice expression $\Delta(\mathbf{k})\propto\cos k_x-\cos k_y$ illustrates a d-wave sign structure. Its symmetry does not supply a gap magnitude, a material's exact Fermi surface or a pairing mediator. Orthorhombicity, disorder and the measurement geometry must remain part of a material-specific interpretation. See the dedicated [d-wave pairing](/scwiki/d-wave) and [gap-node](/scwiki/superconducting-node-structure) pages for the model boundaries.

### scwiki-d3-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Wu's selected final text distinguishes a resistive deviation at 93 K, a sharp drop beginning at 92 K, zero resistance at 80 K and a diamagnetic onset at 91 K. The diamagnetic signal at 4.2 K was compared with a similarly sized lead sample; that relative signal is not an independently corrected superconducting volume fraction. Its 80–180 T upper-critical-field estimate is an extrapolation, whereas the reported field measurements reached 5.7 T. Preserve these criteria and scales separately.

### scwiki-d3-claim-experimental-criteria-2

A later doping-calibration experiment used a different operational criterion: Liang and colleagues chose the midpoint of the field-cooled magnetic transition with 1 Oe along the c axis. Their lattice parameter was measured by room-temperature diffraction. Temperature, field direction, oxygen ordering and the selected calibration therefore belong with the inferred doping, rather than being discarded after assigning a number to a phase diagram. Only the named author-version passages and figure have been checked here.

### scwiki-d3-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Phase-sensitive and magnitude-sensitive probes answer different questions. Tsuei and colleagues' original abstract reports scanning-SQUID measurements of tricrystal rings at 4.2 K, providing a phase-sensitive constraint. Hardy and colleagues' penetration-depth abstract describes a low-temperature linear term in YBa2Cu3O6.95, constraining low-energy excitations. Neither abstract alone verifies all junction assumptions, sample comparisons or raw traces; combine complementary evidence without turning a nodal observation into an unconditional mechanism verdict.

### scwiki-d3-claim-pressure-and-recovered-samples-1

Schilling's historical Hg-based report concerns superconductivity above 130 K at ambient pressure. Gao's original abstract reports resistive measurements under quasihydrostatic pressure up to 45 GPa and a maximum of 164 K for the three-layer member. The often-quoted 31 GPa point and its onset-versus-zero criterion have not been re-extracted from the full original in this review. The comparison record therefore leaves the exact pressure unknown; a study's maximum applied pressure is not the pressure of every reported transition.

### scwiki-d3-claim-pressure-and-recovered-samples-2

The 2026 pressure-quench report now has a selected primary-text and author-figure check inherited from the [pressure-quench](/scwiki/pressure-quenching) page. Sample S4, released from 18.9 GPa at 4.2 K, showed an ambient-pressure resistive onset of 151 K on warming and 150 K on cooling. This is a reported onset in a recovered metastable sample, not a zero-resistance criterion or an equilibrium ambient-pressure phase.

### scwiki-d3-claim-pressure-and-recovered-samples-3

The magnetic onset near 140 K came from retrieved sample S2, not the S4 transport sample. The estimated shielding at 70 K, the separate cold-storage protocol, and an unreproduced broad 172 K anomaly are distinct observations. The latter has no accepted transition-temperature value in this catalogue. Complete final supplementary comparison, raw-data reanalysis and independent replication remain open.

### scwiki-d3-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

A charge-density modulation does not alone establish a pair-density wave; a linear resistivity does not alone determine a scattering time. Pseudogap, magnetic and charge correlations constrain theories without selecting one unique glue. Oxygen rearrangement and pressure history can alter more than carrier concentration, so a changed transition temperature does not by itself identify the causal variable. Complete scientific acceptance remains open for this article and the associated materials.

### scwiki-d3-claim-discovery-implications-1

Compare matched compositions, preparation histories and criteria. Record what each probe measures, what a model infers and what alternative explanation survives. A mechanism proposal should connect an interaction to a symmetry prediction and a falsifiable material trend. For recovered samples, add decompression temperature, storage and subsequent measurement history before comparing them with equilibrium materials. The site preserves those conditions in searchable records and section exports.

articles.body:
## Scope

Iron-based superconductors contain Fe–pnictogen or Fe–chalcogen layers in several structural families. Multiple Fe orbitals contribute to their low-energy electronic structure, and parent magnetic or structural transitions must be distinguished from superconductivity in a substituted sample. Kamihara and colleagues' fluorine-doped LaOFeAs discovery established a high-temperature 1111 platform. Its original abstract reports a transition near 26 K; the exact operational criterion remains unassigned in this review. [R1](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7)

A 122 arsenide, a binary 11 chalcogenide and a single-layer interface are different experimental systems. Rotter and colleagues studied K-substituted BaFe2As2, while Hsu and colleagues reported superconductivity in PbO-type FeSe. Neither result establishes that every related composition has the same gap, transition temperature or magnetic ground state. Starting mixture, refined phase composition and nominal formula should remain separately identifiable. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e) [R3](#ref-source-205024adeb431322)

## Mathematical assumptions

The coefficient $y$ in $\mathrm{BaFe}_{2-y}\mathrm{Co}_y\mathrm{As}_2$ and the site fraction $x$ in $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x}\mathrm{Co}_x)_2\mathrm{As}_2$ obey $y=2x$. Eleven exact atom-count checks verify this normalization. Likewise, nominal $\mathrm{FeSe}_{1-x}$ becomes $\mathrm{Fe}_{1+\delta}\mathrm{Se}$ with $\delta=x/(1-x)$ when normalized to one Se. Five checks preserve the elemental ratio. These conversions do not measure crystal occupancy, mobile-carrier density or the location of a defect. [R7](#ref-source-7bc9538ec7783cf2)

Bulk fractions also have a precise but limited meaning. For superconducting and magnetic fractions $f_S$ and $f_M$ of the same volume, their overlap lies between $\max(0,f_S+f_M-1)$ and $\min(f_S,f_M)$. Two explicit arrangements with 95% and 90% fractions give 85% or 90% overlap. This set-theory bound neither establishes atomic-scale coexistence nor removes probe calibration and sample-matching requirements. A microscopic interpretation must use additional spatial, temporal and model evidence. [R8](#ref-source-c817382f57bbb81d)

A multiband gap $\Delta_i(\mathbf{k})$ is defined on specified bands. Relative sign reversal can arise in a candidate s± pairing solution, but it does not follow simply from the presence of iron. Orbital weights, shallow bands and the accessible scattering channels affect the inference. The [multiband](/scwiki/multiband-pairing) and [s±](/scwiki/s-plus-minus) articles state their model assumptions and preserve alternative interpretations. [R5](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

## Experimental criteria

The revised Rotter author manuscript gives a resistive midpoint of 38.1 K for Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2, a first deviation near 39 K and a reported zero-resistance point of 37.2 K. Figure 4 also labels 37.2 K as its 10% threshold, so the term zero retains an unresolved instrumental-threshold caveat. Its 90–10% width is 1.5 K. Quoting only the rounded 38 K headline loses distinctions that matter in a searchable record. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e)

The same revision measures magnetic cycles at 0.5 and 1 mT, replacing the earlier manuscript's 10 mT example. Diamagnetism begins near 38.3 K; shielding and field-cooled responses differ and depend on density and demagnetization assumptions. The powder contains a minor FeAs impurity. Selected revised-manuscript figures have been checked, but the final published methods and raw data have not been completely compared here. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e)

Hsu's final FeSe report identifies zero resistance near 8 K in a sample labelled by nominal FeSe0.88 composition. Magnetic susceptibility at 30 G and a broad heat-capacity anomaly provide complementary evidence. Its field-dependent transition uses 50% of normal resistance, with applied fields through 9 T; the roughly 16.3 T upper-critical-field value is a fit extrapolation. Nominal selenium deficiency and a fitted critical field must not be promoted to directly measured phase occupancy or field limits. [R3](#ref-source-205024adeb431322)

McQueen and colleagues subsequently found nearly stoichiometric superconducting FeSe and strong preparation sensitivity. Their selected neutron-refinement analysis gives Fe1.01±0.02Se, with limited ability to distinguish tiny deviations. Nominal composition, oxygen contamination and annealing temperature vary across the comparison. A sample labelled Fe1.03Se showed no superconductivity down to 0.6 K; that lower measurement bound is not a superconducting transition. The proposed defect-site explanation remains a hypothesis. [R7](#ref-source-7bc9538ec7783cf2)

## Pressure and magnetism

Medvedev's author manuscript associates a resistive onset of 36.7 K with 8.9 GPa in Fe1.01Se. Broadened transitions and curve offsets require careful interpretation; at 15 GPa the authors report residual resistance associated with a second phase. Their resistance method uses a diamond-anvil cell, platinum contacts, a van der Pauw arrangement and ruby pressure measurements at low and room temperature. The silicone-oil medium specified for the Mössbauer experiment must not automatically be assigned to the separate resistance experiment. [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b)

The earlier Mössbauer nondetection of static order is not a universal FeSe phase diagram. Bendele and colleagues later reported pressure-induced static magnetism using zero-field muon-spin rotation and AC susceptibility in nominal FeSe0.94 and FeSe0.98 samples. Their selected revised manuscript specifies Daphne 7373, pressure-cell background treatment and low-temperature pressure calibration. Its Figure 3 supports a pressure-dependent coexistence interpretation near and above 0.8 GPa, with model-dependent spatial conclusions. Different probes, samples and pressure environments must remain explicit. [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b) [R8](#ref-source-c817382f57bbb81d)

## Evidence for gap structure

Christianson's neutron experiment concerns K-doped Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2. Its superconductivity-related resonance and the relevant coherence-factor model constrain candidate signs, without directly determining every iron-based gap. Background, momentum, orbital matrix elements and independently measured gap scales remain necessary parts of that interpretation. A resonance measurement cannot be substituted for a family-wide phase verdict. [R5](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

At a FeSe/SrTiO3 interface, Lee's replica bands and mean-field gap-closing scale retain their spectroscopic labels. Faeth's later photon-energy comparison supports an intrinsic electron–phonon interpretation within its stated analysis, but does not determine all contributions to pairing enhancement. A gap-closing temperature is not interchangeable with zero resistance or a magnetic transition. These interface results remain linked to the detailed [multiband](/scwiki/multiband-pairing) discussion rather than silently entering a bulk Tc comparison. [R9](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc) [R10](#ref-source-ac66116dfd6e4887)

## Limits and disputes

Several orbitals, correlations, nematicity and magnetic proximity help organize the evidence without selecting one universal pairing mechanism. A mass renormalization is not automatically a larger pairing eigenvalue. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including final-version comparisons, full supplementary methods and raw-data analysis. Differences between a source's claim and this article's review scope are preserved in the references. [R5](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R7](#ref-source-7bc9538ec7783cf2) [R8](#ref-source-c817382f57bbb81d)

## Discovery implications

Test a specific model with controlled composition, structure, pressure or disorder changes, and identify the confounding changes. Preserve actual measurement criteria and sample provenance when comparing results. For a proposed coexistence regime, report what each probe resolves and how sample fractions were calibrated. For a candidate pairing mediator, explain which alternative survives the same observation. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e) [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b) [R8](#ref-source-c817382f57bbb81d)

## Related topics

Continue with [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), [magnetic substitution](/scwiki/magnetic-substitution-and-superconductivity), [nematic order](/scwiki/nematic-order), and [two-dimensional interfaces](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces).

# Iron-based superconductors: families and evidence

A multiorbital materials guide that separates parent compounds, doped superconductors, interface spectra and candidate gap structures.

## Scope

Iron-based superconductors contain Fe–pnictogen or Fe–chalcogen layers in several structural families. Multiple Fe orbitals contribute to their low-energy electronic structure, and parent magnetic or structural transitions must be distinguished from superconductivity in a substituted sample. Kamihara and colleagues' fluorine-doped LaOFeAs discovery established a high-temperature 1111 platform. Its original abstract reports a transition near 26 K; the exact operational criterion remains unassigned in this review. [R1](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7)

A 122 arsenide, a binary 11 chalcogenide and a single-layer interface are different experimental systems. Rotter and colleagues studied K-substituted BaFe2As2, while Hsu and colleagues reported superconductivity in PbO-type FeSe. Neither result establishes that every related composition has the same gap, transition temperature or magnetic ground state. Starting mixture, refined phase composition and nominal formula should remain separately identifiable. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e) [R3](#ref-source-205024adeb431322)

## Mathematical assumptions

The coefficient $y$ in $\mathrm{BaFe}_{2-y}\mathrm{Co}_y\mathrm{As}_2$ and the site fraction $x$ in $\mathrm{Ba}(\mathrm{Fe}_{1-x}\mathrm{Co}_x)_2\mathrm{As}_2$ obey $y=2x$. Eleven exact atom-count checks verify this normalization. Likewise, nominal $\mathrm{FeSe}_{1-x}$ becomes $\mathrm{Fe}_{1+\delta}\mathrm{Se}$ with $\delta=x/(1-x)$ when normalized to one Se. Five checks preserve the elemental ratio. These conversions do not measure crystal occupancy, mobile-carrier density or the location of a defect. [R7](#ref-source-7bc9538ec7783cf2)

Bulk fractions also have a precise but limited meaning. For superconducting and magnetic fractions $f_S$ and $f_M$ of the same volume, their overlap lies between $\max(0,f_S+f_M-1)$ and $\min(f_S,f_M)$. Two explicit arrangements with 95% and 90% fractions give 85% or 90% overlap. This set-theory bound neither establishes atomic-scale coexistence nor removes probe calibration and sample-matching requirements. A microscopic interpretation must use additional spatial, temporal and model evidence. [R8](#ref-source-c817382f57bbb81d)

A multiband gap $\Delta_i(\mathbf{k})$ is defined on specified bands. Relative sign reversal can arise in a candidate s± pairing solution, but it does not follow simply from the presence of iron. Orbital weights, shallow bands and the accessible scattering channels affect the inference. The [multiband](/scwiki/multiband-pairing) and [s±](/scwiki/s-plus-minus) articles state their model assumptions and preserve alternative interpretations. [R5](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

## Experimental criteria

The revised Rotter author manuscript gives a resistive midpoint of 38.1 K for Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2, a first deviation near 39 K and a reported zero-resistance point of 37.2 K. Figure 4 also labels 37.2 K as its 10% threshold, so the term zero retains an unresolved instrumental-threshold caveat. Its 90–10% width is 1.5 K. Quoting only the rounded 38 K headline loses distinctions that matter in a searchable record. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e)

The same revision measures magnetic cycles at 0.5 and 1 mT, replacing the earlier manuscript's 10 mT example. Diamagnetism begins near 38.3 K; shielding and field-cooled responses differ and depend on density and demagnetization assumptions. The powder contains a minor FeAs impurity. Selected revised-manuscript figures have been checked, but the final published methods and raw data have not been completely compared here. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e)

Hsu's final FeSe report identifies zero resistance near 8 K in a sample labelled by nominal FeSe0.88 composition. Magnetic susceptibility at 30 G and a broad heat-capacity anomaly provide complementary evidence. Its field-dependent transition uses 50% of normal resistance, with applied fields through 9 T; the roughly 16.3 T upper-critical-field value is a fit extrapolation. Nominal selenium deficiency and a fitted critical field must not be promoted to directly measured phase occupancy or field limits. [R3](#ref-source-205024adeb431322)

McQueen and colleagues subsequently found nearly stoichiometric superconducting FeSe and strong preparation sensitivity. Their selected neutron-refinement analysis gives Fe1.01±0.02Se, with limited ability to distinguish tiny deviations. Nominal composition, oxygen contamination and annealing temperature vary across the comparison. A sample labelled Fe1.03Se showed no superconductivity down to 0.6 K; that lower measurement bound is not a superconducting transition. The proposed defect-site explanation remains a hypothesis. [R7](#ref-source-7bc9538ec7783cf2)

## Pressure and magnetism

Medvedev's author manuscript associates a resistive onset of 36.7 K with 8.9 GPa in Fe1.01Se. Broadened transitions and curve offsets require careful interpretation; at 15 GPa the authors report residual resistance associated with a second phase. Their resistance method uses a diamond-anvil cell, platinum contacts, a van der Pauw arrangement and ruby pressure measurements at low and room temperature. The silicone-oil medium specified for the Mössbauer experiment must not automatically be assigned to the separate resistance experiment. [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b)

The earlier Mössbauer nondetection of static order is not a universal FeSe phase diagram. Bendele and colleagues later reported pressure-induced static magnetism using zero-field muon-spin rotation and AC susceptibility in nominal FeSe0.94 and FeSe0.98 samples. Their selected revised manuscript specifies Daphne 7373, pressure-cell background treatment and low-temperature pressure calibration. Its Figure 3 supports a pressure-dependent coexistence interpretation near and above 0.8 GPa, with model-dependent spatial conclusions. Different probes, samples and pressure environments must remain explicit. [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b) [R8](#ref-source-c817382f57bbb81d)

## Evidence for gap structure

Christianson's neutron experiment concerns K-doped Ba0.6K0.4Fe2As2. Its superconductivity-related resonance and the relevant coherence-factor model constrain candidate signs, without directly determining every iron-based gap. Background, momentum, orbital matrix elements and independently measured gap scales remain necessary parts of that interpretation. A resonance measurement cannot be substituted for a family-wide phase verdict. [R5](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

At a FeSe/SrTiO3 interface, Lee's replica bands and mean-field gap-closing scale retain their spectroscopic labels. Faeth's later photon-energy comparison supports an intrinsic electron–phonon interpretation within its stated analysis, but does not determine all contributions to pairing enhancement. A gap-closing temperature is not interchangeable with zero resistance or a magnetic transition. These interface results remain linked to the detailed [multiband](/scwiki/multiband-pairing) discussion rather than silently entering a bulk Tc comparison. [R9](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc) [R10](#ref-source-ac66116dfd6e4887)

## Limits and disputes

Several orbitals, correlations, nematicity and magnetic proximity help organize the evidence without selecting one universal pairing mechanism. A mass renormalization is not automatically a larger pairing eigenvalue. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including final-version comparisons, full supplementary methods and raw-data analysis. Differences between a source's claim and this article's review scope are preserved in the references. [R5](#ref-source-716c338ddfa726d3) [R6](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c) [R7](#ref-source-7bc9538ec7783cf2) [R8](#ref-source-c817382f57bbb81d)

## Discovery implications

Test a specific model with controlled composition, structure, pressure or disorder changes, and identify the confounding changes. Preserve actual measurement criteria and sample provenance when comparing results. For a proposed coexistence regime, report what each probe resolves and how sample fractions were calibrated. For a candidate pairing mediator, explain which alternative survives the same observation. [R2](#ref-source-1a3690e5f1d38f3e) [R4](#ref-source-a631bcd83d23567b) [R8](#ref-source-c817382f57bbb81d)

## Related topics

Continue with [s± pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), [magnetic substitution](/scwiki/magnetic-substitution-and-superconductivity), [nematic order](/scwiki/nematic-order), and [two-dimensional interfaces](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces).

articles.body:
## Scope

Nickelate superconductors include infinite-layer reduced films, bilayer Ruddlesden–Popper crystals and engineered layer sequences. The number of NiO2 layers, oxygen coordination and sample preparation distinguish these systems. An ambient-pressure epitaxial film and a compressed bulk crystal should retain separate records even when both contain lanthanum and nickel. Structural resemblance to cuprates motivates comparisons without establishing a shared pairing mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

The 2026 La2PrNi2O7 high-field transport study concerns a bilayer Ruddlesden–Popper film. The inherited draft incorrectly placed it in the infinite-layer family. Its field-induced normal state is also distinct from the Eu-substituted infinite-layer material exhibiting re-entrant resistance suppression. Family, composition and probe must accompany these interpretations. [R6](#ref-source-1b4b1103f747fe70) [R7](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

## Mathematical assumptions

Formal charge neutrality gives nickel valence $v_{\mathrm{Ni}}=1+x+2\delta$ for an idealized $R_{1-x}\mathrm{Sr}_x\mathrm{NiO}_{2+\delta}$ with trivalent $R$, divalent Sr and divalent oxygen. For $R_3\mathrm{Ni}_2\mathrm{O}_{7-\delta}$, it gives $v_{\mathrm{Ni}}=2.5-\delta$. Sixty-six exact bookkeeping checks preserve neutrality. These averages do not measure orbital occupancy, vacancy location, ligand holes or mobile carriers. In particular, an annealing-gas dose does not specify oxygen stoichiometry. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R5](#ref-source-3f4ceab12660ad62)

Even the elementary two-carrier low-field Drude expression $R_H=(p\mu_h^2-n\mu_e^2)/[e(p\mu_h+n\mu_e)^2]$, with $e>0$, prevents a unique carrier count from Hall sign alone. Three explicit counterexamples give negative Hall coefficients with different electron–hole population orderings. This model illustrates nonuniqueness; it is not a fit to nickelate data. Both Li and Hsu discuss multiband limitations, so a negative Hall coefficient must not be silently converted to a single-band electron density. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R6](#ref-source-1b4b1103f747fe70)

## Experimental criteria

For the representative Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 film in Li's 2019 discovery, the published text identifies a 14.9 K onset by maximum curvature, a 13.6 K midpoint and 9.1 K resistance indistinguishable from the noise floor. The final methods describe six-point electrical measurements, 9–11 nm precursor films and topotactic reduction. Two-coil mutual inductance supports a diamagnetic response, but the authors explicitly decline to extract a penetration depth because of finite-size, disorder and other uncertainties. These three temperatures describe different criteria on the selected sample. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

Sun's 2023 bilayer-crystal report gives an 80 K resistance onset at 18.5 GPa in run 1 without pressure medium. Run 2 uses KBr and reaches a 78 K onset at 18.9 GPa. Figure 3 distinguishes the 10 μA run-1 excitation from 300 μA in run 2. Its magnetic response near 77 K is measured separately at 25.2 GPa. Residual resistance and specimen differences prevent combining these observations into one zero-resistance or bulk-fraction record. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## Oxygen, strain and transport

Bhatt's final strain study distinguishes nominal substrate mismatch from measured strain: the strongly compressed film is labelled approximately −1.6% measured strain, rather than the inherited draft's −1.8%. Growth method, oxygen treatment and substrate vary across comparisons. In-plane compression accompanied by out-of-plane expansion is not equivalent to hydrostatic compression. The [strain](/scwiki/strain) article retains the source-specific structural comparison and its confounding variables. [R3](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9)

Xiang's revised author manuscript demonstrates an oxygen-removal and ozone-annealing sequence that can recover degraded bilayer films. Repeating ozone treatment alone can instead damage the superconducting response. Its proposed phase diagram uses cumulative annealing-gas volume; oxygen concentration is not precisely measured, and unknown phases complicate interpretation. Figure 2 identifies a zero-resistance point near 5.5 K for sample S1049-4, far below its onset region. The recovery experiment constrains preparation sensitivity without establishing a calibrated carrier-density axis or a universal recycling recipe. [R5](#ref-source-3f4ceab12660ad62)

Hsu's final La2PrNi2O7 study defines 41 K using 90% of a fitted normal-state resistivity. Pulsed-field measurements access a low-temperature normal state with approximately quadratic resistivity; an extrapolated zero-field normal-state curve is not directly observed below the transition. The film is about 5 nm thick, grown on SrLaAlO4 with a SrTiO3 cap and kept cold between measurements. The reported effective mass uses an empirical Kadowaki–Woods relation, not direct calorimetry. These results describe a strained bilayer specimen, not every nickelate. [R6](#ref-source-1b4b1103f747fe70)

## Recent structures and membranes

Nie's publisher abstract, published in April 2026, reports ambient-pressure onset temperatures spanning 46–50 K in engineered 1212 and 2323 layer sequences, alongside a nonsuperconducting 1313 comparison. The exact operational criterion and lower nondetection bound have not been extracted here, so this range is not assigned to a precise searchable Tc record. Associated orbital and Fermi-surface observations constrain structure–electronic-state relationships; they do not independently prove a unique pairing interaction. [R4](#ref-source-2337a5bf19bca4c4)

Lee's April 2026 membrane preprint reports 74.2 K at 91.5 GPa using 99.5% of an extrapolated normal-state resistance. Extended Data Figure 1 gives 69.1 K with an intersection construction and 75.4 K with a second-derivative construction for the illustrated transition. These differences are criterion dependence, not separate superconducting phases. Zero resistance is defined by the noise floor and occurs lower. The preprint remains explicitly labelled and is not an ambient-pressure result. [R8](#ref-source-0886448b2b71c919)

The same preprint measures six membranes and fits an onset increase near 0.65 K/GPa over its sampled range. It uses room-temperature ruby calibration below 50 GPa and diamond Raman calibration above that, with the latter measured adjacent to the specimen. Silicone-oil solidification and nonhydrostatic stress complicate broadening. Its 13 T field measurements and fitted coherence lengths should not be mistaken for direct measurements of a much larger zero-temperature critical field. Extrapolating the pressure trend beyond the measured range is not a demonstrated materials prediction. [R8](#ref-source-0886448b2b71c919)

## Limits and disputes

Eu-substituted infinite-layer films show field-dependent resistance recovery in a specific sample and temperature window. Magnetic compensation and triplet pairing remain interpretations rather than conclusions forced by re-entrance alone. The [re-entrant superconductivity](/scwiki/field-induced-superconductivity) and [magnetic substitution](/scwiki/magnetic-substitution-and-superconductivity) articles preserve field orientation, measurement temperature and alternative mechanisms. None of these observations establishes a universal nickelate gap symmetry. [R7](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected primary passages, figures and model checks have been reviewed, while full supplements, final-author version comparisons, independent reproduction and raw-data analysis remain incomplete. Onset, midpoint, noise-floor zero, spectroscopic gaps and normal-state measurement temperatures retain distinct meanings. Pressure and strain comparisons require matching phase and preparation rather than ordering headline temperatures. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853) [R3](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9) [R8](#ref-source-0886448b2b71c919)

## Discovery implications

A useful comparison records layer sequence, oxygen history, nominal and measured composition, substrate, thickness, pressure calibration, probe and temperature criterion. Controlled oxygen cycles and structural contrasts are informative only with their phase and interface changes documented. A promising design hypothesis should specify which variable changes, which confounders remain and what observation would distinguish competing mechanisms. [R3](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9) [R4](#ref-source-2337a5bf19bca4c4) [R5](#ref-source-3f4ceab12660ad62)

## Related topics

Continue with [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), [strain](/scwiki/strain), [two-dimensional interfaces](/scwiki/two-dimensional-interfaces), [multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [magnetic substitution](/scwiki/magnetic-substitution-and-superconductivity).

Formal charge neutrality gives nickel valence $v_{\mathrm{Ni}}=1+x+2\delta$ for an idealized $R_{1-x}\mathrm{Sr}_x\mathrm{NiO}_{2+\delta}$ with trivalent $R$, divalent Sr and divalent oxygen. For $R_3\mathrm{Ni}_2\mathrm{O}_{7-\delta}$, it gives $v_{\mathrm{Ni}}=2.5-\delta$. Sixty-six exact bookkeeping checks preserve neutrality. These averages do not measure orbital occupancy, vacancy location, ligand holes or mobile carriers. In particular, an annealing-gas dose does not specify oxygen stoichiometry. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R5](#ref-source-3f4ceab12660ad62)

Even the elementary two-carrier low-field Drude expression $R_H=(p\mu_h^2-n\mu_e^2)/[e(p\mu_h+n\mu_e)^2]$, with $e>0$, prevents a unique carrier count from Hall sign alone. Three explicit counterexamples give negative Hall coefficients with different electron–hole population orderings. This model illustrates nonuniqueness; it is not a fit to nickelate data. Both Li and Hsu discuss multiband limitations, so a negative Hall coefficient must not be silently converted to a single-band electron density. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R6](#ref-source-1b4b1103f747fe70)

sections.title: Experimental criteria
sections.markdown:
## Experimental criteria

For the representative Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 film in Li's 2019 discovery, the published text identifies a 14.9 K onset by maximum curvature, a 13.6 K midpoint and 9.1 K resistance indistinguishable from the noise floor. The final methods describe six-point electrical measurements, 9–11 nm precursor films and topotactic reduction. Two-coil mutual inductance supports a diamagnetic response, but the authors explicitly decline to extract a penetration depth because of finite-size, disorder and other uncertainties. These three temperatures describe different criteria on the selected sample. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

Sun's 2023 bilayer-crystal report gives an 80 K resistance onset at 18.5 GPa in run 1 without pressure medium. Run 2 uses KBr and reaches a 78 K onset at 18.9 GPa. Figure 3 distinguishes the 10 μA run-1 excitation from 300 μA in run 2. Its magnetic response near 77 K is measured separately at 25.2 GPa. Residual resistance and specimen differences prevent combining these observations into one zero-resistance or bulk-fraction record. [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

sections.title: Oxygen, strain and transport
sections.markdown:
## Oxygen, strain and transport

Bhatt's final strain study distinguishes nominal substrate mismatch from measured strain: the strongly compressed film is labelled approximately −1.6% measured strain, rather than the inherited draft's −1.8%. Growth method, oxygen treatment and substrate vary across comparisons. In-plane compression accompanied by out-of-plane expansion is not equivalent to hydrostatic compression. The [strain](/scwiki/strain) article retains the source-specific structural comparison and its confounding variables. [R3](#ref-source-4b5b65a5047eb1a9)

Xiang's revised author manuscript demonstrates an oxygen-removal and ozone-annealing sequence that can recover degraded bilayer films. Repeating ozone treatment alone can instead damage the superconducting response. Its proposed phase diagram uses cumulative annealing-gas volume; oxygen concentration is not precisely measured, and unknown phases complicate interpretation. Figure 2 identifies a zero-resistance point near 5.5 K for sample S1049-4, far below its onset region. The recovery experiment constrains preparation sensitivity without establishing a calibrated carrier-density axis or a universal recycling recipe. [R5](#ref-source-3f4ceab12660ad62)

Hsu's final La2PrNi2O7 study defines 41 K using 90% of a fitted normal-state resistivity. Pulsed-field measurements access a low-temperature normal state with approximately quadratic resistivity; an extrapolated zero-field normal-state curve is not directly observed below the transition. The film is about 5 nm thick, grown on SrLaAlO4 with a SrTiO3 cap and kept cold between measurements. The reported effective mass uses an empirical Kadowaki–Woods relation, not direct calorimetry. These results describe a strained bilayer specimen, not every nickelate. [R6](#ref-source-1b4b1103f747fe70)

sections.markdown:
## Recent structures and membranes

Nie's publisher abstract, published in April 2026, reports ambient-pressure onset temperatures spanning 46–50 K in engineered 1212 and 2323 layer sequences, alongside a nonsuperconducting 1313 comparison. The exact operational criterion and lower nondetection bound have not been extracted here, so this range is not assigned to a precise searchable Tc record. Associated orbital and Fermi-surface observations constrain structure–electronic-state relationships; they do not independently prove a unique pairing interaction. [R4](#ref-source-2337a5bf19bca4c4)

Lee's April 2026 membrane preprint reports 74.2 K at 91.5 GPa using 99.5% of an extrapolated normal-state resistance. Extended Data Figure 1 gives 69.1 K with an intersection construction and 75.4 K with a second-derivative construction for the illustrated transition. These differences are criterion dependence, not separate superconducting phases. Zero resistance is defined by the noise floor and occurs lower. The preprint remains explicitly labelled and is not an ambient-pressure result. [R8](#ref-source-0886448b2b71c919)

The same preprint measures six membranes and fits an onset increase near 0.65 K/GPa over its sampled range. It uses room-temperature ruby calibration below 50 GPa and diamond Raman calibration above that, with the latter measured adjacent to the specimen. Silicone-oil solidification and nonhydrostatic stress complicate broadening. Its 13 T field measurements and fitted coherence lengths should not be mistaken for direct measurements of a much larger zero-temperature critical field. Extrapolating the pressure trend beyond the measured range is not a demonstrated materials prediction. [R8](#ref-source-0886448b2b71c919)
