articles.body:
## Scope

Light can change carrier populations, excite lattice motion and alter collective electronic response. Persistent photodoping, a transient pump–probe state and a periodically driven model are different protocols. Specify wavelength, polarization, pulse duration, fluence, repetition rate, base temperature and probe delay. A temperature at which a driven response is observed is not automatically an equilibrium superconducting transition temperature. [R1](#ref-source-c60f0131e7d25c60) [R2](#ref-source-e8775e639989b8d6) [R4](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1) [R6](#ref-source-30e68110da17974c)

The evidence now extends beyond optical conductivity. Electrical measurements in K3C60, transient magnetic measurements in YBa2Cu3O6.48 and a later sensitivity-limited magnetic experiment on K3C60 ask different questions. Preserve the specimen, geometry and measured observable rather than combining them into one universal light-induced transition. [R5](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690) [R9](#ref-source-65e69ec93039deb9) [R10](#ref-source-930b28b64275da42) [R11](#ref-source-e7138d083320dfd7)

## Mathematical assumptions

With the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention, a normal Drude response is $\sigma(\omega)=D/(\Gamma-i\omega)$, where $D$ is the Drude weight and $\Gamma>0$ the relaxation rate. Thus $\sigma_2=D\omega/(\Gamma^2+\omega^2)\approx D/\omega$ when the measured frequencies greatly exceed $\Gamma$, although the DC conductivity $D/\Gamma$ remains finite. A finite-band inductive trend alone cannot distinguish this limit from a condensate. This elementary counterexample is not a fit to, or refutation of, any particular experiment. [R4](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1) [R7](#ref-source-a85b56be7c62bf11)

Depth reconstruction also matters. For Dodge's illustrative saturating profile, $\Delta\sigma(z)=\Delta\sigma_{\rm sat}f e^{-z/\Lambda}/(1+f e^{-z/\Lambda})$, with $f=F/F_{\rm sat}$, integration gives sheet photoconductance $\Delta G=\Delta\sigma_{\rm sat}\Lambda\ln(1+f)$. The effective thickness grows with fluence even while the surface response saturates. Assuming a fixed exponential profile can therefore bias the inferred surface conductivity. This integral checks the stated profile, not a full electromagnetic inversion; the experimental interpretation is disputed below. [R7](#ref-source-a85b56be7c62bf11) [R8](#ref-source-56a2c1fa63bafe80)

Kennes's minimal quadratic electron–phonon model gives oscillator frequency $\omega(n)=\omega_0\sqrt{1+2gn}$ for site occupation $n=0,1,2$, requiring $g>-1/4$. At fixed phonon occupation $n_B$, its induced interaction is $\Delta U=(n_B+1/2)\hbar\omega_0[\sqrt{1+4g}+1-2\sqrt{1+2g}]$. Concavity makes this nonpositive for either sign of stable $g$, with leading term $-(n_B+1/2)\hbar\omega_0g^2$. The author manuscript sets Planck's constant to one; it is restored here. This is a model mechanism, not a measured coupling or proof of a stable superconducting phase. [R6](#ref-source-30e68110da17974c)

## Experimental criteria

Fausti studied stripe-ordered La1.675Eu0.2Sr0.125CuO4 at a 10 K base temperature. The reported signal is a transient c-axis plasma edge and optical response interpreted as restored interlayer coherence. Figures 2–3 specify a 16 micrometre pump, approximately 1 mJ/cm² fluence and a 5 ps delay for the transient spectrum. The pump excites roughly 200 nm in depth, while the THz probe samples about 10 micrometres; the transformed-layer reconstruction is essential. A near-infrared plateau observed to 100 ps does not directly measure a many-nanosecond lifetime. [R1](#ref-source-c60f0131e7d25c60)

Hu's YBa2Cu3O6.5 specimen has an equilibrium transition near 50 K. Its approximately 300 fs, 15 micrometre pump modifies both inter- and intra-bilayer optical response. The effective-medium analysis separates transformed and untransformed regions; screened plasma-edge positions are not the same as fitted unscreened plasma frequencies. Broadband data at 60 K and narrower-band measurements at 100 and 300 K have different information content. Mankowsky's associated structural study combines diffraction with calculations to connect driven distortions with electronic changes; structural response does not uniquely identify pairing. [R2](#ref-source-e8775e639989b8d6) [R3](#ref-source-b47831832e13ca4e)

Mitrano's K3C60 report compares a transient optical response above the roughly 20 K equilibrium transition with the low-temperature spectrum. Its title deliberately says “Possible”. The reported optical-gap fit and enhanced carrier mobility are not a direct DC resistance or magnetic measurement. Temperature, pump–probe delay and model-dependent gap extraction must remain attached to that evidence. [R4](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1)

Budden extended the response using longer pulses. Figure 4 compares optical extrapolation with electrical measurements at a 100 K base temperature and about 25 mJ/cm² fluence. The optical and transport pump durations are 200 ps and 75 ps, respectively. The electrical experiment is transient two-terminal transport with contact contributions calibrated from static four-terminal measurements; it is not a direct transient four-terminal measurement. Resistance compatible with zero within that calibration and recovery over tens of nanoseconds strengthen the authors' metastable interpretation without establishing a pump-free equilibrium transition at 100 K. [R5](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690)

Adelinia's 2025 thin-film study uses a quasi-DC bias, 300 fs pulses at 7 micrometres and photoconductive switches to resolve voltage dynamics. Granular-film and powder results are not interchangeable. The above-transition voltage response changes sign at 80 K; at 100 K it is positive and linear across the measured current range. Fitted superfluid fractions and weak-link phase-slip dynamics depend on the granular two-fluid model. A 100 K measurement in this paper must not become a 100 K superconducting-transition record. [R10](#ref-source-930b28b64275da42)

Fava's 2024 YBa2Cu3O6.48 experiment detects a transient magnetic-field enhancement near the excited region's edge using Faraday rotation in a nearby GaP detector. Signals at 100 and 300 K last about 1 ps. The inferred diamagnetic susceptibility of order −0.3 depends on geometry and the magnetic-response model; the paper itself cautions that a quasi-static estimate is not fully justified for this dynamics. This provides a complementary magnetic observable, while remaining distinct from a persistent equilibrium Meissner state. [R9](#ref-source-65e69ec93039deb9)

De Vecchi's December 2025 K3C60 study reports no statistically significant photo-induced field signal above roughly 50 nT out to 1 ns in its protocol. Its model-based bound is $\chi_v>-0.1$. The authors explicitly conclude that their resolution does not decide whether Meissner diamagnetism is present or absent. Granularity and a small expected response matter: this null result neither establishes superconductivity nor universally rules it out. [R11](#ref-source-e7138d083320dfd7)

## Limits and disputes

Dodge and colleagues argue that saturation-dependent excitation depth can create misleading superconducting-like reconstructed spectra. Buzzi and colleagues' March 2023 preprint response disputes that interpretation, arguing that the inductive signature survives their alternative reconstructions. The local profile and Drude checks above do not resolve this dispute. Compare raw reflected fields, depth assumptions, spectral bandwidth and independent transport or magnetic evidence rather than treating a fitted gap as a unique diagnosis. [R7](#ref-source-a85b56be7c62bf11) [R8](#ref-source-56a2c1fa63bafe80)

Long-lived after a short pulse does not mean thermodynamic equilibrium. Quantify absorbed energy, depth gradients, carrier and lattice temperatures, relaxation and repetition-rate heating. Selective excitation of a phonon does not establish that equilibrium pairing is phonon-mediated. The present review covers selected original passages and figures; full supplements, remaining version comparisons, experimental raw-data reproduction and complete scientific acceptance remain open. [R3](#ref-source-b47831832e13ca4e) [R5](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690) [R6](#ref-source-30e68110da17974c) [R10](#ref-source-930b28b64275da42)

## Discovery implications

Use synchronized optical, electrical and magnetic probes with explicit controls and uncertainty. Report signal duration separately from formation time and instrumental resolution. Keep equilibrium transition records separate from driven base temperatures and model estimates in databases and search filters. Theory should predict observables under the actual drive protocol, including relaxation, rather than equating an attractive model interaction with an experimentally established superconducting phase. [R5](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690) [R6](#ref-source-30e68110da17974c) [R9](#ref-source-65e69ec93039deb9) [R11](#ref-source-e7138d083320dfd7)

## Related topics

Compare [fullerides](/scwiki/fulleride-superconductors), [electrostatic gating](/scwiki/electrostatic-gating), [magnetic fields](/scwiki/magnetic-field), [pair-density waves](/scwiki/pair-density-wave) and [critical fields](/scwiki/critical-fields).

# Light-driven states: transient evidence and equilibrium limits

Compare optical, electrical and magnetic evidence under explicit drive conditions, with depth reconstruction, granularity and detection limits.

## Scope

Light can change carrier populations, excite lattice motion and alter collective electronic response. Persistent photodoping, a transient pump–probe state and a periodically driven model are different protocols. Specify wavelength, polarization, pulse duration, fluence, repetition rate, base temperature and probe delay. A temperature at which a driven response is observed is not automatically an equilibrium superconducting transition temperature. [R1](#ref-source-c60f0131e7d25c60) [R2](#ref-source-e8775e639989b8d6) [R4](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1) [R6](#ref-source-30e68110da17974c)

The evidence now extends beyond optical conductivity. Electrical measurements in K3C60, transient magnetic measurements in YBa2Cu3O6.48 and a later sensitivity-limited magnetic experiment on K3C60 ask different questions. Preserve the specimen, geometry and measured observable rather than combining them into one universal light-induced transition. [R5](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690) [R9](#ref-source-65e69ec93039deb9) [R10](#ref-source-930b28b64275da42) [R11](#ref-source-e7138d083320dfd7)

## Mathematical assumptions

With the $e^{-i\omega t}$ convention, a normal Drude response is $\sigma(\omega)=D/(\Gamma-i\omega)$, where $D$ is the Drude weight and $\Gamma>0$ the relaxation rate. Thus $\sigma_2=D\omega/(\Gamma^2+\omega^2)\approx D/\omega$ when the measured frequencies greatly exceed $\Gamma$, although the DC conductivity $D/\Gamma$ remains finite. A finite-band inductive trend alone cannot distinguish this limit from a condensate. This elementary counterexample is not a fit to, or refutation of, any particular experiment. [R4](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1) [R7](#ref-source-a85b56be7c62bf11)

Depth reconstruction also matters. For Dodge's illustrative saturating profile, $\Delta\sigma(z)=\Delta\sigma_{\rm sat}f e^{-z/\Lambda}/(1+f e^{-z/\Lambda})$, with $f=F/F_{\rm sat}$, integration gives sheet photoconductance $\Delta G=\Delta\sigma_{\rm sat}\Lambda\ln(1+f)$. The effective thickness grows with fluence even while the surface response saturates. Assuming a fixed exponential profile can therefore bias the inferred surface conductivity. This integral checks the stated profile, not a full electromagnetic inversion; the experimental interpretation is disputed below. [R7](#ref-source-a85b56be7c62bf11) [R8](#ref-source-56a2c1fa63bafe80)

Kennes's minimal quadratic electron–phonon model gives oscillator frequency $\omega(n)=\omega_0\sqrt{1+2gn}$ for site occupation $n=0,1,2$, requiring $g>-1/4$. At fixed phonon occupation $n_B$, its induced interaction is $\Delta U=(n_B+1/2)\hbar\omega_0[\sqrt{1+4g}+1-2\sqrt{1+2g}]$. Concavity makes this nonpositive for either sign of stable $g$, with leading term $-(n_B+1/2)\hbar\omega_0g^2$. The author manuscript sets Planck's constant to one; it is restored here. This is a model mechanism, not a measured coupling or proof of a stable superconducting phase. [R6](#ref-source-30e68110da17974c)

## Experimental criteria

Fausti studied stripe-ordered La1.675Eu0.2Sr0.125CuO4 at a 10 K base temperature. The reported signal is a transient c-axis plasma edge and optical response interpreted as restored interlayer coherence. Figures 2–3 specify a 16 micrometre pump, approximately 1 mJ/cm² fluence and a 5 ps delay for the transient spectrum. The pump excites roughly 200 nm in depth, while the THz probe samples about 10 micrometres; the transformed-layer reconstruction is essential. A near-infrared plateau observed to 100 ps does not directly measure a many-nanosecond lifetime. [R1](#ref-source-c60f0131e7d25c60)

Hu's YBa2Cu3O6.5 specimen has an equilibrium transition near 50 K. Its approximately 300 fs, 15 micrometre pump modifies both inter- and intra-bilayer optical response. The effective-medium analysis separates transformed and untransformed regions; screened plasma-edge positions are not the same as fitted unscreened plasma frequencies. Broadband data at 60 K and narrower-band measurements at 100 and 300 K have different information content. Mankowsky's associated structural study combines diffraction with calculations to connect driven distortions with electronic changes; structural response does not uniquely identify pairing. [R2](#ref-source-e8775e639989b8d6) [R3](#ref-source-b47831832e13ca4e)

Mitrano's K3C60 report compares a transient optical response above the roughly 20 K equilibrium transition with the low-temperature spectrum. Its title deliberately says “Possible”. The reported optical-gap fit and enhanced carrier mobility are not a direct DC resistance or magnetic measurement. Temperature, pump–probe delay and model-dependent gap extraction must remain attached to that evidence. [R4](#ref-source-6ee3670220e24ff1)

Budden extended the response using longer pulses. Figure 4 compares optical extrapolation with electrical measurements at a 100 K base temperature and about 25 mJ/cm² fluence. The optical and transport pump durations are 200 ps and 75 ps, respectively. The electrical experiment is transient two-terminal transport with contact contributions calibrated from static four-terminal measurements; it is not a direct transient four-terminal measurement. Resistance compatible with zero within that calibration and recovery over tens of nanoseconds strengthen the authors' metastable interpretation without establishing a pump-free equilibrium transition at 100 K. [R5](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690)

Adelinia's 2025 thin-film study uses a quasi-DC bias, 300 fs pulses at 7 micrometres and photoconductive switches to resolve voltage dynamics. Granular-film and powder results are not interchangeable. The above-transition voltage response changes sign at 80 K; at 100 K it is positive and linear across the measured current range. Fitted superfluid fractions and weak-link phase-slip dynamics depend on the granular two-fluid model. A 100 K measurement in this paper must not become a 100 K superconducting-transition record. [R10](#ref-source-930b28b64275da42)

Fava's 2024 YBa2Cu3O6.48 experiment detects a transient magnetic-field enhancement near the excited region's edge using Faraday rotation in a nearby GaP detector. Signals at 100 and 300 K last about 1 ps. The inferred diamagnetic susceptibility of order −0.3 depends on geometry and the magnetic-response model; the paper itself cautions that a quasi-static estimate is not fully justified for this dynamics. This provides a complementary magnetic observable, while remaining distinct from a persistent equilibrium Meissner state. [R9](#ref-source-65e69ec93039deb9)

De Vecchi's December 2025 K3C60 study reports no statistically significant photo-induced field signal above roughly 50 nT out to 1 ns in its protocol. Its model-based bound is $\chi_v>-0.1$. The authors explicitly conclude that their resolution does not decide whether Meissner diamagnetism is present or absent. Granularity and a small expected response matter: this null result neither establishes superconductivity nor universally rules it out. [R11](#ref-source-e7138d083320dfd7)

## Limits and disputes

Dodge and colleagues argue that saturation-dependent excitation depth can create misleading superconducting-like reconstructed spectra. Buzzi and colleagues' March 2023 preprint response disputes that interpretation, arguing that the inductive signature survives their alternative reconstructions. The local profile and Drude checks above do not resolve this dispute. Compare raw reflected fields, depth assumptions, spectral bandwidth and independent transport or magnetic evidence rather than treating a fitted gap as a unique diagnosis. [R7](#ref-source-a85b56be7c62bf11) [R8](#ref-source-56a2c1fa63bafe80)

Long-lived after a short pulse does not mean thermodynamic equilibrium. Quantify absorbed energy, depth gradients, carrier and lattice temperatures, relaxation and repetition-rate heating. Selective excitation of a phonon does not establish that equilibrium pairing is phonon-mediated. The present review covers selected original passages and figures; full supplements, remaining version comparisons, experimental raw-data reproduction and complete scientific acceptance remain open. [R3](#ref-source-b47831832e13ca4e) [R5](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690) [R6](#ref-source-30e68110da17974c) [R10](#ref-source-930b28b64275da42)

## Discovery implications

Use synchronized optical, electrical and magnetic probes with explicit controls and uncertainty. Report signal duration separately from formation time and instrumental resolution. Keep equilibrium transition records separate from driven base temperatures and model estimates in databases and search filters. Theory should predict observables under the actual drive protocol, including relaxation, rather than equating an attractive model interaction with an experimentally established superconducting phase. [R5](#ref-source-07be806c0002c690) [R6](#ref-source-30e68110da17974c) [R9](#ref-source-65e69ec93039deb9) [R11](#ref-source-e7138d083320dfd7)

## Related topics

Compare [fullerides](/scwiki/fulleride-superconductors), [electrostatic gating](/scwiki/electrostatic-gating), [magnetic fields](/scwiki/magnetic-field), [pair-density waves](/scwiki/pair-density-wave) and [critical fields](/scwiki/critical-fields).

De Vecchi's December 2025 K3C60 study reports no statistically significant photo-induced field signal above roughly 50 nT out to 1 ns in its protocol. Its model-based bound is $\chi_v>-0.1$. articles.body:
## Scope

Disorder is not one adjustable number. Elastic scattering, magnetic pair breaking, local bound states, localization, vortex pinning and poor grain connectivity affect different observables. Record defect chemistry, irradiation particle and energy, dose, temperature, annealing history and sample geometry. A larger residual resistivity does not by itself specify the pair-breaking rate or prove a change of carrier density. [R1](#ref-source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b) [R6](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83) [R7](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2)

Anderson's time-reversed-state argument explains the robustness of an isotropic, sign-preserving superconducting state to nonmagnetic elastic scattering under restricted assumptions. The participating states must remain extended and the averaged pairing interaction and density of states must not change substantially. It is not immunity to arbitrary chemical substitution, localization, magnetic scattering or spatial granularity. Constant $T_c$ alone does not uniquely determine pairing symmetry. [R1](#ref-source-8d0e592da8ec9c7b) [R6](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83)

## Mathematical assumptions

In the dilute, uncorrelated, weak magnetic-scattering model for an isotropic singlet state, define the pair-breaking **energy** $\Gamma$ by $\ln(T_{c0}/T_c)=\psi(1/2+\Gamma/(2\pi k_BT_c))-\psi(1/2)$, where $\psi$ is the digamma function. With $g=\Gamma/(k_BT_{c0})$ and $t=T_c/T_{c0}$, the initial slope is $dt/dg=-\pi/4$, and $T_c$ vanishes at $g_c=\pi e^{-\gamma_E}/2\approx0.882$. Rate conventions differ; do not substitute a transport lifetime without deriving its relation to this $\Gamma$. Local numerical checks compare the equation with independently bounded Matsubara sums. The original AG paper remains a bibliographic anchor, not a completed original-text audit. [R2](#ref-source-daf8f301de81a726) [R5](#ref-source-3a528aeee1b7cf04) [R6](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83)

For one classical magnetic scattering channel in a particle–hole-symmetric, isotropic host with a fixed gap, use exchange $J\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf s$, $\mathbf s=\boldsymbol\sigma/2$, and normal density of states per spin $N_0$. Defining $\alpha=\pi N_0JS/2$ and potential strength $\beta=\pi N_0V$, one signed Yu–Shiba–Rusinov branch is $E/\Delta=(1+\beta^2-\alpha^2)/\sqrt{(1+\beta^2-\alpha^2)^2+4\alpha^2}$; its particle–hole partner has opposite energy. At $V=0$, this reduces to $(1-\alpha^2)/(1+\alpha^2)$. A zero crossing requires $\alpha^2=1+\beta^2$ in this model. These conventions and phase-shift checks do not solve quantum Kondo screening, multiple orbital channels or self-consistent gap suppression. [R3](#ref-source-c9bed6791b995641) [R4](#ref-source-7383f31da800ca9e) [R5](#ref-source-3a528aeee1b7cf04) [R8](#ref-source-54e8e8bbd28f62fd)

Dose is a separate quantity: an electron charge dose of 1 C/cm² corresponds to approximately $6.24\times10^{18}$ incident electrons/cm². The 3.4 C/cm² exposure in Prozorov's protocol is about $2.12\times10^{19}$ electrons/cm². Neither number is the surviving defect concentration; displacement cross sections, recombination and annealing enter that conversion. [R6](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83)

## Experimental criteria

Prozorov studied Ba(Fe1−xRux)2As2 with WDS composition $x=0.24$ using 2.5 MeV electrons. Irradiation and in-situ resistivity measurements took place near 22 K; the initial superconducting transition is reported as 17.8 K in the methods and 17.85 K in the transport figure. Warming to room temperature between runs partially annealed the damage, by up to about 30%. The same contacts were retained. Increased resistivity and suppressed $T_c$ were compatible with the authors' multiband sign-changing scenario, whose interband/intraband scattering ratio matters. The 22 K irradiation temperature is not $T_c$, and no unverified onset, midpoint or zero-resistance label is assigned here. [R6](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83)

Mizukami's BaFe2(As1−xPx)2 crystals had $x=0.33$–0.36 and initial transitions of 28, 29 or 30 K. The 28/29 K batches were tracked by tunnel-diode-oscillator frequency shifts; the 30 K crystal also supplied the resistivity series. Following 2.5 MeV irradiation, low-temperature penetration-depth curves evolved from nodal behavior to an activated regime, then back to gapless behavior with further disorder. The authors interpreted that sequence with accidental nodes and sign-changing multiband pairing. Here “topological change” concerns the gap's nodal structure; it does not establish a Majorana-carrying topological superconductor. The 80 mK measurement floor and 20–22 K irradiation bath remain separate from transition records. [R7](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2)

Hatter measured manganese phthalocyanine on Pb(111) at 1.2 K with a superconducting Pb tip. The resolved Shiba triplets have 50–100 microelectronvolt widths and separations up to 400 microelectronvolts. The measured conductance includes the tip density of states: near-zero sample excitation energy appears near the tip-gap bias, not necessarily at zero measured bias. The authors numerically deconvolved the spectra and used relative spectral weights to distinguish impurity ground states and magnetic-anisotropy effects. This is local spectroscopy, not a 1.2 K transition measurement or a standalone Majorana demonstration. [R8](#ref-source-54e8e8bbd28f62fd)

## Limits and disputes

A suppression curve alone is not a unique symmetry test. Separate changes in pairing interaction, band filling, magnetic moments and defect morphology from elastic scattering; distinguish intra- and interband processes. Gapless superconductivity is also different from destruction of superconducting order. The classical single-impurity formula cannot establish the quantum impurity parity change on its own; spectroscopy, tip calibration, spatial structure and the appropriate many-body model are needed. [R3](#ref-source-c9bed6791b995641) [R5](#ref-source-3a528aeee1b7cf04) [R6](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83) [R7](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2) [R8](#ref-source-54e8e8bbd28f62fd)

Defects can help current transport by pinning vortices while harming other properties. BaZrO3-containing YBCO films illustrate an in-field current improvement that must be evaluated at specified temperature, field and orientation, rather than equated with higher $T_c$. Dirty two-gap theory also permits enhanced orbital upper critical fields under particular diffusivity and coupling conditions. Neither result implies monotonic improvement with damage, a universal type-I to type-II conversion, or an enhanced Pauli limit. [R9](#ref-source-51c947cf11bea72e) [R10](#ref-source-7ba854cc57960377)

The present article has selected original-paper and equation checks. The original AG full text and Shiba full derivation have not been read; Yu's original abstract and opening discussion were checked from scans. The detailed AG/YSR equation convention was cross-checked in the Balatsky author manuscript, with final-version comparison still open. Full supplements, raw-data reanalysis and complete scientific acceptance remain unfinished. [R2](#ref-source-daf8f301de81a726) [R3](#ref-source-c9bed6791b995641) [R4](#ref-source-7383f31da800ca9e) [R5](#ref-source-3a528aeee1b7cf04)

## Discovery implications

Use controlled defect series with repeat measurements before irradiation, after irradiation and after annealing. Compare $T_c$, gap spectra, residual resistivity, magnetic response, $H_{c2}$ and $J_c$ under matched conditions. Preserve sample identifiers and probe-specific transition criteria in machine-readable records; never merge irradiation temperatures, spectroscopy temperatures and superconducting transitions into a single temperature ranking. [R6](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83) [R7](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2) [R8](#ref-source-54e8e8bbd28f62fd) [R9](#ref-source-51c947cf11bea72e)

## Related topics

Compare [isotropic s-wave pairing](/scwiki/s-wave), [sign-changing s-wave pairing](/scwiki/s-plus-minus), [chemical substitution](/scwiki/chemical-doping), [magnetic fields](/scwiki/magnetic-field) and [critical current](/scwiki/critical-current).

## Experimental criteria

Prozorov studied Ba(Fe1−xRux)2As2 with WDS composition $x=0.24$ using 2.5 MeV electrons. Irradiation and in-situ resistivity measurements took place near 22 K; the initial superconducting transition is reported as 17.8 K in the methods and 17.85 K in the transport figure. Warming to room temperature between runs partially annealed the damage, by up to about 30%. The same contacts were retained. Increased resistivity and suppressed $T_c$ were compatible with the authors' multiband sign-changing scenario, whose interband/intraband scattering ratio matters. The 22 K irradiation temperature is not $T_c$, and no unverified onset, midpoint or zero-resistance label is assigned here. [R6](#ref-source-23c62b46f5681d83)

Mizukami's BaFe2(As1−xPx)2 crystals had $x=0.33$–0.36 and initial transitions of 28, 29 or 30 K. The 28/29 K batches were tracked by tunnel-diode-oscillator frequency shifts; the 30 K crystal also supplied the resistivity series. Following 2.5 MeV irradiation, low-temperature penetration-depth curves evolved from nodal behavior to an activated regime, then back to gapless behavior with further disorder. The authors interpreted that sequence with accidental nodes and sign-changing multiband pairing. Here “topological change” concerns the gap's nodal structure; it does not establish a Majorana-carrying topological superconductor. The 80 mK measurement floor and 20–22 K irradiation bath remain separate from transition records. [R7](#ref-source-c4a5c25b97df43a2)

Hatter measured manganese phthalocyanine on Pb(111) at 1.2 K with a superconducting Pb tip. The resolved Shiba triplets have 50–100 microelectronvolt widths and separations up to 400 microelectronvolts. The measured conductance includes the tip density of states: near-zero sample excitation energy appears near the tip-gap bias, not necessarily at zero measured bias. The authors numerically deconvolved the spectra and used relative spectral weights to distinguish impurity ground states and magnetic-anisotropy effects. This is local spectroscopy, not a 1.2 K transition measurement or a standalone Majorana demonstration. [R8](#ref-source-54e8e8bbd28f62fd)

Separate symmetry-sensitive scattering, impurity spectroscopy and useful vortex pinning, with explicit dose, annealing and temperature criteria.

## Scope

Record defect chemistry, irradiation particle and energy, dose, temperature, annealing history and sample geometry. A larger residual resistivity does not by itself specify the pair-breaking rate or prove a change of carrier density. It is not immunity to arbitrary chemical substitution, localization, magnetic scattering or spatial granularity. Constant $T_c$ alone does not uniquely determine pairing symmetry. Rate conventions differ; do not substitute a transport lifetime without deriving its relation to this $\Gamma$. Local numerical checks compare the equation with independently bounded Matsubara sums. The original AG paper remains a bibliographic anchor, not a completed original-text audit.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-daf8f301de81a726, source-3a528aeee1b7cf04, source-23c62b46f5681d83.

Conditions: Separate magnetic and potential scattering, defect morphology/annealing, irradiation/measurement temperatures, transition criteria and tip spectral convolution.

### scwiki-e7-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

For one classical magnetic scattering channel in a particle–hole-symmetric, isotropic host with a fixed gap, use exchange $J\mathbf S\cdot\mathbf s$, $\mathbf s=\boldsymbol\sigma/2$, and normal density of states per spin $N_0$. Defining $\alpha=\pi N_0JS/2$ and potential strength $\beta=\pi N_0V$, one signed Yu–Shiba–Rusinov branch is $E/\Delta=(1+\beta^2-\alpha^2)/\sqrt{(1+\beta^2-\alpha^2)^2+4\alpha^2}$; its particle–hole partner has opposite energy. At $V=0$, this reduces to $(1-\alpha^2)/(1+\alpha^2)$. A zero crossing requires $\alpha^2=1+\beta^2$ in this model. These conventions and phase-shift checks do not solve quantum Kondo screening, multiple orbital channels or self-consistent gap suppression.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-c9bed6791b995641, source-7383f31da800ca9e, source-3a528aeee1b7cf04, source-54e8e8bbd28f62fd.

Conditions: Separate magnetic and potential scattering, defect morphology/annealing, irradiation/measurement temperatures, transition criteria and tip spectral convolution.

### scwiki-e7-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

Dose is a separate quantity: an electron charge dose of 1 C/cm² corresponds to approximately $6.24\times10^{18}$ incident electrons/cm². The 3.4 C/cm² exposure in Prozorov's protocol is about $2.12\times10^{19}$ electrons/cm². Neither number is the surviving defect concentration; displacement cross sections, recombination and annealing enter that conversion.

### scwiki-e7-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Prozorov studied Ba(Fe1−xRux)2As2 with WDS composition $x=0.24$ using 2.5 MeV electrons. Irradiation and in-situ resistivity measurements took place near 22 K; the initial superconducting transition is reported as 17.8 K in the methods and 17.85 K in the transport figure. Warming to room temperature between runs partially annealed the damage, by up to about 30%. The same contacts were retained. Increased resistivity and suppressed $T_c$ were compatible with the authors' multiband sign-changing scenario, whose interband/intraband scattering ratio matters. The 22 K irradiation temperature is not $T_c$, and no unverified onset, midpoint or zero-resistance label is assigned here.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-23c62b46f5681d83.

### scwiki-e7-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Mizukami's BaFe2(As1−xPx)2 crystals had $x=0.33$–0.36 and initial transitions of 28, 29 or 30 K. The 28/29 K batches were tracked by tunnel-diode-oscillator frequency shifts; the 30 K crystal also supplied the resistivity series. Following 2.5 MeV irradiation, low-temperature penetration-depth curves evolved from nodal behavior to an activated regime, then back to gapless behavior with further disorder. The authors interpreted that sequence with accidental nodes and sign-changing multiband pairing. Here “topological change” concerns the gap's nodal structure; it does not establish a Majorana-carrying topological superconductor. The 80 mK measurement floor and 20–22 K irradiation bath remain separate from transition records.

### scwiki-e7-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Hatter measured manganese phthalocyanine on Pb(111) at 1.2 K with a superconducting Pb tip. The resolved Shiba triplets have 50–100 microelectronvolt widths and separations up to 400 microelectronvolts. The measured conductance includes the tip density of states: near-zero sample excitation energy appears near the tip-gap bias, not necessarily at zero measured bias. The authors numerically deconvolved the spectra and used relative spectral weights to distinguish impurity ground states and magnetic-anisotropy effects. This is local spectroscopy, not a 1.2 K transition measurement or a standalone Majorana demonstration.

### scwiki-e7-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

A suppression curve alone is not a unique symmetry test. Separate changes in pairing interaction, band filling, magnetic moments and defect morphology from elastic scattering; distinguish intra- and interband processes. Gapless superconductivity is also different from destruction of superconducting order. The classical single-impurity formula cannot establish the quantum impurity parity change on its own; spectroscopy, tip calibration, spatial structure and the appropriate many-body model are needed.

### scwiki-e7-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

Defects can help current transport by pinning vortices while harming other properties. BaZrO3-containing YBCO films illustrate an in-field current improvement that must be evaluated at specified temperature, field and orientation, rather than equated with higher $T_c$. Dirty two-gap theory also permits enhanced orbital upper critical fields under particular diffusivity and coupling conditions. Neither result implies monotonic improvement with damage, a universal type-I to type-II conversion, or an enhanced Pauli limit.

Use controlled defect series with repeat measurements before irradiation, after irradiation and after annealing. articles.body:
## Scope

Dimensionality compares geometry with physical length scales. A layered crystal, a two-dimensional electronic band and a superconducting film with a nearly uniform order parameter through its thickness are different descriptions. Compare thickness with the perpendicular coherence length, wire transverse dimensions with coherence lengths, and lateral size with magnetic screening lengths. Interlayer coupling, substrate, disorder and carrier density can change when layers are removed. Reduced thickness alone does not establish an ideal two-dimensional phase transition. [R1](#ref-source-408113812912d816) [R6](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83)

For a short-range two-dimensional phase model, vortex–antivortex unbinding separates quasi-long-range order from a disordered phase. The relevant stiffness is renormalized by fluctuations. In a charged film, magnetic screening changes the vortex interaction at long distance: Kosterlitz and Thouless explicitly identified this limitation in their original paper. BKT-like behavior requires an appropriate range of length, current and temperature scales; do not transfer the neutral infinite-system limit to every finite superconducting sheet. [R1](#ref-source-408113812912d816) [R2](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Mathematical assumptions

Define the sheet phase stiffness $J$ in energy units by $F_\theta=(J/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2$. A single vortex has logarithmic energy $\pi J\ln(L/a)$ and positional entropy $2k_B\ln(L/a)$ within this model, where $a$ is a core cutoff. The universal jump is $J_R(T_{\rm BKT}^-)=2k_BT_{\rm BKT}/\pi$, with the long-distance **renormalized** stiffness $J_R$. The elementary energy–entropy balance explains the scale; it is not a replacement for the renormalization calculation. For a local sheet inductance $L_k$ per square, the corresponding stiffness convention is $J=\hbar^2/(4e^2L_k)$. Frequency, vortex response and finite size matter when comparing a measured inductance with the static jump. [R1](#ref-source-408113812912d816) [R2](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

In a uniform narrow wire near its mean-field transition, the zero-current Ginzburg–Landau saddle gives $\Delta F_0=(8\sqrt2/3)u_c A\xi$, where $u_c=B_c^2/(2\mu_0)$ is the SI condensation-energy density and $A$ is cross-sectional area. A local check integrates the normalized saddle $f(y)=\tanh(y/\sqrt2)$, $y=x/\xi$, in $\int[(1-f^2)^2+2(df/dy)^2]dy$. This checks the barrier factor under those assumptions, not a finite-current barrier, quantum tunneling action or the full LAMH prefactor. The original Langer–Ambegaokar and McCumber–Halperin full derivations have not been retrieved for this review. [R3](#ref-source-aa12d674a498e02d) [R4](#ref-source-866d4492c91f5b39)

For rare independent thermal phase slips, define $r_0$ explicitly as the zero-bias rate **per direction**. With $\Phi_0=h/(2e)$, detailed balance gives $r_\pm=r_0\exp[\pm I\Phi_0/(2k_BT)]$ to leading small-bias barrier tilt, $V=\Phi_0(r_+-r_-)$ and $R_{I\to0}=\Phi_0^2r_0/(k_BT)$. The thermal activation factor belongs inside $r_0$; this definition avoids confusing a total event rate with a directional one. Low-temperature resistance saturation alone does not identify coherent quantum phase slips. [R3](#ref-source-aa12d674a498e02d) [R4](#ref-source-866d4492c91f5b39) [R8](#ref-source-42e0dec220b7b3ea)

## Experimental criteria

Xi's encapsulated NbSe2 devices distinguish several transition definitions. In the checked author manuscript, the monolayer Aslamazov–Larkin fit gives $T_{c0}\approx3.0$ K, close to the 50% normal-resistance criterion; the inferred BKT transition lies near the 1% criterion. Those are separate quantities. Normal resistance was taken at 8 K. The four-terminal field series used a 50% criterion, while a separate two-terminal monolayer device used a rapid-resistance-drop criterion. The 0.3 K measurement floor is not another transition. Large in-plane critical fields support the authors' Ising-pairing interpretation under their model, rather than proving triplet pairing by themselves. The journal issue is from 2016; online publication was 9 November 2015. [R6](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83)

Bezryadin's nanotube-templated amorphous Mo79Ge21 wires were approximately 10 nm or less in diameter and 95–185 nm long. The resistance drop near 5.5 K belongs to the electrodes, after which the wire resistance could be isolated. In the studied series, samples on opposite sides of a normal-resistance scale near $R_Q=h/(4e^2)\approx6.45$ kilohms showed decreasing or increasing resistance on cooling. One superconducting sample was checked down to 50 mK. These are sample-specific transport observations and a quantum-fluctuation interpretation, not a universal wire transition temperature or universal critical resistance for all geometries and environments. [R7](#ref-source-9ebba9ba0616123e)

Astafiev's InOx loop experiment used microwave spectroscopy to investigate coherent coupling between flux states. The checked author version describes a 35 nm film, a narrow segment about 40 nm wide and 400 nm long, and measurements at 40 mK. A two-state fit gave $E_S/h=4.9$ GHz and persistent current 24 nA for the illustrated device; resonator features distorted portions of the spectrum. The film's separately reported 2.7 K transition is distinct from the loop spectroscopy temperature. Coherent coupling evidence is stronger and different in kind from fitting a dissipative resistance tail; the selected readings do not reproduce the complete supplementary analysis. [R8](#ref-source-42e0dec220b7b3ea)

For aluminum nanoparticles, Black, Ralph and Tinkham reported even/odd differences in tunneling excitation thresholds and field suppression of a spectroscopic gap in sufficiently large particles, with radius roughly 5 nm or greater in their abstract. Radius is not diameter. Discrete levels, charging and parity enter the interpretation. Local pairing signatures do not demonstrate zero resistance across an isolated grain or global phase coherence in an array. This entry currently relies on the original publisher abstract, without a complete original-text audit. [R9](#ref-source-9fd1a118a8a9914b)

## Limits and disputes

Use several diagnostics for a BKT interpretation: nonlinear current–voltage behavior, stiffness and resistance scaling over justified windows, together with finite-size, heating and inhomogeneity checks. A convenient fit does not establish its asymptotic assumptions. sections.title: Experimental criteria
sections.markdown:
## Experimental criteria

Xi's encapsulated NbSe2 devices distinguish several transition definitions. In the checked author manuscript, the monolayer Aslamazov–Larkin fit gives $T_{c0}\approx3.0$ K, close to the 50% normal-resistance criterion; the inferred BKT transition lies near the 1% criterion. Those are separate quantities. Normal resistance was taken at 8 K. The four-terminal field series used a 50% criterion, while a separate two-terminal monolayer device used a rapid-resistance-drop criterion. The 0.3 K measurement floor is not another transition. Large in-plane critical fields support the authors' Ising-pairing interpretation under their model, rather than proving triplet pairing by themselves. The journal issue is from 2016; online publication was 9 November 2015. [R6](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83)

Bezryadin's nanotube-templated amorphous Mo79Ge21 wires were approximately 10 nm or less in diameter and 95–185 nm long. The resistance drop near 5.5 K belongs to the electrodes, after which the wire resistance could be isolated. In the studied series, samples on opposite sides of a normal-resistance scale near $R_Q=h/(4e^2)\approx6.45$ kilohms showed decreasing or increasing resistance on cooling. One superconducting sample was checked down to 50 mK. These are sample-specific transport observations and a quantum-fluctuation interpretation, not a universal wire transition temperature or universal critical resistance for all geometries and environments. [R7](#ref-source-9ebba9ba0616123e)

Astafiev's InOx loop experiment used microwave spectroscopy to investigate coherent coupling between flux states. The checked author version describes a 35 nm film, a narrow segment about 40 nm wide and 400 nm long, and measurements at 40 mK. A two-state fit gave $E_S/h=4.9$ GHz and persistent current 24 nA for the illustrated device; resonator features distorted portions of the spectrum. The film's separately reported 2.7 K transition is distinct from the loop spectroscopy temperature. Coherent coupling evidence is stronger and different in kind from fitting a dissipative resistance tail; the selected readings do not reproduce the complete supplementary analysis. [R8](#ref-source-42e0dec220b7b3ea)

For aluminum nanoparticles, Black, Ralph and Tinkham reported even/odd differences in tunneling excitation thresholds and field suppression of a spectroscopic gap in sufficiently large particles, with radius roughly 5 nm or greater in their abstract. Radius is not diameter. Discrete levels, charging and parity enter the interpretation. Local pairing signatures do not demonstrate zero resistance across an isolated grain or global phase coherence in an array. This entry currently relies on the original publisher abstract, without a complete original-text audit. [R9](#ref-source-9fd1a118a8a9914b)

Interlayer coupling, substrate, disorder and carrier density can change when layers are removed. Reduced thickness alone does not establish an ideal two-dimensional phase transition.

### scwiki-e8-claim-scope-2

For a short-range two-dimensional phase model, vortex–antivortex unbinding separates quasi-long-range order from a disordered phase. The relevant stiffness is renormalized by fluctuations. In a charged film, magnetic screening changes the vortex interaction at long distance: Kosterlitz and Thouless explicitly identified this limitation in their original paper. BKT-like behavior requires an appropriate range of length, current and temperature scales; do not transfer the neutral infinite-system limit to every finite superconducting sheet.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-408113812912d816, source-8f81510a80c35e3a.

Conditions: Specify effective dimension, finite size and screening, probe/transition criterion, sample and temperature; distinguish thermal activation, coherent coupling and local pairing.

### scwiki-e8-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

Define the sheet phase stiffness $J$ in energy units by $F_\theta=(J/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2$. A single vortex has logarithmic energy $\pi J\ln(L/a)$ and positional entropy $2k_B\ln(L/a)$ within this model, where $a$ is a core cutoff. The universal jump is $J_R(T_{\rm BKT}^-)=2k_BT_{\rm BKT}/\pi$, with the long-distance **renormalized** stiffness $J_R$. The elementary energy–entropy balance explains the scale; it is not a replacement for the renormalization calculation. For a local sheet inductance $L_k$ per square, the corresponding stiffness convention is $J=\hbar^2/(4e^2L_k)$. Frequency, vortex response and finite size matter when comparing a measured inductance with the static jump.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-408113812912d816, source-8f81510a80c35e3a.

Conditions: Specify effective dimension, finite size and screening, probe/transition criterion, sample and temperature; distinguish thermal activation, coherent coupling and local pairing.

Verification scope: Selected original text, author versions or clearly marked abstracts plus bounded calculations; full scientific acceptance open.

### scwiki-e8-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

In a uniform narrow wire near its mean-field transition, the zero-current Ginzburg–Landau saddle gives $\Delta F_0=(8\sqrt2/3)u_c A\xi$, where $u_c=B_c^2/(2\mu_0)$ is the SI condensation-energy density and $A$ is cross-sectional area. A local check integrates the normalized saddle $f(y)=\tanh(y/\sqrt2)$, $y=x/\xi$, in $\int[(1-f^2)^2+2(df/dy)^2]dy$. This checks the barrier factor under those assumptions, not a finite-current barrier, quantum tunneling action or the full LAMH prefactor. The original Langer–Ambegaokar and McCumber–Halperin full derivations have not been retrieved for this review.

### scwiki-e8-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

For rare independent thermal phase slips, define $r_0$ explicitly as the zero-bias rate **per direction**. With $\Phi_0=h/(2e)$, detailed balance gives $r_\pm=r_0\exp[\pm I\Phi_0/(2k_BT)]$ to leading small-bias barrier tilt, $V=\Phi_0(r_+-r_-)$ and $R_{I\to0}=\Phi_0^2r_0/(k_BT)$. The thermal activation factor belongs inside $r_0$; this definition avoids confusing a total event rate with a directional one. Low-temperature resistance saturation alone does not identify coherent quantum phase slips.

### scwiki-e8-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Xi's encapsulated NbSe2 devices distinguish several transition definitions. In the checked author manuscript, the monolayer Aslamazov–Larkin fit gives $T_{c0}\approx3.0$ K, close to the 50% normal-resistance criterion; the inferred BKT transition lies near the 1% criterion. Those are separate quantities. Normal resistance was taken at 8 K. The four-terminal field series used a 50% criterion, while a separate two-terminal monolayer device used a rapid-resistance-drop criterion. The 0.3 K measurement floor is not another transition. Large in-plane critical fields support the authors' Ising-pairing interpretation under their model, rather than proving triplet pairing by themselves. The journal issue is from 2016; online publication was 9 November 2015.

Bezryadin's nanotube-templated amorphous Mo79Ge21 wires were approximately 10 nm or less in diameter and 95–185 nm long. Astafiev's InOx loop experiment used microwave spectroscopy to investigate coherent coupling between flux states. ### scwiki-e8-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

Use several diagnostics for a BKT interpretation: nonlinear current–voltage behavior, stiffness and resistance scaling over justified windows, together with finite-size, heating and inhomogeneity checks. A convenient fit does not establish its asymptotic assumptions. Likewise, Giordano's early indium-wire work reported low-temperature deviations from thermal-activation predictions consistent with quantum tunneling; it should not be generalized into a rule that every residual resistance tail proves quantum phase slips. Weak links, contacts, normal regions and electromagnetic environment need independent controls.

articles.body:
## Scope

A twist angle controls the relative orientation of two layers, changing the moiré pattern and the coupled electronic Hamiltonian. It does not independently specify carrier filling, interlayer tunneling, disorder, pairing interaction or superconducting topology. The original continuum model explains narrow bands and suppressed Dirac velocity at particular parameter values; observing a moiré pattern alone does not demonstrate a flat band or superconductivity. [R1](#ref-source-28797be9898b68b5)

Magic-angle graphene supplies experimentally accessible correlated phases, but an adjacent insulating state does not uniquely identify a one-band Mott mechanism or a common pairing mediator. The 2018 correlated-insulator and superconductivity papers are distinct sources, with different questions and evidence. Pressure-dependent superconductivity further shows why nominal angle cannot be treated as the only tuning parameter. [R2](#ref-source-be5e45f3ed46d90b) [R3](#ref-source-90c67b111a6e919c) [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

## Mathematical assumptions

For two matched, unstrained hexagonal lattices, define $a=0.246$ nm as graphene's lattice constant, **not** its carbon–carbon bond length. Then $L_m=a/[2\sin(\theta/2)]$, $A_m=\sqrt3L_m^2/2$ and $L_m\approx a/\theta$ for a small angle expressed in radians. Bistritzer–MacDonald's manuscript instead calls the bond length $a$, so its numerator is $\sqrt3a$: these conventions are equivalent. Using the bond length in the lattice-constant formula would underestimate the period by $\sqrt3$ and overestimate the inferred full-filling density by a factor of three. [R1](#ref-source-28797be9898b68b5) [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

With four spin–valley states per moiré band, define the full-band density $n_s=4/A_m$ and filling $\nu=nA_m=4n/n_s$, measured relative to charge neutrality. At 1.10°, the ideal geometry gives $L_m\approx12.81$ nm and $n_s\approx2.81\times10^{12}$ cm⁻². This is a calculated reference, not a measured device value. The small-angle sensitivity is $\delta n_s/n_s\approx2\delta\theta/\theta$; the exact logarithmic derivative is $d\ln n_s/d\theta=\cot(\theta/2)$. A contact-averaged filling estimate cannot resolve a local twist/strain map, and broken-symmetry states need not retain fourfold degeneracy. [R1](#ref-source-28797be9898b68b5) [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

Let $k_\theta=2K\sin(\theta/2)$, $K=4\pi/(3a)$, and $\alpha=w/(\hbar v_Fk_\theta)$, using wavevector units for $k_\theta$. In the first-shell approximation with the small layer-rotation correction neglected, $v_*/v_F=(1-3\alpha^2)/(1+6\alpha^2)$. Its zero at $\alpha=1/\sqrt3$ illustrates velocity cancellation, not an exact experimental magic angle. Tunneling, lattice relaxation and strain affect a realistic calculation. Our local check covers reciprocal geometry, density conversion and the stated algebraic zero; it does not diagonalize the complete continuum Hamiltonian or calculate a superconducting transition. [R1](#ref-source-28797be9898b68b5) [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

## Experimental criteria

Cao's published superconductivity paper labels M1 at 1.16° and M2 at 1.05°. Figure 2 assigns maximum half-normal-resistance transition temperatures of about 0.5 K to M1 and 1.7 K to M2; the figure and caption resolve the device assignment. Both reached the reported zero-resistance state at the 70 mK measurement floor. A separate tentative cubic current–voltage fit for M2 at $n=-1.44\times10^{12}$ cm⁻² gave $T_{\rm BKT}\approx1.0$ K. The midpoint, inferred BKT scale and measurement floor must remain separate records. [R3](#ref-source-90c67b111a6e919c)

Yankowitz's nominal 1.27° device D2 developed superconducting transport under hydrostatic pressure. The published pressure plot defines $T_c$ by the intersection of low- and high-temperature linear fits, and the reported resistance falls to a roughly 10-ohm noise floor. The author supplement lists approximately 3.1 K at 1.33 GPa and 1.7 K at 2.21 GPa; the 300 mK base temperature is separate. These fitted transition temperatures should not be relabeled as exact zero-resistance or half-resistance thresholds. The same supplement reports removal, solvent cleaning and reloading between these pressures, which adds a possible disorder change to the pressure comparison. [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

The same study's ambient-pressure D1, at approximately 1.14°, had fitted transition scales near 0.4 K for holes and 0.25 K for electrons, with a 10 mK base temperature. Different contacts showed different full-filling densities; the final text reports moiré unit-cell-area variations up to roughly 30% within a device. The authors used full-filling features and quantum-oscillation extrapolations to estimate angle. They did not establish a uniform angle at every point merely by quoting two decimal places. [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

Tanaka and colleagues' 2025 paper combines microwave kinetic inductance and transport to study superfluid stiffness. The checked earlier manuscript uses a parallel proximitized-edge circuit model and an assumed active-region aspect ratio to convert inductance into sheet stiffness. It distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base from an approximately 40 mK device temperature and uses a half-normal-resistance transition scale near 1 K over much of the dome. Its comparison supports a quantum-geometric contribution and anisotropic gap interpretation without extracting a model-independent geometric fraction or uniquely determining the pairing mediator. [R5](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

## Limits and disputes

Compare local geometry, filling calibration, contacts and thermal history before interpreting differences between devices. ## Mathematical assumptions

For two matched, unstrained hexagonal lattices, define $a=0.246$ nm as graphene's lattice constant, **not** its carbon–carbon bond length. Then $L_m=a/[2\sin(\theta/2)]$, $A_m=\sqrt3L_m^2/2$ and $L_m\approx a/\theta$ for a small angle expressed in radians. Bistritzer–MacDonald's manuscript instead calls the bond length $a$, so its numerator is $\sqrt3a$: these conventions are equivalent. Using the bond length in the lattice-constant formula would underestimate the period by $\sqrt3$ and overestimate the inferred full-filling density by a factor of three. [R1](#ref-source-28797be9898b68b5) [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

With four spin–valley states per moiré band, define the full-band density $n_s=4/A_m$ and filling $\nu=nA_m=4n/n_s$, measured relative to charge neutrality. At 1.10°, the ideal geometry gives $L_m\approx12.81$ nm and $n_s\approx2.81\times10^{12}$ cm⁻². This is a calculated reference, not a measured device value. The small-angle sensitivity is $\delta n_s/n_s\approx2\delta\theta/\theta$; the exact logarithmic derivative is $d\ln n_s/d\theta=\cot(\theta/2)$. [R1](#ref-source-28797be9898b68b5) [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

Let $k_\theta=2K\sin(\theta/2)$, $K=4\pi/(3a)$, and $\alpha=w/(\hbar v_Fk_\theta)$, using wavevector units for $k_\theta$. Its zero at $\alpha=1/\sqrt3$ illustrates velocity cancellation, not an exact experimental magic angle. Tunneling, lattice relaxation and strain affect a realistic calculation. [R1](#ref-source-28797be9898b68b5) [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

sections.title: Experimental criteria
sections.markdown:
## Experimental criteria

Cao's published superconductivity paper labels M1 at 1.16° and M2 at 1.05°. Figure 2 assigns maximum half-normal-resistance transition temperatures of about 0.5 K to M1 and 1.7 K to M2; the figure and caption resolve the device assignment. Both reached the reported zero-resistance state at the 70 mK measurement floor. A separate tentative cubic current–voltage fit for M2 at $n=-1.44\times10^{12}$ cm⁻² gave $T_{\rm BKT}\approx1.0$ K. The midpoint, inferred BKT scale and measurement floor must remain separate records. [R3](#ref-source-90c67b111a6e919c)

Yankowitz's nominal 1.27° device D2 developed superconducting transport under hydrostatic pressure. The published pressure plot defines $T_c$ by the intersection of low- and high-temperature linear fits, and the reported resistance falls to a roughly 10-ohm noise floor. The author supplement lists approximately 3.1 K at 1.33 GPa and 1.7 K at 2.21 GPa; the 300 mK base temperature is separate. These fitted transition temperatures should not be relabeled as exact zero-resistance or half-resistance thresholds. The same supplement reports removal, solvent cleaning and reloading between these pressures, which adds a possible disorder change to the pressure comparison. [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

The same study's ambient-pressure D1, at approximately 1.14°, had fitted transition scales near 0.4 K for holes and 0.25 K for electrons, with a 10 mK base temperature. Different contacts showed different full-filling densities; the final text reports moiré unit-cell-area variations up to roughly 30% within a device. The authors used full-filling features and quantum-oscillation extrapolations to estimate angle. They did not establish a uniform angle at every point merely by quoting two decimal places. [R4](#ref-source-e80d36514bb4144d)

Tanaka and colleagues' 2025 paper combines microwave kinetic inductance and transport to study superfluid stiffness. The checked earlier manuscript uses a parallel proximitized-edge circuit model and an assumed active-region aspect ratio to convert inductance into sheet stiffness. It distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base from an approximately 40 mK device temperature and uses a half-normal-resistance transition scale near 1 K over much of the dome. Its comparison supports a quantum-geometric contribution and anisotropic gap interpretation without extracting a model-independent geometric fraction or uniquely determining the pairing mediator. [R5](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

Conditions: Distinguish lattice/bond length, radians/degrees, full-band degeneracy, local angle/strain, device/carrier branch, pressure and transition criteria.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and bounded geometry; complete scientific acceptance open.

### scwiki-e9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

For two matched, unstrained hexagonal lattices, define $a=0.246$ nm as graphene's lattice constant, **not** its carbon–carbon bond length. Then $L_m=a/[2\sin(\theta/2)]$, $A_m=\sqrt3L_m^2/2$ and $L_m\approx a/\theta$ for a small angle expressed in radians. Bistritzer–MacDonald's manuscript instead calls the bond length $a$, so its numerator is $\sqrt3a$: these conventions are equivalent. Using the bond length in the lattice-constant formula would underestimate the period by $\sqrt3$ and overestimate the inferred full-filling density by a factor of three.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-28797be9898b68b5, source-e80d36514bb4144d.

Conditions: Distinguish lattice/bond length, radians/degrees, full-band degeneracy, local angle/strain, device/carrier branch, pressure and transition criteria.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and bounded geometry; complete scientific acceptance open.

### scwiki-e9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

With four spin–valley states per moiré band, define the full-band density $n_s=4/A_m$ and filling $\nu=nA_m=4n/n_s$, measured relative to charge neutrality. At 1.10°, the ideal geometry gives $L_m\approx12.81$ nm and $n_s\approx2.81\times10^{12}$ cm⁻². This is a calculated reference, not a measured device value. The small-angle sensitivity is $\delta n_s/n_s\approx2\delta\theta/\theta$; the exact logarithmic derivative is $d\ln n_s/d\theta=\cot(\theta/2)$. A contact-averaged filling estimate cannot resolve a local twist/strain map, and broken-symmetry states need not retain fourfold degeneracy.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-28797be9898b68b5, source-e80d36514bb4144d.

Conditions: Distinguish lattice/bond length, radians/degrees, full-band degeneracy, local angle/strain, device/carrier branch, pressure and transition criteria.

### scwiki-e9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

Let $k_\theta=2K\sin(\theta/2)$, $K=4\pi/(3a)$, and $\alpha=w/(\hbar v_Fk_\theta)$, using wavevector units for $k_\theta$. In the first-shell approximation with the small layer-rotation correction neglected, $v_*/v_F=(1-3\alpha^2)/(1+6\alpha^2)$. Its zero at $\alpha=1/\sqrt3$ illustrates velocity cancellation, not an exact experimental magic angle. Tunneling, lattice relaxation and strain affect a realistic calculation. Our local check covers reciprocal geometry, density conversion and the stated algebraic zero; it does not diagonalize the complete continuum Hamiltonian or calculate a superconducting transition.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-28797be9898b68b5, source-e80d36514bb4144d.

Conditions: Distinguish lattice/bond length, radians/degrees, full-band degeneracy, local angle/strain, device/carrier branch, pressure and transition criteria.

### scwiki-e9-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Cao's published superconductivity paper labels M1 at 1.16° and M2 at 1.05°. Figure 2 assigns maximum half-normal-resistance transition temperatures of about 0.5 K to M1 and 1.7 K to M2; the figure and caption resolve the device assignment. Both reached the reported zero-resistance state at the 70 mK measurement floor. A separate tentative cubic current–voltage fit for M2 at $n=-1.44\times10^{12}$ cm⁻² gave $T_{\rm BKT}\approx1.0$ K. The midpoint, inferred BKT scale and measurement floor must remain separate records.

### scwiki-e9-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Yankowitz's nominal 1.27° device D2 developed superconducting transport under hydrostatic pressure. The published pressure plot defines $T_c$ by the intersection of low- and high-temperature linear fits, and the reported resistance falls to a roughly 10-ohm noise floor. The author supplement lists approximately 3.1 K at 1.33 GPa and 1.7 K at 2.21 GPa; the 300 mK base temperature is separate. These fitted transition temperatures should not be relabeled as exact zero-resistance or half-resistance thresholds. The same supplement reports removal, solvent cleaning and reloading between these pressures, which adds a possible disorder change to the pressure comparison.

The same study's ambient-pressure D1, at approximately 1.14°, had fitted transition scales near 0.4 K for holes and 0.25 K for electrons, with a 10 mK base temperature. Different contacts showed different full-filling densities; the final text reports moiré unit-cell-area variations up to roughly 30% within a device. The authors used full-filling features and quantum-oscillation extrapolations to estimate angle. They did not establish a uniform angle at every point merely by quoting two decimal places.

Tanaka and colleagues' 2025 paper combines microwave kinetic inductance and transport to study superfluid stiffness. The checked earlier manuscript uses a parallel proximitized-edge circuit model and an assumed active-region aspect ratio to convert inductance into sheet stiffness. It distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base from an approximately 40 mK device temperature and uses a half-normal-resistance transition scale near 1 K over much of the dome. Its comparison supports a quantum-geometric contribution and anisotropic gap interpretation without extracting a model-independent geometric fraction or uniquely determining the pairing mediator.

Compare local geometry, filling calibration, contacts and thermal history before interpreting differences between devices. Pressure-dependent transition curves, a nearby insulator or a broadened dome are not unique fingerprints of a pairing mechanism. Distinguish measured resistance, nonlinear response and stiffness from a proposed microscopic explanation. Likewise, normal-state band topology does not alone fix the topology of the superconducting quasiparticles. Transferring graphene conclusions to a lattice-mismatched semiconductor stack requires a new model and platform-specific evidence.

Optimize angle together with tunneling, strain, filling and phase stiffness. Store each transition under its device, carrier branch, pressure and criterion; keep measurement floors separate. articles.body:
## Scope

The quantum metric measures how a normalized quantum state changes with parameters after removing its unobservable overall phase. For Bloch bands, those parameters can be crystal momentum. It describes wavefunctions rather than only energy dispersion. A flat band can therefore have nonzero metric, while a large metric alone neither supplies an attractive interaction nor establishes superconductivity. Provost and Vallée developed a general state-manifold construction; later multiband superconductivity work connected band geometry to current response under specified assumptions. [R1](#ref-source-fbbc7a50ad47a3f8) [R2](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

This page uses a single isolated band or a specified smooth band subspace. It does not identify a single-particle Bloch metric with every many-body fidelity susceptibility. Keep the Hilbert space, parameter coordinates, orbital basis and selected subspace explicit. A geometric quantity can vary continuously without becoming a quantized topological invariant. [R1](#ref-source-fbbc7a50ad47a3f8) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a normalized state $|u\rangle$, let $P=|u\rangle\langle u|$ and $Q_{ij}=\langle\partial_i u|(1-P)|\partial_j u\rangle$. We define $g_{ij}=\mathrm{Re}\,Q_{ij}$ and $\Omega_{ij}=-2\mathrm{Im}\,Q_{ij}$, consistent with $A_i=i\langle u|\partial_i u\rangle$. Thus $Q_{ij}=g_{ij}-i\Omega_{ij}/2$. The nearby-state fidelity obeys $1-|\langle u(\mathbf k)|u(\mathbf k+d\mathbf k)\rangle|^2=g_{ij}dk_i dk_j+O(|d\mathbf k|^3)$. With physical wavevectors, the metric components have units of length squared; dimensionless lattice coordinates change those units. [R1](#ref-source-fbbc7a50ad47a3f8) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

For a rank-one projector, $Q_{ij}=\mathrm{Tr}[P(\partial_iP)(\partial_jP)]$ and $g_{ij}=\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}[(\partial_iP)(\partial_jP)]$. The projector is unchanged by $|u\rangle\rightarrow e^{i\phi(\mathbf k)}|u\rangle$, so this construction removes phase-gauge artifacts. For an isolated group of touching bands, use the smooth subspace projector and state the trace convention. A chosen individual eigenvector can become singular or ambiguous at a degeneracy. Phase-gauge invariance within a fixed orbital representation is not permission to ignore a momentum-dependent change of the underlying basis. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R5](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81)

Positivity of the two-coordinate matrix $Q$ gives $\det g\geq\Omega_{xy}^2/4$ and $g_{xx}+g_{yy}\geq|\Omega_{xy}|$. The trace statement refers to the selected common coordinate convention. For the spinor $u=(\cos(\theta/2),e^{i\varphi}\sin(\theta/2))$, our convention gives $g_{\theta\theta}=1/4$, $g_{\varphi\varphi}=\sin^2\theta/4$ and $\Omega_{\theta\varphi}=-\sin\theta/2$. This two-level example saturates the determinant inequality; a three-level family can satisfy it strictly. These are model checks, not measurements of a material. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

Normalization must be translated before comparing formulas. Liang's checked manuscript defines $\mathcal R_{ij}=2\mathrm{Tr}[P(\partial_iP)(\partial_jP)]$ and calls its real part the metric. Consequently $g^{\rm Liang}=2g$ in this page's convention, and that paper writes the fidelity distance with an extra factor of one half. Its curvature sign must likewise be translated consistently. This is a convention difference, not a contradiction or a factor-of-two enhancement of a physical stiffness. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

As a counterexample to equating metric with topology, take $u=(\cos(k_x/2),\sin(k_x/2))$, independent of $k_y$. The projector is periodic on a $2\pi$ torus, $g_{xx}=1/4$, and the Berry curvature vanishes. The Hamiltonian $H=E_0(2P-I)$ has flat eigenvalues $\pm E_0$ for positive constant $E_0$. It has nonzero metric and zero Chern number without introducing pairing. Our finite-difference checks compare projector derivatives, phase-transformed states and symmetric fidelity curvature; they do not calculate a superconducting response. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

## Experimental criteria

An experimental response may constrain band geometry through a model and matrix elements; it need not uniquely reconstruct every metric component. For superconductivity, distinguish the measured total stiffness from a decomposition into conventional and geometric terms. Report carrier filling, band window, temperature, units and the response-to-metric conversion. A successful fit does not by itself identify a unique microscopic pairing mechanism. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R4](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

Tanaka and colleagues' 2025 MATBG study combines microwave kinetic inductance and transport. The checked author version includes a parallel edge-proximity circuit and an assumed active-region aspect ratio. It distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base from an approximately 40 mK wired-device temperature, and a half-normal-resistance transition near 1 K across much of the gate range. These are different quantities. Its comparison supports a connection to quantum geometry without directly isolating a model-independent geometric fraction. This page stores the 40 mK value only as a measurement condition. [R4](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

## Limits and disputes

Peotta–Törmä's flat-band result assumes an interaction window between the bandwidth and separating band gaps, together with an appropriate uniform-pairing construction. Liang extends the response analysis, but the isolated-band expression retains time-reversal, orbital-uniform pairing and band-separation assumptions. Huhtinen and colleagues subsequently identify missing order-parameter-response terms in earlier formulas and connect isolated-flat-band stiffness to a minimal quantum metric. Therefore an arbitrary raw metric integral should not be presented as an automatically complete quantitative stiffness prediction. [R2](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R5](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81)

The review covers selected Peotta published passages, Liang author-version equations and Tanaka author methods; it does not complete their raw-data, full supplementary or final-version audits. Provost's original is checked at publisher-abstract scope. Huhtinen's published introduction and selected response derivation, pages 1–4, were checked; its full minimal-metric proof and band-touching analysis were not reproduced. The inherited F1 bibliography misattributes the MATBG paper to Randeria; the published authors are Tanaka and colleagues. Complete scientific acceptance remains open. [R1](#ref-source-fbbc7a50ad47a3f8) [R2](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R4](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056) [R5](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81)

## Discovery implications

Calculate geometry with a reproducible orbital convention and subspace, check mesh convergence and preserve normalization factors. Test pairing and total phase stiffness separately. A topological lower bound can be useful under its assumptions, but zero Chern number does not exclude useful geometry, and nonzero metric does not guarantee superconductivity. Geometry is one constraint in a material-specific calculation, alongside interactions, filling, disorder and phase coherence. [R2](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R5](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81)

## Related topics

Compare [geometric superfluid weight](/scwiki/geometric-superfluid-weight), [flat-band pairing](/scwiki/flat-band-pairing), [twist angle](/scwiki/twist-angle) and [dimensionality](/scwiki/dimensionality).

sections.markdown:
## Mathematical assumptions

For a normalized state $|u\rangle$, let $P=|u\rangle\langle u|$ and $Q_{ij}=\langle\partial_i u|(1-P)|\partial_j u\rangle$. We define $g_{ij}=\mathrm{Re}\,Q_{ij}$ and $\Omega_{ij}=-2\mathrm{Im}\,Q_{ij}$, consistent with $A_i=i\langle u|\partial_i u\rangle$. Thus $Q_{ij}=g_{ij}-i\Omega_{ij}/2$. The nearby-state fidelity obeys $1-|\langle u(\mathbf k)|u(\mathbf k+d\mathbf k)\rangle|^2=g_{ij}dk_i dk_j+O(|d\mathbf k|^3)$. With physical wavevectors, the metric components have units of length squared; dimensionless lattice coordinates change those units. [R1](#ref-source-fbbc7a50ad47a3f8) [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

For a rank-one projector, $Q_{ij}=\mathrm{Tr}[P(\partial_iP)(\partial_jP)]$ and $g_{ij}=\tfrac12\mathrm{Tr}[(\partial_iP)(\partial_jP)]$. The projector is unchanged by $|u\rangle\rightarrow e^{i\phi(\mathbf k)}|u\rangle$, so this construction removes phase-gauge artifacts. For an isolated group of touching bands, use the smooth subspace projector and state the trace convention. A chosen individual eigenvector can become singular or ambiguous at a degeneracy. Phase-gauge invariance within a fixed orbital representation is not permission to ignore a momentum-dependent change of the underlying basis. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R5](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81)

Positivity of the two-coordinate matrix $Q$ gives $\det g\geq\Omega_{xy}^2/4$ and $g_{xx}+g_{yy}\geq|\Omega_{xy}|$. The trace statement refers to the selected common coordinate convention. For the spinor $u=(\cos(\theta/2),e^{i\varphi}\sin(\theta/2))$, our convention gives $g_{\theta\theta}=1/4$, $g_{\varphi\varphi}=\sin^2\theta/4$ and $\Omega_{\theta\varphi}=-\sin\theta/2$. This two-level example saturates the determinant inequality; a three-level family can satisfy it strictly. These are model checks, not measurements of a material. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

Normalization must be translated before comparing formulas. Liang's checked manuscript defines $\mathcal R_{ij}=2\mathrm{Tr}[P(\partial_iP)(\partial_jP)]$ and calls its real part the metric. Consequently $g^{\rm Liang}=2g$ in this page's convention, and that paper writes the fidelity distance with an extra factor of one half. Its curvature sign must likewise be translated consistently. This is a convention difference, not a contradiction or a factor-of-two enhancement of a physical stiffness. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

As a counterexample to equating metric with topology, take $u=(\cos(k_x/2),\sin(k_x/2))$, independent of $k_y$. The projector is periodic on a $2\pi$ torus, $g_{xx}=1/4$, and the Berry curvature vanishes. The Hamiltonian $H=E_0(2P-I)$ has flat eigenvalues $\pm E_0$ for positive constant $E_0$. It has nonzero metric and zero Chern number without introducing pairing. Our finite-difference checks compare projector derivatives, phase-transformed states and symmetric fidelity curvature; they do not calculate a superconducting response. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

sections.title: Experimental criteria

## Experimental criteria

An experimental response may constrain band geometry through a model and matrix elements; it need not uniquely reconstruct every metric component. For superconductivity, distinguish the measured total stiffness from a decomposition into conventional and geometric terms. Report carrier filling, band window, temperature, units and the response-to-metric conversion. A successful fit does not by itself identify a unique microscopic pairing mechanism. [R3](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63) [R4](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

Tanaka and colleagues' 2025 MATBG study combines microwave kinetic inductance and transport. The checked author version includes a parallel edge-proximity circuit and an assumed active-region aspect ratio. It distinguishes a 20 mK refrigerator base from an approximately 40 mK wired-device temperature, and a half-normal-resistance transition near 1 K across much of the gate range. These are different quantities. Its comparison supports a connection to quantum geometry without directly isolating a model-independent geometric fraction. This page stores the 40 mK value only as a measurement condition. [R4](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)
