Meul and colleagues reported magnetic-field-induced superconductivity in Eu-Sn molybdenum chalcogenides in 1984. Their original abstract interprets the phase-diagram shape through compensation. URhGe supplies a distinct magnetic setting. Its ambient-pressure discovery includes thermodynamic superconducting evidence; Levy and colleagues subsequently identify a second field pocket near the roughly 12 T spin reorientation for a field along the b axis. Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-scope-2

A resistive decrease can indicate reduced dissipation without demonstrating a new bulk phase. Zero resistance establishes a conducting path; diamagnetic screening or a thermodynamic anomaly provides complementary information. Record whether an intermediate state is demonstrably normal or simply dissipative. A field sweep and a temperature sweep trace different paths through a phase diagram, and must not be joined as though every point belongs to one isotherm.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-3504ee9027165d0a, source-b57e3b2b5a90705f.

Conditions: Same specimen, measurement temperature, field orientation and resistive or bulk criterion; synthetic thresholds explicitly independent of any material fit.

Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

Jaccarino–Peter compensation concerns an exchange contribution opposing the applied field in the electron spin sector. An illustrative effective Zeeman field is $b_{\rm eff}=B-B_J(B,T)$, with every term expressed in tesla and positive $B_J$ defined to oppose positive applied $B$. The exchange term does not automatically cancel orbital coupling to the physical field. The original 1962 paper's identity is verified here; the following threshold example is independently calculated, rather than presented as its complete theory.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-849f7f4f675464de, source-b57e3b2b5a90705f.

Conditions: Same specimen, measurement temperature, field orientation and resistive or bulk criterion; synthetic thresholds explicitly independent of any material fit.

Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

At a fixed temperature, impose the artificial conditions $|b_{\rm eff}|\lt B_P$ and $0\le B\lt B_{\rm orb}$. With a constant saturated exchange field $J$, the permitted interval is the intersection of $(J-B_P,J+B_P)$ with the nonnegative orbital window. Its width is $\max[0,\min(B_{\rm orb},J+B_P)-\max(0,J-B_P)]$. For $J=8$ T and $B_P=2$ T, an orbital ceiling of 7 T leaves only $6\lt B\lt7$ T; a ceiling of 5 T leaves no interval. A universal width of $2B_P$ therefore fails even in this simplified model.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-849f7f4f675464de.

Conditions: Same specimen, measurement temperature, field orientation and resistive or bulk criterion; synthetic thresholds explicitly independent of any material fit.

Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

A constant saturated exchange field is unsuitable near zero field if the moments are unpolarized there. For an explicitly synthetic alternative, take $B_J=J\tanh(B/B_s)$. With $J=10$ T, $B_s=B_P=1$ T and $B_{\rm orb}=15$ T, the threshold model has a low-field interval ending near 0.112 T and a second interval approximately between 9 and 11 T. Reducing the orbital ceiling to 7 T removes the second interval. Reversing the exchange sign removes the compensation pocket. Root finding on monotonic segments agrees with 120,006 independent grid checks across six parameter sets. This is neither a material fit nor a self-consistent gap or free-energy calculation.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-849f7f4f675464de, source-b57e3b2b5a90705f.

Conditions: Same specimen, measurement temperature, field orientation and resistive or bulk criterion; synthetic thresholds explicitly independent of any material fit.

Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Meul and colleagues reported magnetic-field-induced superconductivity in Eu-Sn molybdenum chalcogenides in 1984. Their original abstract interprets the phase-diagram shape through compensation. The detailed composition, measurement protocol and complete curves have not been checked in this review, so an exact stoichiometry or numerical field window is not assigned from that abstract alone.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-d564bee026e788c7.

Conditions: Same specimen, measurement temperature, field orientation and resistive or bulk criterion; synthetic thresholds explicitly independent of any material fit.

Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-experimental-criteria-2

URhGe supplies a distinct magnetic setting. Its ambient-pressure discovery includes thermodynamic superconducting evidence; Levy and colleagues subsequently identify a second field pocket near the roughly 12 T spin reorientation for a field along the b axis. Gourgout and colleagues connect this region to transport and thermoelectric anomalies, a first-order magnetic transition and Fermi-surface changes. These observations constrain the mechanism without establishing a simple continuous quantum critical point or a unique pairing interaction. The original discovery abstracts and selected later author text support this limited comparison.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-15aec45a868e9fb9, source-e917adb251d93c59, source-c690ee5b95521000.

Conditions: Same specimen, measurement temperature, field orientation and resistive or bulk criterion; synthetic thresholds explicitly independent of any material fit.

Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Yang and colleagues' Sm0.95−xCa0.05EuxNiO2 study reports reentrance in Eu-rich films. For the 54-unit-cell x=0.34 specimen, resistance returns to zero above approximately 6.23 T at 2 K; mutual inductance on that specimen shows screening at 9 and 12 T, absent at 3 T. For x=0.32, the 13.04 T recovery is measured at 3 K, while persistence above 32 T refers to 1.7 K. Neither measurement temperature is a transition temperature for database filtering.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-3504ee9027165d0a.

Conditions: Same specimen, measurement temperature, field orientation and resistive or bulk criterion; synthetic thresholds explicitly independent of any material fit.

Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-experimental-criteria-4

Varbaro and colleagues investigate a separate Nd0.7Eu0.3NiO2 system. Their final Figure 3 combines two specimens using 20-percent and 50-percent normal-resistivity criteria; open and filled markers distinguish measurement facilities and specimens. These boundaries are not zero-resistance contours. The low-temperature Hall analysis uses a non-superconducting film on NdGaO3, whereas the superconducting transport uses LSAT-grown films. Their proposed competing Eu and Nd paramagnetic contributions should not be silently substituted for the magnetic interpretation of the Sm/Ca/Eu material.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-b57e3b2b5a90705f.

Conditions: Same specimen, measurement temperature, field orientation and resistive or bulk criterion; synthetic thresholds explicitly independent of any material fit.

Verification scope: Selected original sources and bounded independent calculations; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g3-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

The Sm/Ca/Eu author's revised manuscript does not establish the long-range magnetic structure. Its angular reentrance extends nearly in-plane for some dopings, and the compared angular maps use different temperatures. The 50-percent resistance contours and phenomenological compensation fits do not prove triplet pairing. These qualifications replace stronger statements in the fixed planning source.

### scwiki-g3-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

The public Sm/Ca/Eu dataset predates the checked manuscript revision. A read-only check of its Fig2 workbook preserves small negative baseline readings instead of clipping them to zero. Missing unit labels and an unverified noise floor prevent assigning an independently validated zero-resistance threshold from the spreadsheet alone. Complete correspondence between dataset and revised figures remains open. Separately, the URhGe author manuscript gives 12.75 T in its abstract but 11.75 T in its body; the published abstract gives 12.75 T. The discrepancy remains unresolved here.

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Full historical methods, selected final-version comparisons, absolute screening calibration, supplementary-data checks and independent material-specific model fits remain outstanding. Distinguish evidence supporting a superconducting state from evidence selecting its mechanism, and a measured high-field survival point from a measured upper critical field.

Compare full field paths with matched criteria, preserve field direction and specimen identity, and test temperature control and sweep dependence. Evaluate compensation against magnetic response and orbital limitations; evaluate magnetic reorientation against relevant magnetic and electronic probes. Retain disagreements rather than averaging incompatible definitions. A useful candidate explains several measurements under their actual conditions, not merely a high-field resistance drop.

articles.body:
## Scope

Reentrance describes a path through a phase diagram. Specify which phase returns, which parameter is swept, its direction, and what is held fixed. A field scan can produce superconducting, dissipative, and superconducting regimes in sequence. The historical term reentrant superconductor also covers a different sequence on cooling: normal, superconducting, then normal ferromagnetic. A pair of maxima in a transition-temperature curve does not by itself establish disconnected superconducting regions. [R1](#ref-source-435b794ed32c7604) [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2) [R6](#ref-source-e917adb251d93c59)

Use superconducting and normal labels only to the extent supported by the probes. A resistive intermediate regime may retain pairing or superconducting correlations, while zero resistance may follow a connected minority path. The same plotted boundary can have different meanings when it represents onset, a resistance fraction, a magnetic response or a thermodynamic anomaly. Paths assembled from different samples need explicit specimen labels. [R2](#ref-source-a1eeb97b9380bbe3) [R3](#ref-source-384b3a4f65f6493c) [R8](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

## Mathematical assumptions

An independent dimensionless example separates path geometry from mechanism. Define an imposed transition curve $T_c(x)=\max[0,1+v-(x^2-1)^2]$, and label a point superconducting when $0\lt T\lt T_c(x)$. The variable $x$ is a control coordinate, not an assigned pressure in GPa. With $v=0.2$, both peaks reach 1.2 and the valley remains at 0.2. A horizontal scan at $T=0.6$ crosses two superconducting intervals; at $T=0.1$ it crosses one connected interval. The two higher-temperature pockets therefore belong to one connected region in the full positive-temperature plane. [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2) [R5](#ref-source-da35691a947db0c5)

For $v=-0.2$, the imposed curve has a zero-temperature gap between two lobes. At $T=0.1$, its superconducting intervals run approximately from -1.355 to -0.404 and from 0.404 to 1.355. The analytic endpoints follow from $(x^2-1)^2=1+v-T$. Six cases, including scans above both peaks, agree with 120,000 independent grid evaluations. This construction demonstrates a logical distinction; it does not infer a second order parameter, pairing symmetry or microscopic interaction from the number of lobes. [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2)

A separate homogeneous example represents the historical temperature sequence. Let $f=a(T)s^2+s^4/2$, where $s\ge0$ and $a(T)=(T-1)(T-3)$ in dimensionless units. Its global minimum has $s^2=\max[0,-a(T)]$. Cooling through $T=4,2,0.5$ gives normal, superconducting and normal states. Only one superconducting interval exists. The model has continuous boundaries and no domains or hysteresis, so it cannot reproduce the observed history dependence of ErRh4B4. It illustrates which state reenters, not that material's magnetic mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-435b794ed32c7604) [R2](#ref-source-a1eeb97b9380bbe3)

## Experimental criteria

Sinha and colleagues' 1982 ErRh4B4 study combines neutron diffraction and resistivity. Its abstract reports an intermediate region below 1.2 K with ferromagnetic and modulated magnetic structures, followed below 0.71 K by disappearance of the modulation and superconductivity into a normal ferromagnetic state. The proposed coexistence of ferromagnetic and superconducting domains is an interpretation of these measurements, not proof of uniform coexistence at every microscopic position. The full historical methods remain unchecked here. [R1](#ref-source-435b794ed32c7604)

Prozorov and colleagues later resolve directional and historical differences using dynamic susceptibility. Their approximately 10 MHz probe uses a small excitation field, and their Figure 3 compares multiple temperature-ramp rates. Warming from the ferromagnetic state produces steps; cooling is more gradual. The reported rate insensitivity covers the tested ramps, not every possible relaxation timescale. Superconducting screening can conceal remaining ferromagnetic regions. Minor temperature loops also differ from the initial warming path, so sweep direction alone does not completely specify sample history. [R2](#ref-source-a1eeb97b9380bbe3)

Crespo and colleagues add local tunneling spectroscopy with a superconducting Pb tip. Their analysis deconvolves the tip response to infer the sample density of states. They select about twenty suitable surface locations; many other areas have suppressed or absent superconducting features. The representative heating and cooling transitions differ by about 90 mK. At 0.3 K the measured superconducting features come from the tip, while the inferred sample spectrum is featureless. This is a local, surface-sensitive absence within the measured conditions, not a complete volume census. The author manuscript identifies the crystal as the one previously used in the neutron and transport study. [R3](#ref-source-384b3a4f65f6493c)

Yuan and colleagues' original 2003 abstract reports disconnected pressure domes in partially Ge-substituted CeCu2Si2. Their later institutional report distinguishes the continuous region of the pure compound from the separated domes near substitution x=0.1. The comparison uses relative pressure $\Delta p=p-p_{c1}(x)$; the reference pressure depends on composition. Ge substitution changes both disorder and lattice volume. The report also combines comparison curves from different probes and uses distinct pressure-cell techniques across its range. These conditions prevent a universal pressure window from being assigned to every CeCu2(Si,Ge)2 sample. [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2) [R5](#ref-source-da35691a947db0c5)

URhGe and Eu-rich Sm/Ca/Eu nickelates provide field-scan examples, with different magnetic settings. The former has a second pocket near a b-axis spin reorientation; the latter combines selected high-field zero-resistance and screening observations. Keep these examples distinct from the normal-state reentrance on cooling in ErRh4B4. Similar phase-diagram shapes do not establish a shared microscopic mechanism. The sample-specific field and temperature conditions are treated in the linked field-induced-superconductivity page. [R6](#ref-source-e917adb251d93c59) [R7](#ref-source-c690ee5b95521000) [R8](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

## Limits and disputes

A lowest measured temperature is a detection boundary, not proof that the true transition temperature vanishes. The institutional pressure report describes measurements extending down to 50 mK; its absence of observed superconductivity cannot establish an exact zero-temperature interval without further evidence. Likewise, its discussion of a possible volume collapse cites diffraction on CeCu2Ge2 rather than a direct structural measurement on every specimen in its superconducting phase diagram. Magnetic and valence-mediated pairing remain interpretations to test against additional measurements. [R5](#ref-source-da35691a947db0c5)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The original Sinha and Science pressure papers have only abstract-level checks here; other selected passages and figures have more detailed review. Raw spectra, absolute magnetic calibration, complete final-version comparisons and historical field boundaries remain incomplete. Local gaplessness, resistance, screening and global phase coherence must not be treated as interchangeable observations. The independent examples verify their stated assumptions only. [R1](#ref-source-435b794ed32c7604) [R2](#ref-source-a1eeb97b9380bbe3) [R3](#ref-source-384b3a4f65f6493c) [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2)

## Discovery implications

Record the full path, sample history, parameter uncertainties, measurement floor and transition criterion with each reported pocket. Compare warming, cooling and partial loops before assigning an equilibrium boundary. Separate a new region in a measured slice from a distinct phase in the full diagram, then use magnetic, structural and spectroscopic measurements to test the proposed mechanism. Preserve unresolved differences instead of averaging incompatible temperatures or pressure origins. sections.markdown:
## Mathematical assumptions

An independent dimensionless example separates path geometry from mechanism. Define an imposed transition curve $T_c(x)=\max[0,1+v-(x^2-1)^2]$, and label a point superconducting when $0\lt T\lt T_c(x)$. The variable $x$ is a control coordinate, not an assigned pressure in GPa. With $v=0.2$, both peaks reach 1.2 and the valley remains at 0.2. A horizontal scan at $T=0.6$ crosses two superconducting intervals; at $T=0.1$ it crosses one connected interval. The two higher-temperature pockets therefore belong to one connected region in the full positive-temperature plane. [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2) [R5](#ref-source-da35691a947db0c5)

For $v=-0.2$, the imposed curve has a zero-temperature gap between two lobes. At $T=0.1$, its superconducting intervals run approximately from -1.355 to -0.404 and from 0.404 to 1.355. The analytic endpoints follow from $(x^2-1)^2=1+v-T$. Six cases, including scans above both peaks, agree with 120,000 independent grid evaluations. This construction demonstrates a logical distinction; it does not infer a second order parameter, pairing symmetry or microscopic interaction from the number of lobes. [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2)

A separate homogeneous example represents the historical temperature sequence. Let $f=a(T)s^2+s^4/2$, where $s\ge0$ and $a(T)=(T-1)(T-3)$ in dimensionless units. Its global minimum has $s^2=\max[0,-a(T)]$. Cooling through $T=4,2,0.5$ gives normal, superconducting and normal states. Only one superconducting interval exists. The model has continuous boundaries and no domains or hysteresis, so it cannot reproduce the observed history dependence of ErRh4B4. It illustrates which state reenters, not that material's magnetic mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-435b794ed32c7604) [R2](#ref-source-a1eeb97b9380bbe3)

sections.title: Experimental criteria
sections.markdown:
## Experimental criteria

Sinha and colleagues' 1982 ErRh4B4 study combines neutron diffraction and resistivity. Its abstract reports an intermediate region below 1.2 K with ferromagnetic and modulated magnetic structures, followed below 0.71 K by disappearance of the modulation and superconductivity into a normal ferromagnetic state. The proposed coexistence of ferromagnetic and superconducting domains is an interpretation of these measurements, not proof of uniform coexistence at every microscopic position. The full historical methods remain unchecked here. [R1](#ref-source-435b794ed32c7604)

Prozorov and colleagues later resolve directional and historical differences using dynamic susceptibility. Their approximately 10 MHz probe uses a small excitation field, and their Figure 3 compares multiple temperature-ramp rates. Warming from the ferromagnetic state produces steps; cooling is more gradual. The reported rate insensitivity covers the tested ramps, not every possible relaxation timescale. Superconducting screening can conceal remaining ferromagnetic regions. Minor temperature loops also differ from the initial warming path, so sweep direction alone does not completely specify sample history. [R2](#ref-source-a1eeb97b9380bbe3)

Crespo and colleagues add local tunneling spectroscopy with a superconducting Pb tip. Their analysis deconvolves the tip response to infer the sample density of states. They select about twenty suitable surface locations; many other areas have suppressed or absent superconducting features. The representative heating and cooling transitions differ by about 90 mK. At 0.3 K the measured superconducting features come from the tip, while the inferred sample spectrum is featureless. This is a local, surface-sensitive absence within the measured conditions, not a complete volume census. The author manuscript identifies the crystal as the one previously used in the neutron and transport study. [R3](#ref-source-384b3a4f65f6493c)

Yuan and colleagues' original 2003 abstract reports disconnected pressure domes in partially Ge-substituted CeCu2Si2. Their later institutional report distinguishes the continuous region of the pure compound from the separated domes near substitution x=0.1. The comparison uses relative pressure $\Delta p=p-p_{c1}(x)$; the reference pressure depends on composition. Ge substitution changes both disorder and lattice volume. The report also combines comparison curves from different probes and uses distinct pressure-cell techniques across its range. These conditions prevent a universal pressure window from being assigned to every CeCu2(Si,Ge)2 sample. [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2) [R5](#ref-source-da35691a947db0c5)

URhGe and Eu-rich Sm/Ca/Eu nickelates provide field-scan examples, with different magnetic settings. The former has a second pocket near a b-axis spin reorientation; the latter combines selected high-field zero-resistance and screening observations. Keep these examples distinct from the normal-state reentrance on cooling in ErRh4B4. Similar phase-diagram shapes do not establish a shared microscopic mechanism. The sample-specific field and temperature conditions are treated in the linked field-induced-superconductivity page. [R6](#ref-source-e917adb251d93c59) [R7](#ref-source-c690ee5b95521000) [R8](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

sections.title: Limits and disputes
sections.markdown:
## Limits and disputes

A lowest measured temperature is a detection boundary, not proof that the true transition temperature vanishes. The institutional pressure report describes measurements extending down to 50 mK; its absence of observed superconductivity cannot establish an exact zero-temperature interval without further evidence. Likewise, its discussion of a possible volume collapse cites diffraction on CeCu2Ge2 rather than a direct structural measurement on every specimen in its superconducting phase diagram. Magnetic and valence-mediated pairing remain interpretations to test against additional measurements. [R5](#ref-source-da35691a947db0c5)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The original Sinha and Science pressure papers have only abstract-level checks here; other selected passages and figures have more detailed review. Raw spectra, absolute magnetic calibration, complete final-version comparisons and historical field boundaries remain incomplete. Local gaplessness, resistance, screening and global phase coherence must not be treated as interchangeable observations. The independent examples verify their stated assumptions only. [R1](#ref-source-435b794ed32c7604) [R2](#ref-source-a1eeb97b9380bbe3) [R3](#ref-source-384b3a4f65f6493c) [R4](#ref-source-9be3bcd270b306a2)

sections.markdown:
## Discovery implications

Record the full path, sample history, parameter uncertainties, measurement floor and transition criterion with each reported pocket. Compare warming, cooling and partial loops before assigning an equilibrium boundary. Separate a new region in a measured slice from a distinct phase in the full diagram, then use magnetic, structural and spectroscopic measurements to test the proposed mechanism. Preserve unresolved differences instead of averaging incompatible temperatures or pressure origins. articles.body:
## Scope

The Jaccarino–Peter effect is compensation of the spin-splitting field experienced by conduction electrons. An exchange contribution opposite to the applied field can reduce Zeeman pair breaking near a finite field. It does not cancel the applied field everywhere in space or remove orbital coupling. A large critical field, a second superconducting pocket or the presence of magnetic ions alone does not establish this mechanism. The original proposal dates to 1962; its identity is verified here, but its full derivation has not been reread. [R1](#ref-source-849f7f4f675464de) [R3](#ref-source-7d153b141f652513)

Meul and colleagues' 1984 work reports field-induced superconductivity in a Eu–Sn molybdenum chalcogenide system and interprets it through compensation. The original abstract supports that historical connection. Exact composition, numerical field endpoints and complete measurement methods have not been verified here, so they are not promoted to universal material parameters. A classical example cannot supply the missing exchange measurement for a different compound. [R2](#ref-source-d564bee026e788c7)

## Mathematical assumptions

Choose the positive direction along the applied field and define the signed effective field as $B_{\mathrm{eff}}=B_{\mathrm{ext}}+B_{\mathrm{ex}}$. Compensation requires $B_{\mathrm{ex}}\lt0$ in this convention. In the collinear single-band illustration, spin energies are $E_\pm=\pm h$, with $h=g\mu_B B_{\mathrm{eff}}/2$ and positive $g$. Their full separation is $2|h|=g\mu_B|B_{\mathrm{eff}}|$. A source using another sign for its exchange constant must first be translated into this convention; the sign of a symbol called J is not transferable without its Hamiltonian. [R1](#ref-source-849f7f4f675464de) [R3](#ref-source-7d153b141f652513)

An independent synthetic example isolates an inference used in shift measurements. Suppose corrected frequency shifts obey $y=m(B-B_*)$, with nonzero, field-independent slope and a saturated exchange contribution. A fitted line $y=mB+c$ gives $B_*=-c/m$. Four imposed fields, 14.5, 21, 26 and 28 T, recover six noiseless examples with target intercepts of 20, 32 and 40 T and both slope signs. The latter two targets are extrapolations outside this measurement interval. These calculations reproduce the algebra, not published spectra. [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7)

A residual constant correction $d$ moves the inferred intercept by $-d/m$. In the synthetic examples, a 0.06 MHz offset shifts it by +2 T for a slope of -0.03 MHz/T, or by -1.2 T for +0.05 MHz/T. A zero slope leaves the intercept unidentifiable. Nine separate spin-energy checks verify the distinction between half splitting and full splitting, including negative effective fields. Neither exercise contains orbital coupling, spin-flip scattering or a gap equation, so neither demonstrates a superconducting transition. [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7) [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541)

## Experimental criteria

Balicas and colleagues measured four-terminal transport in lambda-(BETS)2FeCl4 with field near the conducting plane. Their phase diagram distinguishes resistive midpoints from resistance below instrumental sensitivity; the broad 18–41 T field-induced region is not uniformly a zero-resistance region. Below 2 K, resistance reaches the experimental zero near 33 T. Tilting introduces a transverse component that suppresses the state. Figure 3's pairing-state curves are theoretical fits, not direct imaging of a modulated order parameter. These results support a compensation interpretation while retaining orbital and measurement limits. [R3](#ref-source-7d153b141f652513)

Hiraki and colleagues provide a different probe: corrected 77Se NMR shifts in the metallic state at 1.5 K and fields up to 28 T. They infer an exchange-field magnitude of 32 ± 2 T by extrapolating a field-dependent shift. This is not an observed zero crossing at 32 T. Chemical, dipolar and demagnetization corrections enter the analysis; demagnetization dominates their stated uncertainty. The interpretation assumes sufficiently saturated local moments and suitable field-independent electronic response. The transport specimen discussed alongside the NMR came from the same batch, not necessarily the identical crystal. [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7)

Wu and colleagues instead infer an exchange field of -32.7 ± 1.5 T from a 9 T, 5 K angular-shift experiment. Their author manuscript uses a hyperfine calibration partly informed by the nonmagnetic Ga analogue, and explicitly excludes an unknown uncertainty in its axial Knight-shift coefficient. Its predicted value at 33 T is a further model adjustment. Keep the applied field, temperature, inferred exchange field and uncertainty scope separate; the quoted exchange magnitude is not the applied field at which these spectra were taken. [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541)

For a new material, the evidence should connect a measured local-moment response to a signed electronic exchange contribution, then test whether its field and angle dependence account for the superconducting observations. Compare transport with independent magnetic or thermodynamic evidence where available. Different samples, transition criteria, pressure conditions and temperatures must remain identifiable. A numerical similarity between a resistance minimum and an inferred exchange field is supporting evidence, not a replacement for calibration or alternative-mechanism tests. [R3](#ref-source-7d153b141f652513) [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7) [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541)

## Limits and disputes

The selected Wu author manuscript has a convention issue requiring further review: the signed angular-difference formula and the subsequent printed numerical input do not match under direct substitution. The final publisher abstract confirms the reported exchange value, but the full final calibration has not been compared. This page therefore attributes the value to the authors and does not claim to reproduce it independently. The discrepancy is an unresolved source-version issue, not evidence that the experimental phenomenon is false. Complete scientific acceptance remains open. [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541)

The 2026 Eu-rich Sm/Ca/Eu nickelate study reports reentrance and discusses exchange compensation alongside other magnetic physics. Its selected later author version leaves the magnetic order unresolved and includes sample-dependent angular behavior. It does not justify a universal claim of established ferromagnetism or triplet pairing. A separate Nd/Eu nickelate study develops a paramagnetic-compensation interpretation using different material and substrate conditions. Their similarities motivate tests; they do not make the two systems interchangeable or establish one uniquely complete mechanism. [R6](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a) [R7](#ref-source-b57e3b2b5a90705f)

## Discovery implications

Store the exchange-field estimate with its sign convention, probe, applied field, temperature, correction model and uncertainty coverage. Record whether compensation was measured directly, extrapolated or assumed in fitting a phase boundary. Separate those records from superconducting transition temperatures. For multiband systems, test whether one effective exchange field is adequate rather than assuming every band has the same coupling. Preserve the independently measured orbital constraints when evaluating candidate compensation windows. [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7) [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541) [R6](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

## Related topics

[Field-induced superconductivity](/scwiki/field-induced-superconductivity), [reentrant superconductivity](/scwiki/reentrant-superconductivity), [ferromagnetism and superconductivity](/scwiki/ferromagnetism-and-superconductivity), and [nickelates](/scwiki/nickelates).

The original proposal dates to 1962; its identity is verified here, but its full derivation has not been reread. [R1](#ref-source-849f7f4f675464de) [R3](#ref-source-7d153b141f652513)

Meul and colleagues' 1984 work reports field-induced superconductivity in a Eu–Sn molybdenum chalcogenide system and interprets it through compensation. The original abstract supports that historical connection. Exact composition, numerical field endpoints and complete measurement methods have not been verified here, so they are not promoted to universal material parameters. A classical example cannot supply the missing exchange measurement for a different compound. [R2](#ref-source-d564bee026e788c7)

## Mathematical assumptions

Choose the positive direction along the applied field and define the signed effective field as $B_{\mathrm{eff}}=B_{\mathrm{ext}}+B_{\mathrm{ex}}$. Compensation requires $B_{\mathrm{ex}}\lt0$ in this convention. In the collinear single-band illustration, spin energies are $E_\pm=\pm h$, with $h=g\mu_B B_{\mathrm{eff}}/2$ and positive $g$. Their full separation is $2|h|=g\mu_B|B_{\mathrm{eff}}|$. A source using another sign for its exchange constant must first be translated into this convention; the sign of a symbol called J is not transferable without its Hamiltonian. [R1](#ref-source-849f7f4f675464de) [R3](#ref-source-7d153b141f652513)

An independent synthetic example isolates an inference used in shift measurements. Suppose corrected frequency shifts obey $y=m(B-B_*)$, with nonzero, field-independent slope and a saturated exchange contribution. A fitted line $y=mB+c$ gives $B_*=-c/m$. Four imposed fields, 14.5, 21, 26 and 28 T, recover six noiseless examples with target intercepts of 20, 32 and 40 T and both slope signs. The latter two targets are extrapolations outside this measurement interval. These calculations reproduce the algebra, not published spectra. [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7)

A residual constant correction $d$ moves the inferred intercept by $-d/m$. In the synthetic examples, a 0.06 MHz offset shifts it by +2 T for a slope of -0.03 MHz/T, or by -1.2 T for +0.05 MHz/T. A zero slope leaves the intercept unidentifiable. Nine separate spin-energy checks verify the distinction between half splitting and full splitting, including negative effective fields. Neither exercise contains orbital coupling, spin-flip scattering or a gap equation, so neither demonstrates a superconducting transition. [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7) [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541)

## Experimental criteria

Balicas and colleagues measured four-terminal transport in lambda-(BETS)2FeCl4 with field near the conducting plane. Their phase diagram distinguishes resistive midpoints from resistance below instrumental sensitivity; the broad 18–41 T field-induced region is not uniformly a zero-resistance region. Below 2 K, resistance reaches the experimental zero near 33 T. Tilting introduces a transverse component that suppresses the state. Figure 3's pairing-state curves are theoretical fits, not direct imaging of a modulated order parameter. These results support a compensation interpretation while retaining orbital and measurement limits. [R3](#ref-source-7d153b141f652513)

Hiraki and colleagues provide a different probe: corrected 77Se NMR shifts in the metallic state at 1.5 K and fields up to 28 T. They infer an exchange-field magnitude of 32 ± 2 T by extrapolating a field-dependent shift. This is not an observed zero crossing at 32 T. Chemical, dipolar and demagnetization corrections enter the analysis; demagnetization dominates their stated uncertainty. The interpretation assumes sufficiently saturated local moments and suitable field-independent electronic response. The transport specimen discussed alongside the NMR came from the same batch, not necessarily the identical crystal. [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7)

Wu and colleagues instead infer an exchange field of -32.7 ± 1.5 T from a 9 T, 5 K angular-shift experiment. Their author manuscript uses a hyperfine calibration partly informed by the nonmagnetic Ga analogue, and explicitly excludes an unknown uncertainty in its axial Knight-shift coefficient. Its predicted value at 33 T is a further model adjustment. Keep the applied field, temperature, inferred exchange field and uncertainty scope separate; the quoted exchange magnitude is not the applied field at which these spectra were taken. [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541)

For a new material, the evidence should connect a measured local-moment response to a signed electronic exchange contribution, then test whether its field and angle dependence account for the superconducting observations. Compare transport with independent magnetic or thermodynamic evidence where available. Different samples, transition criteria, pressure conditions and temperatures must remain identifiable. A numerical similarity between a resistance minimum and an inferred exchange field is supporting evidence, not a replacement for calibration or alternative-mechanism tests. [R3](#ref-source-7d153b141f652513) [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7) [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541)

## Limits and disputes

The selected Wu author manuscript has a convention issue requiring further review: the signed angular-difference formula and the subsequent printed numerical input do not match under direct substitution. The final publisher abstract confirms the reported exchange value, but the full final calibration has not been compared. This page therefore attributes the value to the authors and does not claim to reproduce it independently. The discrepancy is an unresolved source-version issue, not evidence that the experimental phenomenon is false. Complete scientific acceptance remains open. [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541)

The 2026 Eu-rich Sm/Ca/Eu nickelate study reports reentrance and discusses exchange compensation alongside other magnetic physics. Its selected later author version leaves the magnetic order unresolved and includes sample-dependent angular behavior. It does not justify a universal claim of established ferromagnetism or triplet pairing. A separate Nd/Eu nickelate study develops a paramagnetic-compensation interpretation using different material and substrate conditions. Their similarities motivate tests; they do not make the two systems interchangeable or establish one uniquely complete mechanism. [R6](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a) [R7](#ref-source-b57e3b2b5a90705f)

## Discovery implications

Store the exchange-field estimate with its sign convention, probe, applied field, temperature, correction model and uncertainty coverage. Record whether compensation was measured directly, extrapolated or assumed in fitting a phase boundary. Separate those records from superconducting transition temperatures. For multiband systems, test whether one effective exchange field is adequate rather than assuming every band has the same coupling. Preserve the independently measured orbital constraints when evaluating candidate compensation windows. [R4](#ref-source-473d207bc401a7e7) [R5](#ref-source-f328f3068f201541) [R6](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

claims.statement: The Pauli paramagnetic limit compares the energy gained by a spin-polarized normal state with the condensation energy of a specified superconducting state. It is a model-dependent reference, not a universal upper bound on every superconductor. Exceeding a weak-coupling, g = 2 estimate signals that its assumptions need examination. It does not by itself establish triplet pairing, a spatially modulated state or a topological phase. Chandrasekhar and Clogston's 1962 publication identities are checked here; the following explicit calculation is independent rather than a claimed reproduction of their complete original papers.

claims.statement: Use $B$ in tesla and dimensionless SI volume susceptibilities. With positive zero-field condensation-energy density $U_c$, constant spin susceptibilities and no orbital contribution, the free-energy difference is $F_s-F_n=-U_c+(\chi_n-\chi_s)B^2/(2\mu_0)$. For $\chi_n\gt\chi_s$, its crossing occurs at $B_P=\sqrt{2\mu_0U_c/(\chi_n-\chi_s)}$. If the susceptibilities vary strongly with field, this quadratic expression must be replaced by the appropriate magnetization integral. Equal susceptibilities remove this particular quadratic penalty, not every physical limit on superconductivity.

claims.statement: For a simple uniform, fully gapped spin-singlet state at zero temperature, set $\chi_s=0$. Let $n$ be the single-spin density of states per unit energy and volume. Taking $U_c=n\Delta_0^2/2$ and $\chi_n=\mu_0n(g\mu_B)^2/2$ yields $B_P=\sqrt{2}\Delta_0/(g\mu_B)$. At $g=2$ and $\Delta_0=1.764k_BT_c$, the numerical coefficient is about 1.857 T/K. The familiar approximate 1.84–1.86 T/K benchmark is meaningful only with its gap and response assumptions. It is a zero-temperature reference, not a measured transition curve at arbitrary temperature.

articles.body:
## Scope

The Pauli paramagnetic limit compares the energy gained by a spin-polarized normal state with the condensation energy of a specified superconducting state. It is a model-dependent reference, not a universal upper bound on every superconductor. Exceeding a weak-coupling, g = 2 estimate signals that its assumptions need examination. It does not by itself establish triplet pairing, a spatially modulated state or a topological phase. Chandrasekhar and Clogston's 1962 publication identities are checked here; the following explicit calculation is independent rather than a claimed reproduction of their complete original papers. [R1](#ref-source-d32df19524b2a1c8) [R2](#ref-source-b31f8fbbf312e41d)

Suppressing orbital depairing in a very thin film can expose spin depairing that would otherwise be hidden. Geometry alone does not remove the spin-energy cost. Spin–orbit coupling, an altered gap scale, anisotropic response, exchange compensation and multiband physics require distinct models. Keep the applied field, internal exchange field and spin–orbit energy scale separate when interpreting an apparently large critical field. [R3](#ref-source-16926b3817cff55d) [R4](#ref-source-7ba854cc57960377) [R7](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83)

## Mathematical assumptions

Use $B$ in tesla and dimensionless SI volume susceptibilities. With positive zero-field condensation-energy density $U_c$, constant spin susceptibilities and no orbital contribution, the free-energy difference is $F_s-F_n=-U_c+(\chi_n-\chi_s)B^2/(2\mu_0)$. For $\chi_n\gt\chi_s$, its crossing occurs at $B_P=\sqrt{2\mu_0U_c/(\chi_n-\chi_s)}$. If the susceptibilities vary strongly with field, this quadratic expression must be replaced by the appropriate magnetization integral. Equal susceptibilities remove this particular quadratic penalty, not every physical limit on superconductivity. [R8](#ref-source-804e0c9690bde4d8)

For a simple uniform, fully gapped spin-singlet state at zero temperature, set $\chi_s=0$. Let $n$ be the single-spin density of states per unit energy and volume. Taking $U_c=n\Delta_0^2/2$ and $\chi_n=\mu_0n(g\mu_B)^2/2$ yields $B_P=\sqrt{2}\Delta_0/(g\mu_B)$. At $g=2$ and $\Delta_0=1.764k_BT_c$, the numerical coefficient is about 1.857 T/K. The familiar approximate 1.84–1.86 T/K benchmark is meaningful only with its gap and response assumptions. It is a zero-temperature reference, not a measured transition curve at arbitrary temperature. [R1](#ref-source-d32df19524b2a1c8) [R2](#ref-source-b31f8fbbf312e41d) [R8](#ref-source-804e0c9690bde4d8)

An independent calculation checks eighteen combinations of transition temperature, g factor and gap ratio, and verifies the free-energy sign on both sides of each crossing. Holding the other assumptions fixed, halving g doubles the reference field; increasing the gap ratio from 1.764 to 2.2 multiplies it by about 1.247. A synthetic $T_c=3$ K, g = 2 example gives approximately 5.571 T with the first gap ratio. These parameter changes demonstrate sensitivity, not fitted explanations for a named material. [R1](#ref-source-d32df19524b2a1c8) [R2](#ref-source-b31f8fbbf312e41d)

A further controlled example fixes $U_c$ and $\chi_n$ while assigning $r=\chi_s/\chi_n$. The crossing grows by $1/\sqrt{1-r}$: r = 0, 0.25 and 0.75 give factors 1, approximately 1.155 and 2. This scaling cannot be carried unchanged into a system where spin–orbit coupling also changes the normal susceptibility or condensation energy. The finite checks verify the stated energy comparison; they do not solve a self-consistent gap equation or select the stable pairing state. [R8](#ref-source-804e0c9690bde4d8)

## Experimental criteria

For Xi and colleagues' monolayer NbSe2 study, the approximately 35 T zero-temperature scale comes from fitting a spin–orbit-protected pair-breaking model. An independent contact-conductance measurement extends to 31.5 T and finds a strongly diminished Andreev-related feature. The author text gives 0.3 K, while its Figure 4 caption specifies 0.36 K for the inset; those labels are preserved here. The fitted effective spin–orbit scale near 660 T is not an applied laboratory field. Field-transition criteria and two-terminal versus four-terminal devices must also remain distinct. [R7](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83)

De la Barrera and colleagues report that monolayer TaS2's parallel-field transition remains above their 34.5 T measurement ceiling below 2 K. Their quoted 65.6 T is a near-transition square-root fit parameter, not a directly measured critical field. They define phase-boundary points using half the normal-state resistance, which is distinct from zero resistance. Alignment is optimized at fixed temperature and field by minimizing resistance; maintaining alignment during a temperature sweep is harder. Their 25 mK/12 T and 300 mK/34.5 T apparatus limits must not be combined into one unperformed measurement. [R8](#ref-source-804e0c9690bde4d8)

Calorimetry provides another kind of evidence. Bianchi and colleagues observe a high-field, low-temperature anomaly in CeCoIn5 and interpret it as a possible finite-momentum superconducting state. The final publication explicitly retains “Possible” in its title. Subsequent neutron evidence establishes coupled magnetic order in the high-field superconducting phase. An extra phase boundary therefore requires assessment of competing or coexisting order; it is not an automatic image of a spatially modulated superconducting gap. The older calorimetry and later magnetic observations have different review depths here. [R5](#ref-source-a626e7fcb17b94fa) [R6](#ref-source-fda01ade7737b638)

## Limits and disputes

The orbital field in a Maki ratio must come from an orbital model or suitable independent estimate: $\alpha_M=\sqrt{2}B_{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}/B_P$. Inserting an already Pauli-limited measured field into its numerator changes the meaning. The dirty, single-band orbital estimate involving 0.693 times $T_c$ and the magnitude of the near-transition slope has restricted assumptions. Unequal band diffusivities can change the extrapolation. A large ratio motivates further investigation; it does not certify a finite-momentum state or determine a universal onset threshold. [R3](#ref-source-16926b3817cff55d) [R4](#ref-source-7ba854cc57960377)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected TMD methods and figures have been checked, but raw transport, full supplementary calibration, complete final-version comparisons and material-specific susceptibility reconstructions remain incomplete. A fitted spin–orbit parameter, a resistance midpoint and a bulk thermodynamic boundary are different quantities. Even when a spin-sensitive probe agrees with a proposed interpretation, compare alternative states under the same field direction, temperature and experimental conditions before assigning pairing symmetry. [R5](#ref-source-a626e7fcb17b94fa) [R6](#ref-source-fda01ade7737b638) [R7](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83) [R8](#ref-source-804e0c9690bde4d8)

## Discovery implications

Record the measured field range and any censoring or extrapolation, the superconducting criterion, field direction, sample thickness and transition temperature used in the reference ratio. Report the chosen g factor, gap ratio, susceptibility assumptions and orbital model separately. Use departures from the simple benchmark to design discriminating measurements, not to rank triplet content by the size of a critical-field ratio. A future model must explain both the enhanced direction and the directions in which superconductivity is more easily destroyed. [R3](#ref-source-16926b3817cff55d) [R4](#ref-source-7ba854cc57960377) [R7](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83)

## Related topics

[Magnetic field](/scwiki/magnetic-field), [singlet and triplet pairing](/scwiki/singlet-and-triplet-pairing), [exchange compensation](/scwiki/jaccarino-peter-effect), and [field-induced superconductivity](/scwiki/field-induced-superconductivity).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-g6-claim-scope-1

The Pauli paramagnetic limit compares the energy gained by a spin-polarized normal state with the condensation energy of a specified superconducting state. It is a model-dependent reference, not a universal upper bound on every superconductor. Exceeding a weak-coupling, g = 2 estimate signals that its assumptions need examination. It does not by itself establish triplet pairing, a spatially modulated state or a topological phase. Chandrasekhar and Clogston's 1962 publication identities are checked here; the following explicit calculation is independent rather than a claimed reproduction of their complete original papers.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-d32df19524b2a1c8, source-b31f8fbbf312e41d.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-scope-2

Suppressing orbital depairing in a very thin film can expose spin depairing that would otherwise be hidden. Geometry alone does not remove the spin-energy cost. Spin–orbit coupling, an altered gap scale, anisotropic response, exchange compensation and multiband physics require distinct models. Keep the applied field, internal exchange field and spin–orbit energy scale separate when interpreting an apparently large critical field.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-16926b3817cff55d, source-7ba854cc57960377, source-c80fb39cdf748a83.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

Use $B$ in tesla and dimensionless SI volume susceptibilities. With positive zero-field condensation-energy density $U_c$, constant spin susceptibilities and no orbital contribution, the free-energy difference is $F_s-F_n=-U_c+(\chi_n-\chi_s)B^2/(2\mu_0)$. For $\chi_n\gt\chi_s$, its crossing occurs at $B_P=\sqrt{2\mu_0U_c/(\chi_n-\chi_s)}$. If the susceptibilities vary strongly with field, this quadratic expression must be replaced by the appropriate magnetization integral. Equal susceptibilities remove this particular quadratic penalty, not every physical limit on superconductivity.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-804e0c9690bde4d8.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

For a simple uniform, fully gapped spin-singlet state at zero temperature, set $\chi_s=0$. Let $n$ be the single-spin density of states per unit energy and volume. Taking $U_c=n\Delta_0^2/2$ and $\chi_n=\mu_0n(g\mu_B)^2/2$ yields $B_P=\sqrt{2}\Delta_0/(g\mu_B)$. At $g=2$ and $\Delta_0=1.764k_BT_c$, the numerical coefficient is about 1.857 T/K. The familiar approximate 1.84–1.86 T/K benchmark is meaningful only with its gap and response assumptions. It is a zero-temperature reference, not a measured transition curve at arbitrary temperature.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-d32df19524b2a1c8, source-b31f8fbbf312e41d, source-804e0c9690bde4d8.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

An independent calculation checks eighteen combinations of transition temperature, g factor and gap ratio, and verifies the free-energy sign on both sides of each crossing. Holding the other assumptions fixed, halving g doubles the reference field; increasing the gap ratio from 1.764 to 2.2 multiplies it by about 1.247. A synthetic $T_c=3$ K, g = 2 example gives approximately 5.571 T with the first gap ratio. These parameter changes demonstrate sensitivity, not fitted explanations for a named material.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-d32df19524b2a1c8, source-b31f8fbbf312e41d.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-mathematical-assumptions-4

A further controlled example fixes $U_c$ and $\chi_n$ while assigning $r=\chi_s/\chi_n$. The crossing grows by $1/\sqrt{1-r}$: r = 0, 0.25 and 0.75 give factors 1, approximately 1.155 and 2. This scaling cannot be carried unchanged into a system where spin–orbit coupling also changes the normal susceptibility or condensation energy. The finite checks verify the stated energy comparison; they do not solve a self-consistent gap equation or select the stable pairing state.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-804e0c9690bde4d8.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-experimental-criteria-1

For Xi and colleagues' monolayer NbSe2 study, the approximately 35 T zero-temperature scale comes from fitting a spin–orbit-protected pair-breaking model. An independent contact-conductance measurement extends to 31.5 T and finds a strongly diminished Andreev-related feature. The author text gives 0.3 K, while its Figure 4 caption specifies 0.36 K for the inset; those labels are preserved here. The fitted effective spin–orbit scale near 660 T is not an applied laboratory field. Field-transition criteria and two-terminal versus four-terminal devices must also remain distinct.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-c80fb39cdf748a83.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-experimental-criteria-2

De la Barrera and colleagues report that monolayer TaS2's parallel-field transition remains above their 34.5 T measurement ceiling below 2 K. Their quoted 65.6 T is a near-transition square-root fit parameter, not a directly measured critical field. They define phase-boundary points using half the normal-state resistance, which is distinct from zero resistance. Alignment is optimized at fixed temperature and field by minimizing resistance; maintaining alignment during a temperature sweep is harder. Their 25 mK/12 T and 300 mK/34.5 T apparatus limits must not be combined into one unperformed measurement.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-804e0c9690bde4d8.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Calorimetry provides another kind of evidence. Bianchi and colleagues observe a high-field, low-temperature anomaly in CeCoIn5 and interpret it as a possible finite-momentum superconducting state. The final publication explicitly retains “Possible” in its title. Subsequent neutron evidence establishes coupled magnetic order in the high-field superconducting phase. An extra phase boundary therefore requires assessment of competing or coexisting order; it is not an automatic image of a spatially modulated superconducting gap. The older calorimetry and later magnetic observations have different review depths here.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-a626e7fcb17b94fa, source-fda01ade7737b638.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

The orbital field in a Maki ratio must come from an orbital model or suitable independent estimate: $\alpha_M=\sqrt{2}B_{c2}^{\mathrm{orb}}/B_P$. Inserting an already Pauli-limited measured field into its numerator changes the meaning. The dirty, single-band orbital estimate involving 0.693 times $T_c$ and the magnitude of the near-transition slope has restricted assumptions. Unequal band diffusivities can change the extrapolation. A large ratio motivates further investigation; it does not certify a finite-momentum state or determine a universal onset threshold.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-16926b3817cff55d, source-7ba854cc57960377.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected TMD methods and figures have been checked, but raw transport, full supplementary calibration, complete final-version comparisons and material-specific susceptibility reconstructions remain incomplete. A fitted spin–orbit parameter, a resistance midpoint and a bulk thermodynamic boundary are different quantities. Even when a spin-sensitive probe agrees with a proposed interpretation, compare alternative states under the same field direction, temperature and experimental conditions before assigning pairing symmetry.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-a626e7fcb17b94fa, source-fda01ade7737b638, source-c80fb39cdf748a83, source-804e0c9690bde4d8.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g6-claim-discovery-implications-1

Record the measured field range and any censoring or extrapolation, the superconducting criterion, field direction, sample thickness and transition temperature used in the reference ratio. Report the chosen g factor, gap ratio, susceptibility assumptions and orbital model separately. Use departures from the simple benchmark to design discriminating measurements, not to rank triplet content by the size of a critical-field ratio. A future model must explain both the enhanced direction and the directions in which superconductivity is more easily destroyed.

Evidence: experimental. Sources: source-16926b3817cff55d, source-7ba854cc57960377, source-c80fb39cdf748a83.

Conditions: Explicit SI B/chi/DOS convention, gap/g response assumptions; measurement criterion, fielddirection, sample thickness and observed versus fitted scales retained.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent energy-balance examples; complete scientific acceptance remains open.

articles.body:
## Scope

A quantum spin liquid is not identified simply by an absence of detected magnetic order. A candidate material must be tested against valence-bond order, disorder, freezing and the finite temperature and time windows of the measurements. A spin gap can occur in different states; its observation alone does not identify topological order or fractionalized excitations. Here the organic Mott insulator κ-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3 illustrates how interpretations change when additional probes become available. [R2](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R4](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b) [R5](#ref-source-ef796739e836bb78)

RVB, or resonating valence bond, describes a family of theoretical constructions built from superpositions of singlet configurations. Anderson's cuprate proposal connects this idea to superconductivity in a doped correlated insulator; the abstract is a historical proposal, not a material-level proof of a spin-liquid parent. The allowed coverings, amplitudes and constraints must be specified. A generic U(1) construction is not automatically a Dirac state, and BCS mean-field language does not imply a phonon-only pairing interaction. [R1](#ref-source-5a6026d6455bf7a0)

## Mathematical assumptions

An independent finite example makes one logical limitation explicit. Consider an isolated singlet of energy zero and three triplet states with energies $\Delta-h$, $\Delta$ and $\Delta+h$. Use units $k_B=g\mu_B=1$, so temperatures, gaps and the field variable h are expressed in compatible energy units; the response below is not an SI molar susceptibility. The partition function is $Z=1+e^{-\Delta/T}[1+2\cosh(h/T)]$. Differentiating the mean moment at zero field gives $\chi_0=2e^{-\Delta/T}/\{T[1+3e^{-\Delta/T}]\}$. This illustrative model addresses an inference problem raised by the magnetic measurements, rather than fitting those experiments. [R2](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R5](#ref-source-ef796739e836bb78)

The model has a gap and a nonmagnetic singlet ground state, yet an isolated dimer has neither bulk topological order nor mobile charge. Adding a synthetic Curie contribution gives $\chi_{\mathrm{obs}}=\chi_0+c/T$. With an illustrative gap of 6 K, c = 0.001 and T = 0.1 K, the background exceeds 99.9999% of the total response even though the intrinsic response is exponentially suppressed. The chosen 6 K is a model parameter, not the measured anomaly temperature or a fitted material gap. An inverse-temperature tail cannot by itself establish a gapless intrinsic state. [R5](#ref-source-ef796739e836bb78)

Five finite-difference derivatives agree with the analytic response, and fifteen temperature/background combinations check this counterexample. Its Curie term assumes independent, unsaturated moments; interactions, anisotropy and finite-field saturation are excluded. Singlet correlations in an insulating model also do not demonstrate charge coherence or superconductivity. articles.body:
## Scope

Spin–orbit coupling links electronic motion to spin and changes the normal-state band structure and magnetic response. It does not, by itself, specify the attractive interaction responsible for superconductivity. In a nonmagnetic system without inversion symmetry, antisymmetric spin–orbit coupling can split bands and allow pairing components that inversion would separate. Permission by symmetry is not a measurement of their relative weights. Gor'kov and Rashba's two-dimensional model explicitly leaves the pairing mechanism unspecified and assumes its spin–orbit splitting remains small compared with the Fermi energy. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22) [R2](#ref-source-6c944305286c9cad)

In an ideal Rashba model, the spin texture lies in the plane and winds perpendicular to momentum. In the Ising description used for monolayer NbSe2, opposite valleys have predominantly opposite out-of-plane spin orientations. These are different textures and give different directional responses. A spin–orbit energy expressed as an equivalent field is not an applied laboratory field. Strong spin–orbit coupling and a large upper critical field do not independently certify triplet pairing or topological superconductivity. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22) [R6](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83) [R8](#ref-source-5eb9e7b0c0c3b0cf)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a two-spin effective model, write $h(\mathbf k)=\xi(\mathbf k)I+\mathbf g(\mathbf k)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$, with even $\xi$ and odd $\mathbf g$ under momentum reversal. Its normal energies are $\xi\pm|\mathbf g|$. An even-frequency gap may be written $\widehat\Delta=[\psi+\mathbf d\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma]i\sigma_y$, with even singlet component $\psi$ and odd triplet vector $\mathbf d$. The chosen spin or pseudospin basis matters; this two-component model is not a complete multiorbital classification. Neither the normal splitting nor the algebraic gap decomposition determines a self-consistent interaction. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22) [R2](#ref-source-6c944305286c9cad)

An independent calculation imposes a real, purely singlet gap $\widehat\Delta=\psi i\sigma_y$. Its Bogoliubov excitation energies are $E_\pm=\sqrt{(\xi\pm g)^2+\psi^2}$, where $g=|\mathbf g|$. For a nonzero Matsubara frequency, define $f_\pm=-\psi/(\omega^2+E_\pm^2)$. The anomalous propagator decomposes as $F=[f_s+\mathbf f_t\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma]i\sigma_y$, with $f_s=(f_++f_-)/2$ and $\mathbf f_t=(f_+-f_-)\hat{\mathbf g}/2$. Thus a momentum-resolved triplet pair amplitude can be nonzero although the imposed gap has no triplet component. These quantities should not both be labeled an experimental “triplet fraction.” [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22)

One hundred independently assembled matrices reproduce the spectra and fermionic relation $F(\mathbf k,i\omega)=-F^T(-\mathbf k,-i\omega)$; one hundred decompositions match the analytic amplitudes. Three controls check cancellation at zero spin–orbit coupling or at $\xi=0$, and a nonzero amplitude at generic parameters. The result distinguishes a propagator from a gap interaction. It does not compute a momentum-integrated mixing ratio, susceptibility, transition temperature or topological invariant. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22)

Frigeri and colleagues' weak-coupling treatment neglects small particle-hole-asymmetry mixing terms and studies pairing channels separately. Alignment of $\mathbf d$ with $\mathbf g$ avoids a leading suppression term; it does not select the stable material state. Their erratum adds an omitted linear contribution to the MnSi spin–orbit vector and rescales the original Figure 2 parameter by dividing by $\sqrt{3/2}$. Claims about which p-wave component is suppressed therefore require the corrected vector and its relative coefficients. [R2](#ref-source-6c944305286c9cad) [R3](#ref-source-46e49166d702226d)

## Experimental criteria

Nishiyama and colleagues report a nearly unchanged Knight shift and approximately cubic temperature dependence of the relaxation rate in Li2Pt3B, interpreted as evidence for triplet pairing with nodes. Their crushed polycrystalline sample has a zero-field susceptibility transition at 2.68 K. For boron NMR, 0.26 T gives a transition near 2.1 K, while 0.35 T gives approximately 1.8 K. The 0.1 K spectrum is a measurement temperature, not a transition. The Li2Pd3B comparison uses a different field, 1.46 T, and the Knight-shift interpretation includes an orbital contribution and a fitted gap model. [R4](#ref-source-876de9124496abcb)

Häfliger and colleagues instead find low-temperature saturation in μSR-derived penetration depth and activated specific heat in Li2Pt3B, favoring a fully gapped interpretation. Their final text nevertheless notes that a simple single-gap fit to the penetration-depth data is unsatisfactory and that triplet states cannot be excluded. The low-field temperature scans extend to 30 mK, while the field-dependent comparison is made at 1 K; calorimetry reaches 0.1 K and uses a 4 T normal-state reference. These different probes and protocols must remain separately identifiable. [R5](#ref-source-30ad27b0f37b6baf)

Ising-protected superconductivity provides another route to an enhanced field scale. In the NbSe2 study, the approximately 35 T scale is fitted, whereas contact-conductance data extend to 31.5 T. In the TaS2 study, 34.5 T is an experimental ceiling and 65.6 T is a fit parameter. Orbital geometry, alignment, gap scale and the resistance criterion accompany any comparison with a weak-coupling Pauli estimate. A larger ratio alone does not determine the spin structure of the gap. [R6](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83) [R7](#ref-source-804e0c9690bde4d8)

## Limits and disputes

The Li2Pt3B disagreement cannot be settled by labeling one result “bulk” and another “surface”: NMR also probes bulk material. The μSR/calorimetry paper discusses sample inhomogeneity and metallic inclusions, but those possibilities are not independently demonstrated explanations for every contrasting measurement. Retain both experimental interpretations and their assumptions. Absence of a coherence peak is not, by itself, a unique nodal or triplet diagnostic. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including raw-data comparisons, final-version checks and the wider subsequent literature. [R4](#ref-source-876de9124496abcb) [R5](#ref-source-30ad27b0f37b6baf)

A topological assignment requires a specified superconducting Hamiltonian, symmetry class and appropriate invariant, together with evidence that the physical system realizes the assumed state. Normal-state spin splitting, absence of inversion and a superconducting transition do not supply those steps. Likewise, a crystal's effective spin–orbit texture cannot be inferred quantitatively from a simple atomic-number scaling rule. Use a material-specific band model and experimentally constrained parameters before proposing a pairing mechanism or device advantage. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22) [R8](#ref-source-5eb9e7b0c0c3b0cf)

## Discovery implications

Separate normal-state texture, superconducting gap, pair correlations and measured magnetic response in both language and data records. Compare field directions and sample conditions; retain corrections to theoretical papers and competing experimental interpretations. Useful spin–orbit engineering should predict an observable change under controlled gating, thickness or symmetry changes, then test it against alternatives such as orbital depairing and multiband response. An adjustable model parameter is a research hypothesis until the same model explains independent observations. [R2](#ref-source-6c944305286c9cad) [R3](#ref-source-46e49166d702226d) [R6](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83) [R7](#ref-source-804e0c9690bde4d8)

## Related topics

[Singlet and triplet pairing](/scwiki/singlet-and-triplet-pairing), [Pauli limit](/scwiki/pauli-limit), and [Majorana zero modes](/scwiki/majorana-zero-modes).
