# Spin–orbit coupling and superconductivity

Distinguish spin textures, gap components and pair amplitudes, with measured conditions and competing interpretations for noncentrosymmetric superconductors.

## Scope

Spin–orbit coupling links electronic motion to spin and changes the normal-state band structure and magnetic response. It does not, by itself, specify the attractive interaction responsible for superconductivity. In a nonmagnetic system without inversion symmetry, antisymmetric spin–orbit coupling can split bands and allow pairing components that inversion would separate. Permission by symmetry is not a measurement of their relative weights. Gor'kov and Rashba's two-dimensional model explicitly leaves the pairing mechanism unspecified and assumes its spin–orbit splitting remains small compared with the Fermi energy. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22) [R2](#ref-source-6c944305286c9cad)

In an ideal Rashba model, the spin texture lies in the plane and winds perpendicular to momentum. In the Ising description used for monolayer NbSe2, opposite valleys have predominantly opposite out-of-plane spin orientations. These are different textures and give different directional responses. A spin–orbit energy expressed as an equivalent field is not an applied laboratory field. Strong spin–orbit coupling and a large upper critical field do not independently certify triplet pairing or topological superconductivity. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22) [R6](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83) [R8](#ref-source-5eb9e7b0c0c3b0cf)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a two-spin effective model, write $h(\mathbf k)=\xi(\mathbf k)I+\mathbf g(\mathbf k)\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma$, with even $\xi$ and odd $\mathbf g$ under momentum reversal. Its normal energies are $\xi\pm|\mathbf g|$. An even-frequency gap may be written $\widehat\Delta=[\psi+\mathbf d\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma]i\sigma_y$, with even singlet component $\psi$ and odd triplet vector $\mathbf d$. The chosen spin or pseudospin basis matters; this two-component model is not a complete multiorbital classification. Neither the normal splitting nor the algebraic gap decomposition determines a self-consistent interaction. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22) [R2](#ref-source-6c944305286c9cad)

An independent calculation imposes a real, purely singlet gap $\widehat\Delta=\psi i\sigma_y$. Its Bogoliubov excitation energies are $E_\pm=\sqrt{(\xi\pm g)^2+\psi^2}$, where $g=|\mathbf g|$. For a nonzero Matsubara frequency, define $f_\pm=-\psi/(\omega^2+E_\pm^2)$. The anomalous propagator decomposes as $F=[f_s+\mathbf f_t\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma]i\sigma_y$, with $f_s=(f_++f_-)/2$ and $\mathbf f_t=(f_+-f_-)\hat{\mathbf g}/2$. Thus a momentum-resolved triplet pair amplitude can be nonzero although the imposed gap has no triplet component. These quantities should not both be labeled an experimental “triplet fraction.” [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22)

One hundred independently assembled matrices reproduce the spectra and fermionic relation $F(\mathbf k,i\omega)=-F^T(-\mathbf k,-i\omega)$; one hundred decompositions match the analytic amplitudes. Three controls check cancellation at zero spin–orbit coupling or at $\xi=0$, and a nonzero amplitude at generic parameters. The result distinguishes a propagator from a gap interaction. It does not compute a momentum-integrated mixing ratio, susceptibility, transition temperature or topological invariant. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22)

Frigeri and colleagues' weak-coupling treatment neglects small particle-hole-asymmetry mixing terms and studies pairing channels separately. Alignment of $\mathbf d$ with $\mathbf g$ avoids a leading suppression term; it does not select the stable material state. Their erratum adds an omitted linear contribution to the MnSi spin–orbit vector and rescales the original Figure 2 parameter by dividing by $\sqrt{3/2}$. Claims about which p-wave component is suppressed therefore require the corrected vector and its relative coefficients. [R2](#ref-source-6c944305286c9cad) [R3](#ref-source-46e49166d702226d)

## Experimental criteria

Nishiyama and colleagues report a nearly unchanged Knight shift and approximately cubic temperature dependence of the relaxation rate in Li2Pt3B, interpreted as evidence for triplet pairing with nodes. Their crushed polycrystalline sample has a zero-field susceptibility transition at 2.68 K. For boron NMR, 0.26 T gives a transition near 2.1 K, while 0.35 T gives approximately 1.8 K. The 0.1 K spectrum is a measurement temperature, not a transition. The Li2Pd3B comparison uses a different field, 1.46 T, and the Knight-shift interpretation includes an orbital contribution and a fitted gap model. [R4](#ref-source-876de9124496abcb)

Häfliger and colleagues instead find low-temperature saturation in μSR-derived penetration depth and activated specific heat in Li2Pt3B, favoring a fully gapped interpretation. Their final text nevertheless notes that a simple single-gap fit to the penetration-depth data is unsatisfactory and that triplet states cannot be excluded. The low-field temperature scans extend to 30 mK, while the field-dependent comparison is made at 1 K; calorimetry reaches 0.1 K and uses a 4 T normal-state reference. These different probes and protocols must remain separately identifiable. [R5](#ref-source-30ad27b0f37b6baf)

Ising-protected superconductivity provides another route to an enhanced field scale. In the NbSe2 study, the approximately 35 T scale is fitted, whereas contact-conductance data extend to 31.5 T. In the TaS2 study, 34.5 T is an experimental ceiling and 65.6 T is a fit parameter. Orbital geometry, alignment, gap scale and the resistance criterion accompany any comparison with a weak-coupling Pauli estimate. A larger ratio alone does not determine the spin structure of the gap. [R6](#ref-source-c80fb39cdf748a83) [R7](#ref-source-804e0c9690bde4d8)

## Limits and disputes

The Li2Pt3B disagreement cannot be settled by labeling one result “bulk” and another “surface”: NMR also probes bulk material. The μSR/calorimetry paper discusses sample inhomogeneity and metallic inclusions, but those possibilities are not independently demonstrated explanations for every contrasting measurement. Retain both experimental interpretations and their assumptions. Absence of a coherence peak is not, by itself, a unique nodal or triplet diagnostic. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including raw-data comparisons, final-version checks and the wider subsequent literature. [R4](#ref-source-876de9124496abcb) [R5](#ref-source-30ad27b0f37b6baf)

A topological assignment requires a specified superconducting Hamiltonian, symmetry class and appropriate invariant, together with evidence that the physical system realizes the assumed state. Normal-state spin splitting, absence of inversion and a superconducting transition do not supply those steps. Likewise, a crystal's effective spin–orbit texture cannot be inferred quantitatively from a simple atomic-number scaling rule. Use a material-specific band model and experimentally constrained parameters before proposing a pairing mechanism or device advantage. [R1](#ref-source-81c0e16fd118df22) [R8](#ref-source-5eb9e7b0c0c3b0cf)

Useful spin–orbit engineering should predict an observable change under controlled gating, thickness or symmetry changes, then test it against alternatives such as orbital depairing and multiband response. An adjustable model parameter is a research hypothesis until the same model explains independent observations. claims.statement: Altermagnetism describes compensated collinear magnetic order whose opposite-spin sectors are related by crystal operations such as rotations. articles.body:
## Scope

Altermagnetism describes compensated collinear magnetic order whose opposite-spin sectors are related by crystal operations such as rotations. It can produce momentum-dependent spin splitting without requiring spin–orbit coupling. Cancellation of the total magnetic moment does not imply degeneracy of opposite spins at every momentum. Nor does the absence of a uniform moment remove every constraint on superconducting pairing. The magnetic symmetry, the occupied bands and the proposed superconducting state must be specified separately. [R1](#ref-source-ea3e0a10f6917658) [R2](#ref-source-7258aa669504806d)

Three questions should remain distinct: whether a specimen has altermagnetic order, whether it becomes intrinsically superconducting, and whether superconducting electrodes induce correlations in a hybrid device. Evidence for one does not establish the others. A 2026 In–CrSb–In experiment provides a concrete proximity platform, so a blanket statement that experimental altermagnet–superconductor systems do not exist is outdated. That device does not establish intrinsic bulk superconductivity in CrSb. [R3](#ref-source-26b1bd116249a6d3) [R4](#ref-source-807f7414e83e5e4c)

## Mathematical assumptions

A useful symmetry relation is $E_\uparrow(\mathbf k)=E_\downarrow(R\mathbf k)$ for an appropriate crystal operation $R$. It need not imply $E_\uparrow(\mathbf k)=E_\downarrow(\mathbf k)$. In a simple even-parity texture, $\delta(\mathbf k)=d(\cos k_x-\cos k_y)$ changes sign under a right-angle rotation and vanishes along diagonal directions. This illustrates a possible angular pattern, rather than identifying a material or determining its superconducting gap. [R1](#ref-source-ea3e0a10f6917658) [R2](#ref-source-7258aa669504806d)

The Chakraborty–Black-Schaffer construction retains two low-energy states with opposite spins on different sublattices. Its onsite singlet restriction depends on those projected states: opposite spins on the same site are absent from that retained space. A two-component band Hamiltonian must therefore preserve what its components represent. Reading its Pauli matrices as ordinary spin while discarding sublattice information changes the pairing problem. The result should not be promoted to an unconditional ban covering every multiband or strongly hybridized material. [R2](#ref-source-7258aa669504806d)

An independent local calculation illustrates the projection explicitly. For spin $\sigma=\pm1$, take $h_\sigma=(\delta+\sigma M)\tau_z+t\tau_x$, with $M>0$, real hybridization $t$ and sublattice Pauli matrices $\tau$. Let $u_\sigma$ be the normalized lower-band eigenvector. An imposed unit onsite singlet has projected magnitude $P=|u_\uparrow^T u_\downarrow|$. When $t=0$ and $|\delta|<M$, the two vectors occupy opposite sublattices and $P=0$. At $\delta=0$, direct diagonalization gives $P=|t|/\sqrt{M^2+t^2}$. Thus finite mixing changes the projection even when the imposed interaction is unchanged. [R2](#ref-source-7258aa669504806d)

Forty-five parameter cases verify these limits and the exchange of spin branches under $\delta\rightarrow-\delta$. This is an algebraic illustration, not a reproduction of the paper's full lattice calculation. It computes neither a stable superconducting phase nor a transition temperature. A nonzero projected matrix element does not establish that pairing wins over competing states; a zero matrix element in a truncated space does not by itself exclude higher-band processes. Self-consistency, available states and interaction structure remain additional questions. [R2](#ref-source-7258aa669504806d)

## Experimental criteria

Long and colleagues map CrSb's bulk angular electronic structure using magnetic quantum oscillations. Measurements use a 41.5 T magnet and include 0.4 K traces. Figure 3 compares angular oscillation branches with a g-wave interpretation; its displayed map is symmetrized. The comparison uses adjusted electronic bands, including a −0.11 eV shift for one pocket family and a compensating +0.015 eV shift for another. Oscillation frequencies constrain extremal orbit areas; assigning an order-parameter structure involves symmetry and band modeling. This is magnetic evidence, not a superconducting transition measurement. [R3](#ref-source-26b1bd116249a6d3)

Esin and colleagues use superconducting indium contacts separated by 2 μm beneath CrSb flakes thicker than 1 μm. At 30 mK, the device shows a zero-resistance current interval; a 1.2 K trace shows suppression. They compare directional switching currents and average ten sweeps. Keep switching and return currents separate, and compare opposite current directions at the same field when assessing a diode effect. A relation involving simultaneous current and field reversal is a different test. The lowest measurement temperature is not a bulk CrSb transition temperature. [R4](#ref-source-807f7414e83e5e4c)

## Limits and disputes

The CrSb device authors interpret transport asymmetries using surface and bulk spin structure and discuss finite-momentum pairing. Such interpretations are not a direct image of pair momentum or a unique measurement of triplet content. Interface transparency, field history, geometry and alternative transport mechanisms still matter. The angular quantum-oscillation result and the proximity experiment also concern different specimens and observables; they should not be combined into a single specimen-level proof of a superconducting mechanism. [R3](#ref-source-26b1bd116249a6d3) [R4](#ref-source-807f7414e83e5e4c)

RuO2 illustrates why candidate labels require evidence dates and methods. Liu and colleagues report spin-resolved photoemission inconsistent with the proposed altermagnetic splitting in their investigated films and crystals. This challenges the assignment; it does not authorize transferring either a positive or a negative result to every strained film or interface. A superconducting transport report in a candidate material cannot establish magnetic coexistence without magnetic evidence for the relevant state. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including broader competing literature, final-version comparisons and specimen-specific verification. [R5](#ref-source-2a6a831bcc73374f)

## Discovery implications

Use experiments that can distinguish mechanisms: establish the magnetic symmetry, state the interface orientation, compare current and field reversals separately, and retain the orbital or sublattice content of the model. Proposed finite-momentum or topological states require their own discriminating observations. An altermagnetic label is a starting point for a testable pairing problem, not a shortcut from zero net moment to a confirmed superconducting device mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-ea3e0a10f6917658) [R2](#ref-source-7258aa669504806d) [R4](#ref-source-807f7414e83e5e4c)

## Related topics

[Antiferromagnetism and superconductivity](/scwiki/antiferromagnetism-and-superconductivity), [Spin–orbit coupling](/scwiki/spin-orbit-coupling), and [Singlet and triplet pairing](/scwiki/singlet-and-triplet-pairing).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-g9-claim-scope-1

Altermagnetism describes compensated collinear magnetic order whose opposite-spin sectors are related by crystal operations such as rotations. It can produce momentum-dependent spin splitting without requiring spin–orbit coupling. Cancellation of the total magnetic moment does not imply degeneracy of opposite spins at every momentum. Nor does the absence of a uniform moment remove every constraint on superconducting pairing. The magnetic symmetry, the occupied bands and the proposed superconducting state must be specified separately.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-ea3e0a10f6917658, source-7258aa669504806d.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-scope-2

Three questions should remain distinct: whether a specimen has altermagnetic order, whether it becomes intrinsically superconducting, and whether superconducting electrodes induce correlations in a hybrid device. Evidence for one does not establish the others. A 2026 In–CrSb–In experiment provides a concrete proximity platform, so a blanket statement that experimental altermagnet–superconductor systems do not exist is outdated. That device does not establish intrinsic bulk superconductivity in CrSb.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-26b1bd116249a6d3, source-807f7414e83e5e4c.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

A useful symmetry relation is $E_\uparrow(\mathbf k)=E_\downarrow(R\mathbf k)$ for an appropriate crystal operation $R$. It need not imply $E_\uparrow(\mathbf k)=E_\downarrow(\mathbf k)$. In a simple even-parity texture, $\delta(\mathbf k)=d(\cos k_x-\cos k_y)$ changes sign under a right-angle rotation and vanishes along diagonal directions. This illustrates a possible angular pattern, rather than identifying a material or determining its superconducting gap.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-ea3e0a10f6917658, source-7258aa669504806d.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

The Chakraborty–Black-Schaffer construction retains two low-energy states with opposite spins on different sublattices. Its onsite singlet restriction depends on those projected states: opposite spins on the same site are absent from that retained space. A two-component band Hamiltonian must therefore preserve what its components represent. Reading its Pauli matrices as ordinary spin while discarding sublattice information changes the pairing problem. The result should not be promoted to an unconditional ban covering every multiband or strongly hybridized material.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-7258aa669504806d.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

An independent local calculation illustrates the projection explicitly. For spin $\sigma=\pm1$, take $h_\sigma=(\delta+\sigma M)\tau_z+t\tau_x$, with $M>0$, real hybridization $t$ and sublattice Pauli matrices $\tau$. Let $u_\sigma$ be the normalized lower-band eigenvector. An imposed unit onsite singlet has projected magnitude $P=|u_\uparrow^T u_\downarrow|$. When $t=0$ and $|\delta|<M$, the two vectors occupy opposite sublattices and $P=0$. At $\delta=0$, direct diagonalization gives $P=|t|/\sqrt{M^2+t^2}$. Thus finite mixing changes the projection even when the imposed interaction is unchanged.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-7258aa669504806d.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-mathematical-assumptions-4

Forty-five parameter cases verify these limits and the exchange of spin branches under $\delta\rightarrow-\delta$. This is an algebraic illustration, not a reproduction of the paper's full lattice calculation. It computes neither a stable superconducting phase nor a transition temperature. A nonzero projected matrix element does not establish that pairing wins over competing states; a zero matrix element in a truncated space does not by itself exclude higher-band processes. Self-consistency, available states and interaction structure remain additional questions.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-7258aa669504806d.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Long and colleagues map CrSb's bulk angular electronic structure using magnetic quantum oscillations. Measurements use a 41.5 T magnet and include 0.4 K traces. Figure 3 compares angular oscillation branches with a g-wave interpretation; its displayed map is symmetrized. The comparison uses adjusted electronic bands, including a −0.11 eV shift for one pocket family and a compensating +0.015 eV shift for another. Oscillation frequencies constrain extremal orbit areas; assigning an order-parameter structure involves symmetry and band modeling. This is magnetic evidence, not a superconducting transition measurement.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-26b1bd116249a6d3.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Esin and colleagues use superconducting indium contacts separated by 2 μm beneath CrSb flakes thicker than 1 μm. At 30 mK, the device shows a zero-resistance current interval; a 1.2 K trace shows suppression. They compare directional switching currents and average ten sweeps. Keep switching and return currents separate, and compare opposite current directions at the same field when assessing a diode effect. A relation involving simultaneous current and field reversal is a different test. The lowest measurement temperature is not a bulk CrSb transition temperature.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-807f7414e83e5e4c.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

The CrSb device authors interpret transport asymmetries using surface and bulk spin structure and discuss finite-momentum pairing. Such interpretations are not a direct image of pair momentum or a unique measurement of triplet content. Interface transparency, field history, geometry and alternative transport mechanisms still matter. The angular quantum-oscillation result and the proximity experiment also concern different specimens and observables; they should not be combined into a single specimen-level proof of a superconducting mechanism.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-26b1bd116249a6d3, source-807f7414e83e5e4c.

Conditions: Projected spin–sublattice basis and hybridization assumptions; separate magnetic quantum oscillations from superconducting proximity devices and intrinsic bulk transitions.

Verification scope: Selected primary passages and figures, plus an independent projection illustration; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-g9-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

RuO2 illustrates why candidate labels require evidence dates and methods. Liu and colleagues report spin-resolved photoemission inconsistent with the proposed altermagnetic splitting in their investigated films and crystals. This challenges the assignment; it does not authorize transferring either a positive or a negative result to every strained film or interface. A superconducting transport report in a candidate material cannot establish magnetic coexistence without magnetic evidence for the relevant state. Complete scientific acceptance remains open, including broader competing literature, final-version comparisons and specimen-specific verification.

### scwiki-g9-claim-discovery-implications-1

Use experiments that can distinguish mechanisms: establish the magnetic symmetry, state the interface orientation, compare current and field reversals separately, and retain the orbital or sublattice content of the model. Proposed finite-momentum or topological states require their own discriminating observations. An altermagnetic label is a starting point for a testable pairing problem, not a shortcut from zero net moment to a confirmed superconducting device mechanism.

articles.body:
## Scope

A strange metal is identified through unusual normal-state behavior, often including resistivity approximately proportional to temperature after superconductivity is suppressed. It is an observational category, not a uniquely established microscopic phase or order parameter. The early Bi-based transport work and later overdoped-cuprate experiments concern particular specimens and temperature ranges. Their results do not provide a universal slope for all superconductors. Ordinary high-temperature electron–phonon transport can also be linear, so a room-temperature straight line alone is insufficient. [R1](#ref-source-a5d6480d08ee8555) [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225) [R4](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

This article focuses on how observations constrain explanations. Linear resistivity, a transport relaxation rate near a thermal quantum scale, proximity to a quantum critical point and a high superconducting transition temperature are separate propositions. Each requires additional evidence. Even the identity of a relevant lifetime matters: a single-particle linewidth and a current-relaxation rate need not weight scattering processes in the same way. [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8) [R4](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8) [R6](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a fitted normal-state curve, write $\rho(T)=\rho_0+AT+BT^2$. This is an empirical decomposition over a stated interval; its terms do not automatically identify independent microscopic mechanisms. Define a local exponent relative to a trial residual $\rho_r$ by $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=d\ln(\rho-\rho_r)/d\ln T$, wherever the logarithm is defined. Derivatives amplify noise and depend on the residual subtraction. An exponent should therefore accompany its temperature window, uncertainty and treatment of the superconducting region. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225) [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

An independent illustration uses exactly quadratic data, $\rho=\rho_0+BT^2$. If the trial residual differs by $\epsilon=\rho_r-\rho_0$, then $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=2BT^2/(BT^2-\epsilon)$. One hundred and eight finite-difference checks verify this relation. With the correct residual, a positive mixture of linear and quadratic terms gives $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=(A+2BT)/(A+BT)$, continuously between one and two; nine parameter cases confirm that limit. No abrupt phase boundary is required by this smooth crossover. These are synthetic checks, not fits to a paper's measurements. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225)

Two additional synthetic fits use $\rho=10+0.1T^2$ in arbitrary consistent units. A best straight line over $9\leq T\leq11$ has maximum deviation below 0.4% of the mean resistivity; extending the interval to $1\leq T\leq20$ raises it above 20%. Thus apparent linearity over a narrow interval can hide curvature. These percentages depend on the chosen example and are not universal acceptance thresholds. Real analysis needs residual plots, independent temperature calibration and a measurement-specific noise model. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225)

For parallel conducting channels, conductivities add: $\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}=\sigma_0+S/\Gamma$ in a specified Drude convention. If $S$ and $\sigma_0$ are constant and $\Gamma\propto T$, the resulting resistivity is $\rho=1/(a+b/T)$, which is generally nonlinear. Adding channel resistivities would describe a different circuit. Temperature-dependent spectral weight and finite frequency coverage must also be tested before assigning a lifetime from the total d.c. curve. [R6](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Experimental criteria

Grissonnanche and colleagues measured angle-dependent magnetoresistance in Nd-LSCO at hole concentration $p=0.24\pm0.005$. The sample's zero-resistance transition is 11 K; the transport measurements use 45 T at 6, 12, 20 and 25 K. At the two lower temperatures, some field orientations still enter a superconducting region. A high field alone therefore does not certify that every angular data point is normal-state transport. [R4](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Their fit separates a temperature-independent anisotropic contribution from an isotropic temperature-dependent rate, giving $\alpha=1.2\pm0.4$ in $\hbar/\tau_{\mathrm{inel}}=\alpha k_BT$. Total scattering is not isotropic. The analysis uses a bandwidth scale $160\pm30$ meV constrained by specific heat and omits a low-temperature correction that could change it by about 20% at 6 K. Temperature stability of ±1 mK differs from absolute uncertainty of approximately ±1 K at 6 and 12 K. These qualifications belong with the extracted coefficient. [R4](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Romero and colleagues resolve a narrower Drude channel and a broad background in two FeTe1−xSex films. The final abstract associates most condensate spectral weight with the narrower channel. In the checked author version, the scattering-rate fits use 20–40 K, and linewidths below the approximately 0.2 THz measurement limit cannot be resolved directly. Its frequency variable uses cycles per second, so $h$ appears in $\Gamma=\Gamma_0+\alpha k_BT/h$; an angular-frequency rate instead uses $\hbar$. A fitted spectral decomposition is stronger evidence than assigning a lifetime from total resistance alone, but it does not uniquely determine the pairing interaction. [R6](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Cooper and colleagues report that a low-temperature linear contribution extends over a range of LSCO dopings and tracks superconductivity. The checked abstract supports that association, not a reanalysis of its numerical curves. Magic-angle graphene measurements provide another material setting with nearly linear transport; a similar temperature exponent across systems does not prove identical scattering or pairing mechanisms. Material geometry, filling and fit assumptions must accompany cross-system comparisons. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225) [R5](#ref-source-8135909144b6b16b)

## Limits and disputes

The marginal-Fermi-liquid proposal organizes anomalies using an assumed charge- and spin-response spectrum. Its phenomenological success would not identify a unique microscopic origin. The original article has an erratum; this review records the correction's identity but has not independently read its contents, and therefore does not reproduce a supposedly corrected derivation. Quantum critical, incoherent-metal and phonon-based explanations require separate discriminating evidence rather than a choice made from one resistivity exponent. [R7](#ref-source-5880a61b06ec84e6) [R8](#ref-source-2cdc898b9c5e504c) [R4](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected final passages and figures have been checked, but full version comparisons and raw-data fits remain incomplete. A slope correlation with superconductivity does not establish causation, and a channel contributing to the condensate does not identify the interaction binding its electrons. Retain alternative explanations and distinguish an experimental observable from quantities inferred through a model. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225) [R6](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Discovery implications

Compare transport, spectroscopy and superconducting response on well-characterized samples, with field, geometry and temperature windows recorded. Use independent changes in disorder, pressure or filling to test whether a proposed scattering process also controls pairing. A useful discovery claim predicts an observable change and survives alternative fits; simply finding another straight resistivity curve adds a candidate observation, not a complete microscopic explanation. sections.title: Mathematical assumptions
sections.markdown:
## Mathematical assumptions

For a fitted normal-state curve, write $\rho(T)=\rho_0+AT+BT^2$. This is an empirical decomposition over a stated interval; its terms do not automatically identify independent microscopic mechanisms. Define a local exponent relative to a trial residual $\rho_r$ by $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=d\ln(\rho-\rho_r)/d\ln T$, wherever the logarithm is defined. Derivatives amplify noise and depend on the residual subtraction. An exponent should therefore accompany its temperature window, uncertainty and treatment of the superconducting region. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225) [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

An independent illustration uses exactly quadratic data, $\rho=\rho_0+BT^2$. If the trial residual differs by $\epsilon=\rho_r-\rho_0$, then $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=2BT^2/(BT^2-\epsilon)$. One hundred and eight finite-difference checks verify this relation. With the correct residual, a positive mixture of linear and quadratic terms gives $n_{\mathrm{eff}}=(A+2BT)/(A+BT)$, continuously between one and two; nine parameter cases confirm that limit. No abrupt phase boundary is required by this smooth crossover. These are synthetic checks, not fits to a paper's measurements. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225)

Two additional synthetic fits use $\rho=10+0.1T^2$ in arbitrary consistent units. A best straight line over $9\leq T\leq11$ has maximum deviation below 0.4% of the mean resistivity; extending the interval to $1\leq T\leq20$ raises it above 20%. Thus apparent linearity over a narrow interval can hide curvature. These percentages depend on the chosen example and are not universal acceptance thresholds. Real analysis needs residual plots, independent temperature calibration and a measurement-specific noise model. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225)

For parallel conducting channels, conductivities add: $\sigma_{\mathrm{dc}}=\sigma_0+S/\Gamma$ in a specified Drude convention. If $S$ and $\sigma_0$ are constant and $\Gamma\propto T$, the resulting resistivity is $\rho=1/(a+b/T)$, which is generally nonlinear. Adding channel resistivities would describe a different circuit. Temperature-dependent spectral weight and finite frequency coverage must also be tested before assigning a lifetime from the total d.c. curve. [R6](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

sections.title: Experimental criteria
sections.markdown:
## Experimental criteria

Grissonnanche and colleagues measured angle-dependent magnetoresistance in Nd-LSCO at hole concentration $p=0.24\pm0.005$. The sample's zero-resistance transition is 11 K; the transport measurements use 45 T at 6, 12, 20 and 25 K. At the two lower temperatures, some field orientations still enter a superconducting region. A high field alone therefore does not certify that every angular data point is normal-state transport. [R4](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Their fit separates a temperature-independent anisotropic contribution from an isotropic temperature-dependent rate, giving $\alpha=1.2\pm0.4$ in $\hbar/\tau_{\mathrm{inel}}=\alpha k_BT$. Total scattering is not isotropic. The analysis uses a bandwidth scale $160\pm30$ meV constrained by specific heat and omits a low-temperature correction that could change it by about 20% at 6 K. Temperature stability of ±1 mK differs from absolute uncertainty of approximately ±1 K at 6 and 12 K. These qualifications belong with the extracted coefficient. [R4](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Romero and colleagues resolve a narrower Drude channel and a broad background in two FeTe1−xSex films. The final abstract associates most condensate spectral weight with the narrower channel. In the checked author version, the scattering-rate fits use 20–40 K, and linewidths below the approximately 0.2 THz measurement limit cannot be resolved directly. Its frequency variable uses cycles per second, so $h$ appears in $\Gamma=\Gamma_0+\alpha k_BT/h$; an angular-frequency rate instead uses $\hbar$. A fitted spectral decomposition is stronger evidence than assigning a lifetime from total resistance alone, but it does not uniquely determine the pairing interaction. [R6](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Cooper and colleagues report that a low-temperature linear contribution extends over a range of LSCO dopings and tracks superconductivity. The checked abstract supports that association, not a reanalysis of its numerical curves. Magic-angle graphene measurements provide another material setting with nearly linear transport; a similar temperature exponent across systems does not prove identical scattering or pairing mechanisms. Material geometry, filling and fit assumptions must accompany cross-system comparisons. [R2](#ref-source-1610fd228e679225) [R5](#ref-source-8135909144b6b16b)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected final passages and figures have been checked, but full version comparisons and raw-data fits remain incomplete. A slope correlation with superconductivity does not establish causation, and a channel contributing to the condensate does not identify the interaction binding its electrons. articles.body:
## Scope

A quantum spin liquid is a quantum magnetic state with correlations and excitations beyond a conventional ordered magnet. Absence of static magnetic order alone is not a definition that identifies it experimentally: a trivial singlet state, disorder or a finite measurement window can also suppress the expected signal. Candidate materials require positive evidence and tests of alternatives. Chiral spin liquids can break time-reversal symmetry, so preserving every conventional symmetry is not a universal requirement. [R1](#ref-source-779d3cdcbcd5a620) [R2](#ref-source-4619c72961e466c5) [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

The connection to superconductivity is a research route, not an automatic consequence. Anderson's RVB proposal motivates doping a correlated singlet state, but undoped La2CuO4 has antiferromagnetic order. A spin-only Hamiltonian has no mobile electrical charge or superconducting stiffness. Emergent neutral Majorana fermions in such a model do not make its material a topological superconductor. A specific charge sector and gauge-invariant superconducting response must be established separately. [R1](#ref-source-779d3cdcbcd5a620) [R3](#ref-source-5a6026d6455bf7a0) [R11](#ref-source-9dda11fbf0c41f73) [R12](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

## Mathematical assumptions

An explicit counterexample clarifies the diagnostic problem. A product of disconnected spin singlets has $\langle\mathbf S_i\rangle=0$ and vanishing correlations between different dimers, yet is not thereby a long-range-entangled spin liquid. For two spin-one-half singlets, direct matrix evaluation gives $\langle\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_2\rangle=-3/4$ and $\langle\mathbf S_1\cdot\mathbf S_3\rangle=0$. These finite-state checks disprove the inference from zero local moments alone; they do not classify an interacting bulk material. [R2](#ref-source-4619c72961e466c5) [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

Use the honeycomb convention $H=-\sum_{\langle ij\rangle_\alpha}J_\alpha\sigma_i^\alpha\sigma_j^\alpha$, with Pauli matrices $\sigma=2S$. A Hamiltonian written with spin operators requires couplings $K_\alpha=4J_\alpha$ for the same energy. The vortex-free zero-field matter spectrum has zeros when the three $|J_\alpha|$ satisfy triangle inequalities. Kitaev calls this the gapless B region, including isotropy; the dominant-coupling A regions are gapped. The source draft had these labels reversed. [R1](#ref-source-779d3cdcbcd5a620)

Near isotropy, a weak field with all three spin-axis components nonzero generates a time-reversal-breaking term scaling as $h_xh_yh_z/J^2$ at third order. This perturbative result is not exact solvability at arbitrary field. For an ideal equilibrated chiral Majorana edge above a gapped bulk, $\kappa_{xy}^{2D}/T=c_-\pi^2k_B^2/(3h)$ with $c_-=\pm1/2$. This is thermal conductance per layer, not three-dimensional conductivity or electrical Hall conductance. Independent checks verify the phase-boundary algebra, spin normalization and positive-energy thermal integral. [R1](#ref-source-779d3cdcbcd5a620)

For a gapped two-dimensional topologically ordered ground state and a sufficiently large smooth region, $S=\alpha L-\gamma+\cdots$ with $\gamma=\ln\mathcal D$ and $\mathcal D=\sqrt{\sum_a d_a^2}$. The Abelian Z2 example gives $\gamma=\ln2$. This expression is not a universal entropy formula for every gapless spin liquid, and a single entropy constant does not fully specify anyon statistics. Finite geometry, boundaries and correlation length matter before identifying a universal term. [R2](#ref-source-4619c72961e466c5)

## Experimental criteria

Shimizu's organic candidate kappa-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3 shows no proton-NMR signature of long-range magnetic order down to 32 mK. The single-crystal experiment applied 2.2 T perpendicular to the conducting planes; the susceptibility-derived exchange scale around 250 K came from a separate fit. Neither number is a superconducting transition temperature, and the experiment does not directly observe the zero-field, zero-temperature ground state. Kurosaki's pressure phase diagram separately connects the correlated insulator with metallic and superconducting regions; it does not identify a unique pairing mechanism. [R4](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R5](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c)

Pustogow's 2023 strain-transport study instead favors a low-entropy, spin-gapped valence-bond-solid interpretation of the organic material's 6 K anomaly. Its hydrostatic-equivalent pressure is inferred from comparison with transport data, rather than directly applied hydrostatic pressure. The paper retains a gapped chiral-spin-liquid alternative and discusses mounting-related microcracks. Thus a revised interpretation must preserve both the measured anomaly and the remaining discrimination problem. [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

Han's neutron study used deuterated herbertsmithite, ZnCu3(OD)6Cl2, at 1.6 K. Broad momentum-energy scattering supports the authors' fractionalization interpretation, but the measured low-energy signal can include interlayer Cu defects. The apparent absence of a gap down to the measured energy limit does not establish a universally gapless intrinsic kagome state. A later primary study explicitly analyzes correlated impurity contributions. Preserve isotope, background subtraction, resolution and momentum window before comparing these results with a theoretical continuum. [R7](#ref-source-43fba6076983bec0) [R8](#ref-source-7a6863ba09a1c037)

In alpha-RuCl3, zero-field magnetic order and candidate field-induced behavior must be separated. Xing's 2025 ultraclean-crystal study reports a narrower near-half-quantized thermal Hall plateau and weakened oscillation-like features. It discusses sample-dependent magnetic boundaries, possible stacking faults and phonon-edge coupling. The 5.0 K Hall measurement used heat current along b and field along a; the comparison crystal was measured at 4.3 K. These are not identical conditions or a universal material threshold. [R9](#ref-source-f089ec733f27462c)

Shragai's 2026 ultrasound study measures acoustic Faraday rotation and infers a phonon Hall-viscosity contribution. Its conversion to thermal transport requires assumptions about frequency, phonon branches and viscosity components; the directly measured single-component estimate does not independently measure every thermal carrier. One displayed comparison also combines 2 K, 55-degree-tilted ultrasound with 4.9 K, 45-degree-tilted thermal data. This supplies substantive phonon evidence without making every field geometry or claimed quantized plateau equivalent. [R10](#ref-source-4a3e383e4c71604e)

## Limits and disputes

A continuum, a low-temperature heat-capacity term, absent NMR splitting and a thermal Hall signal test different observables. Their interpretation depends on defects, phonons, magnetic order, probe time scales and sample history. Do not turn one positive signal into a sufficient spin-liquid criterion, or one disputed material interpretation into a claim about every possible quantum spin liquid. Broad statements that all materials are settled or that none can ever be established would exceed this review. [R4](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b) [R7](#ref-source-43fba6076983bec0) [R9](#ref-source-f089ec733f27462c) [R10](#ref-source-4a3e383e4c71604e)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The present check covers selected primary passages, figures and restricted independent models. Several references retain abstract-only or earlier manuscript scopes; complete final-version comparisons, defect subtraction, thermal calibration and raw-data reproduction remain unfinished. The exact-model results and experimental interpretations are therefore presented at different evidence levels. [R1](#ref-source-779d3cdcbcd5a620) [R2](#ref-source-4619c72961e466c5) [R4](#ref-source-9d15cd9236072f5c) [R5](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c) [R7](#ref-source-43fba6076983bec0) [R8](#ref-source-7a6863ba09a1c037) [R9](#ref-source-f089ec733f27462c) [R10](#ref-source-4a3e383e4c71604e)

## Discovery implications

Track the insulating magnetic state, tuning parameter and superconducting response independently. For a pressure or doping trajectory, distinguish structural changes and disorder from changed bandwidth or filling. Compare several probes on characterized samples and ask what would exclude a trivial singlet, ordered or disordered alternative. A successful spin-liquid model provides testable mechanisms and excitations; establishing superconductivity additionally requires mobile charge, phase coherence and the corresponding experimental criteria. [R5](#ref-source-0443485ac20d3a8c) [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b) [R11](#ref-source-9dda11fbf0c41f73) [R12](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

## Related topics

[Spin-liquid routes to superconductivity](/scwiki/spin-liquids-and-superconductivity), [RVB pairing](/scwiki/rvb-and-doped-mott-insulators), [Organic superconductors](/scwiki/organic-charge-transfer-superconductors), and [Mottness](/scwiki/mottness-and-superconductivity).

## Experimental criteria

Shimizu's organic candidate kappa-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3 shows no proton-NMR signature of long-range magnetic order down to 32 mK. The single-crystal experiment applied 2.2 T perpendicular to the conducting planes; the susceptibility-derived exchange scale around 250 K came from a separate fit. Neither number is a superconducting transition temperature, and the experiment does not directly observe the zero-field, zero-temperature ground state. Pustogow's 2023 strain-transport study instead favors a low-entropy, spin-gapped valence-bond-solid interpretation of the organic material's 6 K anomaly. Its hydrostatic-equivalent pressure is inferred from comparison with transport data, rather than directly applied hydrostatic pressure. The paper retains a gapped chiral-spin-liquid alternative and discusses mounting-related microcracks. Thus a revised interpretation must preserve both the measured anomaly and the remaining discrimination problem. [R6](#ref-source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b)

[R9](#ref-source-f089ec733f27462c)

Shragai's 2026 ultrasound study measures acoustic Faraday rotation and infers a phonon Hall-viscosity contribution. Its conversion to thermal transport requires assumptions about frequency, phonon branches and viscosity components; the directly measured single-component estimate does not independently measure every thermal carrier. ### scwiki-h10-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Shimizu's organic candidate kappa-(BEDT-TTF)2Cu2(CN)3 shows no proton-NMR signature of long-range magnetic order down to 32 mK. The single-crystal experiment applied 2.2 T perpendicular to the conducting planes; the susceptibility-derived exchange scale around 250 K came from a separate fit. Neither number is a superconducting transition temperature, and the experiment does not directly observe the zero-field, zero-temperature ground state. Kurosaki's pressure phase diagram separately connects the correlated insulator with metallic and superconducting regions; it does not identify a unique pairing mechanism.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-9d15cd9236072f5c, source-0443485ac20d3a8c.

Conditions: Distinguish exact spin model, restricted illustrations and material interpretations. Preserve field, temperature, isotope, normalizations, defects and charge-sector criteria.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and independent model checks; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-h10-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Pustogow's 2023 strain-transport study instead favors a low-entropy, spin-gapped valence-bond-solid interpretation of the organic material's 6 K anomaly. Its hydrostatic-equivalent pressure is inferred from comparison with transport data, rather than directly applied hydrostatic pressure. The paper retains a gapped chiral-spin-liquid alternative and discusses mounting-related microcracks. Thus a revised interpretation must preserve both the measured anomaly and the remaining discrimination problem.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-5e0dcd80e8b64a1b.

Conditions: Distinguish exact spin model, restricted illustrations and material interpretations. Preserve field, temperature, isotope, normalizations, defects and charge-sector criteria.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and independent model checks; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-h10-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Han's neutron study used deuterated herbertsmithite, ZnCu3(OD)6Cl2, at 1.6 K. Broad momentum-energy scattering supports the authors' fractionalization interpretation, but the measured low-energy signal can include interlayer Cu defects. The apparent absence of a gap down to the measured energy limit does not establish a universally gapless intrinsic kagome state. A later primary study explicitly analyzes correlated impurity contributions. Preserve isotope, background subtraction, resolution and momentum window before comparing these results with a theoretical continuum.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-43fba6076983bec0, source-7a6863ba09a1c037.

Conditions: Distinguish exact spin model, restricted illustrations and material interpretations. Preserve field, temperature, isotope, normalizations, defects and charge-sector criteria.

### scwiki-h10-claim-experimental-criteria-4

In alpha-RuCl3, zero-field magnetic order and candidate field-induced behavior must be separated. Xing's 2025 ultraclean-crystal study reports a narrower near-half-quantized thermal Hall plateau and weakened oscillation-like features. It discusses sample-dependent magnetic boundaries, possible stacking faults and phonon-edge coupling. The 5.0 K Hall measurement used heat current along b and field along a; the comparison crystal was measured at 4.3 K. These are not identical conditions or a universal material threshold.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-f089ec733f27462c.

Shragai's 2026 ultrasound study measures acoustic Faraday rotation and infers a phonon Hall-viscosity contribution. Its conversion to thermal transport requires assumptions about frequency, phonon branches and viscosity components; the directly measured single-component estimate does not independently measure every thermal carrier. One displayed comparison also combines 2 K, 55-degree-tilted ultrasound with 4.9 K, 45-degree-tilted thermal data. This supplies substantive phonon evidence without making every field geometry or claimed quantized plateau equivalent.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-4a3e383e4c71604e.

A continuum, a low-temperature heat-capacity term, absent NMR splitting and a thermal Hall signal test different observables. Their interpretation depends on defects, phonons, magnetic order, probe time scales and sample history. Do not turn one positive signal into a sufficient spin-liquid criterion, or one disputed material interpretation into a claim about every possible quantum spin liquid. Broad statements that all materials are settled or that none can ever be established would exceed this review.

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The present check covers selected primary passages, figures and restricted independent models. Several references retain abstract-only or earlier manuscript scopes; complete final-version comparisons, defect subtraction, thermal calibration and raw-data reproduction remain unfinished. articles.body:
## Scope

A Planckian-scale claim compares a defined relaxation rate with $k_BT/\hbar$. It must identify the observable, residual subtraction and uncertainty. Charge transport, optical response, single-particle decay and quantum scrambling need not share one lifetime. An approximate coefficient near unity is an empirical observation within a model, not a universal theorem obtained from a straight resistivity curve. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

The evidence has several levels: measured conductivity, an extracted rate, a cross-material scaling relation, and a proposed bound. Moving between them adds assumptions. Bruin's transport comparison, Legros's cuprate analysis, angular magnetoresistance and frequency-resolved film measurements test different parts of this chain. A useful comparison retains each experiment's conditions instead of pooling every quoted coefficient. [R2](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae) [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8) [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R6](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

## Mathematical assumptions

Write $\gamma_{\mathrm{tr}}=\gamma_0+\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}k_BT/\hbar$. Then $\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}=\hbar\gamma_{\mathrm{tr}}/(k_BT)=\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}+\hbar\gamma_0/(k_BT)$. A constant residual rate makes the total ratio temperature dependent even when the inelastic slope is fixed. Twenty-seven independent synthetic parameter checks verify this algebra; they do not justify additive scattering in a material. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

With temperature-independent density and mass in a single-band Drude model, $\rho=m^\ast\gamma_{\mathrm{tr}}/(ne^2)$ gives $\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}=(\hbar ne^2/k_Bm^\ast)d\rho/dT$. A two-dimensional, spin-degenerate parabolic band instead uses sheet slope $A_1^\square$, areal density $n_{2D}$ and $T_F=\pi\hbar^2n_{2D}/(m^\ast k_B)$, yielding $A_1^\square T_F=\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}h/(2e^2)$. The geometric conversion and mass estimate are essential inputs, not outputs of a resistivity slope. Noncircular or multiple Fermi surfaces require additional analysis. [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

An independent angular-scattering illustration makes the lifetime distinction explicit. On a circular Fermi line, define an elastic event kernel $W(\theta)=\gamma[1+a\cos\theta]/(2\pi)$ with $|a|\leq1$. The event rate is $\int_0^{2\pi}W\,d\theta=\gamma$, whereas current relaxation weights changes of direction: $\int_0^{2\pi}W(1-\cos\theta)\,d\theta=\gamma(1-a/2)$. Fifteen numerical quadratures verify both integrals. Forward-weighted events therefore relax current less efficiently in this specified model. The event rate is explicitly defined; it is not silently identified with a spectral half-width. This elastic Boltzmann example proves neither a quantum bound nor a superconducting mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

For a fitted Drude denominator $\Gamma-i\nu$, both variables use cycles per second. The corresponding decay rate is $\gamma=2\pi\Gamma$, so $\Gamma=\alpha k_BT/h$ and $\gamma=\alpha k_BT/\hbar$ have the same dimensionless coefficient after conversion. Mixing the conventions without converting the fitted width changes the apparent coefficient by $2\pi$. Parallel channels add conductivities, further limiting inference from total resistance. [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Experimental criteria

Bruin and colleagues report linear resistivity in Sr3Ru2O7 at 7.9 T and use independently characterized Fermi-surface inputs to estimate scattering. The retrieved opening page describes a 1.5–400 K transport study and a field-induced nematic region below 1.2 K near that field. Those boundaries matter: the available page does not justify extending the measured law through the intervening phase or verify every cross-material fit. The remaining article pages and supplementary tables are outside this check. [R2](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae)

Legros's author manuscript compares sheet-resistance slopes with Fermi-temperature estimates. Its electron-doped comparison gives $\alpha=1.0\pm0.3$; the hole-doped estimates require more approximate geometry and specific-heat masses, with temperature-dependent mass an explicit complication in Nd-LSCO. The displayed $\alpha=1$ prediction is a tested assumption, not an independent lifetime measurement. This article uses selected author-version passages; a complete comparison with the final publication remains open. [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

Grissonnanche's final Nd-LSCO analysis separates an isotropic temperature-dependent component from anisotropic elastic scattering and reports $\alpha=1.2\pm0.4$. The band-energy scale is constrained by specific heat, and the quoted uncertainty includes fitting and sample-geometry contributions. Measurements at 45 T include superconducting angular sectors at the lower temperatures; those sectors are excluded. Neither a large applied field nor the isotropic inelastic term makes every datum normal-state or the total scattering isotropic. [R6](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Romero's author manuscript fits two FeTe1−xSex films over 20–40 K using a narrow Drude contribution plus a broad background. It reports cycle-frequency coefficients 3.02 for $x=0.45$ and 2.42 for $x=0.35$, with widths below 0.2 THz unresolved in its spectral window. These are author-version fit values, not newly reproduced final-paper estimates. The published abstract confirms a parallel-channel interpretation; complete version comparison and fitting covariance remain open. A linear narrow-channel width can coexist with nonlinear total resistivity. [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Limits and disputes

The conditional chaos result $\lambda_L\leq2\pi k_BT/\hbar$ bounds exponential growth of a suitable regularized out-of-time-order correlator. Its argument requires thermal-strip analyticity and boundedness, controlled factorization errors and separated dissipation and scrambling scales. This is not a measured charge-transport rate; identifying the exponent with one requires another, model-specific argument. The theorem alone neither fixes a transport coefficient to one nor verifies a material's inferred mass. [R5](#ref-source-8339743a9f1c3239) [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected primary passages, figures and independent model checks do not constitute raw-data reproduction. Distinguish published results from the author's interpretation of universality; preserve unresolved frequency coverage, final-version and calibration limits. Spectral weight entering a condensate also does not identify the pairing mediator. [R2](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae) [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8) [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Discovery implications

Compare rates only after aligning channel definitions, sample conditions and frequency units. Test whether alternative band weights or a temperature-dependent mass can explain the same measured curve. Then seek independent optical or angle-dependent constraints. A connection between normal-state relaxation and superconductivity is a research hypothesis to test; faster scattering does not, by itself, predict a higher transition temperature. [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8) [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R6](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

## Related topics

[Strange metals](/scwiki/strange-metals), [Linear-T resistivity](/scwiki/linear-t-resistivity), and [Iron-based superconductors](/scwiki/iron-based-superconductors).

sections.title: Mathematical assumptions
sections.markdown:
## Mathematical assumptions

Write $\gamma_{\mathrm{tr}}=\gamma_0+\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}k_BT/\hbar$. Then $\alpha_{\mathrm{tot}}=\hbar\gamma_{\mathrm{tr}}/(k_BT)=\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}+\hbar\gamma_0/(k_BT)$. A constant residual rate makes the total ratio temperature dependent even when the inelastic slope is fixed. Twenty-seven independent synthetic parameter checks verify this algebra; they do not justify additive scattering in a material. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

With temperature-independent density and mass in a single-band Drude model, $\rho=m^\ast\gamma_{\mathrm{tr}}/(ne^2)$ gives $\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}=(\hbar ne^2/k_Bm^\ast)d\rho/dT$. A two-dimensional, spin-degenerate parabolic band instead uses sheet slope $A_1^\square$, areal density $n_{2D}$ and $T_F=\pi\hbar^2n_{2D}/(m^\ast k_B)$, yielding $A_1^\square T_F=\alpha_{\mathrm{inel}}h/(2e^2)$. The geometric conversion and mass estimate are essential inputs, not outputs of a resistivity slope. Noncircular or multiple Fermi surfaces require additional analysis. [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

An independent angular-scattering illustration makes the lifetime distinction explicit. On a circular Fermi line, define an elastic event kernel $W(\theta)=\gamma[1+a\cos\theta]/(2\pi)$ with $|a|\leq1$. The event rate is $\int_0^{2\pi}W\,d\theta=\gamma$, whereas current relaxation weights changes of direction: $\int_0^{2\pi}W(1-\cos\theta)\,d\theta=\gamma(1-a/2)$. Fifteen numerical quadratures verify both integrals. Forward-weighted events therefore relax current less efficiently in this specified model. The event rate is explicitly defined; it is not silently identified with a spectral half-width. This elastic Boltzmann example proves neither a quantum bound nor a superconducting mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

For a fitted Drude denominator $\Gamma-i\nu$, both variables use cycles per second. The corresponding decay rate is $\gamma=2\pi\Gamma$, so $\Gamma=\alpha k_BT/h$ and $\gamma=\alpha k_BT/\hbar$ have the same dimensionless coefficient after conversion. Mixing the conventions without converting the fitted width changes the apparent coefficient by $2\pi$. Parallel channels add conductivities, further limiting inference from total resistance. [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

sections.title: Experimental criteria
sections.markdown:
## Experimental criteria

Bruin and colleagues report linear resistivity in Sr3Ru2O7 at 7.9 T and use independently characterized Fermi-surface inputs to estimate scattering. The retrieved opening page describes a 1.5–400 K transport study and a field-induced nematic region below 1.2 K near that field. Those boundaries matter: the available page does not justify extending the measured law through the intervening phase or verify every cross-material fit. The remaining article pages and supplementary tables are outside this check. [R2](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae)

Legros's author manuscript compares sheet-resistance slopes with Fermi-temperature estimates. Its electron-doped comparison gives $\alpha=1.0\pm0.3$; the hole-doped estimates require more approximate geometry and specific-heat masses, with temperature-dependent mass an explicit complication in Nd-LSCO. The displayed $\alpha=1$ prediction is a tested assumption, not an independent lifetime measurement. This article uses selected author-version passages; a complete comparison with the final publication remains open. [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8)

Grissonnanche's final Nd-LSCO analysis separates an isotropic temperature-dependent component from anisotropic elastic scattering and reports $\alpha=1.2\pm0.4$. The band-energy scale is constrained by specific heat, and the quoted uncertainty includes fitting and sample-geometry contributions. Measurements at 45 T include superconducting angular sectors at the lower temperatures; those sectors are excluded. Neither a large applied field nor the isotropic inelastic term makes every datum normal-state or the total scattering isotropic. [R6](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Romero's author manuscript fits two FeTe1−xSex films over 20–40 K using a narrow Drude contribution plus a broad background. It reports cycle-frequency coefficients 3.02 for $x=0.45$ and 2.42 for $x=0.35$, with widths below 0.2 THz unresolved in its spectral window. These are author-version fit values, not newly reproduced final-paper estimates. The published abstract confirms a parallel-channel interpretation; complete version comparison and fitting covariance remain open. A linear narrow-channel width can coexist with nonlinear total resistivity. [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

sections.title: Limits and disputes
sections.markdown:
## Limits and disputes

The conditional chaos result $\lambda_L\leq2\pi k_BT/\hbar$ bounds exponential growth of a suitable regularized out-of-time-order correlator. Its argument requires thermal-strip analyticity and boundedness, controlled factorization errors and separated dissipation and scrambling scales. This is not a measured charge-transport rate; identifying the exponent with one requires another, model-specific argument. The theorem alone neither fixes a transport coefficient to one nor verifies a material's inferred mass. [R5](#ref-source-8339743a9f1c3239) [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected primary passages, figures and independent model checks do not constitute raw-data reproduction. Distinguish published results from the author's interpretation of universality; preserve unresolved frequency coverage, final-version and calibration limits. Spectral weight entering a condensate also does not identify the pairing mediator. [R2](#ref-source-e6d342432f3409ae) [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8) [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

sections.title: Discovery implications
sections.markdown:
## Discovery implications

Compare rates only after aligning channel definitions, sample conditions and frequency units. Test whether alternative band weights or a temperature-dependent mass can explain the same measured curve. Then seek independent optical or angle-dependent constraints. A connection between normal-state relaxation and superconductivity is a research hypothesis to test; faster scattering does not, by itself, predict a higher transition temperature. [R3](#ref-source-c1ae7869b672a8e8) [R4](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R6](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

articles.body:
## Scope

A pseudogap denotes suppressed low-energy spectral weight without requiring a fully gapped insulator or coherent superconductivity. In cuprates the term connects observations from nuclear magnetic resonance, photoemission, tunnelling and transport, but those probes interrogate different responses. A reported $T^*$ must retain its material, doping, observable and onset criterion. It need not be one universal transition temperature shared by every probe. [R1](#ref-source-2ecda5a1c9258a07) [R2](#ref-source-ce431fada9b3a183) [R3](#ref-source-b8f71a71e90d00ff)

The central question is which microscopic processes produce these changes and how they relate to superconductivity. Pairing, charge or magnetic order and strong-correlation scenarios remain distinguishable explanations. Observing a gap above $T_c$, a charge modulation or a Hall anomaly does not independently identify a unique origin. The original source chapter is retained, but its misattribution of Wise's STM sample to Na-CCOC is corrected here to Pb/La-substituted Bi2201. [R3](#ref-source-b8f71a71e90d00ff) [R4](#ref-source-07213acd01bb9b90) [R5](#ref-source-377dc0bc5c5160fa) [R6](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72) [R7](#ref-source-4fa5e96f6d9eec1b)

## Mathematical assumptions

A useful non-uniqueness example is the two-level matrix $H=\begin{pmatrix}\xi&\Delta\\\Delta&-\xi\end{pmatrix}$ with real $\Delta$. Its diagonal retarded resolvent is $G_{11}(z)=(z+\xi)/(z^2-\xi^2-\Delta^2)$, where $z=\omega+i\eta$ and $\eta>0$. The spectral function is $A_{11}=-\operatorname{Im}G_{11}/\pi$. Its poles lie at $E_\pm=\pm\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}$, with positive weights $(1\pm\xi/\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2})/2$. Three hundred fifteen numerical comparisons verify the resolvent against this pole decomposition; four finite-window integrations recover almost all spectral weight, with small Lorentzian tails outside the window. [R3](#ref-source-b8f71a71e90d00ff) [R7](#ref-source-4fa5e96f6d9eec1b)

In a perfectly nested density-wave illustration, the matrix acts on two electron momenta; in a BCS illustration it acts on a particle–hole Nambu basis. The same diagonal spectrum can therefore accompany physically different off-diagonal correlations. This independently checked example does not model an actual cuprate, establish nesting or calculate phase stiffness. It shows why a spectral gap alone cannot select the broken symmetry. Additional momentum, spin, phase-sensitive and thermodynamic information must constrain the interpretation. [R3](#ref-source-b8f71a71e90d00ff) [R7](#ref-source-4fa5e96f6d9eec1b)

For the Hall comparison, $n_H=V/(eR_H)$ expresses a number per chosen structural unit when $V$ is the corresponding volume. Its interpretation as carrier density requires transport assumptions; multiple bands, mobility imbalance, Fermi-surface reconstruction and scattering anisotropy can alter $R_H$. The high-field inference is consequently stronger when accompanied by magnetoresistance and specimen calibration, and it cannot be transferred unchanged to zero-field spectra. [R6](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72)

## Experimental criteria

Warren's YBa2Cu3O6.7 study reports a decrease of planar Cu nuclear relaxation below about 100 K, above its bulk superconducting transition. The authors discuss spin pairing as a possibility; the abstract does not establish Cooper-pair phase coherence. Alloul's 89Y NMR work separately constrains spin susceptibility through shifts and relaxation. Ding's underdoped Bi2212 ARPES reports an anisotropic normal-state pseudogap evolving into the superconducting gap. These historical results are checked at primary-abstract scope here, without reproducing their lineshape or calibration analyses. [R1](#ref-source-2ecda5a1c9258a07) [R2](#ref-source-ce431fada9b3a183) [R3](#ref-source-b8f71a71e90d00ff)

Wise's final paper measures Pb/La-substituted Bi2201. Its Figures 1–2 compare conductance maps at 6 K: specimens labelled by $T_c=35,32,25$ K have modulation periods approximately $6.2,5.1,4.5a_0$, respectively. The wavelength varies with doping, while the reported modulation is nondispersive over the investigated bias window. That supports the authors' charge-order interpretation within these measurements; it neither proves a universal pseudogap mechanism nor assigns their data to Ca2−xNaxCuO2Cl2, which appears as cited earlier work. The 6 K mapping temperature is not a transition. [R4](#ref-source-07213acd01bb9b90)

Rullier-Albenque's YBCO analysis uses pulsed fields up to 55–60 T along the c axis and a normal-state magnetoresistance background to extract excess conductivity. The author v2 defines a fluctuation-onset threshold of $10^3\,(\Omega\,\mathrm{m})^{-1}$; the earlier v1 prints $10^{-3}$ at that location, so version choice matters. Figure 8 shows distinct doping trends for the fluctuation onset and pseudogap scale. This constrains the identification of the entire pseudogap region with superconducting fluctuations. The threshold is an operational sensitivity criterion, not a universal thermodynamic boundary. [R5](#ref-source-377dc0bc5c5160fa)

Badoux's Hall measurements reach 88 T. The author Figure 4 compares YBCO samples at 50 K using values measured or extrapolated to 80 T, with about 15% uncertainty in the absolute Hall coefficient. The inferred change near $p^*=0.19\pm0.01$ is separated from the charge-reconstruction endpoint near $p=0.16$. Those values belong to this material analysis. The two highest dopings use Ca substitution, and the figure also incorporates comparison data from other cuprates; it must not be presented as one homogeneous specimen series or an unconditional carrier count. [R6](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72)

## Limits and disputes

Sordi's calculation obtains a pseudogap and a nearby Widom crossover in a square-lattice Hubbard model using a 2 × 2 plaquette CDMFT approximation at $U=6.2t$. Spectral, spin and singlet-probability criteria approach the compressibility crossover near the model's critical endpoint. Competing broken symmetries are unnecessary for that calculation to produce a pseudogap, but this does not exclude their role in real materials. The plotted conversion using $t=0.35$ eV is a model choice, not a universal experimental temperature calibration. [R7](#ref-source-4fa5e96f6d9eec1b)

Magnetic interpretations also remain contested. Fauqué reports translation-preserving polarized-neutron magnetic order; Croft reports no corresponding order in two underdoped YBCO specimens. Croft's upper bound depends on the assumed current pattern and experimental sensitivity. The linked 2018 Comment and Reply are recorded as identities, not as a dispute resolved by this review. Neither one positive signal nor one null result establishes the origin of every pseudogap observation. [R8](#ref-source-5e00a8860f823681) [R9](#ref-source-1642be5ac014792d) [R10](#ref-source-e18dc1cf556fc915) [R11](#ref-source-2e937b94b8b7edc6)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Historical abstracts, selected figures and toy spectra do not replace full final-version comparisons, raw-data reproduction or a comprehensive competing-literature assessment. Maintain separate definitions for a gap magnitude, crossover onset, charge modulation and superconducting transition. [R3](#ref-source-b8f71a71e90d00ff) [R4](#ref-source-07213acd01bb9b90) [R5](#ref-source-377dc0bc5c5160fa)

## Discovery implications

Seek predictions that discriminate between explanations on characterized specimens. Compare the same doping and field conditions across spectroscopy, transport and symmetry probes; test whether disorder or controlled tuning separates pairing fluctuations from the larger spectral suppression. A promising theory should explain both supporting observations and boundary cases instead of treating every normal-state anomaly as its confirmation. [R5](#ref-source-377dc0bc5c5160fa) [R6](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72) [R7](#ref-source-4fa5e96f6d9eec1b)

## Related topics

[Strange metals](/scwiki/strange-metals), [Planckian dissipation](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation), and [Pair-density waves](/scwiki/pair-density-wave).

## Limits and disputes

Sordi's calculation obtains a pseudogap and a nearby Widom crossover in a square-lattice Hubbard model using a 2 × 2 plaquette CDMFT approximation at $U=6.2t$. Magnetic interpretations also remain contested. Fauqué reports translation-preserving polarized-neutron magnetic order; Croft reports no corresponding order in two underdoped YBCO specimens. # Pseudogap: probes, crossovers and competing explanations

Distinguish spectral suppression, superconducting fluctuations and ordered phases using material-specific probes, criteria and source versions.

## Scope

A pseudogap denotes suppressed low-energy spectral weight without requiring a fully gapped insulator or coherent superconductivity. In cuprates the term connects observations from nuclear magnetic resonance, photoemission, tunnelling and transport, but those probes interrogate different responses. A reported $T^*$ must retain its material, doping, observable and onset criterion. It need not be one universal transition temperature shared by every probe. The central question is which microscopic processes produce these changes and how they relate to superconductivity. ## Mathematical assumptions

A useful non-uniqueness example is the two-level matrix $H=\begin{pmatrix}\xi&\Delta\\\Delta&-\xi\end{pmatrix}$ with real $\Delta$. Its poles lie at $E_\pm=\pm\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2}$, with positive weights $(1\pm\xi/\sqrt{\xi^2+\Delta^2})/2$. Three hundred fifteen numerical comparisons verify the resolvent against this pole decomposition; four finite-window integrations recover almost all spectral weight, with small Lorentzian tails outside the window. In a perfectly nested density-wave illustration, the matrix acts on two electron momenta; in a BCS illustration it acts on a particle–hole Nambu basis. The same diagonal spectrum can therefore accompany physically different off-diagonal correlations. This independently checked example does not model an actual cuprate, establish nesting or calculate phase stiffness. It shows why a spectral gap alone cannot select the broken symmetry. Additional momentum, spin, phase-sensitive and thermodynamic information must constrain the interpretation. [R3](#ref-source-b8f71a71e90d00ff) [R7](#ref-source-4fa5e96f6d9eec1b)

Its interpretation as carrier density requires transport assumptions; multiple bands, mobility imbalance, Fermi-surface reconstruction and scattering anisotropy can alter $R_H$.
