articles.body:
## Scope

A charge-density wave (CDW) modulates the electronic density at a finite wave vector, often together with atomic displacements. Cuprates and kagome compounds exhibit several distinct charge-order patterns. Their coexistence or competition with superconductivity depends on composition, temperature, field, pressure and the probe's spatial and temporal resolution. Neither a density modulation nor a nearby superconducting dome identifies the pairing interaction. [R2](#ref-source-9ae65971bc3eb5b8) [R3](#ref-source-c4a9d4e1b52d95bb) [R8](#ref-source-80eda571fc6d710c) [R11](#ref-source-74169f2f9bc31219)

This page addresses observations and their interpretation. Pair-density waves instead modulate the superconducting pair field; spin-density waves modulate magnetization. Charge order, structural chirality, broken time-reversal symmetry and superconducting chirality are different claims. The retained source chapter's citation of Stahl for the conjoined-CDW paper is corrected: that paper is by Li and colleagues; Stahl's temperature-dependent stacking study has a different DOI. [R7](#ref-source-d773a884dacbd7c9) [R8](#ref-source-80eda571fc6d710c) [R9](#ref-source-484da7abcc165cd3) [R10](#ref-source-057c43c86174f961)

## Mathematical assumptions

A single-component modulation can be written as $\rho(\mathbf r)=\rho_0+\operatorname{Re}[\rho_{\mathbf Q}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}]$. Peak position identifies periodicity, while width constrains correlations under a stated line-shape model. For the illustrative lattice correlation $C(n)=r^{|n|}$, with $r=e^{-1/\xi}$ and $\xi$ in lattice spacings, the Fourier sum is $S(q)=(1-r^2)/(1+r^2-2r\cos q)$. Here $q$ is dimensionless radians per spacing, measured from the ordering wave vector. Finite $\xi$ produces a finite-width peak; observing that peak does not establish infinite-range order. This is an independent correlation model, not a fit to the cited specimens. [R4](#ref-source-d9477b85392d03f9) [R5](#ref-source-b89f6bcf54acb4d8)

Correlation lengths also depend on resolution and conventions. If both intrinsic and instrumental profiles are Gaussian, $\sigma_{\rm obs}^2=\sigma_{\rm int}^2+\sigma_R^2$. The convention $\xi=1/\sigma_{\rm int}$ then requires momentum widths in inverse-length units. Reciprocal-lattice widths need the appropriate lattice conversion. Uncorrected $1/\sigma_{\rm obs}$ is a lower bound within this model. Gaussian standard deviations, Lorentzian half-widths and full widths are not interchangeable; a resolution-limited peak yields a bound rather than a precisely measured divergence. [R4](#ref-source-d9477b85392d03f9) [R5](#ref-source-b89f6bcf54acb4d8)

A phenomenological free energy $F=a_s|\Delta|^2+b_s|\Delta|^4+a_c|\rho_{\mathbf Q}|^2+b_c|\rho_{\mathbf Q}|^4+g|\Delta|^2|\rho_{\mathbf Q}|^2$ illustrates static competition when $g>0$. With positive quartic coefficients, a stable interior coexistence minimum additionally requires $4b_sb_c-g^2>0$ and positive equilibrium squared amplitudes. Competition alone neither guarantees coexistence nor determines the frequency-dependent pairing kernel. Charge fluctuations could contribute to an effective interaction in a specified microscopic model without making every observed CDW a pairing mechanism. [R3](#ref-source-c4a9d4e1b52d95bb) [R11](#ref-source-74169f2f9bc31219)

## Experimental criteria

Tranquada's historical neutron result concerns Nd-substituted La1.6−xNd0.4SrxCuO4 at $x=0.12$. Its static stripe evidence and suppressed superconductivity should not be assigned indiscriminately to every one-eighth-doped cuprate. Ghiringhelli's resonant X-ray study adds an element-sensitive charge response in underdoped YBCO. The selected author text uses 130 meV instrumental resolution and argues for a much smaller energy bound; that bound is not a separately resolved sharp collective mode. [R1](#ref-source-b33aab72ae697f3a) [R2](#ref-source-9ae65971bc3eb5b8)

Chang's 2012 experiment on detwinned ortho-VIII YBa2Cu3O6.67 finds charge-order intensity suppressed on entering the superconducting regime and enhanced by magnetic field below it. Those controlled changes support competition in this specimen. They do not isolate every field-induced change in vortices or electronic structure, and do not identify a unique microscopic interaction. [R3](#ref-source-c4a9d4e1b52d95bb)

Gerber's high-field diffraction shows additional interlayer-correlated order developing above about 15 T at 10 K. The author Figure 3 separates peaks near integer and half-integer out-of-plane coordinates and extracts Gaussian widths. Its reported lengths are explicitly uncorrected for resolution. Chang's 2016 study instead reports resolution-corrected widths: for YBCO6.67, the c-axis scale reaches about four lattice periods within the measured field range. Finite three-dimensional correlations must remain distinct from unlimited long-range coherence. These analyses cannot be combined by silently treating corrected and uncorrected widths as equivalent. [R4](#ref-source-d9477b85392d03f9) [R5](#ref-source-b89f6bcf54acb4d8)

Kagome studies probe different structures and surfaces. Liang's STM step-edge phase shift suggests $2\times2\times2$ order. Stahl's bulk diffraction reports a low-temperature $2\times2\times2$ structure changing to $2\times2\times4$ near 60 K on warming; its null response to fields up to 10 T does not rule out broken time-reversal symmetry. Li's separate CsV3Sb5 study resolves conjoined $2\times2\times1$ and $2\times2\times2$ charge-order responses, with distinct resonant behavior and a roughly 4 K onset separation at 1 GPa. That separation concerns charge order, not two superconducting transitions. [R6](#ref-source-7746049011a0e640) [R7](#ref-source-d773a884dacbd7c9) [R8](#ref-source-80eda571fc6d710c)

## Limits and disputes

A scattering superlattice peak needs electronic, structural and instrumental interpretation; it is not by itself proof of an exclusively electronic instability. STM conductance modulations must be compared across bias, surface termination and bulk probes. Li's surface modulation and bulk-null comparison illustrates why a surface pattern cannot automatically be promoted to a universal bulk phase. The present review does not independently reproduce those sensitivity limits or resolve every reported stacking structure. [R6](#ref-source-7746049011a0e640) [R8](#ref-source-80eda571fc6d710c)

Mielke's accepted-manuscript abstract reports enhanced internal-field widths in KV3Sb5 below charge ordering, interpreted as time-reversal symmetry breaking. This is a normal-state charge-order claim, not a direct determination of chiral superconducting pairing. Chen's spatially modulated tunnelling signatures motivate a kagome PDW interpretation, but interpretation of the pair field requires additional evidence beyond ordinary charge contrast. Material identity, probe coupling and the superconducting transition must remain explicit. [R9](#ref-source-484da7abcc165cd3) [R10](#ref-source-057c43c86174f961)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected methods and figures, historical abstracts and independent line-shape checks do not replace full source-version comparisons, raw diffraction reproduction, all supplementary calibrations or competing-structure assessment. A Hall anomaly, a Fermi-surface pocket or a charge onset below a pseudogap scale cannot alone specify which charge structure causes reconstruction or whether it mediates pairing. [R3](#ref-source-c4a9d4e1b52d95bb) [R4](#ref-source-d9477b85392d03f9) [R5](#ref-source-b89f6bcf54acb4d8)

## Discovery implications

Preserve the measured wave vector and reciprocal units, sample composition, oxygen order, field direction, pressure medium, line shape and resolution treatment. Compare competing-order amplitudes on characterized specimens and distinguish a static order parameter from dynamic spectral weight. Useful predictions should connect a particular charge structure to a testable electronic reconstruction and superconducting response, including results that could falsify the proposed connection. [R2](#ref-source-9ae65971bc3eb5b8) [R3](#ref-source-c4a9d4e1b52d95bb) [R5](#ref-source-b89f6bcf54acb4d8) [R11](#ref-source-74169f2f9bc31219)

## Related topics

[Pseudogap](/scwiki/pseudogap), [Charge-fluctuation pairing](/scwiki/charge-fluctuation-pairing), and [Pair-density waves](/scwiki/pair-density-wave).

# Charge-density waves: observations, competition and reconstruction

Read charge-order evidence with its material, wave vector, dimensionality and resolution limits; distinguish competition from a pairing mechanism.

## Scope

A charge-density wave (CDW) modulates the electronic density at a finite wave vector, often together with atomic displacements. Cuprates and kagome compounds exhibit several distinct charge-order patterns. Their coexistence or competition with superconductivity depends on composition, temperature, field, pressure and the probe's spatial and temporal resolution. Neither a density modulation nor a nearby superconducting dome identifies the pairing interaction. This page addresses observations and their interpretation. Pair-density waves instead modulate the superconducting pair field; spin-density waves modulate magnetization. Charge order, structural chirality, broken time-reversal symmetry and superconducting chirality are different claims. The retained source chapter's citation of Stahl for the conjoined-CDW paper is corrected: that paper is by Li and colleagues; Stahl's temperature-dependent stacking study has a different DOI. ## Mathematical assumptions

A single-component modulation can be written as $\rho(\mathbf r)=\rho_0+\operatorname{Re}[\rho_{\mathbf Q}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}]$. Peak position identifies periodicity, while width constrains correlations under a stated line-shape model. For the illustrative lattice correlation $C(n)=r^{|n|}$, with $r=e^{-1/\xi}$ and $\xi$ in lattice spacings, the Fourier sum is $S(q)=(1-r^2)/(1+r^2-2r\cos q)$. The convention $\xi=1/\sigma_{\rm int}$ then requires momentum widths in inverse-length units. Reciprocal-lattice widths need the appropriate lattice conversion. Uncorrected $1/\sigma_{\rm obs}$ is a lower bound within this model. Gaussian standard deviations, Lorentzian half-widths and full widths are not interchangeable; a resolution-limited peak yields a bound rather than a precisely measured divergence. With positive quartic coefficients, a stable interior coexistence minimum additionally requires $4b_sb_c-g^2>0$ and positive equilibrium squared amplitudes. Competition alone neither guarantees coexistence nor determines the frequency-dependent pairing kernel. Charge fluctuations could contribute to an effective interaction in a specified microscopic model without making every observed CDW a pairing mechanism. articles.body:
## Scope

A spin-density wave (SDW) is a spatial modulation of magnetization. Static order, fluctuating magnetism and superconductivity are distinct observations. Chromium, iron arsenides and cuprate stripes supply different examples; their microscopic interactions need not be identical. A spin order parameter can couple to charge and lattice distortions. Calling a state magnetic does not imply that the lattice is uninvolved. [R2](#ref-source-e29f9b7d08a70596) [R3](#ref-source-9ab5e43d0018f0b0) [R13](#ref-source-b33aab72ae697f3a)

Overhauser demonstrated an instability of the uniform electron gas within Hartree–Fock theory, near twice the Fermi wave vector. This is a foundational model result, not an exact solution for all interacting metals. Similarly, a spin-fluctuation calculation that favors a sign-changing superconducting gap establishes a candidate mechanism under its assumptions, not a measurement of the pairing phase. [R1](#ref-source-b957bb3d98eba2a8) [R10](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

## Mathematical assumptions

Write $\mathbf M(\mathbf r)=\operatorname{Re}[\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}]$. A complex vector amplitude describes either collinear or rotating magnetization. In a continuum single-harmonic example, the Fourier coefficient of $|\mathbf M(\mathbf r)|^2$ at $+2\mathbf Q$ is $(\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q}\cdot\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q})/4$. This dot product has no complex conjugation. For $\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q}=m e^{i\phi}(1,i\epsilon,0)$ it is proportional to $1-\epsilon^2$: a collinear wave has a scalar second harmonic, while a circular helix has constant magnitude. These independent algebraic examples illustrate possible couplings, not fits to chromium data. [R2](#ref-source-e29f9b7d08a70596)

For the illustrative free energy $F=\kappa|\rho_{2\mathbf Q}|^2+\lambda[\rho_{2\mathbf Q}^{*}(\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q}\cdot\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q})+\mathrm{c.c.}]$, with $\kappa>0$ and real $\lambda$, minimization gives $\rho_{2\mathbf Q}=-\lambda(\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q}\cdot\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q})/\kappa$. The coupling absorbs normalization conventions. Vanishing of this particular scalar coupling for a circular helix does not exclude other spin–orbit or lattice responses. Commensurate harmonics that coincide modulo a reciprocal vector require a separate treatment. [R2](#ref-source-e29f9b7d08a70596)

Wave-vector notation is part of an experimental claim. Lumsden uses a tetragonal in-plane lattice spacing $a$, while the Fe square lattice has $\tilde a=a/\sqrt 2$ and rotated axes. Its tetragonal $(1/2,1/2)$ corresponds to square-lattice $(1/2,0)$ in reciprocal-lattice units, or $(\pi/\tilde a,0)$ in inverse-length coordinates. Huang's crystallographic $(101)$ and Wang's orthorhombic $(1,0,0)$ must retain their own basis and out-of-plane convention. Identical-looking tuples need not identify identical momenta. [R4](#ref-source-820cf342501963df) [R6](#ref-source-7aa630cb9480eb85) [R8](#ref-source-3686ada319d8a30c)

## Experimental criteria

Rotter's parent BaFe2As2 study reports a magnetic/structural anomaly near 140 K. Its 5.2 T Mössbauer hyperfine field at 77 K is a local internal field, not an applied-field threshold for superconductivity. Huang's neutron abstract reports a $0.87(3)\,\mu_B$ ordered moment per Fe along the longer orthorhombic axis. These parent studies must remain separate from Rotter's K-doped superconducting discovery. [R3](#ref-source-9ab5e43d0018f0b0) [R4](#ref-source-820cf342501963df)

In de la Cruz's LaOFeAs parent specimen, the structural transition near 155 K precedes magnetic ordering at $137(3)$ K. Nuclear-normalized neutron intensities give $0.36(5)\,\mu_B$ per Fe at 8 K. The fluorinated superconducting specimen is separate. The paper's constrained structural refinement admits an orthorhombic description under specified atomic coordinates; its in-plane moment direction is not resolved. These qualifications prevent a structural label or moment direction from being transferred uncritically between compounds. [R5](#ref-source-d2760cbcecab6071)

Lumsden's BaFe1.84Co0.16As2 exhibits a superconducting-state resonance at $8.6\pm0.5$ meV, compared at 10 K and 30 K, without detected long-range antiferromagnetic order. The dynamical peak is not a static magnetic Bragg peak. The composition is Ba(Fe0.92Co0.08)2As2: Co fractions in these two formula conventions differ by a factor of two. An intensity-onset fit is not an independently established bulk superconducting transition criterion. [R6](#ref-source-7aa630cb9480eb85)

FeSe makes the probe distinction concrete. Böhmer's low-frequency NMR relaxation increases below the structural transition; the authors argue against a magnetic driver of nematicity. Wang's later neutron study observes finite-energy stripe fluctuations already above that transition and enhanced below it. Its neutron spectra use orthorhombic coordinates and a different energy window from NMR. The results must be compared through probe sensitivity, not reduced to “magnetism absent” versus “magnetism present.” Wang interprets the enhancement as supporting spin-driven proposals; it does not uniquely prove causation. [R7](#ref-source-229de7733ef6e2b5) [R8](#ref-source-3686ada319d8a30c)

## Limits and disputes

The absence of conventional static magnetic order in ambient-pressure FeSe does not exclude magnetic fluctuations or imply the same behavior under pressure. Conversely, a magnetic resonance supports particular coherence-factor interpretations only with a specified gap structure, continuum and susceptibility model. It does not uniquely establish the pairing interaction. This page makes no blanket claim that an entire materials family lacks phase-sensitive experiments. [R6](#ref-source-7aa630cb9480eb85) [R8](#ref-source-3686ada319d8a30c) [R10](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

Coexisting magnetic and superconducting signals require spatial and sample controls. Pratt's experiments and Fernandes's model address competition and coexistence under particular conditions; neither makes a bulk-average signal a universal microscopic-coexistence proof. Pratt's author manuscript and final abstract give different transition numbers, so this page imports no transition record from that unresolved comparison. [R11](#ref-source-8e3f1211aced222f) [R12](#ref-source-01629af670cc7358)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Chromium is checked here at review-abstract scope; several historical sources remain abstract-only. Selected author manuscripts still require final-version comparisons. Wang's PDF states that it was corrected online, and an erratum is identified, but its exact changes have not been independently compared. The de la Cruz figure-label discrepancy also remains recorded. These limitations must travel with exported claims. [R2](#ref-source-e29f9b7d08a70596) [R5](#ref-source-d2760cbcecab6071) [R6](#ref-source-7aa630cb9480eb85) [R7](#ref-source-229de7733ef6e2b5) [R9](#ref-source-8792c0e7a8d3b7e3)

## Discovery implications

Keep composition, coordinate basis, resolution, energy transfer, temperature, field direction and sample identity attached to each measurement. Compare static order and dynamical spectral weight separately while testing superconducting responses on characterized samples. A useful mechanism prediction should distinguish alternatives under controlled tuning, rather than infer a pairing interaction solely from neighboring magnetic and superconducting regions. [R5](#ref-source-d2760cbcecab6071) [R6](#ref-source-7aa630cb9480eb85) [R8](#ref-source-3686ada319d8a30c) [R10](#ref-source-7c2b55d128348e6c)

## Related topics

[Charge-density waves](/scwiki/charge-density-waves), [Antiferromagnetic spin fluctuations](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), and [Superconductivity with antiferromagnetism](/scwiki/antiferromagnetism-and-superconductivity).

# Spin-density waves: static order, fluctuations and superconductivity

Distinguish magnetic order from dynamic spin response, preserve reciprocal coordinates, and compare iron arsenides with ambient-pressure FeSe.

## Scope

A spin-density wave (SDW) is a spatial modulation of magnetization. Static order, fluctuating magnetism and superconductivity are distinct observations. Chromium, iron arsenides and cuprate stripes supply different examples; their microscopic interactions need not be identical. A spin order parameter can couple to charge and lattice distortions. Calling a state magnetic does not imply that the lattice is uninvolved. [R2](#ref-source-e29f9b7d08a70596) [R3](#ref-source-9ab5e43d0018f0b0) [R13](#ref-source-b33aab72ae697f3a)

Overhauser demonstrated an instability of the uniform electron gas within Hartree–Fock theory, near twice the Fermi wave vector. This is a foundational model result, not an exact solution for all interacting metals. Similarly, a spin-fluctuation calculation that favors a sign-changing superconducting gap establishes a candidate mechanism under its assumptions, not a measurement of the pairing phase. ## Mathematical assumptions

Write $\mathbf M(\mathbf r)=\operatorname{Re}[\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q}e^{i\mathbf Q\cdot\mathbf r}]$. A complex vector amplitude describes either collinear or rotating magnetization. In a continuum single-harmonic example, the Fourier coefficient of $|\mathbf M(\mathbf r)|^2$ at $+2\mathbf Q$ is $(\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q}\cdot\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q})/4$. This dot product has no complex conjugation. For $\mathbf M_{\mathbf Q}=m e^{i\phi}(1,i\epsilon,0)$ it is proportional to $1-\epsilon^2$: a collinear wave has a scalar second harmonic, while a circular helix has constant magnitude. These independent algebraic examples illustrate possible couplings, not fits to chromium data. [R2](#ref-source-e29f9b7d08a70596)

The coupling absorbs normalization conventions. Vanishing of this particular scalar coupling for a circular helix does not exclude other spin–orbit or lattice responses. Commensurate harmonics that coincide modulo a reciprocal vector require a separate treatment. [R2](#ref-source-e29f9b7d08a70596)

Its tetragonal $(1/2,1/2)$ corresponds to square-lattice $(1/2,0)$ in reciprocal-lattice units, or $(\pi/\tilde a,0)$ in inverse-length coordinates. Huang's crystallographic $(101)$ and Wang's orthorhombic $(1,0,0)$ must retain their own basis and out-of-plane convention. Identical-looking tuples need not identify identical momenta. Rotter's parent BaFe2As2 study reports a magnetic/structural anomaly near 140 K. articles.body:
## Scope

Electronic nematic order makes symmetry-related directions inequivalent without requiring a new translation period. For a tetragonal crystal, a common example is spontaneous fourfold-to-twofold symmetry reduction. Resistivity anisotropy is a possible response, not a universal definition of the order parameter: external strain, pre-existing orthorhombicity and domain populations can also make transport anisotropic. Establishing spontaneous order requires identifying the symmetry-breaking field and its zero-field limit. [R1](#ref-source-bd2e7b2930bdd775) [R2](#ref-source-bac80c20c1347e23) [R3](#ref-source-d29c3c764d26edfd)

Electronic and lattice degrees of freedom with the same symmetry couple. Evidence for an electronic instability does not make the lattice irrelevant, and the small size of a distortion alone does not prove which subsystem drives the transition. Orbital polarization, unequal fluctuations at two magnetic wave vectors and structural strain are candidate coupled variables; their appearance together is not a causal ranking. [R1](#ref-source-bd2e7b2930bdd775) [R5](#ref-source-643062e6ad91fafe)

## Mathematical assumptions

A uniform illustrative free energy is $F=a\phi^2/2+b\phi^4/4+C_0\epsilon^2/2-\lambda\phi\epsilon-\sigma\epsilon$, with nematic variable $\phi$, symmetry-matched strain $\epsilon$ and stress $\sigma$. In the stable symmetric regime, the relaxed modulus is $C=C_0-\lambda^2/a$. At fixed strain, $\partial\phi/\partial\epsilon=\lambda/a$; stress control instead allows the lattice to relax. For $a=A(T-T_0)$, a continuous mean-field coupled instability occurs at $T_s=T_0+\lambda^2/(AC_0)$. The extrapolated bare scale $T_0$ is neither automatically the measured transition nor a superconducting temperature. Positive quartic stabilization and explicit strain conventions are required. [R3](#ref-source-d29c3c764d26edfd) [R5](#ref-source-643062e6ad91fafe)

Band splitting also needs a symmetry test. At a symmetry point, the independent two-orbital illustration $H=\lambda_{\rm so}\tau_y\sigma_z+\phi\tau_z$ has energies $E_\pm=\pm\sqrt{\lambda_{\rm so}^2+\phi^2}$, each twice degenerate. Pauli matrices $\tau$ and $\sigma$ act on orbital and spin space. The spin–orbit term can preserve fourfold and time-reversal symmetries even when the bands are split; the nematic term reverses sign under a quarter rotation. Thus an observed splitting alone is not a symmetry-breaking diagnosis. This minimal model omits realistic dispersions and is not a fit to FeSe. [R7](#ref-source-82e36852ee3c27b9)

For pre-existing nematic order, symmetry can permit $\phi(\Delta_s^*\Delta_d+\mathrm{c.c.})$ when the chosen d-wave component transforms like $\phi$. In the illustrative quadratic matrix with diagonal entries $a_s(T-T_{s0})$, $a_d(T-T_{d0})$ and real off-diagonal $h=g\phi$, the highest instability is $T_c=(T_{s0}+T_{d0})/2+\sqrt{(T_{s0}-T_{d0})^2/4+h^2/(a_sa_d)}$, for positive slopes. The mixed gap has a common onset; anisotropic gap magnitude or critical fields do not imply separate a-axis and b-axis thermodynamic transition temperatures. Quartic terms can permit additional lower-temperature phases, which this calculation does not solve. [R10](#ref-source-03c03feac2435b1b)

## Experimental criteria

Chu's detwinned Co-substituted Ba122 crystals show larger resistivity along the shorter orthorhombic b axis. Above the structural transition, applied uniaxial stress already induces anisotropy, consistent with a substantial susceptibility. That induced response must not be relabelled spontaneous high-temperature order. Differential elastoresistance adds a strain-response measurement, with geometric backgrounds, strain transfer and residual bias requiring control. [R2](#ref-source-bac80c20c1347e23) [R3](#ref-source-d29c3c764d26edfd)

Böhmer's three-point bending experiment measures a normalized Young modulus along tetragonal [110]. Inferring the shear modulus uses an approximation, a noncritical background and normalization choices. Its thermodynamic treatment cannot by itself distinguish spin-driven from orbital-driven order. The Co- and K-substituted series show different Curie–Weiss behavior; the study does not establish an identical quantum critical point beneath every superconducting dome. [R5](#ref-source-643062e6ad91fafe)

Shimojima's FeSe ARPES assigns a roughly 50 meV zone-corner separation to orbital order in detwinned samples. The experiment uses different photon energies and resolutions for zone-center, zone-corner and detwinned measurements; these are not interchangeable spectra. Watson's later zone-center study resolves a spin–orbit contribution above the structural transition and additional splitting below it. Its constrained peak fits have larger uncertainty for a band partly above the Fermi cutoff. Momentum location, orbital assignment and fitting assumptions must accompany each energy scale. [R6](#ref-source-43471709790b0a92) [R7](#ref-source-82e36852ee3c27b9)

FeSe also separates static magnetism from dynamical evidence. Böhmer's NMR interpretation and Wang's later finite-energy neutron results sample different frequency windows. The absence of conventional ambient-pressure magnetic order does not exclude spin fluctuations or settle the microscopic nematic driver. Neither a structural onset nor an ARPES measurement temperature is a superconducting transition record. [R8](#ref-source-229de7733ef6e2b5) [R9](#ref-source-3686ada319d8a30c)

Cuprates require their own controls. Ando reports anisotropic transport in untwinned crystals and interprets it in terms of conducting stripes. Lawler analyzes intra-unit-cell STM contrast near the pseudogap energy, with oxygen-site differences and precise lattice registration. This is not an ARPES image of Fermi arcs. Existing lattice anisotropy, chain contributions where present, spatial inhomogeneity and charge modulation must be assessed before inferring a distinct bulk nematic transition from any one signal. [R11](#ref-source-34e188caa8191123) [R12](#ref-source-b70aa455468dbc62)

## Limits and disputes

A susceptibility enhancement or extrapolated Curie–Weiss scale supports a proposed instability within its analysis model; it is not direct observation of an uncovered zero-temperature critical point. A superconducting dome near that scale does not establish the pairing interaction. Controlled theories of nematic fluctuation enhancement remain distinct from a unique material-level mechanism, and composition-dependent deviations must stay visible. [R3](#ref-source-d29c3c764d26edfd) [R13](#ref-source-24dd77640a555a0f) [R14](#ref-source-f9ae22fe4f6ed654)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Chu's correction text still needs primary verification. Selected author manuscripts require final-version comparisons, including Watson's abstract/body difference in the quoted splitting increase and Shimojima's transition labels. Full strain calibration, ARPES fitting and STM registration have not been independently reproduced. No precise transition record is extracted from unresolved version differences. [R4](#ref-source-052b3d26e6f02b35) [R6](#ref-source-43471709790b0a92) [R7](#ref-source-82e36852ee3c27b9) [R12](#ref-source-b70aa455468dbc62)

## Discovery implications

Combine symmetry-resolved strain response with structural, magnetic and momentum-resolved measurements on documented samples. Track domain history, mechanical boundary conditions, energy resolution and the reference axes used for symmetry-channel names. Predictions should specify which measurement distinguishes a primary instability from a coupled response, and whether the proposed tuning changes static order, fluctuations or both. Keep proposed pairing benefits separate from demonstrated superconducting transition shifts. [R3](#ref-source-d29c3c764d26edfd) [R5](#ref-source-643062e6ad91fafe) [R7](#ref-source-82e36852ee3c27b9) [R10](#ref-source-03c03feac2435b1b)

## Related topics

[Nematic-fluctuation pairing](/scwiki/nematic-fluctuation-pairing), [Spin-density waves](/scwiki/spin-density-waves), and [Strain and elastic control](/scwiki/strain).

The experiment uses different photon energies and resolutions for zone-center, zone-corner and detwinned measurements; these are not interchangeable spectra. Watson's later zone-center study resolves a spin–orbit contribution above the structural transition and additional splitting below it. Its constrained peak fits have larger uncertainty for a band partly above the Fermi cutoff. Momentum location, orbital assignment and fitting assumptions must accompany each energy scale.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-43471709790b0a92, source-82e36852ee3c27b9.

Conditions: Retain symmetry axes, stress versus strain, sample domains, probe window, momentum and version. Band splitting and induced anisotropy alone do not establish spontaneous nematic order.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent quadratic models; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-h6-claim-experimental-criteria-4

FeSe also separates static magnetism from dynamical evidence. Böhmer's NMR interpretation and Wang's later finite-energy neutron results sample different frequency windows. The absence of conventional ambient-pressure magnetic order does not exclude spin fluctuations or settle the microscopic nematic driver. Neither a structural onset nor an ARPES measurement temperature is a superconducting transition record.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-229de7733ef6e2b5, source-3686ada319d8a30c.

Conditions: Retain symmetry axes, stress versus strain, sample domains, probe window, momentum and version. Band splitting and induced anisotropy alone do not establish spontaneous nematic order.

### scwiki-h6-claim-experimental-criteria-5

Cuprates require their own controls. Ando reports anisotropic transport in untwinned crystals and interprets it in terms of conducting stripes. Lawler analyzes intra-unit-cell STM contrast near the pseudogap energy, with oxygen-site differences and precise lattice registration. This is not an ARPES image of Fermi arcs. A susceptibility enhancement or extrapolated Curie–Weiss scale supports a proposed instability within its analysis model; it is not direct observation of an uncovered zero-temperature critical point. A superconducting dome near that scale does not establish the pairing interaction. Controlled theories of nematic fluctuation enhancement remain distinct from a unique material-level mechanism, and composition-dependent deviations must stay visible.

articles.body:
## Scope

A nonlinear Hall effect is a transverse response beyond first order in the driving electric field. A curved Hall-resistivity trace versus magnetic field can instead arise within ordinary linear-response transport. An anomalous Hall effect, a second-order Hall response, magnetic hysteresis and a superconducting diode signal therefore require separate measurement definitions. The second-order effect can appear in time-reversal-symmetric conductors; a zero-field linear Hall conductivity requires the relevant time-reversal symmetry to be broken. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f) [R3](#ref-source-72e6507348216a06) [R4](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32)

The familiar empirical separation into ordinary Hall and a term proportional to magnetization is not a universal definition of anomalous Hall physics. Noncollinear Mn3Sn provides a counterexample to requiring a large net ferromagnetic moment. Its magnetic symmetry matters even though the net moment is small. A hysteresis loop alone establishes history dependence, not the microscopic origin of a Hall signal. [R4](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32) [R8](#ref-source-40175a38d94ec950)

## Mathematical assumptions

In a fixed laboratory frame, write $j_a=\sigma_{ab}E_b+\chi_{abc}E_bE_c+\cdots$, summing repeated indices. The spatially uniform electric-dipole second-order tensor vanishes when inversion symmetry is present. Breaking inversion is necessary for this contribution but does not guarantee an allowed nonzero component. Boundaries, finite-wave-vector effects and other response mechanisms require separate treatment. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f)

For the illustrative voltage law $V_y=\alpha I+\beta I^2$ and peak-amplitude drive $I=I_0\cos\omega t$, the quadratic contribution is $\beta I_0^2[1+\cos(2\omega t)]/2$. A controlled quadratic DC measurement can also establish second-order transport; detecting $2\omega$ is not an exclusive definition. Conversely, a thermal voltage proportional to dissipated power has the same harmonic structure, so a second harmonic is not sufficient evidence for a Berry-curvature mechanism. Phase and peak-versus-RMS conventions must be reported. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f) [R2](#ref-source-44bfe8a945b93dfd)

In the two-dimensional semiclassical constant-relaxation-time model, $D_a=\sum_n\int d^2k/(2\pi)^2\,f_{n0}\partial_{k_a}\Omega_{n,z}$ has dimensions of length. Time reversal makes Berry curvature odd in momentum, allowing its occupied-state integral to vanish while its dipole remains finite. The model gives a second-harmonic current proportional to $[\tau/(1+i\omega\tau)](\hat{z}\times\mathcal{E})(\mathbf{D}\cdot\mathcal{E})$. Here $\mathcal{E}$ is a complex field amplitude; omitted charge and Planck-constant factors must be restored consistently before numerical comparison. This is a model contribution, not the complete measured nonlinear conductivity. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f) [R3](#ref-source-72e6507348216a06)

In this two-dimensional setting, a surviving mirror permits a dipole perpendicular to the mirror line, whereas an in-plane twofold rotation forces it to vanish. Thus fourfold-to-twofold nematic symmetry reduction alone does not establish a finite dipole, even before checking inversion. These two-dimensional vector rules should not be transferred unchanged to the three-dimensional dipole tensor. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f)

## Experimental criteria

Ma's bilayer WTe2 experiment measures transverse second-harmonic voltages while independently tuning two gates. Figure 2d compares transverse and longitudinal contacts at 50 K and 177.77 Hz; Figure 2e uses 100 K, and the systematic Figure 3 gate maps use 10 K. Those temperatures describe different measurements, not superconducting transitions. The methods test several low frequencies and specify a sine-reference phase convention. The gate-dependent hysteresis associated with ferroelectric switching is not a magnetic-field hysteresis measurement. [R2](#ref-source-44bfe8a945b93dfd)

Kang's few-layer WTe2 work combines Hall bars with circular devices for angular measurements. Its five-layer example is measured at 1.8 K and 137 Hz, while an eight-layer disk maps the angular response. Longitudinal and transverse first-harmonic signals help identify geometric mixing, and the disk analysis antisymmetrizes opposing injection angles. Temperature-dependent scaling suggests both intrinsic and extrinsic contributions; layer number, scattering and device geometry prevent assigning one universal nonlinear coefficient to all WTe2 samples. [R3](#ref-source-72e6507348216a06)

A credible identification records raw longitudinal and transverse channels, amplitude and frequency dependence, contact permutations, crystal axes, thermal stability and sweep history. Quadratic current scaling and allowed angular symmetry are necessary consistency checks for the proposed second-order contribution, but they do not alone eliminate heating or separate every scattering mechanism. Keep fixed-axis current reversal distinct from rotating the injection and voltage-measurement frame; the latter can change a reported transverse component's sign without changing the quadratic field law. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f) [R2](#ref-source-44bfe8a945b93dfd) [R3](#ref-source-72e6507348216a06)

## Limits and disputes

The superconducting diode effect concerns unequal positive- and negative-direction critical-current magnitudes. Ando's Nb/V/Ta superlattice demonstrates this through DC resistance–current measurements, rather than a transverse Hall channel. A zero-resistance window in one direction does not make the whole switching cycle lossless. Later conventional-film work identifies asymmetric vortex barriers and screening currents as possible diode mechanisms, so nonreciprocity alone does not establish exotic pairing. [R5](#ref-source-a39214fe64a9445d) [R9](#ref-source-b5ffaf6a410b9a65)

Romero's longitudinal terahertz/DC study and Yang's high-field re-entrant nickelate measurements do not supply nonlinear Hall evidence in the portions checked here. A scattering rate, nematic motivation or re-entrant zero-resistance field must not be relabelled a Hall coefficient or Hall switching field. Magnetic history can motivate additional measurements but cannot fill a missing transverse dataset. [R6](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R7](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Selected Ma final figures and methods, Kang author-manuscript methods and figures, and Sodemann's theory were checked; full artifact controls, final-version comparisons and raw-data reproduction remain incomplete. Kang's current-reversal wording additionally requires complete wiring and reference-frame reconciliation before a sign rule is exported. Ando, Nakatsuji and Hou are used at primary-abstract scope. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f) [R2](#ref-source-44bfe8a945b93dfd) [R3](#ref-source-72e6507348216a06) [R5](#ref-source-a39214fe64a9445d) [R8](#ref-source-40175a38d94ec950) [R9](#ref-source-b5ffaf6a410b9a65)

## Discovery implications

Design a discrimination experiment before assigning a mechanism: state which response order is measured, which symmetry allows it, and which contact or thermal control could falsify the interpretation. When magnetic or superconducting states coexist, compare magnetization, longitudinal resistance, transverse harmonics and field history on the same documented device. Preserve two-dimensional versus bulk units and distinguish a calculated Berry-curvature dipole from the total experimental response. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f) [R2](#ref-source-44bfe8a945b93dfd) [R3](#ref-source-72e6507348216a06) [R9](#ref-source-b5ffaf6a410b9a65)

## Related topics

[Berry curvature](/scwiki/berry-curvature), [Nematic order](/scwiki/nematic-order), and [Magnetism and re-entrant superconductivity](/scwiki/field-induced-superconductivity).

## Experimental criteria

Ma's bilayer WTe2 experiment measures transverse second-harmonic voltages while independently tuning two gates. Figure 2d compares transverse and longitudinal contacts at 50 K and 177.77 Hz; Figure 2e uses 100 K, and the systematic Figure 3 gate maps use 10 K. Those temperatures describe different measurements, not superconducting transitions. The methods test several low frequencies and specify a sine-reference phase convention. The gate-dependent hysteresis associated with ferroelectric switching is not a magnetic-field hysteresis measurement. [R2](#ref-source-44bfe8a945b93dfd)

Kang's few-layer WTe2 work combines Hall bars with circular devices for angular measurements. Its five-layer example is measured at 1.8 K and 137 Hz, while an eight-layer disk maps the angular response. # Nonlinear Hall effect: response order, symmetry and hysteresis

Distinguish second-order Hall transport from ordinary field nonlinearity, anomalous Hall response, hysteresis and superconducting diode signals.

## Scope

A nonlinear Hall effect is a transverse response beyond first order in the driving electric field. A curved Hall-resistivity trace versus magnetic field can instead arise within ordinary linear-response transport. An anomalous Hall effect, a second-order Hall response, magnetic hysteresis and a superconducting diode signal therefore require separate measurement definitions. The second-order effect can appear in time-reversal-symmetric conductors; a zero-field linear Hall conductivity requires the relevant time-reversal symmetry to be broken. Noncollinear Mn3Sn provides a counterexample to requiring a large net ferromagnetic moment. Its magnetic symmetry matters even though the net moment is small. A hysteresis loop alone establishes history dependence, not the microscopic origin of a Hall signal. [R4](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32) [R8](#ref-source-40175a38d94ec950)

In a fixed laboratory frame, write $j_a=\sigma_{ab}E_b+\chi_{abc}E_bE_c+\cdots$, summing repeated indices. The spatially uniform electric-dipole second-order tensor vanishes when inversion symmetry is present. Breaking inversion is necessary for this contribution but does not guarantee an allowed nonzero component. Boundaries, finite-wave-vector effects and other response mechanisms require separate treatment. [R1](#ref-source-8c7527f0a5a94d1f)

articles.body:
## Scope

Two bands, two Drude components, two scattering processes and two pairing channels are different claims. Independent channels experiencing the same electric field add their conductivities. Scattering events within one channel instead enter a collision problem and can add as rates only under appropriate approximations. A good fit to DC resistivity alone rarely identifies which microscopic description is correct. MgB2 illustrates why band-resolved superconducting gaps must also be distinguished from independently conducting subsystems. [R1](#ref-source-b0fd79e990759ecc) [R2](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221) [R3](#ref-source-6f7229021dc0a92a) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

This entry concerns transport decomposition and spectral-weight accounting. A fitted component can represent a band, an orbital sector, a spatial layer or an effective relaxation scale; the label must be justified with additional evidence. Identifying carriers that contribute to the condensate does not by itself identify the interaction responsible for pairing. [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Mathematical assumptions

For independent isotropic channels, use angular frequency $\omega$ and the convention $e^{-i\omega t}$: $\sigma(\omega)=\sum_j S_j/(\Gamma_j-i\omega)$, where $S_j=n_je^2/m_j$ and $\Gamma_j>0$ in the elementary Drude model. At zero field, $\rho_{\rm DC}=1/\sum_j(S_j/\Gamma_j)$, not the sum of channel resistivities. A broad component has $\sigma_j\simeq S_j/\Gamma_j$ only within a window where $\omega\ll\Gamma_j$; its constant approximation cannot be integrated to infinite frequency. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Even exact DC data admit infinitely many positive pairs with the same total conductivity. Frequency information helps, but if two linewidths are identical, their sum is exactly a single Drude peak with weight $S_1+S_2$ at every frequency. A finite frequency window can also leave a very broad component's weight and linewidth strongly correlated. Report uncertainty and competing models, not just a residual sum of squares. [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Independent scattering contributions can approximately give $\Gamma=\Gamma_{\rm imp}+\Gamma_{\rm ph}+\cdots$ within one relaxation model. This Matthiessen approximation is not a prescription for adding the resistivities of parallel bands. Interchannel momentum exchange generally couples their kinetic equations: an illustrative positive relaxation matrix has diagonals $\gamma_1+g,\gamma_2+g$ and off-diagonals $-g$. In normalized equal-density units its conductivity is $\mathbf{1}^{T}C^{-1}\mathbf{1}$, reducing to $1/\gamma_1+1/\gamma_2$ at $g=0$. This toy model exposes the independence assumption; it is not a material fit. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Normalization matters in spectral-weight sums. For one Drude term, $\int_0^\infty\sigma_1(\omega)d\omega=\pi S/2$. With condensate response $\sigma_{2,s}=S_s/\omega$, the positive-frequency missing area is $\pi S_s/2$, provided the relevant total optical weight is conserved and backgrounds are treated consistently. Thus $S_s=(2/\pi)\int_0^\infty[\sigma_{1,N}-\sigma_{1,S}^{\rm reg}]d\omega$ in this convention. Cyclic frequency $\nu=\omega/(2\pi)$ requires $\Gamma_\nu=\Gamma/(2\pi)$ and $S_\nu=S/(2\pi)$ in the same Drude form. Delta-function boundary conventions must also be stated. The numerical checks establish these model identities, not the complete historical derivation or experimental sum-rule saturation. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R6](#ref-source-7284fbccd4e5d459) [R7](#ref-source-0d95fb4e6b9629c5)

## Experimental criteria

Romero's FeTe1−xSex study uses complex terahertz conductivity with a DC constraint to distinguish a narrow response from a broad background. The checked author version covers two films, x=0.45 and x=0.35, over 0.2–3 THz. The broad component is not resolved as a second complete peak, so assigning it a unique scattering rate or a second Planckian coefficient would exceed the measurement. Its displayed rate uses cycle frequency and a thermal scale proportional to $k_BT/h$; substituting $\hbar$ without conversion changes the convention. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

The same study compares a fitted superconducting term, a low-frequency extrapolation of $\nu\sigma_2$, and a missing-area analysis. These are useful consistency comparisons but share measured spectra and modeling assumptions; they are not three independent experimental replications. Near the transition, a finite-width low-frequency response complicates extrapolation to zero frequency. The normal reference temperature, unmeasured low-frequency region and residual background must remain part of any condensate-weight claim. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Qazilbash's LaFePO experiment combines in-plane reflectance with ellipsometry and Kramers–Kronig-compatible optical extraction. The final paper analyzes a low-frequency Drude response, higher-energy interband transitions and an extended-Drude scattering rate. Its comparison of integrated optical weight with band theory supports a correlation interpretation under that analysis; it does not establish exactly two independent Drude carriers throughout the iron-based family. The reported kinetic-energy ratio has extraction bounds, rather than being an exact universal one-half. [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3)

MgB2 supplies a complementary comparison. Liu and Choi calculate band-dependent electron–phonon pairing, while Souma resolves different superconducting gaps on sigma and pi bands by photoemission. Choi's coupled calculation has a common transition. These results do not authorize treating the bands as two unrelated superconductors with separately assigned transition temperatures, or translating gap values into Drude scattering rates. Surface-sensitive spectroscopy and bulk optical transport retain different measurement conditions. [R1](#ref-source-b0fd79e990759ecc) [R2](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221) [R3](#ref-source-6f7229021dc0a92a)

## Limits and disputes

A spectral decomposition is not unique simply because it is causal or fits both real and imaginary conductivity. Independent Fermi-surface, mass, Hall and magnetoresistance constraints can narrow possibilities, while interband optical transitions and coupled scattering can invalidate a simple channel interpretation. Optical spectral weight, a transport lifetime and a superconducting gap are different quantities; no universal cross-material conversion is justified here. [R2](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221) [R3](#ref-source-6f7229021dc0a92a) [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The Romero author manuscript's printed missing-area prefactor differs from the normalization implied by its Drude numerator; the final paper and calibration must be compared before importing precise condensate fractions. The LaFePO supplement and complete historical sum-rule derivations have not been checked. Independent model integrations do not resolve those source-version questions or reproduce the experimental data. [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R6](#ref-source-7284fbccd4e5d459) [R7](#ref-source-0d95fb4e6b9629c5)

## Discovery implications

First specify what would distinguish two physical channels from an effective two-component fit. Extend the measurement window where possible, constrain the DC limit, document tensor geometry, and test whether fitted weights and rates remain stable when backgrounds or cutoffs change. For superconducting spectral transfer, compare a justified normal-state reference with the regular superconducting response and quantify missing bandwidth. A successful transport decomposition constrains candidate mechanisms; it does not identify a unique pairing interaction. [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Related topics

[Planckian dissipation](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation), [Multiband pairing](/scwiki/multiband-pairing), and [MgB2](/scwiki/magnesium-diboride).

# Parallel conduction channels: multiband transport and identifiability

Distinguish parallel conductivities from additive scattering rates, test model identifiability, and track superconducting spectral weight with explicit conventions.

## Scope

Two bands, two Drude components, two scattering processes and two pairing channels are different claims. Independent channels experiencing the same electric field add their conductivities. Scattering events within one channel instead enter a collision problem and can add as rates only under appropriate approximations. A good fit to DC resistivity alone rarely identifies which microscopic description is correct. MgB2 illustrates why band-resolved superconducting gaps must also be distinguished from independently conducting subsystems. [R1](#ref-source-b0fd79e990759ecc) [R2](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221) [R3](#ref-source-6f7229021dc0a92a) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

This entry concerns transport decomposition and spectral-weight accounting. A fitted component can represent a band, an orbital sector, a spatial layer or an effective relaxation scale; the label must be justified with additional evidence. Identifying carriers that contribute to the condensate does not by itself identify the interaction responsible for pairing. [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Mathematical assumptions

For independent isotropic channels, use angular frequency $\omega$ and the convention $e^{-i\omega t}$: $\sigma(\omega)=\sum_j S_j/(\Gamma_j-i\omega)$, where $S_j=n_je^2/m_j$ and $\Gamma_j>0$ in the elementary Drude model. At zero field, $\rho_{\rm DC}=1/\sum_j(S_j/\Gamma_j)$, not the sum of channel resistivities. A broad component has $\sigma_j\simeq S_j/\Gamma_j$ only within a window where $\omega\ll\Gamma_j$; its constant approximation cannot be integrated to infinite frequency. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Even exact DC data admit infinitely many positive pairs with the same total conductivity. Frequency information helps, but if two linewidths are identical, their sum is exactly a single Drude peak with weight $S_1+S_2$ at every frequency. A finite frequency window can also leave a very broad component's weight and linewidth strongly correlated. Report uncertainty and competing models, not just a residual sum of squares. [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3) [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Independent scattering contributions can approximately give $\Gamma=\Gamma_{\rm imp}+\Gamma_{\rm ph}+\cdots$ within one relaxation model. This Matthiessen approximation is not a prescription for adding the resistivities of parallel bands. Interchannel momentum exchange generally couples their kinetic equations: an illustrative positive relaxation matrix has diagonals $\gamma_1+g,\gamma_2+g$ and off-diagonals $-g$. In normalized equal-density units its conductivity is $\mathbf{1}^{T}C^{-1}\mathbf{1}$, reducing to $1/\gamma_1+1/\gamma_2$ at $g=0$. This toy model exposes the independence assumption; it is not a material fit. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Normalization matters in spectral-weight sums. For one Drude term, $\int_0^\infty\sigma_1(\omega)d\omega=\pi S/2$. With condensate response $\sigma_{2,s}=S_s/\omega$, the positive-frequency missing area is $\pi S_s/2$, provided the relevant total optical weight is conserved and backgrounds are treated consistently. Thus $S_s=(2/\pi)\int_0^\infty[\sigma_{1,N}-\sigma_{1,S}^{\rm reg}]d\omega$ in this convention. Cyclic frequency $\nu=\omega/(2\pi)$ requires $\Gamma_\nu=\Gamma/(2\pi)$ and $S_\nu=S/(2\pi)$ in the same Drude form. Delta-function boundary conventions must also be stated. The numerical checks establish these model identities, not the complete historical derivation or experimental sum-rule saturation. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R6](#ref-source-7284fbccd4e5d459) [R7](#ref-source-0d95fb4e6b9629c5)

## Experimental criteria

Romero's FeTe1−xSex study uses complex terahertz conductivity with a DC constraint to distinguish a narrow response from a broad background. The checked author version covers two films, x=0.45 and x=0.35, over 0.2–3 THz. The broad component is not resolved as a second complete peak, so assigning it a unique scattering rate or a second Planckian coefficient would exceed the measurement. Its displayed rate uses cycle frequency and a thermal scale proportional to $k_BT/h$; substituting $\hbar$ without conversion changes the convention. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

The same study compares a fitted superconducting term, a low-frequency extrapolation of $\nu\sigma_2$, and a missing-area analysis. These are useful consistency comparisons but share measured spectra and modeling assumptions; they are not three independent experimental replications. Near the transition, a finite-width low-frequency response complicates extrapolation to zero frequency. The normal reference temperature, unmeasured low-frequency region and residual background must remain part of any condensate-weight claim. [R5](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

Qazilbash's LaFePO experiment combines in-plane reflectance with ellipsometry and Kramers–Kronig-compatible optical extraction. The final paper analyzes a low-frequency Drude response, higher-energy interband transitions and an extended-Drude scattering rate. Its comparison of integrated optical weight with band theory supports a correlation interpretation under that analysis; it does not establish exactly two independent Drude carriers throughout the iron-based family. The reported kinetic-energy ratio has extraction bounds, rather than being an exact universal one-half. [R4](#ref-source-8c3a5887a7e6b1a3)

MgB2 supplies a complementary comparison. Liu and Choi calculate band-dependent electron–phonon pairing, while Souma resolves different superconducting gaps on sigma and pi bands by photoemission. Choi's coupled calculation has a common transition. These results do not authorize treating the bands as two unrelated superconductors with separately assigned transition temperatures, or translating gap values into Drude scattering rates. Surface-sensitive spectroscopy and bulk optical transport retain different measurement conditions. [R1](#ref-source-b0fd79e990759ecc) [R2](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221) [R3](#ref-source-6f7229021dc0a92a)

articles.body:
## Scope

A Hall-coefficient sign reversal is a change in the sign of the transverse response under a declared wiring and field convention. It is distinct from a change in Hall magnitude, a peak, or an inferred Hall number. Electron and hole contributions can exchange transport weight without either Fermi-surface pocket disappearing. Neither a sign change nor a Hall anomaly by itself proves superconductivity, a Lifshitz transition or a particular pairing mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-7acbaed4e62141d9) [R2](#ref-source-8c3b378d8802f683) [R3](#ref-source-e24f6678715b4917) [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72)

Here $E_y=R_HJ_xB_z$ defines the sign. The elementary single-band Drude values are $R_H=-1/(n_e e)$ for electrons and $R_H=1/(n_h e)$ for holes, with $e>0$. These density interpretations require restrictive assumptions. Even a single crystalline band can have a complicated Hall response because Fermi-surface curvature and a momentum-dependent mean free path affect the weak-field conductivity. A temperature-dependent Hall coefficient is therefore not sufficient evidence for multiple bands. [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

## Mathematical assumptions

For independent isotropic electron and hole Drude channels with positive mobilities and $\mu_i B\ll1$, $R_H=(n_h\mu_h^2-n_e\mu_e^2)/[e(n_h\mu_h+n_e\mu_e)^2]$. The sign changes when the mobility-squared weights cross. Fixed carrier densities can therefore produce a reversal as the mobility ratio varies. At zero field $\sigma_0=e(n_h\mu_h+n_e\mu_e)$; even simultaneous values of $\sigma_0$ and weak-field $R_H$ do not uniquely determine four density/mobility parameters. Independent tensor-inversion checks illustrate this degeneracy without fitting a material. [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3) [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

Beyond weak field, add conductivity tensors and invert the sum. In the same classical model, when both $\mu_iB\gg1$ and $n_h\ne n_e$, the asymptotic slope is $\rho_{yx}/B\to1/[e(n_h-n_e)]$. Exact compensation is a different limit: for $n_h=n_e=n$, $\rho_{yx}/B=(\mu_h-\mu_e)/[en(\mu_h+\mu_e)]$ at all fields in this model. A large laboratory field alone establishes neither of these asymptotic conditions. Quantum effects, coupled scattering and reconstructed bands may require a different model. [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3) [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

Ordinary and anomalous contributions must also be distinguished. A schematic $\rho_{yx}=R_0B+\rho_{yx}^{A}$ is not a universal fit, and an anomalous term need not be proportional to magnetization with a constant coefficient. Intrinsic Berry curvature, skew scattering and side jump are distinct mechanisms. Field antisymmetrization, $[\rho_{yx}(B)-\rho_{yx}(-B)]/2$, removes even longitudinal contact leakage but retains an odd anomalous Hall contribution. It does not isolate ordinary Hall transport by itself. [R6](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32)

## Experimental criteria

Tsukada and Ono studied epitaxial La2−xSrxCuO4 films on SrTiO3 with residual tensile strain. Their room-temperature Hall coefficient changes from positive to negative between x=0.28 and x=0.32. The heavily overdoped samples used field sweeps to ±6 T. This is a sample-series result at 300 K, not a universal cuprate doping boundary. The x=0.32 film lacks zero resistance but has a reported resistive onset, which the authors discuss in relation to possible oxygen inhomogeneity. Describing it simply as having no superconducting evidence would erase that distinction. [R1](#ref-source-7acbaed4e62141d9)

Brouet's Ba(Fe0.65Ru0.35)2As2 study reports a temperature-dependent Hall sign together with electron and hole pockets. The checked primary abstract supports that limited statement; complete transport methods and a precise reversal temperature remain unreviewed here. Mun's Co- and Cu-substituted BaFe2As2 crystals provide a separate comparison: thermopower and Hall changes occur at comparable added-electron counts, but the Cu comparison does not show the corresponding resistive superconductivity. These Hall anomalies are not a superconductivity criterion or a universal sign-change threshold. [R2](#ref-source-8c3b378d8802f683) [R3](#ref-source-e24f6678715b4917)

Mun's experiment measured composition by wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy and applied the Hall field along the crystal c axis, reversing field polarity to reduce contact offsets. Its 25 K comparison is a measurement temperature, not a transition temperature. Sample exfoliation can alter geometric factors, so normalized trends and absolute Hall magnitudes carry different uncertainties. Co/Cu substitution fraction and inferred added-electron count are also different horizontal axes. [R3](#ref-source-e24f6678715b4917)

Iida's strained Ba(Fe1−xCox)2As2 films used MgO and CaF2 substrates and Hall measurements at 9 T. Their effective Hall number $n_H=V/(4e|R_H|)$, with unit-cell volume $V$, is positive by construction and expressed per Fe. It discards the Hall sign and is not a direct count of all mobile carriers in a multiband metal. The reported phase-diagram alignment concerns the studied strained films and selected bulk comparisons. The superconducting temperature uses a resistive onset criterion, rather than silently substituting zero resistance or magnetic shielding. [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3)

Badoux's YBa2Cu3Oy experiment distinguishes a charge-order reconstruction endpoint near p=0.16 from a pseudogap endpoint near p=0.19. The Hall-number interpretation changes from approximately 1+p toward p; this is not evidence for a mandatory Hall-sign reversal at the latter point. Pulsed fields reached 88 T, with a 50 K, 80 T cross-sample comparison. The author manuscript establishes normal-state access down to at least 40 K and explicitly leaves the lower-temperature p=0.16 behavior unresolved. Its vortex-melting field is not automatically the upper critical field. [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72)

## Limits and disputes

Normal-state extraction needs more than a high-field label. Retain temperature, current, field direction, hysteresis branch and the independently justified superconducting boundary; vortex motion and magnetic contributions can contaminate a transverse signal. Yang's field-induced superconductivity study is a boundary example, not a source of an ordinary-Hall reversal field. Its superconducting phase-diagram scales must not be relabeled as Hall or anomalous-Hall thresholds. [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72) [R6](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32) [R8](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Most experimental checks here cover selected author-manuscript methods, results and figures, not complete final articles or raw-data reproduction. Brouet remains abstract-scoped; Ong's full geometric derivation and the anomalous-Hall review remain incompletely read. Apparent numeric typographical inconsistencies in the Mun and Iida author versions require final-version comparison; those uncertain composition values are not adopted. The independent Drude checks establish model algebra, not a unique interpretation of any experimental Hall curve. [R1](#ref-source-7acbaed4e62141d9) [R2](#ref-source-8c3b378d8802f683) [R3](#ref-source-e24f6678715b4917) [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3) [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72) [R6](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32) [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

## Discovery implications

Treat a sign change as a prompt to test competing transport explanations. Combine field-dependent longitudinal and transverse resistivity, magnetoresistance, magnetic characterization and independent Fermi-surface information. Compare constrained models and retain geometry, strain, oxygen content and uncertainty. A mobility crossover, reconstructed Fermi surface and anomalous contribution can produce different predictions beyond a single Hall slope; a defensible conclusion specifies which alternatives the measurements actually exclude. [R1](#ref-source-7acbaed4e62141d9) [R2](#ref-source-8c3b378d8802f683) [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3) [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72) [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

## Related topics

[Parallel conduction channels](/scwiki/parallel-conduction-channels), [Nonlinear Hall effect](/scwiki/nonlinear-hall-effect), and [Field-induced superconductivity](/scwiki/field-induced-superconductivity).

# Hall-coefficient sign reversal: carriers, mobility and evidence

Separate a Hall sign change from a Hall-number inference, account for multiband mobility and anomalous terms, and retain each experiment's normal-state boundary.

## Scope

A Hall-coefficient sign reversal is a change in the sign of the transverse response under a declared wiring and field convention. It is distinct from a change in Hall magnitude, a peak, or an inferred Hall number. Electron and hole contributions can exchange transport weight without either Fermi-surface pocket disappearing. Neither a sign change nor a Hall anomaly by itself proves superconductivity, a Lifshitz transition or a particular pairing mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-7acbaed4e62141d9) [R2](#ref-source-8c3b378d8802f683) [R3](#ref-source-e24f6678715b4917) [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72)

Here $E_y=R_HJ_xB_z$ defines the sign. The elementary single-band Drude values are $R_H=-1/(n_e e)$ for electrons and $R_H=1/(n_h e)$ for holes, with $e>0$. These density interpretations require restrictive assumptions. Even a single crystalline band can have a complicated Hall response because Fermi-surface curvature and a momentum-dependent mean free path affect the weak-field conductivity. A temperature-dependent Hall coefficient is therefore not sufficient evidence for multiple bands. [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

## Mathematical assumptions

For independent isotropic electron and hole Drude channels with positive mobilities and $\mu_i B\ll1$, $R_H=(n_h\mu_h^2-n_e\mu_e^2)/[e(n_h\mu_h+n_e\mu_e)^2]$. The sign changes when the mobility-squared weights cross. Fixed carrier densities can therefore produce a reversal as the mobility ratio varies. At zero field $\sigma_0=e(n_h\mu_h+n_e\mu_e)$; even simultaneous values of $\sigma_0$ and weak-field $R_H$ do not uniquely determine four density/mobility parameters. Independent tensor-inversion checks illustrate this degeneracy without fitting a material. [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3) [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

Beyond weak field, add conductivity tensors and invert the sum. In the same classical model, when both $\mu_iB\gg1$ and $n_h\ne n_e$, the asymptotic slope is $\rho_{yx}/B\to1/[e(n_h-n_e)]$. Exact compensation is a different limit: for $n_h=n_e=n$, $\rho_{yx}/B=(\mu_h-\mu_e)/[en(\mu_h+\mu_e)]$ at all fields in this model. A large laboratory field alone establishes neither of these asymptotic conditions. Quantum effects, coupled scattering and reconstructed bands may require a different model. [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3) [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

Ordinary and anomalous contributions must also be distinguished. A schematic $\rho_{yx}=R_0B+\rho_{yx}^{A}$ is not a universal fit, and an anomalous term need not be proportional to magnetization with a constant coefficient. Intrinsic Berry curvature, skew scattering and side jump are distinct mechanisms. Field antisymmetrization, $[\rho_{yx}(B)-\rho_{yx}(-B)]/2$, removes even longitudinal contact leakage but retains an odd anomalous Hall contribution. It does not isolate ordinary Hall transport by itself. [R6](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32)

## Experimental criteria

Tsukada and Ono studied epitaxial La2−xSrxCuO4 films on SrTiO3 with residual tensile strain. Their room-temperature Hall coefficient changes from positive to negative between x=0.28 and x=0.32. The heavily overdoped samples used field sweeps to ±6 T. This is a sample-series result at 300 K, not a universal cuprate doping boundary. The x=0.32 film lacks zero resistance but has a reported resistive onset, which the authors discuss in relation to possible oxygen inhomogeneity. Describing it simply as having no superconducting evidence would erase that distinction. [R1](#ref-source-7acbaed4e62141d9)

Brouet's Ba(Fe0.65Ru0.35)2As2 study reports a temperature-dependent Hall sign together with electron and hole pockets. The checked primary abstract supports that limited statement; complete transport methods and a precise reversal temperature remain unreviewed here. Mun's Co- and Cu-substituted BaFe2As2 crystals provide a separate comparison: thermopower and Hall changes occur at comparable added-electron counts, but the Cu comparison does not show the corresponding resistive superconductivity. These Hall anomalies are not a superconductivity criterion or a universal sign-change threshold. [R2](#ref-source-8c3b378d8802f683) [R3](#ref-source-e24f6678715b4917)

Mun's experiment measured composition by wavelength-dispersive spectroscopy and applied the Hall field along the crystal c axis, reversing field polarity to reduce contact offsets. Its 25 K comparison is a measurement temperature, not a transition temperature. Sample exfoliation can alter geometric factors, so normalized trends and absolute Hall magnitudes carry different uncertainties. Co/Cu substitution fraction and inferred added-electron count are also different horizontal axes. [R3](#ref-source-e24f6678715b4917)

Iida's strained Ba(Fe1−xCox)2As2 films used MgO and CaF2 substrates and Hall measurements at 9 T. Their effective Hall number $n_H=V/(4e|R_H|)$, with unit-cell volume $V$, is positive by construction and expressed per Fe. It discards the Hall sign and is not a direct count of all mobile carriers in a multiband metal. The reported phase-diagram alignment concerns the studied strained films and selected bulk comparisons. The superconducting temperature uses a resistive onset criterion, rather than silently substituting zero resistance or magnetic shielding. [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3)

Badoux's YBa2Cu3Oy experiment distinguishes a charge-order reconstruction endpoint near p=0.16 from a pseudogap endpoint near p=0.19. The Hall-number interpretation changes from approximately 1+p toward p; this is not evidence for a mandatory Hall-sign reversal at the latter point. Pulsed fields reached 88 T, with a 50 K, 80 T cross-sample comparison. The author manuscript establishes normal-state access down to at least 40 K and explicitly leaves the lower-temperature p=0.16 behavior unresolved. Its vortex-melting field is not automatically the upper critical field. [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72)

## Limits and disputes

Normal-state extraction needs more than a high-field label. Retain temperature, current, field direction, hysteresis branch and the independently justified superconducting boundary; vortex motion and magnetic contributions can contaminate a transverse signal. Yang's field-induced superconductivity study is a boundary example, not a source of an ordinary-Hall reversal field. Its superconducting phase-diagram scales must not be relabeled as Hall or anomalous-Hall thresholds. [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72) [R6](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32) [R8](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. Most experimental checks here cover selected author-manuscript methods, results and figures, not complete final articles or raw-data reproduction. Brouet remains abstract-scoped; Ong's full geometric derivation and the anomalous-Hall review remain incompletely read. Apparent numeric typographical inconsistencies in the Mun and Iida author versions require final-version comparison; those uncertain composition values are not adopted. The independent Drude checks establish model algebra, not a unique interpretation of any experimental Hall curve. [R1](#ref-source-7acbaed4e62141d9) [R2](#ref-source-8c3b378d8802f683) [R3](#ref-source-e24f6678715b4917) [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3) [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72) [R6](#ref-source-7faba5d556864a32) [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

## Discovery implications

Treat a sign change as a prompt to test competing transport explanations. Combine field-dependent longitudinal and transverse resistivity, magnetoresistance, magnetic characterization and independent Fermi-surface information. Compare constrained models and retain geometry, strain, oxygen content and uncertainty. A mobility crossover, reconstructed Fermi surface and anomalous contribution can produce different predictions beyond a single Hall slope; a defensible conclusion specifies which alternatives the measurements actually exclude. [R1](#ref-source-7acbaed4e62141d9) [R2](#ref-source-8c3b378d8802f683) [R4](#ref-source-362cf0fd861683c3) [R5](#ref-source-fae77f2c38d4cf72) [R7](#ref-source-fd33407c49db2caf)

## Related topics

[Parallel conduction channels](/scwiki/parallel-conduction-channels), [Nonlinear Hall effect](/scwiki/nonlinear-hall-effect), and [Field-induced superconductivity](/scwiki/field-induced-superconductivity).

Values describe individual reports, not a ranking. Unknown means the checked source did not supply the field at this review scope.

claims.statement: Choose a probe by the observable it measures and the inference that is needed. A spectral gap, a resistance drop, a magnetic response and a thermodynamic anomaly answer different questions. This handbook connects fifteen experimental methods to concrete original studies and their limitations. It is a guide to interpreting evidence, not a universal instrument operating procedure or a catalogue of confirmed transition temperatures. The fixed I1–I15 identifiers preserve the approved reference structure.

claims.statement: Every inversion needs a forward model: the measured signal is affected by sample response, instrument resolution and background. Parameters are identifiable only if different allowed parameter sets produce distinguishable signals within uncertainty. The independent calculations accompanying this handbook check a triangular London-limit lattice sum, a Gaussian field-distribution transform and additive broadening. They do not reproduce an interacting material or calibrate an instrument. See I6 for the physical assumptions behind the example.

claims.statement: Angle-resolved photoemission maps the energy and emission direction of electrons leaving a surface. Relating those counts to an electronic spectral function requires occupation factors, matrix elements, energy and angular resolution, and a specified momentum conversion. Photon energy and polarization can change which bands are visible; a weak feature is not automatically an absent band. Record surface preparation, sample temperature, energy reference and the fitting or symmetrization procedure alongside an extracted gap. Synchrotron access does not itself establish bulk sensitivity or remove these assumptions.

claims.statement: The selected single-layer FeSe study illustrates the inference boundary. He and colleagues tracked annealing-dependent spectra and fitted the temperature dependence of symmetrized energy-distribution curves. The reported high temperature scale is a spectroscopic indication; it is not a simultaneous demonstration of zero resistance or magnetic screening in that measured layer. Band counting also used a degeneracy assumption. Compare the same preparation and carrier state across probes before identifying a superconducting transition or a causal effect of annealing.

claims.statement: STM resolves a surface through a tunnelling junction, while STS measures its differential conductance versus bias. Interpreting that conductance as a local density of states assumes an adequately characterized tip, tunnelling matrix element and junction regime. Temperature, modulation broadening, setpoint and drift affect the apparent gap or spatial contrast. Preserve the topographic channel and acquisition conditions rather than treating every conductance feature as an intrinsic bulk excitation. A Fourier peak also needs its energy dependence and relation to the atomic lattice.

claims.statement: Wise and colleagues' selected final figures concern Pb/La-substituted Bi2201; Na-CCOC appears as earlier work, not their specimen. Their spatial maps provide an example of separating a checkerboard modulation from a dispersing quasiparticle-interference interpretation. Such an assignment requires competing explanations and energy-dependent controls, rather than one visually striking image. A local gap or zero-bias peak alone does not establish bulk superconductivity, a unique gap phase or a Majorana state. Surface termination and reproducibility across fields of view belong in the evidence record.

claims.statement: INS resolves energy and momentum transferred between neutrons and a sample. Extracting a magnetic spectrum requires resolution, normalization, background and the distinction between magnetic, phonon and nuclear scattering. Single crystals preserve directional information; a powder measurement averages orientations. A resonance at a superconducting transition can constrain a model of the gap and magnetic susceptibility, but the assignment depends on coherence factors, band structure and competing explanations. The measured peak is not by itself a unique identification of the pairing interaction.

Elastic, orbital and magnetic channels must be separated with the actual resolution and model. A measured magnetic dispersion can inform a pairing theory, but does not alone prove that the observed excitation is the pairing mediator. Small-volume sensitivity also does not eliminate surface, self-absorption or normalization questions.

claims.statement: Ament and colleagues' local tetragonal Cu model makes the selection rule concrete: a direct spin flip forbidden for a moment along the orbital normal can become allowed for an in-plane moment at the L or M edge. The accessible momentum range at the M edge is much smaller than at L3. Preserve these conditions when comparing intensities or calling a missing peak evidence against magnetism.

claims.statement: NMR probes nuclei through resonance shifts and relaxation. A Knight-shift interpretation must separate spin, orbital and diamagnetic contributions and specify the field direction, site and hyperfine coupling. The spin susceptibility inferred in an applied field is not automatically the zero-field response of an unperturbed condensate. Relaxation and shift provide complementary information; neither can be replaced by a single pairing-symmetry label without its model and control measurements. Temperature calibration is especially important when the excitation pulse itself can heat a small sample.

claims.statement: Muon polarization samples an internal-field distribution. Transverse-field vortex measurements can constrain penetration depth through a field-profile model; zero-field relaxation and a muon Knight shift address different questions. Brandt's ideal triangular London limit gives $\langle\delta B^2\rangle\simeq0.00371\Phi_0^2/\lambda^4$ only in its restricted field and large-$\kappa$ regime. An independent reciprocal-lattice sum converges to 0.0037107353. This does not validate the approximation near either critical field or for a strongly disordered lattice. The paper's variance symbol must not be mistaken for a relaxation rate.
