claims.statement: Ginzburg–Landau theory organizes a free-energy expansion in a complex order parameter and its spatial gradients. Its coefficients and applicable temperature range must be specified; in its conventional derivation it is controlled near the transition. A homogeneous minimum, a linearized upper-critical-field calculation and a vortex-lattice solution are different problems. The type-I/type-II boundary of the elementary isotropic model should not be transferred without qualification to every anisotropic or multicomponent material.

claims.statement: Brandt's ideal vortex-lattice calculation illustrates how field, the Ginzburg–Landau parameter and lattice structure affect magnetic observables. Its assumptions exclude arbitrary disorder and pinning, and the commonly used London-limit variance is valid only in a restricted regime. Solving a phenomenological equation with chosen coefficients does not identify a microscopic pairing mechanism. Report boundary conditions, gauge, mesh and free-energy comparisons when several solutions exist; numerical convergence to one stationary configuration alone does not establish that it is the global equilibrium state.

claims.statement: Bogoliubov–de Gennes theory writes a quadratic paired Hamiltonian in a particle-and-hole basis. For a complete finite fermionic basis, Hermitian normal block $h$ and antisymmetric pairing matrix $\Delta$, one convention is $\mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta\\\Delta^\dagger&-h^T\end{pmatrix}$. The doubled description has particle-hole redundancy, not twice as many independent physical states. Independent complex-matrix checks verify Hermiticity and paired eigenvalues in this convention; a reduced spin block can use different notation.

claims.statement: Specify whether the pairing field is imposed or determined self-consistently, together with density, boundaries and the physical basis. Kitaev's selected chain model provides a controlled example of bulk and boundary structure, but a near-zero eigenvalue by itself does not prove a protected experimental Majorana mode. Finite-size splitting, competing localized states and model perturbations must be considered. A self-consistent mean-field solution also does not include every collective or correlation effect. Numerical particle-hole symmetry is a necessary algebra check, not a topological classification or material validation.

articles.body:
## Scope

Theoretical tools answer different questions: whether a model has a pairing instability, how a sample responds, or which approximation is defensible. This handbook connects twelve approved topics to their inputs, outputs and limitations. A solver result is conditional on the Hamiltonian, numerical convergence and physical approximations; it is not an experimental transition record. The J1–J12 identifiers remain stable even where an old planning label needed scientific correction. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9) [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

## Mathematical assumptions

State the degrees of freedom, interactions, energy and length units, boundary conditions and limit being taken before comparing calculations. Distinguish an exact identity within a model from an approximation to a real material. The accompanying independent checks cover mass weighting, a four-state atomic Green function, Fourier interpolation, a scalar Cooper-channel flow and complex Bogoliubov matrices. They do not run a material DFT calculation, an interacting impurity solver or a full multichannel renormalization group. [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9) [R8](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194) [R11](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c) [R12](#ref-source-0aec6d266727d631)

## J1 — BCS mean-field theory

BCS theory constructs a coherent many-electron paired state and a self-consistent gap. In the elementary isotropic model, the quasiparticle energy is $E_k=\sqrt{\xi_k^2+|\Delta|^2}$, with energies measured relative to the chemical potential. The familiar exponential transition scale assumes a weak attractive interaction, an energy shell and a sufficiently smooth density of states. Specify whether that density counts one spin or both; changing the convention without changing the coupling produces a different exponent. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

The Cooper problem instead places two added electrons above an inert Fermi sea. Its instability motivates pairing but does not replace the many-body gap and number equations. A BCS gap solution describes pair formation within the approximation; phase fluctuations, spatial inhomogeneity and competing order can alter the observed transition. A material's similar gap ratio is therefore a consistency check, not unique proof of a phonon mechanism. Use the full band and symmetry assumptions when extending the elementary model. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R2](#ref-source-d0ec754310a67e88)

## J2 — Eliashberg theory

Eliashberg theory retains the frequency dependence of the interaction and electronic self-energy. A phonon-mediated calculation needs an electron–phonon spectral function, a treatment of the effective Coulomb interaction and an explicitly chosen isotropic, anisotropic or multiband approximation. The gap and mass-renormalization functions are coupled. A converged solution on a Matsubara grid also needs frequency-cutoff and temperature checks; numerical precision alone does not justify neglecting vertex corrections or changes in the phonon system. [R3](#ref-source-d56b04dc0b32c796)

The selected Marsiglio review provides a simple Einstein-spectrum benchmark, while Choi and colleagues' MgB2 calculation illustrates why band-dependent interactions and gaps can matter. Neither example licenses using one averaged coupling for every material. A Matsubara gap value is not automatically the measured tunnelling gap: real-frequency continuation and spectral features require care. Preserve how the Coulomb parameter was chosen and which electronic and phonon inputs were computed, fitted or assumed. The reviewed examples are scoped checks, not independent reproduction of every numerical result. [R3](#ref-source-d56b04dc0b32c796) [R4](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221)

## J3 — McMillan and Allen–Dynes estimates

Compact transition-temperature estimates summarize solutions of a specified electron–phonon theory; they do not replace its inputs. Allen and Dynes use a logarithmic phonon-frequency scale and introduce strong-coupling and spectral-shape corrections. An implementation should name which version it evaluates, preserve the effective Coulomb parameter, and state whether its frequency input is an energy, angular frequency or temperature. A number copied between these conventions without conversion can be wrong even when the expression looks familiar. [R5](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66)

The original abstract describes the accuracy of the modified McMillan estimate for the materials known at that time and its failure at larger coupling. That historical comparison is not a universal modern applicability boundary. Report sensitivity to the spectrum and Coulomb input, and compare a compact estimate with a suitably converged Eliashberg solution when justified. Here the original abstract was checked; the inaccessible original fit derivation and dataset are not claimed as fully reviewed. No fitted or hypothetical estimate is entered into the experimental Tc filter. [R5](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66) [R3](#ref-source-d56b04dc0b32c796)

## J4 — DFT and density-functional perturbation theory

DFT and DFPT connect an electronic-structure approximation to forces, harmonic phonons and response functions. The mass-weighted force-constant matrix $D=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ has eigenvalues $\omega^2$, where $K$ is the energy Hessian. Its eigenvalues are not superconducting transition temperatures. An independent two-mass calculation checks the translational zero mode and shows that negative curvature produces a negative squared frequency; removing that sign would conceal an instability. [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9)

Baroni and colleagues' selected formulation requires self-consistent induced charge and potential. Metallic calculations couple momentum sampling to the smearing treatment; arbitrary numerical smearing is not a physical electronic temperature. The electron–phonon spectral function also differs from the transport-weighted spectrum. Specify structure, exchange-correlation approximation, basis, sampling and response convergence before interpreting a prediction. Harmonic stability alone neither establishes superconductivity nor tests anharmonic effects, strong correlations or every competing structure. The independent checks here verify elementary mechanics, not a full first-principles workflow. [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9)

## J5 — Hubbard-model QMC and DMRG

Quantum Monte Carlo and density-matrix renormalization group methods address interacting lattice models across different coupling regimes; they are not collectively weak-correlation methods. LeBlanc and colleagues compare several algorithms for specified two-dimensional Hubbard parameters. Agreement must be assessed observable by observable and after the relevant finite-size, temperature and algorithmic extrapolations. Agreement in ground-state energy alone does not establish a particular pairing state or a finite superconducting transition temperature. [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

In the reviewed auxiliary-field formulation, particle-hole symmetry protects the half-filled model with zero next-nearest hopping from the sign problem. Away from that setting, a constrained-path calculation adds trial-state-dependent systematic error and is not generally variational. DMRG requires checks of retained states or bond dimension, truncation error, cylinder length and width, boundary conditions and competing metastable patterns. Taking cylinder length to infinity does not take its width to the two-dimensional thermodynamic limit. Historical computational sizes in a 2015 benchmark are not current hardware limits. [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

## J6 — Dynamical mean-field theory

Single-site DMFT replaces a lattice environment by a self-consistent quantum impurity bath. It retains local temporal fluctuations through a frequency-dependent self-energy; it is not simply static Hartree-Fock theory. For the specified local-interaction models, its large-coordination limit becomes exact with the appropriate hopping scaling. Applied in finite dimensions, the single-site construction omits nonlocal self-energy components, so spatial correlations may require extensions or independent checks. [R8](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194)

The impurity Green function must equal the local lattice Green function after self-consistency. The Weiss propagator describing the bath is not generally the bare local lattice propagator. An independent four-state thermal calculation verifies the atomic-limit spectral weights and Green function, but does not validate a finite-hopping DMFT solution. State the impurity solver, bath or frequency discretization, interaction convention and convergence criteria. Two lattices with the same noninteracting density of states need not have identical magnetic response or ordered phases; local single-particle agreement is a narrower result. [R8](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194)

## J7 — RPA, fluctuation exchange and pairing kernels

Random-phase and fluctuation-exchange approaches organize selected interaction diagrams into response and pairing approximations. Their names do not specify the entire calculation: identify the bare or dressed propagators, orbital interaction matrix, retained channels and self-consistency. Bickers, Scalapino and White's original abstract describes self-consistent conserving approximations for two-particle correlations. Conservation properties are useful constraints, but do not make an approximation exact for arbitrary coupling or establish a measured material's pairing mechanism. [R10](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0)

Scalapino's selected review passages discuss a DCA vertex decomposition and a particle-particle Bethe–Salpeter eigenproblem. They illustrate how a momentum-dependent interaction and dressed propagators enter pairing analysis; those particular results must not be relabelled as an RPA or FLEX benchmark. An eigenvalue reaching the stated instability condition is conditional on the kernel and approximation. Check competing channels, resolution and the treatment of fluctuations before equating its temperature scale with a bulk experimental Tc. The full original conserving-functional derivation remains outside the reviewed scope. [R9](#ref-source-eaa3beeed4368f46) [R10](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0)

## J8 — Tight-binding and Wannier models

Wannier functions provide a localized representation of a chosen Bloch subspace. Unitary rotations within an isolated manifold preserve its projector but change the orbital shapes and hopping representation. With entangled bands, selecting the subspace and selecting its gauge are distinct tasks. The frozen inner energy window constrains which states are retained; outside it, projected bands can differ from the original calculation. A compact model therefore needs its orbital basis and energy windows, not just an attractive band plot. [R11](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c)

Interpolation relies on localization, a sufficient momentum mesh and adequate real-space hopping range. Independent Fourier recovery of a known finite-range model succeeds, while an undersampled distant hopping aliases into a different term despite perfect agreement on the sampled grid. Validate intermediate momenta and relevant observables. Nonzero Chern invariants can obstruct an exponentially localized representation of the isolated manifold; a different subspace or hybrid construction must be described explicitly. This check is not a material wannierization or proof that an empirical tight-binding fit is unique. [R11](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c)

## J9 — Renormalization group

Renormalization group methods track how an effective description changes as higher-energy modes are removed. The retained channels, cutoff, self-energy treatment and truncation determine what a flow can establish. In Shankar's stated Fermi-surface setting, angular Cooper channels decouple at one loop. With the normalization $g=V_l/(4\pi)$ and $\ell=\ln(\Lambda_0/\Lambda)$, the selected equation gives $dg/d\ell=-g^2$. Negative coupling is attractive in this convention. [R12](#ref-source-0aec6d266727d631)

Independent numerical integration agrees with $g(\ell)=g_0/(1+g_0\ell)$ before its pole: attraction grows and repulsion decreases in this restricted flow. The divergence marks an instability and loss of perturbative control, not a measured Tc or a solved ordered state. The source explicitly warns that otherwise irrelevant terms can generate an attractive channel through the Kohn–Luttinger mechanism. Thus the simple positive-channel flow does not prove that every repulsive system remains a stable normal metal. Nested surfaces and additional channels require their own analysis. [R12](#ref-source-0aec6d266727d631)

## J10 — Quantum geometry and Berry methods

Band eigenvectors carry geometric information beyond the dispersion. A quantum metric and Berry curvature can be constructed from the projector onto a specified band or subspace, with carefully stated normalization and gauge conventions. The selected Liang manuscript uses a metric normalization twice the convention used in the linked Wiki geometry article. Comparing numerical coefficients without reconciling that factor would produce a false disagreement. Degenerate or touching bands also require a suitable subspace treatment rather than unstable single-band derivatives. [R13](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

Geometric quantities can enter superfluid response, but a nonzero metric alone does not prove superconductivity. Peotta and Törmä's flat-band result has explicit interaction, isolation and pairing assumptions. Huhtinen and colleagues further show why order-parameter relaxation and representation dependence matter when differentiating the free energy. State what is held fixed and what is reoptimized before calling a curvature a physical stiffness. A frozen-field derivative and a relaxed response are not interchangeable; the full multiband response calculation remains a separate task. [R14](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81) [R15](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f)

## J11 — Ginzburg–Landau theory

Ginzburg–Landau theory organizes a free-energy expansion in a complex order parameter and its spatial gradients. Its coefficients and applicable temperature range must be specified; in its conventional derivation it is controlled near the transition. A homogeneous minimum, a linearized upper-critical-field calculation and a vortex-lattice solution are different problems. The type-I/type-II boundary of the elementary isotropic model should not be transferred without qualification to every anisotropic or multicomponent material. [R16](#ref-source-89f5503f5e470385)

Brandt's ideal vortex-lattice calculation illustrates how field, the Ginzburg–Landau parameter and lattice structure affect magnetic observables. Its assumptions exclude arbitrary disorder and pinning, and the commonly used London-limit variance is valid only in a restricted regime. Solving a phenomenological equation with chosen coefficients does not identify a microscopic pairing mechanism. Report boundary conditions, gauge, mesh and free-energy comparisons when several solutions exist; numerical convergence to one stationary configuration alone does not establish that it is the global equilibrium state. [R17](#ref-source-65b23b74f5402e26)

## J12 — Bogoliubov–de Gennes equations

Bogoliubov–de Gennes theory writes a quadratic paired Hamiltonian in a particle-and-hole basis. For a complete finite fermionic basis, Hermitian normal block $h$ and antisymmetric pairing matrix $\Delta$, one convention is $\mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta\\\Delta^\dagger&-h^T\end{pmatrix}$. The doubled description has particle-hole redundancy, not twice as many independent physical states. Independent complex-matrix checks verify Hermiticity and paired eigenvalues in this convention; a reduced spin block can use different notation. [R18](#ref-source-ade538b429fdd847)

Specify whether the pairing field is imposed or determined self-consistently, together with density, boundaries and the physical basis. Kitaev's selected chain model provides a controlled example of bulk and boundary structure, but a near-zero eigenvalue by itself does not prove a protected experimental Majorana mode. Finite-size splitting, competing localized states and model perturbations must be considered. A self-consistent mean-field solution also does not include every collective or correlation effect. Numerical particle-hole symmetry is a necessary algebra check, not a topological classification or material validation. [R18](#ref-source-ade538b429fdd847)

## Experimental criteria

Compare calculated and measured quantities with matching sample conditions and definitions. A pairing eigenvalue, a harmonic phonon, a local spectral gap and an experimental zero-resistance criterion are different observables. Keep model temperatures out of the measured-Tc catalogue. Predictions should specify independent tests that could reject the assumed mechanism, structure or parameter set. [R4](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221) [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9) [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

## Limits and disputes

Each of the twelve sections has a named review scope. Some references were checked only at abstract level; others use selected author-manuscript passages with final-version comparisons still open. Independent small-model checks verify the stated algebra and counterexamples, not all numerical methods or every cited material. Complete scientific acceptance, full derivations, supplementary datasets and material-level reproduction remain open. [R5](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66) [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472) [R10](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0) [R12](#ref-source-0aec6d266727d631)

## Discovery implications

Choose the simplest defensible model that can distinguish the proposed explanation from a concrete alternative. Carry its uncertainty into any material ranking. A useful workflow moves between structural evidence, electronic and interaction models, numerical convergence and experimentally testable observables; agreement at one stage does not remove assumptions at the next. Retain failed fits and competing states rather than reporting only the most favorable transition estimate. [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9) [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472) [R11](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c)

## Related topics

Read [BCS theory](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), [Eliashberg theory](/scwiki/eliashberg-strong-coupling), [spin fluctuations](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), [quantum metric](/scwiki/quantum-metric), [geometric superfluid weight](/scwiki/geometric-superfluid-weight), [Majorana states](/scwiki/majorana-zero-modes), [experimental methods](/scwiki/experimental-methods), and [flat-band temperature limits](/scwiki/open-questions/n10).

sections.markdown:
## J10 — Quantum geometry and Berry methods

Band eigenvectors carry geometric information beyond the dispersion. A quantum metric and Berry curvature can be constructed from the projector onto a specified band or subspace, with carefully stated normalization and gauge conventions. The selected Liang manuscript uses a metric normalization twice the convention used in the linked Wiki geometry article. Comparing numerical coefficients without reconciling that factor would produce a false disagreement. Degenerate or touching bands also require a suitable subspace treatment rather than unstable single-band derivatives. [R13](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

Geometric quantities can enter superfluid response, but a nonzero metric alone does not prove superconductivity. Peotta and Törmä's flat-band result has explicit interaction, isolation and pairing assumptions. Huhtinen and colleagues further show why order-parameter relaxation and representation dependence matter when differentiating the free energy. State what is held fixed and what is reoptimized before calling a curvature a physical stiffness. [R14](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81) [R15](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f)

sections.title: J11 — Ginzburg–Landau theory
sections.markdown:
## J11 — Ginzburg–Landau theory

Ginzburg–Landau theory organizes a free-energy expansion in a complex order parameter and its spatial gradients. Its coefficients and applicable temperature range must be specified; in its conventional derivation it is controlled near the transition. A homogeneous minimum, a linearized upper-critical-field calculation and a vortex-lattice solution are different problems. The type-I/type-II boundary of the elementary isotropic model should not be transferred without qualification to every anisotropic or multicomponent material. [R16](#ref-source-89f5503f5e470385)

sections.title: J12 — Bogoliubov–de Gennes equations
sections.markdown:
## J12 — Bogoliubov–de Gennes equations

Bogoliubov–de Gennes theory writes a quadratic paired Hamiltonian in a particle-and-hole basis. For a complete finite fermionic basis, Hermitian normal block $h$ and antisymmetric pairing matrix $\Delta$, one convention is $\mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta\\\Delta^\dagger&-h^T\end{pmatrix}$. Compare calculated and measured quantities with matching sample conditions and definitions. A pairing eigenvalue, a harmonic phonon, a local spectral gap and an experimental zero-resistance criterion are different observables. Keep model temperatures out of the measured-Tc catalogue. articles.markdown:
# Theoretical tools for superconductivity

Twelve theoretical and computational approaches, with their inputs, convergence checks, physical assumptions and limits on predicting superconductivity.

## Scope

Theoretical tools answer different questions: whether a model has a pairing instability, how a sample responds, or which approximation is defensible. This handbook connects twelve approved topics to their inputs, outputs and limitations. A solver result is conditional on the Hamiltonian, numerical convergence and physical approximations; it is not an experimental transition record. The J1–J12 identifiers remain stable even where an old planning label needed scientific correction. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9) [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

## Mathematical assumptions

State the degrees of freedom, interactions, energy and length units, boundary conditions and limit being taken before comparing calculations. Distinguish an exact identity within a model from an approximation to a real material. The accompanying independent checks cover mass weighting, a four-state atomic Green function, Fourier interpolation, a scalar Cooper-channel flow and complex Bogoliubov matrices. They do not run a material DFT calculation, an interacting impurity solver or a full multichannel renormalization group. [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9) [R8](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194) [R11](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c) [R12](#ref-source-0aec6d266727d631)

## J1 — BCS mean-field theory

BCS theory constructs a coherent many-electron paired state and a self-consistent gap. In the elementary isotropic model, the quasiparticle energy is $E_k=\sqrt{\xi_k^2+|\Delta|^2}$, with energies measured relative to the chemical potential. The familiar exponential transition scale assumes a weak attractive interaction, an energy shell and a sufficiently smooth density of states. Specify whether that density counts one spin or both; changing the convention without changing the coupling produces a different exponent. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

The Cooper problem instead places two added electrons above an inert Fermi sea. Its instability motivates pairing but does not replace the many-body gap and number equations. A BCS gap solution describes pair formation within the approximation; phase fluctuations, spatial inhomogeneity and competing order can alter the observed transition. A material's similar gap ratio is therefore a consistency check, not unique proof of a phonon mechanism. Use the full band and symmetry assumptions when extending the elementary model. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R2](#ref-source-d0ec754310a67e88)

## J2 — Eliashberg theory

Eliashberg theory retains the frequency dependence of the interaction and electronic self-energy. A phonon-mediated calculation needs an electron–phonon spectral function, a treatment of the effective Coulomb interaction and an explicitly chosen isotropic, anisotropic or multiband approximation. The gap and mass-renormalization functions are coupled. A converged solution on a Matsubara grid also needs frequency-cutoff and temperature checks; numerical precision alone does not justify neglecting vertex corrections or changes in the phonon system. [R3](#ref-source-d56b04dc0b32c796)

The selected Marsiglio review provides a simple Einstein-spectrum benchmark, while Choi and colleagues' MgB2 calculation illustrates why band-dependent interactions and gaps can matter. Neither example licenses using one averaged coupling for every material. A Matsubara gap value is not automatically the measured tunnelling gap: real-frequency continuation and spectral features require care. Preserve how the Coulomb parameter was chosen and which electronic and phonon inputs were computed, fitted or assumed. The reviewed examples are scoped checks, not independent reproduction of every numerical result. [R3](#ref-source-d56b04dc0b32c796) [R4](#ref-source-7c4eac077ae5e221)

## J3 — McMillan and Allen–Dynes estimates

Compact transition-temperature estimates summarize solutions of a specified electron–phonon theory; they do not replace its inputs. Allen and Dynes use a logarithmic phonon-frequency scale and introduce strong-coupling and spectral-shape corrections. An implementation should name which version it evaluates, preserve the effective Coulomb parameter, and state whether its frequency input is an energy, angular frequency or temperature. A number copied between these conventions without conversion can be wrong even when the expression looks familiar. [R5](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66)

The original abstract describes the accuracy of the modified McMillan estimate for the materials known at that time and its failure at larger coupling. That historical comparison is not a universal modern applicability boundary. Report sensitivity to the spectrum and Coulomb input, and compare a compact estimate with a suitably converged Eliashberg solution when justified. Here the original abstract was checked; the inaccessible original fit derivation and dataset are not claimed as fully reviewed. No fitted or hypothetical estimate is entered into the experimental Tc filter. [R5](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66) [R3](#ref-source-d56b04dc0b32c796)

## J4 — DFT and density-functional perturbation theory

DFT and DFPT connect an electronic-structure approximation to forces, harmonic phonons and response functions. The mass-weighted force-constant matrix $D=M^{-1/2}KM^{-1/2}$ has eigenvalues $\omega^2$, where $K$ is the energy Hessian. Its eigenvalues are not superconducting transition temperatures. An independent two-mass calculation checks the translational zero mode and shows that negative curvature produces a negative squared frequency; removing that sign would conceal an instability. [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9)

Baroni and colleagues' selected formulation requires self-consistent induced charge and potential. Metallic calculations couple momentum sampling to the smearing treatment; arbitrary numerical smearing is not a physical electronic temperature. The electron–phonon spectral function also differs from the transport-weighted spectrum. Specify structure, exchange-correlation approximation, basis, sampling and response convergence before interpreting a prediction. Harmonic stability alone neither establishes superconductivity nor tests anharmonic effects, strong correlations or every competing structure. The independent checks here verify elementary mechanics, not a full first-principles workflow. [R6](#ref-source-b06e417872e240c9)

## J5 — Hubbard-model QMC and DMRG

Quantum Monte Carlo and density-matrix renormalization group methods address interacting lattice models across different coupling regimes; they are not collectively weak-correlation methods. LeBlanc and colleagues compare several algorithms for specified two-dimensional Hubbard parameters. Agreement must be assessed observable by observable and after the relevant finite-size, temperature and algorithmic extrapolations. Agreement in ground-state energy alone does not establish a particular pairing state or a finite superconducting transition temperature. [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

In the reviewed auxiliary-field formulation, particle-hole symmetry protects the half-filled model with zero next-nearest hopping from the sign problem. Away from that setting, a constrained-path calculation adds trial-state-dependent systematic error and is not generally variational. DMRG requires checks of retained states or bond dimension, truncation error, cylinder length and width, boundary conditions and competing metastable patterns. Taking cylinder length to infinity does not take its width to the two-dimensional thermodynamic limit. Historical computational sizes in a 2015 benchmark are not current hardware limits. [R7](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

## J6 — Dynamical mean-field theory

Single-site DMFT replaces a lattice environment by a self-consistent quantum impurity bath. It retains local temporal fluctuations through a frequency-dependent self-energy; it is not simply static Hartree-Fock theory. For the specified local-interaction models, its large-coordination limit becomes exact with the appropriate hopping scaling. Applied in finite dimensions, the single-site construction omits nonlocal self-energy components, so spatial correlations may require extensions or independent checks. [R8](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194)

The impurity Green function must equal the local lattice Green function after self-consistency. The Weiss propagator describing the bath is not generally the bare local lattice propagator. An independent four-state thermal calculation verifies the atomic-limit spectral weights and Green function, but does not validate a finite-hopping DMFT solution. State the impurity solver, bath or frequency discretization, interaction convention and convergence criteria. Two lattices with the same noninteracting density of states need not have identical magnetic response or ordered phases; local single-particle agreement is a narrower result. [R8](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194)

Conservation properties are useful constraints, but do not make an approximation exact for arbitrary coupling or establish a measured material's pairing mechanism. [R10](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0)

They illustrate how a momentum-dependent interaction and dressed propagators enter pairing analysis; those particular results must not be relabelled as an RPA or FLEX benchmark. An eigenvalue reaching the stated instability condition is conditional on the kernel and approximation. Check competing channels, resolution and the treatment of fluctuations before equating its temperature scale with a bulk experimental Tc. The full original conserving-functional derivation remains outside the reviewed scope. [R9](#ref-source-eaa3beeed4368f46) [R10](#ref-source-822deb97a8e9dde0)

Unitary rotations within an isolated manifold preserve its projector but change the orbital shapes and hopping representation. With entangled bands, selecting the subspace and selecting its gauge are distinct tasks. The frozen inner energy window constrains which states are retained; outside it, projected bands can differ from the original calculation. A compact model therefore needs its orbital basis and energy windows, not just an attractive band plot. [R11](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c)

Independent Fourier recovery of a known finite-range model succeeds, while an undersampled distant hopping aliases into a different term despite perfect agreement on the sampled grid. Validate intermediate momenta and relevant observables. Nonzero Chern invariants can obstruct an exponentially localized representation of the isolated manifold; a different subspace or hybrid construction must be described explicitly. ## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-j-claim-scope-1

Theoretical tools answer different questions: whether a model has a pairing instability, how a sample responds, or which approximation is defensible. This handbook connects twelve approved topics to their inputs, outputs and limitations. A solver result is conditional on the Hamiltonian, numerical convergence and physical approximations; it is not an experimental transition record. The J1–J12 identifiers remain stable even where an old planning label needed scientific correction.

### scwiki-j-claim-j1-1

BCS theory constructs a coherent many-electron paired state and a self-consistent gap. In the elementary isotropic model, the quasiparticle energy is $E_k=\sqrt{\xi_k^2+|\Delta|^2}$, with energies measured relative to the chemical potential. The familiar exponential transition scale assumes a weak attractive interaction, an energy shell and a sufficiently smooth density of states. Specify whether that density counts one spin or both; changing the convention without changing the coupling produces a different exponent.

### scwiki-j-claim-j1-2

The Cooper problem instead places two added electrons above an inert Fermi sea. Its instability motivates pairing but does not replace the many-body gap and number equations. A BCS gap solution describes pair formation within the approximation; phase fluctuations, spatial inhomogeneity and competing order can alter the observed transition. A material's similar gap ratio is therefore a consistency check, not unique proof of a phonon mechanism. Use the full band and symmetry assumptions when extending the elementary model.

### scwiki-j-claim-j12-1

Bogoliubov–de Gennes theory writes a quadratic paired Hamiltonian in a particle-and-hole basis. For a complete finite fermionic basis, Hermitian normal block $h$ and antisymmetric pairing matrix $\Delta$, one convention is $\mathcal H=\begin{pmatrix}h&\Delta\\\Delta^\dagger&-h^T\end{pmatrix}$. The doubled description has particle-hole redundancy, not twice as many independent physical states. Independent complex-matrix checks verify Hermiticity and paired eigenvalues in this convention; a reduced spin block can use different notation.

## Scope

Superconducting applications combine materials with cryogenics, mechanical support, electronics and protection. This handbook connects ten approved topics to the physical function that superconductivity provides and the conditions required to assess a device. Historical demonstrations, design specifications and current operator explanations are identified separately. A material's transition temperature is not an equipment operating temperature, and a successful component does not establish the performance of an entire installation. ## Mathematical assumptions

Compare like quantities: magnetic field at a named location, current with a stated criterion, power versus stored energy, and sensor efficiency referenced to a defined input. Independent calculations here test an ideal two-junction interference model, a finite charge-basis qubit Hamiltonian and a hypothetical rotating annulus. They do not certify a magnet, reproduce a detector calibration or establish service life. Engineering margins and uncertainty must accompany device-level claims. [R5](#ref-source-654ce5462e87aa22) [R8](#ref-source-4807a9ed7d6653f1) [R12](#ref-source-70cba2aaed2e7595)

## K1 — Power transmission cables

Superconducting cables aim to carry large currents in a compact conductor, but the conductor choice is project-specific. The selected MRI review describes conventional whole-body systems using liquid-helium-cooled NbTi coils, commonly operating near 4.2 K. That temperature is a cooling condition, not the material's transition temperature. The main magnet must provide a field with suitable spatial uniformity and stability across the intended imaging region. A larger central field alone does not specify image quality or make two scanners equivalent. Geometry, gradients, radio-frequency hardware and reconstruction also matter. [R2](#ref-source-684ee630b8b083a8)

Shorter magnets and wider bores change the balance between conductor quantity, peak field, field uniformity and accessibility. Reduced-helium and conduction-cooled designs can change installation requirements, but they still need refrigeration, thermal margins and protection against local heating. The source's product examples describe the state considered in its 2022 manuscript; they are not a current market ranking. The engineering discussion here does not provide clinical advice or assert that every magnet of a named material has the same operating limits. Detailed scanner qualification, final review-version comparison and the underlying device datasets remain separate checks. [R2](#ref-source-684ee630b8b083a8)

## K3 — Accelerator magnets

Accelerator dipoles bend charged-particle trajectories; quadrupoles focus the beam. Their field profiles, apertures and operating cycles impose different requirements. CERN's 5 December 2023 report describes a 7.2 m Nb3Sn quadrupole prototype for the High-Luminosity LHC, following earlier LHC use of NbTi. The reported third full-length prototype reached 16.53 kA in tests at both 1.9 K and 4.5 K, while planned operation was at 1.9 K. These are distinct test conditions, not interchangeable operating specifications. [R3](#ref-source-c43ec6c74bbdf714)

The same report links improved performance to changes in support-shell dimensions, assembly stress and production procedures after earlier prototypes were limited at 4.5 K. A useful comparison therefore includes conductor properties, mechanical loading, cooling and the specific magnet test, rather than attributing every improvement to chemical composition. Reaching a current target is an important milestone but does not independently establish beam performance, complete series-production acceptance or current fleet readiness. The Wiki records this as a dated prototype result; further system qualification requires its own evidence. [R3](#ref-source-c43ec6c74bbdf714)

## K4 — Fusion magnets

Magnetic-confinement fusion devices use different coils for different field functions. ITER's technical overview describes Nb3Sn in its toroidal-field and central-solenoid systems, and NbTi in the four largest poloidal-field coils. Its quoted peak fields refer to named parts of the magnet system: the toroidal-coil maximum and the central-solenoid maximum are not the same measurement location. Cooling near liquid-helium temperatures is also distinct from the plasma temperature. [R4](#ref-source-9ca58981555e968d)

Coils, structural supports, cable jackets, cooling circuits and feeders form an engineered system. High-temperature superconducting current leads in a feeder should not be confused with the material used throughout the main winding. Nor are all ITER coils superconducting: the overview identifies copper conductors for in-vessel vertical-stability and edge-localized-mode coils. Treat the page's design capabilities and intended operation as design information. A magnet specification does not demonstrate a completed fusion campaign, sustained net electricity generation or commercial reactor availability. Those outcomes require separately dated operational evidence. [R4](#ref-source-9ca58981555e968d)

## K5 — SQUID sensors and readout

A superconducting quantum interference device converts flux-dependent Josephson interference into an electrical signal. For an ideal loop with two identical sinusoidal junctions and negligible self-inductance, maximizing their summed currents gives $I_{\max}=2I_0|\cos(\pi\Phi/\Phi_0)|$. This independently checked limit explains periodicity; unequal junctions leave a nonzero minimum at half a flux quantum. It is not a complete sensor-noise calculation. Tesche and Clarke's original abstract explicitly includes inductance, junction asymmetry, resistive shunts and noise when assessing performance. [R5](#ref-source-654ce5462e87aa22)

Practical sensitivity depends on the pickup geometry, flux-to-voltage transfer, bandwidth and noise environment. A noise density must carry its frequency normalization and refer to the correct input quantity. NIST's detector-readout project illustrates SQUID ammeters and multiplexing used to read cryogenic sensor arrays, together with room-temperature electronics. The SQUID readout and the sensor that absorbs a photon are distinct components. Neither an ideal interference curve nor the presence of a SQUID establishes the final instrument's energy resolution. The complete original noise derivation and device-specific calibration remain outside this scoped check. [R5](#ref-source-654ce5462e87aa22) [R6](#ref-source-3fd82d6f06095581)

## K6 — Superconducting nanowire photon detectors

An SNSPD uses a biased superconducting nanowire and readout circuit to register photon-induced detection events. Efficiency, timing jitter, dark counts, recovery and maximum usable rate are separate metrics. Reddy and colleagues' 2020 experiment reported 98.0 ± 0.5% system detection efficiency at 1550 nm using MoSi, not WSi or NbN. Its definition refers to photons entering the fiber pigtail outside the cryostat, so the reported system efficiency must not be replaced by an internal absorption or conversion efficiency. [R7](#ref-source-f2533bc529f46a76)

The selected final-paper passages describe operation at 720–780 mK with optimized polarization. For the 50 μm device, series resistance in the readout changed pulse behavior and suppressed problems that otherwise affected operation. These conditions belong with the headline value. Do not combine this efficiency with another paper's best timing or dark-count result as though one device achieved them together. This is a dated experimental example, not an assertion of a current world record. The full calibration supplement, uncertainty reconstruction and raw detection traces have not yet been independently reviewed. [R7](#ref-source-f2533bc529f46a76)

## K7 — Superconducting qubits

Josephson circuits supply a nonlinear quantum element whose lowest levels can encode a qubit. The transmon model uses $H=4E_C(\hat n-n_g)^2-E_J\cos\hat\varphi$, where $E_C=e^2/(2C_\Sigma)$ and $\hat n$ counts Cooper pairs. Koch and colleagues show that increasing $E_J/E_C$ strongly suppresses sensitivity to offset charge, while reducing relative anharmonicity more slowly. The latter must remain sufficient to distinguish the intended transition from leakage to higher levels. [R8](#ref-source-4807a9ed7d6653f1)

Independent diagonalization in the charge basis checks this tradeoff across six energy ratios and verifies convergence under an increased charge cutoff. Absolute anharmonicity approaches a scale of order $E_C$; confusing it with relative anharmonicity would misstate the result. The calculation does not include fabricated junction defects, all environmental noise, driven gates or measurement electronics. A stable transition in this model is not a measured coherence time, gate fidelity or fault-tolerant processor. The original 2007 design paper supplies a foundational model, not a benchmark for present-day hardware. [R8](#ref-source-4807a9ed7d6653f1)

## K8 — Magnetic levitation

Magnetic levitation is a family of systems, not a single superconducting material. JR Central's operator explanation describes liquid-helium-cooled NbTi magnets onboard SCMAGLEV vehicles. Propulsion uses powered guideway coils, while motion relative to other guideway coils generates levitation and guidance forces. This architecture must not be described simply as a YBCO bulk floating over permanent magnets. A low-loss superconducting magnet also does not imply a train that consumes no electrical energy. [R9](#ref-source-5cdba326c3439d40)

Bulk-superconductor demonstrations provide a different example. The publisher-indexed abstract and excerpt of Wang and colleagues' 2002 paper describe a YBaCuO-bulk test vehicle over an NdFeB guideway and date the first reported test to 31 December 2000. That limited source access does not establish all load, speed or stability claims. Distinguish the demonstrated configuration from a transport service: propulsion, guidance, cooling, emergency support and operating reliability must be assessed for the actual system. This handbook preserves both examples and their evidence boundaries without declaring every maglev system superconducting or every prototype commercially deployed. [R9](#ref-source-5cdba326c3439d40) [R10](#ref-source-7be734c7e3d7c08e)

## K9 — Microwave resonators and filters

Superconducting films can reduce conductor loss in microwave structures, but zero direct-current resistance does not imply zero microwave surface resistance. Resonator measurements must distinguish loaded from unloaded quality factor and account for coupling, dielectric loss, packaging and heating. Xin and colleagues compared unpatterned YBCO wafers with patterned stripline structures using different current distributions. Their selected methods include thermal control and a change of measurement method at high input power. [R11](#ref-source-579a5cc38efb09e7)

The observed absence of patterning-induced degradation applied to the tested films and procedures; it is not a theorem about every fabrication process. Some comparisons also rescaled between frequencies using an assumed frequency-squared resistance dependence. Retain that assumption when interpreting agreement. Nonlinear response can limit power handling and generate unwanted frequencies even where small-signal loss is low. For a filter, quote frequency, temperature, bandwidth, insertion loss and power conditions together. The reviewed resonator experiment motivates these checks but does not establish the performance or current deployment of a particular communications filter. [R11](#ref-source-579a5cc38efb09e7)

## K10 — Flywheel energy storage

A superconducting flywheel stores kinetic energy in a rotating mass; its superconducting bearing reduces contact friction. This differs from storing energy directly in a magnetic field. RTRI's 15 April 2015 system description reports a four-ton rotor supported by a bearing cooled to 50 K, with a yttrium-containing superconducting coil and a superconducting bulk on the shaft. It lists 300 kW output, 100 kWh storage and a maximum speed of 6,000 rpm; grid-connection tests were still planned in that document. [R12](#ref-source-70cba2aaed2e7595)

Rotational energy is $E=I\omega^2/2$. Usable energy between two speeds depends on their squared difference, not just the maximum speed. Dividing the stated 100 kWh by 300 kW gives an ideal 20 minutes, not a measured discharge duration or round-trip efficiency. An independent uniform-annulus calculation illustrates why mass distribution matters; it does not reconstruct the actual layered rotor. Vacuum equipment, cooling, motor-generator losses, containment and maintenance remain part of system assessment. The source's historical capacity claim is preserved without repeating an absolute promise of unlimited lifetime or zero total loss. [R12](#ref-source-70cba2aaed2e7595)

## Experimental criteria

For each device, retain material, geometry, cooling, measurement reference, date and operating conditions. Identify whether the cited result is a model, component test, integrated demonstration or operational report. Reliability and efficiency need a stated duration and system boundary. Current or field targets, detector efficiency and storage capacity cannot be merged into a generic measure of superconducting quality. [R3](#ref-source-c43ec6c74bbdf714) [R7](#ref-source-f2533bc529f46a76) [R12](#ref-source-70cba2aaed2e7595)

## Limits and disputes

The ten sections have individual review records. Some use selected final-paper passages; others use author manuscripts, institutional engineering reports, reviews or explicitly limited abstract access. Full scientific acceptance remains open, including supplementary calibration, final-version comparisons and complete device records. The historical examples establish neither present-day records nor universal superiority over alternative technologies. ## Discovery implications

Select materials against the application: usable current and mechanical margin for a cable, field quality for a magnet, noise and coupling for a sensor, or losses and control for a quantum circuit. A higher transition temperature can change cooling options but does not settle every engineering constraint. A useful development claim specifies which independently measurable system property should improve and which tradeoffs may worsen. Do not combine this efficiency with another paper's best timing or dark-count result as though one device achieved them together. This is a dated experimental example, not an assertion of a current world record. The full calibration supplement, uncertainty reconstruction and raw detection traces have not yet been independently reviewed.

### scwiki-k-claim-k7-1

Josephson circuits supply a nonlinear quantum element whose lowest levels can encode a qubit. The transmon model uses $H=4E_C(\hat n-n_g)^2-E_J\cos\hat\varphi$, where $E_C=e^2/(2C_\Sigma)$ and $\hat n$ counts Cooper pairs. Koch and colleagues show that increasing $E_J/E_C$ strongly suppresses sensitivity to offset charge, while reducing relative anharmonicity more slowly. The latter must remain sufficient to distinguish the intended transition from leakage to higher levels.

### scwiki-k-claim-k7-2

Independent diagonalization in the charge basis checks this tradeoff across six energy ratios and verifies convergence under an increased charge cutoff. Absolute anharmonicity approaches a scale of order $E_C$; confusing it with relative anharmonicity would misstate the result. The calculation does not include fabricated junction defects, all environmental noise, driven gates or measurement electronics. A stable transition in this model is not a measured coherence time, gate fidelity or fault-tolerant processor. The original 2007 design paper supplies a foundational model, not a benchmark for present-day hardware.

### scwiki-k-claim-k8-1

Magnetic levitation is a family of systems, not a single superconducting material. JR Central's operator explanation describes liquid-helium-cooled NbTi magnets onboard SCMAGLEV vehicles. Propulsion uses powered guideway coils, while motion relative to other guideway coils generates levitation and guidance forces. This architecture must not be described simply as a YBCO bulk floating over permanent magnets. A low-loss superconducting magnet also does not imply a train that consumes no electrical energy.

### scwiki-k-claim-k8-2

Bulk-superconductor demonstrations provide a different example. The publisher-indexed abstract and excerpt of Wang and colleagues' 2002 paper describe a YBaCuO-bulk test vehicle over an NdFeB guideway and date the first reported test to 31 December 2000. That limited source access does not establish all load, speed or stability claims. Distinguish the demonstrated configuration from a transport service: propulsion, guidance, cooling, emergency support and operating reliability must be assessed for the actual system. This handbook preserves both examples and their evidence boundaries without declaring every maglev system superconducting or every prototype commercially deployed.

### scwiki-k-claim-k9-1

Superconducting films can reduce conductor loss in microwave structures, but zero direct-current resistance does not imply zero microwave surface resistance. Resonator measurements must distinguish loaded from unloaded quality factor and account for coupling, dielectric loss, packaging and heating. Xin and colleagues compared unpatterned YBCO wafers with patterned stripline structures using different current distributions. Their selected methods include thermal control and a change of measurement method at high input power.

The observed absence of patterning-induced degradation applied to the tested films and procedures; it is not a theorem about every fabrication process. Some comparisons also rescaled between frequencies using an assumed frequency-squared resistance dependence. Retain that assumption when interpreting agreement. ### scwiki-k-claim-k10-1

A superconducting flywheel stores kinetic energy in a rotating mass; its superconducting bearing reduces contact friction. This differs from storing energy directly in a magnetic field. RTRI's 15 April 2015 system description reports a four-ton rotor supported by a bearing cooled to 50 K, with a yttrium-containing superconducting coil and a superconducting bulk on the shaft. It lists 300 kW output, 100 kWh storage and a maximum speed of 6,000 rpm; grid-connection tests were still planned in that document.

### scwiki-k-claim-k10-2

Rotational energy is $E=I\omega^2/2$. Usable energy between two speeds depends on their squared difference, not just the maximum speed. Dividing the stated 100 kWh by 300 kW gives an ideal 20 minutes, not a measured discharge duration or round-trip efficiency. An independent uniform-annulus calculation illustrates why mass distribution matters; it does not reconstruct the actual layered rotor. These eighteen milestones preserve the approved topic identities while correcting dates and oversimplified temperature labels. A later author's recollection, an original discovery report and a modern reanalysis answer different historical questions. The cited review scope tells the reader which was checked.

claims.statement: There is no single mathematical curve that makes all reported transition temperatures directly comparable. The linked material articles preserve detailed records; this history does not create duplicate experimental Tc entries from narrative summaries.

claims.statement: Onnes's 1911 mercury work opened the study of superconductivity. The lecture also discusses a current threshold above which a voltage appeared, anticipating the need to specify measuring current.

claims.statement: Meissner and Ochsenfeld's 1933 work added magnetic behavior to the definition of the superconducting state. The selected original reproduction describes field redistribution around tin and lead as the samples became superconducting. This changed the question from whether a conductor can sustain current without detectable resistance to which magnetic state it reaches. An ideal conductor's history-dependent trapped field does not by itself supply the same equilibrium magnetic condition.

claims.statement: The London brothers' 1935 paper supplied an electromagnetic description of superconductors that accommodates magnetic screening. An integration constant associated with the initial field is therefore not a trivial detail: dropping it without stating the physical postulate would conceal what the theory adds.

claims.statement: The London description links current and electromagnetic fields under its stated local assumptions. It does not determine a material's microscopic pairing interaction or explain every spatially nonuniform state. Modern equations often use SI units and different notation from the original scan; a historical formula should not be copied into a modern calculation without checking those conventions. This milestone concerns a phenomenological advance in electrodynamics, not an experimental discovery of a new transition-temperature record.

claims.statement: Ginzburg and Landau introduced a complex order parameter and a free-energy description of superconductivity in 1950. Ginzburg's later firsthand lecture explains the motivation to extend the London treatment, including spatial variation and interfaces. The resulting framework connects electromagnetic response to the amplitude and phase of an order parameter and provides a basis for studying boundaries and competing configurations near a transition.

claims.statement: Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer's 1957 theory constructed a coherent paired many-electron state and related its excitation spectrum to superconducting observables. It moved beyond identifying macroscopic signatures by providing a microscopic explanation within a specified interaction model. The energy gap and thermodynamic behavior arise together in that framework, rather than being independent empirical labels attached to a zero-resistance state.

claims.statement: The achievement should not be turned into a claim that one elementary approximation describes every later material. The familiar isotropic weak-coupling results assume a particular pairing structure and energy-scale hierarchy. Strong coupling, multiple bands, unconventional symmetry and substantial fluctuations require further treatment. A historical timeline should distinguish the theory's established role from a material-specific mechanism assignment. Agreement with one BCS-like ratio is a consistency check, not proof that a newly observed superconductor has the same microscopic interaction.

Earlier zero-voltage currents could instead have involved metallic shorts, and unsuccessful measurements were part of the development. Phase-dependent response, magnetic interference and microwave-induced voltage steps provided more specific tests than a zero-voltage branch alone.
