articles.body:
## Scope

The history of superconductivity includes discoveries, theories, material families and changing standards of evidence. These eighteen milestones connect major developments to their dates, measurement conditions and original evidence. A later author's recollection, an original discovery report and a modern reanalysis answer different historical questions. The cited review scope tells the reader which was checked. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f) [R4](#ref-source-9ccf1f17448aae3d) [R7](#ref-source-2e9437c55bb758da)

## Mathematical assumptions

There is no single mathematical curve that makes all reported transition temperatures directly comparable. A resistance onset, a midpoint, a noise-floor zero and a magnetic response can occur at different temperatures, even in one specimen. Pressure, composition, sample history and measurement field must remain attached to any point. The linked material articles preserve detailed records; this history does not create duplicate experimental Tc entries from narrative summaries. [R12](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e) [R21](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f) [R22](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

## L1 — 1911: mercury and the resistance transition

Onnes's 1911 mercury work opened the study of superconductivity. His 1913 Nobel lecture provides a firsthand account of the abrupt resistance decrease near 4.2 K and the limits of the electrical measurement. Resistance too small to resolve is an experimental statement; mathematical exactness is not read directly from an instrument. The lecture also discusses a current threshold above which a voltage appeared, anticipating the need to specify measuring current. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f)

The checked scan contains later notes, including a 1914 addendum. Those observations must not all be assigned to the original 1911 discovery. Nor should the initial resistance experiment be described as already establishing the later Meissner effect or a complete microscopic theory. The original 1911 communication itself remains outside the directly reviewed material; the author lecture is identified as the historical source used here. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f)

## L2 — 1933: the Meissner–Ochsenfeld effect

Meissner and Ochsenfeld's 1933 work added magnetic behavior to the definition of the superconducting state. The selected original reproduction describes field redistribution around tin and lead as the samples became superconducting. This changed the question from whether a conductor can sustain current without detectable resistance to which magnetic state it reaches. An ideal conductor's history-dependent trapped field does not by itself supply the same equilibrium magnetic condition. [R2](#ref-source-512705f3e64d88d7)

Geometry remains essential to reading the experiment. The original report also discusses retained field in a lead-tube cavity; a cavity is not the same region as the superconducting material. A simplified statement that every field everywhere becomes zero would erase this distinction. The historical paper's apparatus, uncertainty and complete translation have not been independently reconstructed here. The milestone records the new magnetic evidence while retaining the limits of the selected primary reproduction. [R2](#ref-source-512705f3e64d88d7)

## L3 — 1935: London electrodynamics

The London brothers' 1935 paper supplied an electromagnetic description of superconductors that accommodates magnetic screening. The selected original pages distinguish the consequence of perfect conductivity from an additional condition selecting the superconducting magnetic state. An integration constant associated with the initial field is therefore not a trivial detail: dropping it without stating the physical postulate would conceal what the theory adds. [R3](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

The London description links current and electromagnetic fields under its stated local assumptions. It does not determine a material's microscopic pairing interaction or explain every spatially nonuniform state. Modern equations often use SI units and different notation from the original scan; a historical formula should not be copied into a modern calculation without checking those conventions. This milestone concerns a phenomenological advance in electrodynamics, not an experimental discovery of a new transition-temperature record. [R3](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

## L4 — 1950: Ginzburg–Landau theory

Ginzburg and Landau introduced a complex order parameter and a free-energy description of superconductivity in 1950. Ginzburg's later firsthand lecture explains the motivation to extend the London treatment, including spatial variation and interfaces. The resulting framework connects electromagnetic response to the amplitude and phase of an order parameter and provides a basis for studying boundaries and competing configurations near a transition. [R4](#ref-source-9ccf1f17448aae3d)

The history is not identical to today's textbook presentation. Ginzburg recounts that the effective charge was not correctly settled at twice the electron charge in the original work; the later microscopic interpretation clarified that point. Their early analysis also focused on what are now called type-I superconductors. Avoid projecting every subsequent vortex result or the complete BCS interpretation back into 1950. The checked source is the 2004 retrospective, with its original-paper citation, rather than a full direct audit of the 1950 article. [R4](#ref-source-9ccf1f17448aae3d)

## L5 — 1957: the BCS microscopic theory

Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer's 1957 theory constructed a coherent paired many-electron state and related its excitation spectrum to superconducting observables. It moved beyond identifying macroscopic signatures by providing a microscopic explanation within a specified interaction model. The energy gap and thermodynamic behavior arise together in that framework, rather than being independent empirical labels attached to a zero-resistance state. [R5](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

The achievement should not be turned into a claim that one elementary approximation describes every later material. The familiar isotropic weak-coupling results assume a particular pairing structure and energy-scale hierarchy. Strong coupling, multiple bands, unconventional symmetry and substantial fluctuations require further treatment. A historical timeline should distinguish the theory's established role from a material-specific mechanism assignment. Agreement with one BCS-like ratio is a consistency check, not proof that a newly observed superconductor has the same microscopic interaction. [R5](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## L6 — 1962: tunnelling supercurrents and field compensation

Josephson's 1962 paper predicted new tunnelling effects between superconductors. His 1973 lecture distinguishes the theoretical prediction from the later experiments that convincingly attributed observed supercurrents to tunnelling. Earlier zero-voltage currents could instead have involved metallic shorts, and unsuccessful measurements were part of the development. Phase-dependent response, magnetic interference and microwave-induced voltage steps provided more specific tests than a zero-voltage branch alone. [R6](#ref-source-ee44c3aab4e6fdee) [R7](#ref-source-2e9437c55bb758da)

Another development in 1962 was Jaccarino and Peter's proposal of ultra-high-field superconductivity through compensation of an external field by an internal exchange effect. This is a separate idea, not part of Josephson tunnelling. Its original bibliographic identity is checked here; the full original derivation is not. Later field-induced experiments and their limits are discussed in the linked exchange-compensation article. Keeping the two contributions distinct prevents a shared calendar year from becoming a misleading shared mechanism. [R8](#ref-source-849f7f4f675464de)

## L7 — 1973: Nb–Ge films above 22 K

Gavaler's 1973 report describes superconductivity in sputtered Nb–Ge films above 22 K. The checked original abstract reports 22.3 K. The often-quoted 23.2 K value is not the value reported in this specific discovery abstract. A later optimized result, if added, needs its own citation, sample description and date rather than being silently attached to the earlier report. [R9](#ref-source-82a0df3d764cd0bc)

Processing is central to the historical interpretation: the source describes high-pressure sputtering, which is a deposition condition, not evidence that the superconducting transition was measured under high external pressure. Film composition, phase formation and preparation affect the result. Neither the reported temperature nor the A15 label defines a universal transition for all Nb–Ge samples or a strict ceiling for the entire structural family. Full methods and the exact operational transition criterion remain unreviewed at this abstract-level scope. [R9](#ref-source-82a0df3d764cd0bc)

## L8 — 1979: CeCu2Si2 and heavy fermions

The 1979 CeCu2Si2 report established a superconducting state in a system with strong Pauli paramagnetism and an unusually large electronic response. Its original abstract gives a transition scale around 0.5 K. The historical importance lies in opening a strongly correlated setting for superconductivity, not in raising the maximum known transition temperature. Different measures of progress therefore belong in a scientific timeline. [R10](#ref-source-0ebda9b697c1f7fd)

This original observation should be separated from later debates over gap structure, magnetic coexistence and sample classification. Modern CeCu2Si2 experiments distinguish crystals and transitions that cannot be reduced to a universal 0.5 K constant. The presence of a heavy-electron normal state also does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction from the discovery abstract alone. The original full measurements have not been reconstructed in this review; the linked heavy-fermion article follows the subsequent evidence and its competing interpretations. [R10](#ref-source-0ebda9b697c1f7fd)

## L9 — 1986: the Ba–La–Cu–O discovery

Bednorz and Müller's 1986 paper deliberately used the title “Possible high Tc superconductivity” for its Ba–La–Cu–O result. The publisher's original abstract describes multiphase polycrystals and a current-dependent, percolative resistive onset in the 30 K range. That is the evidence actually checked here. This abstract does not establish a precise bulk magnetic transition at 35 K. [R11](#ref-source-ad4ee05105f93caf)

The milestone initiated a new materials direction, but the discovery report's sample and uncertainty deserve to remain visible. A connected superconducting path can strongly affect resistance without establishing that the whole sample occupies one superconducting phase. Later synthesis, phase identification and complementary measurements must retain their own citations. The original abstract and publication record were checked; the complete figures, apparatus and raw measurements remain outside this review scope. Historical significance does not remove the need to distinguish an initial report from later confirmation. [R11](#ref-source-ad4ee05105f93caf)

## L10 — 1987: Y–Ba–Cu–O above liquid-nitrogen temperature

Wu and colleagues reported a transition above liquid-nitrogen temperature in mixed-phase Y–Ba–Cu–O material. The selected final paper distinguishes a resistance deviation at 93 K, a sharp drop beginning near 92 K, zero resistance at 80 K and a magnetic onset near 91 K. These values describe different criteria in the reported experiment; the 93 K headline is not a 93 K zero-resistance result. [R12](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e)

The original nominal sample composition was not a phase-pure YBa2Cu3O7 crystal. A subsequent structural, transport and magnetic study identified the principal YBa2Cu3Ox phase. Combining those papers is useful only when their roles remain distinct. Likewise, a low-temperature diamagnetic signal compared with lead is not automatically an independently corrected volume fraction. This milestone records both the striking temperature advance and the continuing work needed to establish the responsible phase and quantitative superconducting properties. [R12](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e) [R13](#ref-source-82098193516b8d9a)

## L11 — 1993: mercury-based cuprates above 130 K

Schilling and colleagues' 1993 report describes superconductivity above 130 K in the Hg–Ba–Ca–Cu–O system, with magnetic and resistive evidence summarized near 133 K. The commonly cited 135 K value should not replace the approximately 133 K result in this specific original report. Oxygen content, phase composition and the experimental criterion matter when later samples yield somewhat different quoted temperatures. [R14](#ref-source-d95477ebe515f481)

Gao and colleagues' 1994 pressure study is a separate milestone in the development of this material family. Its abstract reports resistive superconductivity up to 164 K under quasihydrostatic pressure. That high-pressure result is neither an ambient-pressure value nor evidence that the state survives unloading. The exact pressure of the maximum and its onset-versus-zero criterion have not been re-extracted here. A plot that joins these numbers without marking conditions would confuse distinct experiments; the linked cuprate and pressure-quench pages preserve those boundaries. [R14](#ref-source-d95477ebe515f481) [R15](#ref-source-6d09a24a26a15997)

## L12 — 2001: MgB2 at 39 K

Nagamatsu and colleagues' 2001 MgB2 paper showed that a chemically simple binary compound could superconduct at a surprisingly high temperature for that class of material. In the selected final report, resistance begins to fall at 39 K and reaches its endpoint near 38 K; a separate low-field magnetization measurement supports the interpretation. The two criteria should not be merged into one exact temperature independent of the measurement. [R16](#ref-source-fade6558e7eafb2b)

The synthesis pressure quoted in the methods is a preparation condition, not the pressure at which the reported transition was measured. The discovery also precedes the detailed body of isotope, spectroscopy and anisotropic electron–phonon work that established MgB2 as a multigap benchmark. Those later results do not all belong to the original discovery paper. Its role in the timeline is the 2001 observation with the sample and probes actually described, while the linked material article develops the subsequent microscopic evidence. [R16](#ref-source-fade6558e7eafb2b)

## L13 — 2008: the iron-arsenide expansion

The 2008 fluorine-substituted LaOFeAs report brought a transition near 26 K to the iron-pnictide field. The publisher record distinguishes its February online publication from the later journal issue. The selected original abstract supports the composition range and reported temperature, but the detailed operational transition criterion remains unassigned at this review scope. Do not infer that criterion from the title alone. [R17](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7)

This was not the first superconducting iron-containing compound or even the first reported layered iron pnictide: the same research group's LaOFeP paper appeared in 2006. That earlier source is retained to avoid compressing the family history into an incorrect first-discovery claim. The 2008 advance instead marks the higher-temperature arsenide platform and the beginning of rapid diversification into related systems. Iron-based materials subsequently require separate structural, magnetic and pairing analyses; the presence of iron does not fix a universal gap symmetry. [R17](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7) [R18](#ref-source-2c26a22bac7d742e)

## L14 — 2015: sulfur hydride near 203 K

The 2015 sulfur-hydride report extended superconducting temperatures into a much higher range under extreme pressure. The selected author passages and published captions distinguish resistance measurements from the magnetic response, including a reported onset near 203 K at 155 GPa for the magnetic specimen. The pressure and measurement definition belong with the number; the result is not an ambient-pressure material property. [R19](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434)

The superconducting phase assignment also developed through further structural work. A sulfur-hydride starting composition is not by itself proof of the final high-pressure stoichiometry, and the later diffraction study must remain separately cited when discussing H3S. The selected scientific review did not independently reconstruct magnetization background subtraction or all raw transport data. This milestone records the reported evidence and the pressure-enabled material setting without treating the historical headline as a complete audit of every experimental inference. [R19](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434) [R20](#ref-source-e7837a18f3252cb9)

## L15 — 2019: lanthanum hydride and infinite-layer nickelates

Two distinct materials developments occurred in 2019. The lanthanum-hydride experiment reported a resistive transition around 250 K near 170 GPa. The selected final paper includes resistance, isotope comparison and field suppression, but no SQUID measurement. Applied magnetic fields and extrapolated upper-critical-field estimates are different quantities. This high-pressure result should not be plotted as an ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductor. [R21](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

In a different materials setting, Li and colleagues reported superconductivity in reduced, Sr-substituted infinite-layer nickelate films. A representative Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 sample has separately defined onset, midpoint and noise-floor zero values of 14.9, 13.6 and 9.1 K. The result must not be relabelled as superconductivity in undoped bulk NdNiO2. Epitaxy, reduction, capping and sample preparation are part of the observation. The common year links these discoveries chronologically, not through an established common mechanism. [R22](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

## L16 — 2018: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

Cao and colleagues' superconductivity report appeared in 2018, not 2022. The discovery year should remain separate from the dates of later studies. In the selected final paper, two devices with different nominal twist angles have different transition scales: approximately 0.5 K and 1.7 K under the stated half-normal-resistance criterion. A device label, carrier density and transport definition belong with each number. [R23](#ref-source-90c67b111a6e919c)

The paper's tentative BKT analysis supplies another temperature scale, while a 70 mK measurement floor is not a transition temperature. These distinctions prevent one figure from becoming several apparently interchangeable records. The broader advance is geometric control of electronic bands and interactions through a moiré structure; it does not establish that every magic-angle device has the same phase diagram or that a flat band alone guarantees superconductivity. The chronological guide places this discovery before the 2019 hydride and nickelate results. [R23](#ref-source-90c67b111a6e919c)

## L17 — 2023: bilayer nickelate signatures near 80 K

The 2023 La3Ni2O7 paper reported signatures near 80 K under pressure. For the selected run, the resistance onset occurs near 18.5 GPa, with nonzero residual resistance. A separate magnetic measurement is part of the broader paper, but its sample and pressure must not be silently attached to that particular resistance record. The wording “signatures” and the operational criterion are scientifically meaningful. [R24](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

The checked passages also distinguish applied fields from an upper-critical-field extrapolation and retain pressure calibration and measurement-current conditions. A later zero-resistance result, thin-film experiment or structurally modified nickelate would be a separate entry with its own evidence. The historical milestone therefore establishes the reported pressure-induced phenomenon and the questions it raised, rather than declaring an independently reproduced 80 K bulk transition for every bilayer nickelate. Full raw-data and replication review remains open. [R24](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## L18 — 2026: recovered cuprates, re-entrance and transport

Three recent papers illustrate different research directions; their dates and observables must remain separate. Deng and colleagues' pressure-quench article appeared online on 9 March 2026. Its highest retained ambient-pressure value, 151 K, is a resistive onset after a specific pressure-and-temperature preparation. A magnetic result on a different retrieved sample and cold-storage tests cannot be reassigned to that highest-onset specimen. [R25](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

The Eu-substituted infinite-layer nickelate paper and the iron-chalcogenide Planckian-scattering paper were published on 23 April 2026. The first concerns field-dependent re-entrance under specified conditions; the second analyzes normal-state transport with parallel conduction channels. A model-dependent scattering rate is not a new Tc record or proof of a universal pairing mechanism. These studies are recent research directions with scoped checks, not one combined discovery or a completed independent replication programme. [R26](#ref-source-3504ee9027165d0a) [R27](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Chronological guide

Follow the links to the evidence for each milestone. The graphene discovery appears in 2018, before the 2019 hydride and nickelate results. Temperatures in the detailed sections are conditional reported values, not a uniform record-ranking dataset.

| Period | Milestones |
| --- | --- |
| 1911–1935 | [Mercury](#l1), [Meissner–Ochsenfeld](#l2), [London electrodynamics](#l3) |
| 1950–1962 | [Ginzburg–Landau](#l4), [BCS](#l5), [Josephson and field compensation](#l6) |
| 1973–1987 | [Nb–Ge films](#l7), [heavy fermions](#l8), [Ba–La–Cu–O](#l9), [Y–Ba–Cu–O](#l10) |
| 1993–2015 | [Hg cuprates](#l11), [MgB2](#l12), [iron arsenides](#l13), [sulfur hydride](#l14) |
| 2018–2023 | [Twisted bilayer graphene](#l16), [hydrides and nickelates](#l15), [bilayer nickelates](#l17) |
| 2026 | [Pressure quench, re-entrance and transport](#l18) |

## Experimental criteria

A reported milestone is not a standardized material benchmark. Preserve the experimental criterion and distinguish the year of observation, first public report, journal publication and later author account. An accurate timeline can include a theory, a measurement or a material platform without assigning each one a transition-temperature point. Links to primary evidence make the interpretation inspectable. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f) [R7](#ref-source-2e9437c55bb758da) [R12](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e) [R22](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

## Limits and disputes

Some early sources remain checked only at abstract or bibliographic level; other entries reuse selected original-paper reviews from the linked core articles. Those limitations remain attached rather than being upgraded by appearing in a history handbook. Later recollections help explain reasoning but are not the original laboratory record. Complete scientific acceptance, full final-version comparisons, supplementary data and independent replication remain open where stated. [R4](#ref-source-9ccf1f17448aae3d) [R6](#ref-source-ee44c3aab4e6fdee) [R9](#ref-source-82a0df3d764cd0bc) [R18](#ref-source-2c26a22bac7d742e)

## Discovery implications

Progress has come from new materials, better preparation, more discriminating probes and theories that make testable predictions. A higher reported onset is only one kind of advance. The historical examples encourage a workflow that separates initial observations from phase identification, reproducibility and mechanism tests, preserving negative results and corrections instead of rewriting them out of the story. [R7](#ref-source-2e9437c55bb758da) [R12](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e) [R16](#ref-source-fade6558e7eafb2b) [R24](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

## Related topics

Continue with [experimental methods](/scwiki/experimental-methods), [theoretical tools](/scwiki/theoretical-tools), [applications](/scwiki/applications), [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), [iron-based materials](/scwiki/iron-based-superconductors), [nickelates](/scwiki/nickelates), [hydrides](/scwiki/hydride-superconductors), [pressure quenching](/scwiki/pressure-quenching), and [exchange compensation](/scwiki/jaccarino-peter-effect).

sections.title: Scope
sections.markdown:
## Scope

The history of superconductivity includes discoveries, theories, material families and changing standards of evidence. These eighteen milestones connect major developments to their dates, measurement conditions and original evidence. A later author's recollection, an original discovery report and a modern reanalysis answer different historical questions. The cited review scope tells the reader which was checked. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f) [R4](#ref-source-9ccf1f17448aae3d) [R7](#ref-source-2e9437c55bb758da)

sections.title: Mathematical assumptions
sections.markdown:
## Mathematical assumptions

There is no single mathematical curve that makes all reported transition temperatures directly comparable. A resistance onset, a midpoint, a noise-floor zero and a magnetic response can occur at different temperatures, even in one specimen. Pressure, composition, sample history and measurement field must remain attached to any point. The linked material articles preserve detailed records; this history does not create duplicate experimental Tc entries from narrative summaries. [R12](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e) [R21](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f) [R22](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

sections.title: L1 — 1911: mercury and the resistance transition
sections.markdown:
## L1 — 1911: mercury and the resistance transition

Onnes's 1911 mercury work opened the study of superconductivity. His 1913 Nobel lecture provides a firsthand account of the abrupt resistance decrease near 4.2 K and the limits of the electrical measurement. Resistance too small to resolve is an experimental statement; mathematical exactness is not read directly from an instrument. The lecture also discusses a current threshold above which a voltage appeared, anticipating the need to specify measuring current. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f)

The checked scan contains later notes, including a 1914 addendum. Those observations must not all be assigned to the original 1911 discovery. Nor should the initial resistance experiment be described as already establishing the later Meissner effect or a complete microscopic theory. The original 1911 communication itself remains outside the directly reviewed material; the author lecture is identified as the historical source used here. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f)

sections.title: L2 — 1933: the Meissner–Ochsenfeld effect
sections.markdown:
## L2 — 1933: the Meissner–Ochsenfeld effect

Meissner and Ochsenfeld's 1933 work added magnetic behavior to the definition of the superconducting state. The selected original reproduction describes field redistribution around tin and lead as the samples became superconducting. This changed the question from whether a conductor can sustain current without detectable resistance to which magnetic state it reaches. An ideal conductor's history-dependent trapped field does not by itself supply the same equilibrium magnetic condition. [R2](#ref-source-512705f3e64d88d7)

Geometry remains essential to reading the experiment. The original report also discusses retained field in a lead-tube cavity; a cavity is not the same region as the superconducting material. A simplified statement that every field everywhere becomes zero would erase this distinction. The historical paper's apparatus, uncertainty and complete translation have not been independently reconstructed here. The milestone records the new magnetic evidence while retaining the limits of the selected primary reproduction. [R2](#ref-source-512705f3e64d88d7)

sections.title: L3 — 1935: London electrodynamics
sections.markdown:
## L3 — 1935: London electrodynamics

The London brothers' 1935 paper supplied an electromagnetic description of superconductors that accommodates magnetic screening. The selected original pages distinguish the consequence of perfect conductivity from an additional condition selecting the superconducting magnetic state. An integration constant associated with the initial field is therefore not a trivial detail: dropping it without stating the physical postulate would conceal what the theory adds. [R3](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

The London description links current and electromagnetic fields under its stated local assumptions. It does not determine a material's microscopic pairing interaction or explain every spatially nonuniform state. Modern equations often use SI units and different notation from the original scan; a historical formula should not be copied into a modern calculation without checking those conventions. This milestone concerns a phenomenological advance in electrodynamics, not an experimental discovery of a new transition-temperature record. [R3](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

Nagamatsu and colleagues' 2001 MgB2 paper showed that a chemically simple binary compound could superconduct at a surprisingly high temperature for that class of material. In the selected final report, resistance begins to fall at 39 K and reaches its endpoint near 38 K; a separate low-field magnetization measurement supports the interpretation. The two criteria should not be merged into one exact temperature independent of the measurement. [R16](#ref-source-fade6558e7eafb2b)

The synthesis pressure quoted in the methods is a preparation condition, not the pressure at which the reported transition was measured. The discovery also precedes the detailed body of isotope, spectroscopy and anisotropic electron–phonon work that established MgB2 as a multigap benchmark. Those later results do not all belong to the original discovery paper. Its role in the timeline is the 2001 observation with the sample and probes actually described, while the linked material article develops the subsequent microscopic evidence. [R16](#ref-source-fade6558e7eafb2b)

sections.title: L13 — 2008: the iron-arsenide expansion
sections.markdown:
## L13 — 2008: the iron-arsenide expansion

The 2008 fluorine-substituted LaOFeAs report brought a transition near 26 K to the iron-pnictide field. The publisher record distinguishes its February online publication from the later journal issue. The selected original abstract supports the composition range and reported temperature, but the detailed operational transition criterion remains unassigned at this review scope. Do not infer that criterion from the title alone. [R17](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7)

This was not the first superconducting iron-containing compound or even the first reported layered iron pnictide: the same research group's LaOFeP paper appeared in 2006. That earlier source is retained to avoid compressing the family history into an incorrect first-discovery claim. The 2008 advance instead marks the higher-temperature arsenide platform and the beginning of rapid diversification into related systems. Iron-based materials subsequently require separate structural, magnetic and pairing analyses; the presence of iron does not fix a universal gap symmetry. [R17](#ref-source-62a72493865c59d7) [R18](#ref-source-2c26a22bac7d742e)

sections.title: L14 — 2015: sulfur hydride near 203 K
sections.markdown:
## L14 — 2015: sulfur hydride near 203 K

The 2015 sulfur-hydride report extended superconducting temperatures into a much higher range under extreme pressure. The selected author passages and published captions distinguish resistance measurements from the magnetic response, including a reported onset near 203 K at 155 GPa for the magnetic specimen. The pressure and measurement definition belong with the number; the result is not an ambient-pressure material property. [R19](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434)

The superconducting phase assignment also developed through further structural work. A sulfur-hydride starting composition is not by itself proof of the final high-pressure stoichiometry, and the later diffraction study must remain separately cited when discussing H3S. The selected scientific review did not independently reconstruct magnetization background subtraction or all raw transport data. This milestone records the reported evidence and the pressure-enabled material setting without treating the historical headline as a complete audit of every experimental inference. [R19](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434) [R20](#ref-source-e7837a18f3252cb9)

sections.title: L15 — 2019: lanthanum hydride and infinite-layer nickelates
sections.markdown:
## L15 — 2019: lanthanum hydride and infinite-layer nickelates

Two distinct materials developments occurred in 2019. The lanthanum-hydride experiment reported a resistive transition around 250 K near 170 GPa. The selected final paper includes resistance, isotope comparison and field suppression, but no SQUID measurement. Applied magnetic fields and extrapolated upper-critical-field estimates are different quantities. This high-pressure result should not be plotted as an ambient-pressure room-temperature superconductor. [R21](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

In a different materials setting, Li and colleagues reported superconductivity in reduced, Sr-substituted infinite-layer nickelate films. A representative Nd0.8Sr0.2NiO2 sample has separately defined onset, midpoint and noise-floor zero values of 14.9, 13.6 and 9.1 K. The result must not be relabelled as superconductivity in undoped bulk NdNiO2. Epitaxy, reduction, capping and sample preparation are part of the observation. The common year links these discoveries chronologically, not through an established common mechanism. [R22](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

sections.title: L16 — 2018: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene
sections.markdown:
## L16 — 2018: magic-angle twisted bilayer graphene

Cao and colleagues' superconductivity report appeared in 2018, not 2022. The discovery year should remain separate from the dates of later studies. In the selected final paper, two devices with different nominal twist angles have different transition scales: approximately 0.5 K and 1.7 K under the stated half-normal-resistance criterion. A device label, carrier density and transport definition belong with each number. [R23](#ref-source-90c67b111a6e919c)

The paper's tentative BKT analysis supplies another temperature scale, while a 70 mK measurement floor is not a transition temperature. These distinctions prevent one figure from becoming several apparently interchangeable records. The broader advance is geometric control of electronic bands and interactions through a moiré structure; it does not establish that every magic-angle device has the same phase diagram or that a flat band alone guarantees superconductivity. The chronological guide places this discovery before the 2019 hydride and nickelate results. [R23](#ref-source-90c67b111a6e919c)

sections.title: L17 — 2023: bilayer nickelate signatures near 80 K
sections.markdown:
## L17 — 2023: bilayer nickelate signatures near 80 K

The 2023 La3Ni2O7 paper reported signatures near 80 K under pressure. For the selected run, the resistance onset occurs near 18.5 GPa, with nonzero residual resistance. A separate magnetic measurement is part of the broader paper, but its sample and pressure must not be silently attached to that particular resistance record. The wording “signatures” and the operational criterion are scientifically meaningful. [R24](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

The checked passages also distinguish applied fields from an upper-critical-field extrapolation and retain pressure calibration and measurement-current conditions. A later zero-resistance result, thin-film experiment or structurally modified nickelate would be a separate entry with its own evidence. The historical milestone therefore establishes the reported pressure-induced phenomenon and the questions it raised, rather than declaring an independently reproduced 80 K bulk transition for every bilayer nickelate. Full raw-data and replication review remains open. [R24](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

sections.title: L18 — 2026: recovered cuprates, re-entrance and transport

## L18 — 2026: recovered cuprates, re-entrance and transport

These studies are recent research directions with scoped checks, not one combined discovery or a completed independent replication programme. ## Experimental criteria

A reported milestone is not a standardized material benchmark. Preserve the experimental criterion and distinguish the year of observation, first public report, journal publication and later author account. An accurate timeline can include a theory, a measurement or a material platform without assigning each one a transition-temperature point. Links to primary evidence make the interpretation inspectable. ## Limits and disputes

Some early sources remain checked only at abstract or bibliographic level; other entries reuse selected original-paper reviews from the linked core articles. Those limitations remain attached rather than being upgraded by appearing in a history handbook. Later recollections help explain reasoning but are not the original laboratory record. sections.title: Discovery implications
sections.markdown:
## Discovery implications

Progress has come from new materials, better preparation, more discriminating probes and theories that make testable predictions. A higher reported onset is only one kind of advance. The historical examples encourage a workflow that separates initial observations from phase identification, reproducibility and mechanism tests, preserving negative results and corrections instead of rewriting them out of the story. articles.markdown:
# A history of superconductivity: milestones and evidence

Eighteen milestones from mercury to recent research, with original-source links, corrected chronology and the conditions behind reported temperatures.

## Scope

The history of superconductivity includes discoveries, theories, material families and changing standards of evidence. These eighteen milestones connect major developments to their dates, measurement conditions and original evidence. A later author's recollection, an original discovery report and a modern reanalysis answer different historical questions. The cited review scope tells the reader which was checked. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f) [R4](#ref-source-9ccf1f17448aae3d) [R7](#ref-source-2e9437c55bb758da)

## Mathematical assumptions

There is no single mathematical curve that makes all reported transition temperatures directly comparable. A resistance onset, a midpoint, a noise-floor zero and a magnetic response can occur at different temperatures, even in one specimen. Pressure, composition, sample history and measurement field must remain attached to any point. The linked material articles preserve detailed records; this history does not create duplicate experimental Tc entries from narrative summaries. [R12](#ref-source-9350a30b2eabe27e) [R21](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f) [R22](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c)

## L1 — 1911: mercury and the resistance transition

Onnes's 1911 mercury work opened the study of superconductivity. His 1913 Nobel lecture provides a firsthand account of the abrupt resistance decrease near 4.2 K and the limits of the electrical measurement. Resistance too small to resolve is an experimental statement; mathematical exactness is not read directly from an instrument. The lecture also discusses a current threshold above which a voltage appeared, anticipating the need to specify measuring current. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f)

The checked scan contains later notes, including a 1914 addendum. Those observations must not all be assigned to the original 1911 discovery. Nor should the initial resistance experiment be described as already establishing the later Meissner effect or a complete microscopic theory. The original 1911 communication itself remains outside the directly reviewed material; the author lecture is identified as the historical source used here. [R1](#ref-source-d36e5a81b57e823f)

## L2 — 1933: the Meissner–Ochsenfeld effect

Meissner and Ochsenfeld's 1933 work added magnetic behavior to the definition of the superconducting state. The selected original reproduction describes field redistribution around tin and lead as the samples became superconducting. This changed the question from whether a conductor can sustain current without detectable resistance to which magnetic state it reaches. An ideal conductor's history-dependent trapped field does not by itself supply the same equilibrium magnetic condition. [R2](#ref-source-512705f3e64d88d7)

Geometry remains essential to reading the experiment. The original report also discusses retained field in a lead-tube cavity; a cavity is not the same region as the superconducting material. A simplified statement that every field everywhere becomes zero would erase this distinction. The historical paper's apparatus, uncertainty and complete translation have not been independently reconstructed here. The milestone records the new magnetic evidence while retaining the limits of the selected primary reproduction. [R2](#ref-source-512705f3e64d88d7)

## L3 — 1935: London electrodynamics

The London brothers' 1935 paper supplied an electromagnetic description of superconductors that accommodates magnetic screening. The selected original pages distinguish the consequence of perfect conductivity from an additional condition selecting the superconducting magnetic state. An integration constant associated with the initial field is therefore not a trivial detail: dropping it without stating the physical postulate would conceal what the theory adds. [R3](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

The London description links current and electromagnetic fields under its stated local assumptions. It does not determine a material's microscopic pairing interaction or explain every spatially nonuniform state. Modern equations often use SI units and different notation from the original scan; a historical formula should not be copied into a modern calculation without checking those conventions. This milestone concerns a phenomenological advance in electrodynamics, not an experimental discovery of a new transition-temperature record. [R3](#ref-source-0590b237a1d87de4)

## L4 — 1950: Ginzburg–Landau theory

Ginzburg and Landau introduced a complex order parameter and a free-energy description of superconductivity in 1950. Ginzburg's later firsthand lecture explains the motivation to extend the London treatment, including spatial variation and interfaces. The resulting framework connects electromagnetic response to the amplitude and phase of an order parameter and provides a basis for studying boundaries and competing configurations near a transition. [R4](#ref-source-9ccf1f17448aae3d)

The history is not identical to today's textbook presentation. Ginzburg recounts that the effective charge was not correctly settled at twice the electron charge in the original work; the later microscopic interpretation clarified that point. Their early analysis also focused on what are now called type-I superconductors. Avoid projecting every subsequent vortex result or the complete BCS interpretation back into 1950. The checked source is the 2004 retrospective, with its original-paper citation, rather than a full direct audit of the 1950 article. [R4](#ref-source-9ccf1f17448aae3d)

## L5 — 1957: the BCS microscopic theory

Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer's 1957 theory constructed a coherent paired many-electron state and related its excitation spectrum to superconducting observables. It moved beyond identifying macroscopic signatures by providing a microscopic explanation within a specified interaction model. The energy gap and thermodynamic behavior arise together in that framework, rather than being independent empirical labels attached to a zero-resistance state. [R5](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

The achievement should not be turned into a claim that one elementary approximation describes every later material. The familiar isotropic weak-coupling results assume a particular pairing structure and energy-scale hierarchy. Strong coupling, multiple bands, unconventional symmetry and substantial fluctuations require further treatment. A historical timeline should distinguish the theory's established role from a material-specific mechanism assignment. Agreement with one BCS-like ratio is a consistency check, not proof that a newly observed superconductor has the same microscopic interaction. [R5](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6)

## L6 — 1962: tunnelling supercurrents and field compensation

Josephson's 1962 paper predicted new tunnelling effects between superconductors. His 1973 lecture distinguishes the theoretical prediction from the later experiments that convincingly attributed observed supercurrents to tunnelling. Earlier zero-voltage currents could instead have involved metallic shorts, and unsuccessful measurements were part of the development. Phase-dependent response, magnetic interference and microwave-induced voltage steps provided more specific tests than a zero-voltage branch alone. [R6](#ref-source-ee44c3aab4e6fdee) [R7](#ref-source-2e9437c55bb758da)

Another development in 1962 was Jaccarino and Peter's proposal of ultra-high-field superconductivity through compensation of an external field by an internal exchange effect. This is a separate idea, not part of Josephson tunnelling. Its original bibliographic identity is checked here; the full original derivation is not. Later field-induced experiments and their limits are discussed in the linked exchange-compensation article. Keeping the two contributions distinct prevents a shared calendar year from becoming a misleading shared mechanism. [R8](#ref-source-849f7f4f675464de)

Gavaler's 1973 report describes superconductivity in sputtered Nb–Ge films above 22 K. The checked original abstract reports 22.3 K. The often-quoted 23.2 K value is not the value reported in this specific discovery abstract. A later optimized result, if added, needs its own citation, sample description and date rather than being silently attached to the earlier report. [R9](#ref-source-82a0df3d764cd0bc)

Processing is central to the historical interpretation: the source describes high-pressure sputtering, which is a deposition condition, not evidence that the superconducting transition was measured under high external pressure. Film composition, phase formation and preparation affect the result. Neither the reported temperature nor the A15 label defines a universal transition for all Nb–Ge samples or a strict ceiling for the entire structural family. Full methods and the exact operational transition criterion remain unreviewed at this abstract-level scope. [R9](#ref-source-82a0df3d764cd0bc)

The 1979 CeCu2Si2 report established a superconducting state in a system with strong Pauli paramagnetism and an unusually large electronic response. Its original abstract gives a transition scale around 0.5 K. Different measures of progress therefore belong in a scientific timeline. [R10](#ref-source-0ebda9b697c1f7fd)

This original observation should be separated from later debates over gap structure, magnetic coexistence and sample classification. Modern CeCu2Si2 experiments distinguish crystals and transitions that cannot be reduced to a universal 0.5 K constant. The presence of a heavy-electron normal state also does not uniquely identify a pairing interaction from the discovery abstract alone. The original full measurements have not been reconstructed in this review; the linked heavy-fermion article follows the subsequent evidence and its competing interpretations. [R10](#ref-source-0ebda9b697c1f7fd)

This abstract does not establish a precise bulk magnetic transition at 35 K. [R11](#ref-source-ad4ee05105f93caf)

The milestone initiated a new materials direction, but the discovery report's sample and uncertainty deserve to remain visible. A connected superconducting path can strongly affect resistance without establishing that the whole sample occupies one superconducting phase. Later synthesis, phase identification and complementary measurements must retain their own citations. The original abstract and publication record were checked; the complete figures, apparatus and raw measurements remain outside this review scope. Historical significance does not remove the need to distinguish an initial report from later confirmation. [R11](#ref-source-ad4ee05105f93caf)

Combining those papers is useful only when their roles remain distinct. Likewise, a low-temperature diamagnetic signal compared with lead is not automatically an independently corrected volume fraction. This milestone records both the striking temperature advance and the continuing work needed to establish the responsible phase and quantitative superconducting properties. A reported milestone is not a standardized material benchmark. Preserve the experimental criterion and distinguish the year of observation, first public report, journal publication and later author account. An accurate timeline can include a theory, a measurement or a material platform without assigning each one a transition-temperature point. Links to primary evidence make the interpretation inspectable. ## Discovery implications

Progress has come from new materials, better preparation, more discriminating probes and theories that make testable predictions. A higher reported onset is only one kind of advance. The historical examples encourage a workflow that separates initial observations from phase identification, reproducibility and mechanism tests, preserving negative results and corrections instead of rewriting them out of the story. ## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-l-claim-scope-1

The history of superconductivity includes discoveries, theories, material families and changing standards of evidence. These eighteen milestones preserve the approved topic identities while correcting dates and oversimplified temperature labels. A later author's recollection, an original discovery report and a modern reanalysis answer different historical questions. The cited review scope tells the reader which was checked.

### scwiki-l-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

There is no single mathematical curve that makes all reported transition temperatures directly comparable. A resistance onset, a midpoint, a noise-floor zero and a magnetic response can occur at different temperatures, even in one specimen. The linked material articles preserve detailed records; this history does not create duplicate experimental Tc entries from narrative summaries.

### scwiki-l-claim-l1-1

Onnes's 1911 mercury work opened the study of superconductivity. His 1913 Nobel lecture provides a firsthand account of the abrupt resistance decrease near 4.2 K and the limits of the electrical measurement. Resistance too small to resolve is an experimental statement; mathematical exactness is not read directly from an instrument. The lecture also discusses a current threshold above which a voltage appeared, anticipating the need to specify measuring current.

### scwiki-l-claim-l2-1

Meissner and Ochsenfeld's 1933 work added magnetic behavior to the definition of the superconducting state. The selected original reproduction describes field redistribution around tin and lead as the samples became superconducting. An ideal conductor's history-dependent trapped field does not by itself supply the same equilibrium magnetic condition.

### scwiki-l-claim-l4-1

Ginzburg and Landau introduced a complex order parameter and a free-energy description of superconductivity in 1950. Ginzburg's later firsthand lecture explains the motivation to extend the London treatment, including spatial variation and interfaces. The resulting framework connects electromagnetic response to the amplitude and phase of an order parameter and provides a basis for studying boundaries and competing configurations near a transition.

### scwiki-l-claim-l5-1

Bardeen, Cooper and Schrieffer's 1957 theory constructed a coherent paired many-electron state and related its excitation spectrum to superconducting observables. It moved beyond identifying macroscopic signatures by providing a microscopic explanation within a specified interaction model. The energy gap and thermodynamic behavior arise together in that framework, rather than being independent empirical labels attached to a zero-resistance state.

### scwiki-l-claim-l5-2

The achievement should not be turned into a claim that one elementary approximation describes every later material. The familiar isotropic weak-coupling results assume a particular pairing structure and energy-scale hierarchy. Strong coupling, multiple bands, unconventional symmetry and substantial fluctuations require further treatment. A historical timeline should distinguish the theory's established role from a material-specific mechanism assignment. Agreement with one BCS-like ratio is a consistency check, not proof that a newly observed superconductor has the same microscopic interaction.

### scwiki-l-claim-l6-1

Josephson's 1962 paper predicted new tunnelling effects between superconductors. His 1973 lecture distinguishes the theoretical prediction from the later experiments that convincingly attributed observed supercurrents to tunnelling. Earlier zero-voltage currents could instead have involved metallic shorts, and unsuccessful measurements were part of the development. Phase-dependent response, magnetic interference and microwave-induced voltage steps provided more specific tests than a zero-voltage branch alone.

## Scope

Reliable superconductivity research connects a question to a traceable dataset, a suitable method and an observation that could disprove the proposed answer. This handbook follows six parts of that process: finding data, predicting transitions, screening with calculations, checking claims, reviewing interpretations and reading papers closely. The aim is a reproducible chain of evidence, with the limits of each step visible. [R3](#ref-source-219632ed94597bf3) [R4](#ref-source-158dac7a4c8f8fb7) [R7](#ref-source-d4daeb7c4b4ef52a)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a binary classifier, TP and TN count correct positive and negative predictions; FP and FN count the corresponding errors. With a fixed positive-class definition and test set,

$$
\mathrm{accuracy}=\frac{TP+TN}{TP+TN+FP+FN},\qquad
\mathrm{precision}=\frac{TP}{TP+FP},\qquad
\mathrm{recall}=\frac{TP}{TP+FN}.
$$

These are dimensionless fractions, not transition temperatures or discovery rates. Precision is undefined if no positive prediction exists; recall is undefined if the test set contains no positives. An original teaching example with 34 positive and 966 negative labels gives 96.6% accuracy and zero positive recall when every label is predicted negative. Its precision is undefined. This arithmetic illustrates class imbalance; it is not a fitted superconductivity model. [R10](#ref-source-05f057efe73a6cda)

## M1 — Databases, structures and provenance

NIMS is the institution that publishes SuperCon; the two names should not be counted as independent confirmations. The MDR SuperCon datasheet provides a versioned release with a DOI and a stated reuse license. Record the release identifier and original literature reference when extracting a value. A database row is a route to evidence, not a substitute for checking how the reported transition was measured. The checked Ver.220808 release is an explicit snapshot, not a claim to be today's latest dataset. [R1](#ref-source-4a9ab24336f6fcc3)

ICSD serves a different purpose: inorganic crystal structures support structural identification and calculation inputs, but a structure match does not establish superconductivity. Its access and reuse terms differ from an openly licensed SuperCon release. Check the applicable license before redistributing records. In SCLib, use the [data guide](/docs/data) and [reading guide](/scwiki/using-sclib) to follow retrieved results back to their publications. Preserve the query, returned identifier and retrieval date so another researcher can repeat the search. [R1](#ref-source-4a9ab24336f6fcc3) [R2](#ref-source-7b0fd1ede1525615)

Keep composition, phase, sample treatment, pressure, magnetic field and transition criterion together. Separate records can share a formula while describing different experiments. Conversely, copies of the same measurement across databases are not independent evidence. For model evaluation, related compositions may need to share a train/test group even though their experimental records remain separate; this prevents data organization from silently becoming a claim of independent validation. [R3](#ref-source-219632ed94597bf3) [R4](#ref-source-158dac7a4c8f8fb7)

## M2 — Machine learning for transition temperatures

Composition descriptors and neural representations can help prioritize experiments, but the target and validation design determine what a score means. Stanev and colleagues used random forests for classification and regression; their methods explicitly discuss inconsistent records and missing pressure information. Their proposed materials remain candidates. Predicting a threshold class is a different task from predicting a numerical Tc, and neither guarantees successful synthesis. [R3](#ref-source-219632ed94597bf3)

Pogue and colleagues tested a neural-network approach with both uniform and leave-one-cluster-out validation. The latter exposed much poorer generalization. Their experimental loop combined model suggestions with expert filtering and new measurements. The reported counts are five successes among 190 suggestions and five among 65 after filtering. The printed second percentage is 7.5%; arithmetic from its stated count gives approximately 7.69%. These overlapping selections are not independent randomized trial arms, and the result should not be attributed to the model alone. [R4](#ref-source-158dac7a4c8f8fb7)

In the recommended evaluation workflow, declare the candidate space, grouping rule, held-out data, selection threshold and error metric before inspecting the test results. Report unsuccessful synthesis separately from a successfully prepared sample with no transition in the measured range. Compare against a simple baseline, and retain uncertainty and known family limits when ranking new candidates. The majority-class counterexample above shows why accuracy alone can hide complete failure to identify the desired class. [R10](#ref-source-05f057efe73a6cda)

## M3 — High-throughput first-principles screening

A phonon-mediated screening workflow first specifies composition, crystal structure and pressure, then checks electronic structure, phonons and electron–phonon coupling under stated approximations. A calculated Eliashberg spectral function can inform an estimated transition temperature within that model. It is not a universal treatment of every unconventional pairing mechanism, nor a measurement of a synthesized material. [R5](#ref-source-f080f572de65a123)

Gibson and colleagues report 818 retained calculated spectra after screening and numerical quality checks. Their methods specify commensurate electronic and phonon meshes, smearing, pseudopotentials and numerical cutoffs. They also discuss imaginary modes caused by numerical issues or a mismatch between ideal stoichiometry and experimental composition. Thus, a calculation that converges is not automatically physically valid, while an imaginary mode requires diagnosis before drawing a materials conclusion. Their high-pressure extrapolation remains unvalidated. [R5](#ref-source-f080f572de65a123)

For a new candidate, save the input structure, code and pseudopotential versions, convergence evidence and failed calculations as well as successful outputs. Recheck finalists with tighter settings and the relevant stability assumptions. Report a predicted Tc with its model parameters and pressure rather than adding it to a table of experimental transitions. These workflow recommendations extend the documented calculation controls; they do not certify a new calculation or reproduce the published training run. [R5](#ref-source-f080f572de65a123)

## M4 — Preventing unsupported claims

A DOI helps identify a research object. It does not prove that the linked paper contains the proposed claim, that the claim concerns the right material, or that later work confirmed it. Check the title and authors, then locate the relevant passage, equation, figure or dataset. Crossmark can expose registered corrections and retractions; the service itself states that its presence is not a guarantee. Missing update metadata should not be treated as a certificate of validity. [R6](#ref-source-dedff231d5c3d3cd)

For each factual statement, retain the source version, location, sample identity, observable, conditions and review scope. Distinguish a publisher abstract from selected full text and a complete supplementary-data review. If a source has no DOI, preserve its official URL, title, version or date and, where appropriate, a local file checksum; inventing a DOI would weaken traceability. Versioned data and institutional documentation illustrate why the identifier must fit the source type. [R1](#ref-source-4a9ab24336f6fcc3) [R6](#ref-source-dedff231d5c3d3cd)

Resolve contradictions at the level of the underlying evidence. For example, onset and zero resistance should not be averaged into one transition, and a calculated field limit must not be relabelled as the highest applied field. Mark an unresolved difference explicitly, revise downstream summaries when evidence changes, and keep a correction history. This is an editorial verification workflow, not a guarantee that every indexed claim has already passed it. [R6](#ref-source-dedff231d5c3d3cd) [R7](#ref-source-d4daeb7c4b4ef52a)

## M5 — Peer review and assisted critique

Scientific criticism should test a specific inference. Ask which alternative explanation fits the same measurement, whether a numerical result changes under a reasonable control, and whether the cited source actually supports the wording. A useful review records the disputed claim, supporting evidence and a concrete way to resolve it. COPE guidance emphasizes relevant expertise, declared conflicts, clear scope and constructive feedback rather than personal accusations. [R7](#ref-source-d4daeb7c4b4ef52a)

Model-generated critiques can suggest missing checks, but agreement among several models is not independent peer review or experimental replication. They may repeat the same source error or overlook the same missing condition. Treat each objection as a hypothesis to inspect against primary evidence, and document who performed the substantive verification. A journal's peer-review decision and a wiki's editorial check are distinct events and should be labelled separately. [R7](#ref-source-d4daeb7c4b4ef52a) [R8](#ref-source-e45bc5804b6aaa96)

Follow the actual publisher's confidentiality and AI-use policy when reviewing a submitted manuscript. Nature Portfolio's checked policy retains human scholarly accountability and distinguishes assistance from delegating evaluative judgment. These publisher-specific rules do not establish a universal policy for every venue. For public scientific discussion, preserve the same practical discipline: make the critique inspectable, state its limitations and change the conclusion when a counterexample survives checking. [R8](#ref-source-e45bc5804b6aaa96)

## M6 — Close reading and PDF extraction

Begin with the question the paper claims to answer, its publication version and any linked correction. Read the methods needed to interpret the central observable before summarizing the headline. Build a small evidence record containing the sample label, control conditions, definition of each reported quantity, figure location and remaining uncertainty. Compare the conclusion with the actual result rather than assuming that a familiar title supplies the necessary details. COPE's review guidance also distinguishes reading the manuscript and ancillary material from a specifically commissioned raw-data audit. [R7](#ref-source-d4daeb7c4b4ef52a)

OpenDataLoader PDF is one tool for converting a paper into structured text with reading order and element coordinates. Its documentation describes extraction capabilities; that description does not validate any particular extracted equation or table. Inspect the original page when columns interleave, symbols disappear, subscripts move or a legend changes the interpretation. Keep the original file and extraction version, and link a quoted or summarized finding to its page or bounding box. A parser output is a navigation aid, not the final authority on the paper. [R9](#ref-source-7d4fe3e5598a78a4)

Record unavailable supplements and unresolved version differences as specific missing evidence. A practical reading note separates the author's conclusion, the observation supporting it and the reader's remaining objection. Keep the public summary within the material actually reviewed; if a figure has not been inspected, do not describe its contents from a citation title alone. [R7](#ref-source-d4daeb7c4b4ef52a)

## Experimental criteria

A null observation is bounded by the prepared sample, measurement range and sensitivity. A failed synthesis is not the same result as no superconducting transition in a well-characterized specimen. Complementary transport, magnetic and thermodynamic probes address different possibilities; retain their separate conditions and uncertainty. These distinctions matter both when curating training labels and when deciding whether a model suggestion became an experimental discovery. [R3](#ref-source-219632ed94597bf3) [R4](#ref-source-158dac7a4c8f8fb7)

## Limits and disputes

Selected original methods, figures and official documentation were checked for this handbook. The independent arithmetic examples test definitions and denominators only. Complete scientific acceptance remains open: the published machine-learning models, full supplemental datasets, first-principles convergence and laboratory results were not independently reproduced. Policies and software documentation can change, so their checked date and source must remain visible. [R3](#ref-source-219632ed94597bf3) [R5](#ref-source-f080f572de65a123) [R8](#ref-source-e45bc5804b6aaa96) [R9](#ref-source-7d4fe3e5598a78a4)

## Discovery implications

A productive research loop records both useful predictions and informative failures, then updates the next experiment without erasing provenance. Separate the question “does the method rank this test set well?” from “does it identify a new, reproducible superconducting phase?” The answer to the second question requires evidence about the material itself. [R3](#ref-source-219632ed94597bf3) [R4](#ref-source-158dac7a4c8f8fb7)

## Related topics

Continue with [experimental methods](/scwiki/experimental-methods), [theoretical tools](/scwiki/theoretical-tools), [historical milestones](/scwiki/history), [material search](/materials), and [SCWiki source and interface guidance](/scwiki/using-sclib).

claims.statement: Room-temperature superconductivity at ambient pressure remains an open materials question in the evidence reviewed here. The cited theoretical models do not establish a universal prohibition at 300 K, but they also do not supply an experimentally verified ambient-pressure material at that temperature. Mathematical permission, a candidate calculation and a reproducible specimen are different levels of evidence. A negative experiment or a retracted claim does not prove that every possible material must fail.

claims.statement: A hypothetical BCS transition at 300 K would therefore correspond to a zero-temperature gap of about 45.60 meV. This is a conditional conversion: observing a gap of that size does not determine its origin, phase coherence or transition temperature. Strong coupling, anisotropy and competing orders can invalidate the weak-coupling ratio. Independent quadrature of the finite-cutoff BCS equations approaches the stated limiting ratio; it does not identify a viable compound.

claims.statement: For a strictly two-dimensional system with a BKT transition, define phase stiffness by $F=(D_s/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2$. The renormalized stiffness just below the transition satisfies $D_s(T_c^-)=2k_BT_c/\pi$. At 300 K this would require about 16.46 meV in that convention. A zero-temperature mean-field stiffness is not automatically this finite-temperature response. The [flat-band bounds question](/scwiki/open-questions/n10) explains why model-specific upper bounds are necessary constraints rather than sufficient evidence of superconductivity. The BKT relation is not a universal three-dimensional temperature limit.

articles.body:
## Scope

Room-temperature superconductivity at ambient pressure remains an open materials question in the evidence reviewed here. The cited theoretical models do not establish a universal prohibition at 300 K, but they also do not supply an experimentally verified ambient-pressure material at that temperature. Mathematical permission, a candidate calculation and a reproducible specimen are different levels of evidence. A negative experiment or a retracted claim does not prove that every possible material must fail. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R2](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66) [R7](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c) [R10](#ref-source-151c87f0eda0236f)

For a precise target, this page uses 300 K, approximately 27 °C, and near-atmospheric operating pressure. This is an explicit convention rather than a universal definition of room temperature. Preparation at high pressure and measurement after decompression must be reported separately. A recovered specimen may operate at ambient pressure while remaining metastable, cold-stored or difficult to manufacture; those are different practical questions. [R3](#ref-source-ba29a1eb0f9df263) [R6](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

## Mathematical assumptions

A temperature target first sets a thermal energy, not a pairing mechanism. At 300 K,

$$
k_BT=25.852\ {\rm meV}.
$$

In the isotropic weak-coupling BCS limit, the zero-temperature gap obeys

$$
\frac{\Delta(0)}{k_BT_c}=\frac{\pi}{e^\gamma}\simeq1.764.
$$

A hypothetical BCS transition at 300 K would therefore correspond to a zero-temperature gap of about 45.60 meV. This is a conditional conversion: observing a gap of that size does not determine its origin, phase coherence or transition temperature. Strong coupling, anisotropy and competing orders can invalidate the weak-coupling ratio. Independent quadrature of the finite-cutoff BCS equations approaches the stated limiting ratio; it does not identify a viable compound. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R2](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66)

For a strictly two-dimensional system with a BKT transition, define phase stiffness by $F=(D_s/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2$. The renormalized stiffness just below the transition satisfies $D_s(T_c^-)=2k_BT_c/\pi$. At 300 K this would require about 16.46 meV in that convention. A zero-temperature mean-field stiffness is not automatically this finite-temperature response. The [flat-band bounds question](/scwiki/open-questions/n10) explains why model-specific upper bounds are necessary constraints rather than sufficient evidence of superconductivity. The BKT relation is not a universal three-dimensional temperature limit. [R7](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

## Pairing, coherence and stability

For phonon-mediated candidates, raising a characteristic frequency or electron–phonon coupling cannot be assessed in isolation. The Allen–Dynes analysis depends on coupling, screened Coulomb repulsion and spectral moments; it does not justify an arbitrary extrapolation of one fitted parameter. Ashcroft's hydrogen-dominant-alloy proposal motivates chemical precompression, but its proposal is not a demonstration of ambient-pressure superconductivity. The existence, stability and synthesis of the required structure remain separate problems. [R2](#ref-source-0620df96ebbf2a66) [R3](#ref-source-ba29a1eb0f9df263)

A useful candidate must sustain pair formation and a coherent current response in the same accessible state. In two dimensions, phase fluctuations can constrain a transition even when pairing is strong. For a metastable recovered state, the pressure–temperature–time path and the lifetime at the intended operating temperature also matter. Neither a large calculated pairing scale nor a specimen recovered briefly at ambient pressure establishes all of these conditions. [R6](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb) [R7](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

## What experiments establish

High-pressure hydrides show why temperature and pressure must remain paired. The 2015 sulfur-hydride work reports a magnetic onset of 203(1) K at 155 GPa in the checked author figure; its transport comparison uses a different pressure. Drozdov and colleagues' final 2019 lanthanum-hydride paper reports a resistive onset near 250–252 K around 170 GPa, zero resistance and field/isotope observations, while explicitly noting the sample was below their available SQUID sensitivity. These are substantial high-pressure results, not ambient-pressure demonstrations or interchangeable magnetic criteria. The [hydrides article](/scwiki/hydride-superconductors) preserves the measurement-specific qualifications. [R4](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434) [R5](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f)

Deng and colleagues' 2026 Hg-1223 report separates preparation from observation: S4 was quenched from 18.9 GPa at 4.2 K, then showed derivative-defined resistive onsets of 151 K on warming and 150 K on cooling at ambient pressure. Those are not 300 K transitions or a 151 K zero-resistance threshold. The retrieved-sample magnetic estimate belongs to S2, while cold-storage tests used S3; neither can be silently assigned to the highest-onset S4 specimen. An unreproduced anomaly extending to 172 K remains unassigned. [R6](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

These examples establish different experimental constraints and motivate follow-up; this selection is not an exhaustive world-record survey. The 2026 final main text and selected author figures were checked, but the final supplementary file and raw data remain outside the completed review. Independent laboratory replication of that pressure-quench result has not been verified here; this does not establish that no replication exists. [R6](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

## Experimental criteria

A persuasive room-temperature claim needs mutually consistent evidence tied to identified samples: composition and structure, calibrated temperature and pressure, resistance with a stated noise floor and contact geometry, field/current dependence, and an appropriately calibrated magnetic or thermodynamic response. Their evidential weight depends on geometry and scale; a thin film cannot simply be judged by an uncorrected bulk shielding fraction. Preserve unsuccessful preparations and differences among specimens instead of combining each specimen's strongest result into an imaginary single sample. This is a synthesis of the measurement limitations in the cited primary studies. [R4](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434) [R5](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f) [R6](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

Independent replication should reproduce the synthesis and relevant observations, with raw traces, calibration, backgrounds and transition criteria available for examination. An onset, midpoint, instrumental zero and magnetic onset answer different questions. Near-atmospheric operation should also survive the specified temperature cycle and useful measurement duration; a claim of practical applicability requires additional current, field, mechanical and manufacturing evidence beyond this scientific existence question. [R4](#ref-source-8b901b9c6008c434) [R5](#ref-source-1e6e868a12cdd34f) [R6](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb)

## Limits and disputes

The carbonaceous-sulfur-hydride and nitrogen-doped lutetium-hydride reports were retracted in 2022 and 2023, respectively. Their claimed transition temperatures cannot be treated as established benchmarks. In particular, a near-ambient label must not replace the numerical pressure: 10 kbar equals 1 GPa, about ten thousand times atmospheric pressure. Publication status, sample identity and the actual operating conditions must accompany any historical mention. [R8](#ref-source-754d75026e52d9ac) [R9](#ref-source-98bc73a5e1c86c78)

The independent LuH₂±xNᵧ study found no superconductivity above 2 K in its tested samples across 0.4–40.1 GPa. That negative result constrains the tested preparation and composition, not every possible member of a chemical system. Likewise, the absence of a demonstrated 300 K material in the sources reviewed here is not a mathematical impossibility proof. It is a reason to demand better, reproducible evidence for a new claim. [R10](#ref-source-151c87f0eda0236f)

## Discovery implications

The productive question is which concrete composition, structure and preparation route could supply pairing, phase coherence and sufficient stability under the same stated conditions. Predictions should identify their approximation, uncertainty and falsifying observations; experiments should test the same conditions and distinguish reproduction within one laboratory from independent confirmation. This page offers a framework for evaluating that question, not a prediction that a room-temperature material will or will not be discovered. [R1](#ref-source-ba10e800a1246bf6) [R3](#ref-source-ba29a1eb0f9df263) [R6](#ref-source-14d1e9e0097f7ffb) [R7](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

## Related topics

Continue with [BCS theory](/scwiki/bcs-weak-coupling), [hydrides](/scwiki/hydride-superconductors), [experimental methods](/scwiki/experimental-methods), [research methods](/scwiki/research-methodology), and [flat-band temperature bounds](/scwiki/open-questions/n10).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-n1-claim-scope-1

Room-temperature superconductivity at ambient pressure remains an open materials question in the evidence reviewed here. The cited theoretical models do not establish a universal prohibition at 300 K, but they also do not supply an experimentally verified ambient-pressure material at that temperature. Mathematical permission, a candidate calculation and a reproducible specimen are different levels of evidence. A negative experiment or a retracted claim does not prove that every possible material must fail.

### scwiki-n1-claim-mathematical-assumptions-5

A hypothetical BCS transition at 300 K would therefore correspond to a zero-temperature gap of about 45.60 meV. This is a conditional conversion: observing a gap of that size does not determine its origin, phase coherence or transition temperature. Strong coupling, anisotropy and competing orders can invalidate the weak-coupling ratio. Independent quadrature of the finite-cutoff BCS equations approaches the stated limiting ratio; it does not identify a viable compound.
