### scwiki-n1-claim-mathematical-assumptions-6

For a strictly two-dimensional system with a BKT transition, define phase stiffness by $F=(D_s/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2$. The renormalized stiffness just below the transition satisfies $D_s(T_c^-)=2k_BT_c/\pi$. At 300 K this would require about 16.46 meV in that convention. A zero-temperature mean-field stiffness is not automatically this finite-temperature response. The [flat-band bounds question](/scwiki/open-questions/n10) explains why model-specific upper bounds are necessary constraints rather than sufficient evidence of superconductivity. The BKT relation is not a universal three-dimensional temperature limit.

### scwiki-n1-claim-experimental-criteria-1

A persuasive room-temperature claim needs mutually consistent evidence tied to identified samples: composition and structure, calibrated temperature and pressure, resistance with a stated noise floor and contact geometry, field/current dependence, and an appropriately calibrated magnetic or thermodynamic response. Their evidential weight depends on geometry and scale; a thin film cannot simply be judged by an uncorrected bulk shielding fraction. Preserve unsuccessful preparations and differences among specimens instead of combining each specimen's strongest result into an imaginary single sample. This is a synthesis of the measurement limitations in the cited primary studies.

Independent replication should reproduce the synthesis and relevant observations, with raw traces, calibration, backgrounds and transition criteria available for examination. ### scwiki-n1-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

The carbonaceous-sulfur-hydride and nitrogen-doped lutetium-hydride reports were retracted in 2022 and 2023, respectively. Their claimed transition temperatures cannot be treated as established benchmarks. In particular, a near-ambient label must not replace the numerical pressure: 10 kbar equals 1 GPa, about ten thousand times atmospheric pressure. Publication status, sample identity and the actual operating conditions must accompany any historical mention.

### scwiki-n1-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

The independent LuH₂±xNᵧ study found no superconductivity above 2 K in its tested samples across 0.4–40.1 GPa. That negative result constrains the tested preparation and composition, not every possible member of a chemical system. Likewise, the absence of a demonstrated 300 K material in the sources reviewed here is not a mathematical impossibility proof. It is a reason to demand better, reproducible evidence for a new claim.

### scwiki-n1-claim-discovery-implications-1

The productive question is which concrete composition, structure and preparation route could supply pairing, phase coherence and sufficient stability under the same stated conditions. Predictions should identify their approximation, uncertainty and falsifying observations; experiments should test the same conditions and distinguish reproduction within one laboratory from independent confirmation. This page offers a framework for evaluating that question, not a prediction that a room-temperature material will or will not be discovered.

articles.body:
## Scope

There is no single numerical temperature ceiling supplied by the phrase “flat band.” A meaningful limit specifies the Hamiltonian, density, dimensionality, interaction and current response. A bound is also different from a predicted transition: satisfying an upper bound does not establish that superconductivity occurs. This question concerns constraints on phase coherence and their relation to pair formation. [R1](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c) [R2](#ref-source-0f28a13259b6faed)

A narrow dispersion can enhance pairing while suppressing ordinary band transport. In a multiorbital system, however, the wavefunctions and interband matrix elements can support a geometric contribution to superfluid weight. Flattening the eigenvalues alone does not determine that contribution. The relevant question is whether a particular interacting system can develop a robust total phase stiffness, with the required electromagnetic and thermodynamic limits. [R3](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R8](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

## Mathematical assumptions

Define the two-dimensional phase stiffness $D_s$ by $F=(D_s/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2$. Hazra and colleagues bound it by the optical spectral weight, $D_s(T)\leq\widetilde D(T)$. With a BKT transition, $k_BT_c\leq\pi\widetilde D(T_c)/2$. Replacing the right-hand side by its zero-temperature value requires an additional monotonic-stiffness assumption. Their derivation couples the vector potential to the kinetic Hamiltonian; its interaction assumptions must accompany applications. [R1](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

For the specified two-spin parabolic band, $E_F=\pi\hbar^2n/m$ and $\widetilde D=\hbar^2n/(4m)$ give $k_BT_c\leq E_F/8$. This is a strictly two-dimensional BKT result, not a generic multiband or three-dimensional formula. In an anisotropic sheet the corresponding bound uses $\sqrt{\widetilde D_x\widetilde D_y}$. Independent density-convention and coordinate-Jacobian checks reproduce these relations; they do not determine a material's input stiffness. [R1](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

The BKT jump concerns the renormalized total response at the transition. It does not isolate a geometric share or convert a pairing gap directly into phase stiffness. A mean-field amplitude can remain nonzero after phase coherence has been lost. The [BKT article](/scwiki/bkt-transition) discusses current-window, finite-size and resistance-fit ambiguities that also matter when testing a proposed bound experimentally. [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Isolated-band constraints

Verma and colleagues examine on-site attraction in a controlled hierarchy $w\ll|U|\ll E_0$, with bandwidth $w$ and isolation gap $E_0$. Projecting to localized Wannier states produces pair hopping and an interaction-dependent current operator. For their trivial-band construction, $\widetilde D_{\rm low}\leq\widetilde n|U|\Omega/2$, where $\widetilde n=\min(n,2-n)$ and $\Omega$ is the Wannier spread in the stated normalization. The Lieb-lattice symmetry sharpens the coefficient; it is not a universal constant for every lattice. [R2](#ref-source-0f28a13259b6faed)

Their zero-temperature lower bound concerns optical spectral weight and requires the stated long-range-order and correlation assumptions. It is not a general lower bound on finite-temperature superconductivity. Topological bands require care with the Wannier basis: relaxing the Kramers-pair constraint permits localized functions and a generalized overlap bound. Extrapolating the linear interaction trend beyond the isolated-band hierarchy is unjustified; interband physics becomes important. [R2](#ref-source-0f28a13259b6faed)

## Pair formation is not pair mobility

A simple independent check makes the distinction concrete. An attractive Hubbard dimer was assembled directly in its six-dimensional two-electron Fock space. Sixteen spectra agree with the analytic ground-state energy $E_0=(-|U|-\sqrt{|U|^2+16t^2})/2$. At zero hopping the local pairs have no intersite splitting. In the strong-attraction limit, the low pair-sector splitting approaches $4t^2/|U|$, corresponding to pair hopping $2t^2/|U|$. Stronger local binding can therefore accompany slower pair motion. The dimer has no thermodynamic transition and supplies no predicted Tc. [R1](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c) [R2](#ref-source-0f28a13259b6faed)

Flat-band geometry can change this mobility argument because overlapping Wannier orbitals generate interaction-mediated pair motion. That is a model-specific route, not permission to discard self-consistency. Peotta and Törmä's geometric response assumes a defined isolated-band and pairing regime. The Chern-trivial Lieb example also demonstrates why nonzero Chern number is not necessary for every geometric contribution. Its existence does not establish superconductivity in an arbitrary flat-band material. [R3](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R7](#ref-source-b43340ce5c356e49)

## Experimental criteria

Measure a total sheet response with units, frequency, device geometry and fitting uncertainties. Tanaka and colleagues infer stiffness from microwave kinetic inductance using a circuit that includes a parallel edge contribution. Their active-region aspect ratio is an assumption in converting the measured inductance to sheet response. A comparison with a conventional estimate may support a geometric interpretation, but it does not directly measure an independently separable geometric component. [R5](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

The selected Tanaka author manuscript distinguishes refrigerator base temperature, wired-device temperature and a half-normal-resistance transition. These are separate observables. A finite-frequency stiffness should be connected to the low-frequency, long-wavelength response before applying an equilibrium BKT criterion. Experimental comparison also needs a stated pairing scale, a temperature-dependent stiffness and evidence that sample inhomogeneity or finite size does not dominate the inferred transition. [R5](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056) [R6](#ref-source-8f81510a80c35e3a)

## Limits and disputes

Multiband bounds depend on the actual band structure and occupation assumptions; an approximate estimate is not a universal material ceiling. Hazra's three-dimensional discussion does not establish a general linear stiffness bound there. A successful two-dimensional derivation cannot simply be carried into three dimensions with the same prefactor. [R1](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

A calculated mean-field stiffness may itself be overstated when internal pairing fields are held fixed during a phase twist. Huhtinen and colleagues show a relaxation correction under their time-reversal and equilibrium assumptions. In the isolated uniform-pairing setting, the relevant integrated metric is minimized over orbital positions. A frozen-field geometric answer can therefore differ qualitatively from the relaxed response. This correction must be considered before interpreting a mean-field value as a usable bound on an experimental transition. [R4](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81)

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The selected original passages, figures and independent algebra are documented, while full projection-error control, interacting response calculations, final-author comparisons and raw experimental data have not all been reviewed. No model temperature in this page is entered as an experimental material transition. The open problem is to obtain useful, controlled limits for realistic multiband and correlated systems, rather than to maximize one isolated formula. [R1](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c) [R2](#ref-source-0f28a13259b6faed) [R4](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81) [R5](#ref-source-be7282623ca96056)

## Discovery implications

Specify the density, isolation gap, interaction scale, orbital structure and measurement convention before comparing designs. Check whether a change enhances pairing, pair mobility or both, and whether it changes the assumptions behind the calculation. Report the full relaxed response and its uncertainty alongside any decomposition. A useful prediction should identify the observation that would falsify it; a large density of states or geometric metric alone does not meet that standard. [R3](#ref-source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f) [R4](#ref-source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81) [R8](#ref-source-fa7a165c8c344a63)

## Related topics

Continue with [flat-band pairing](/scwiki/flat-band-pairing), [flat-band superconductivity](/scwiki/flat-band-superconductivity), [geometric superfluid weight](/scwiki/geometric-superfluid-weight), [quantum metric](/scwiki/quantum-metric), and [BKT transitions](/scwiki/bkt-transition).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-n10-claim-scope-1

There is no single numerical temperature ceiling supplied by the phrase “flat band.” A meaningful limit specifies the Hamiltonian, density, dimensionality, interaction and current response. A bound is also different from a predicted transition: satisfying an upper bound does not establish that superconductivity occurs. This question concerns constraints on phase coherence and their relation to pair formation.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-a57ef549f45fe74c, source-0f28a13259b6faed.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-scope-2

A narrow dispersion can enhance pairing while suppressing ordinary band transport. In a multiorbital system, however, the wavefunctions and interband matrix elements can support a geometric contribution to superfluid weight. Flattening the eigenvalues alone does not determine that contribution. The relevant question is whether a particular interacting system can develop a robust total phase stiffness, with the required electromagnetic and thermodynamic limits.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f, source-fa7a165c8c344a63.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-mathematical-assumptions-1

Define the two-dimensional phase stiffness $D_s$ by $F=(D_s/2)\int d^2r\,|\nabla\theta|^2$. Hazra and colleagues bound it by the optical spectral weight, $D_s(T)\leq\widetilde D(T)$. With a BKT transition, $k_BT_c\leq\pi\widetilde D(T_c)/2$. Replacing the right-hand side by its zero-temperature value requires an additional monotonic-stiffness assumption. Their derivation couples the vector potential to the kinetic Hamiltonian; its interaction assumptions must accompany applications.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-a57ef549f45fe74c.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-mathematical-assumptions-2

For the specified two-spin parabolic band, $E_F=\pi\hbar^2n/m$ and $\widetilde D=\hbar^2n/(4m)$ give $k_BT_c\leq E_F/8$. This is a strictly two-dimensional BKT result, not a generic multiband or three-dimensional formula. In an anisotropic sheet the corresponding bound uses $\sqrt{\widetilde D_x\widetilde D_y}$. Independent density-convention and coordinate-Jacobian checks reproduce these relations; they do not determine a material's input stiffness.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-a57ef549f45fe74c.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

The BKT jump concerns the renormalized total response at the transition. It does not isolate a geometric share or convert a pairing gap directly into phase stiffness. A mean-field amplitude can remain nonzero after phase coherence has been lost. The [BKT article](/scwiki/bkt-transition) discusses current-window, finite-size and resistance-fit ambiguities that also matter when testing a proposed bound experimentally.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-8f81510a80c35e3a.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-isolated-band-constraints-1

Verma and colleagues examine on-site attraction in a controlled hierarchy $w\ll|U|\ll E_0$, with bandwidth $w$ and isolation gap $E_0$. Projecting to localized Wannier states produces pair hopping and an interaction-dependent current operator. For their trivial-band construction, $\widetilde D_{\rm low}\leq\widetilde n|U|\Omega/2$, where $\widetilde n=\min(n,2-n)$ and $\Omega$ is the Wannier spread in the stated normalization. The Lieb-lattice symmetry sharpens the coefficient; it is not a universal constant for every lattice.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-0f28a13259b6faed.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-isolated-band-constraints-2

Their zero-temperature lower bound concerns optical spectral weight and requires the stated long-range-order and correlation assumptions. It is not a general lower bound on finite-temperature superconductivity. Topological bands require care with the Wannier basis: relaxing the Kramers-pair constraint permits localized functions and a generalized overlap bound. Extrapolating the linear interaction trend beyond the isolated-band hierarchy is unjustified; interband physics becomes important.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-0f28a13259b6faed.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-pair-formation-is-not-pair-mobility-1

A simple independent check makes the distinction concrete. An attractive Hubbard dimer was assembled directly in its six-dimensional two-electron Fock space. Sixteen spectra agree with the analytic ground-state energy $E_0=(-|U|-\sqrt{|U|^2+16t^2})/2$. At zero hopping the local pairs have no intersite splitting. In the strong-attraction limit, the low pair-sector splitting approaches $4t^2/|U|$, corresponding to pair hopping $2t^2/|U|$. Stronger local binding can therefore accompany slower pair motion. The dimer has no thermodynamic transition and supplies no predicted Tc.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-a57ef549f45fe74c, source-0f28a13259b6faed.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-pair-formation-is-not-pair-mobility-2

Flat-band geometry can change this mobility argument because overlapping Wannier orbitals generate interaction-mediated pair motion. That is a model-specific route, not permission to discard self-consistency. Peotta and Törmä's geometric response assumes a defined isolated-band and pairing regime. The Chern-trivial Lieb example also demonstrates why nonzero Chern number is not necessary for every geometric contribution. Its existence does not establish superconductivity in an arbitrary flat-band material.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f, source-b43340ce5c356e49.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Measure a total sheet response with units, frequency, device geometry and fitting uncertainties. Tanaka and colleagues infer stiffness from microwave kinetic inductance using a circuit that includes a parallel edge contribution. Their active-region aspect ratio is an assumption in converting the measured inductance to sheet response. A comparison with a conventional estimate may support a geometric interpretation, but it does not directly measure an independently separable geometric component.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-be7282623ca96056.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-experimental-criteria-2

The selected Tanaka author manuscript distinguishes refrigerator base temperature, wired-device temperature and a half-normal-resistance transition. These are separate observables. A finite-frequency stiffness should be connected to the low-frequency, long-wavelength response before applying an equilibrium BKT criterion. Experimental comparison also needs a stated pairing scale, a temperature-dependent stiffness and evidence that sample inhomogeneity or finite size does not dominate the inferred transition.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-be7282623ca96056, source-8f81510a80c35e3a.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

Multiband bounds depend on the actual band structure and occupation assumptions; an approximate estimate is not a universal material ceiling. Hazra's three-dimensional discussion does not establish a general linear stiffness bound there. A successful two-dimensional derivation cannot simply be carried into three dimensions with the same prefactor.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-a57ef549f45fe74c.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-limits-and-disputes-2

A calculated mean-field stiffness may itself be overstated when internal pairing fields are held fixed during a phase twist. Huhtinen and colleagues show a relaxation correction under their time-reversal and equilibrium assumptions. In the isolated uniform-pairing setting, the relevant integrated metric is minimized over orbital positions. A frozen-field geometric answer can therefore differ qualitatively from the relaxed response. This correction must be considered before interpreting a mean-field value as a usable bound on an experimental transition.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-limits-and-disputes-3

Complete scientific acceptance remains open. The selected original passages, figures and independent algebra are documented, while full projection-error control, interacting response calculations, final-author comparisons and raw experimental data have not all been reviewed. No model temperature in this page is entered as an experimental material transition. The open problem is to obtain useful, controlled limits for realistic multiband and correlated systems, rather than to maximize one isolated formula.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-a57ef549f45fe74c, source-0f28a13259b6faed, source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81, source-be7282623ca96056.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

Verification scope: Named selected primary passages/figures or explicitly independent model arithmetic; full scientific acceptance remains open.

### scwiki-n10-claim-discovery-implications-1

Specify the density, isolation gap, interaction scale, orbital structure and measurement convention before comparing designs. Check whether a change enhances pairing, pair mobility or both, and whether it changes the assumptions behind the calculation. Report the full relaxed response and its uncertainty alongside any decomposition. A useful prediction should identify the observation that would falsify it; a large density of states or geometric metric alone does not meet that standard.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-fdf091e09e7f4a6f, source-72f7ddb9f13bbd81, source-fa7a165c8c344a63.

Conditions: Retain dimensionality, density convention, response units, band-isolation hierarchy and stated approximation. Bounds and synthetic models are not measured material transitions.

claims.statement: A shared mathematical language is available, but it is not yet a demonstrated, quantitatively predictive microscopic explanation of every unconventional superconductor in the sources reviewed here. Three goals should be distinguished: classifying order parameters, identifying a common dominant interaction, and predicting material-specific observables from independently constrained inputs. Success at one level does not establish the others. Scalapino's spin-fluctuation framework is an influential proposed connection across several families, not a proof that every family has an identical mechanism.

claims.statement: This question asks what would count as unification and what current examples actually test. ## Scope

A shared mathematical language is available, but it is not yet a demonstrated, quantitatively predictive microscopic explanation of every unconventional superconductor in the sources reviewed here. Three goals should be distinguished: classifying order parameters, identifying a common dominant interaction, and predicting material-specific observables from independently constrained inputs. Success at one level does not establish the others. Scalapino's spin-fluctuation framework is an influential proposed connection across several families, not a proof that every family has an identical mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-eaa3beeed4368f46) [R2](#ref-source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4) [R10](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

This question asks what would count as unification and what current examples actually test. It does not assume that cuprates, iron compounds, heavy-fermion materials and every newer platform must reduce to the same minimal Hamiltonian. Conversely, different gap symmetries do not by themselves require unrelated interactions: the same bilayer model can favor different pairing channels when its electronic structure changes. [R1](#ref-source-eaa3beeed4368f46) [R2](#ref-source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4)

## Mathematical assumptions

A schematic linearized singlet pairing equation is

$$
-\frac{T}{N}\sum_{K'}\Gamma^{pp}(K,K')G(K')G(-K')\phi(K')
=\lambda\phi(K).
$$

Here $K$ combines momentum and fermionic Matsubara frequency, $G$ is the normal-state dressed propagator, and $\Gamma^{pp}$ is the irreducible particle–particle vertex in a consistent normalization. Units use $k_B=1$; $N$ denotes the momentum-mesh normalization. Within the specified approximation, a leading eigenvalue reaching one signals a pairing instability. The eigenfunction describes a pairing structure, whereas the vertex and propagators encode more of the microscopic physics. Writing this equation does not solve for those inputs or establish the actual phase-ordering temperature. [R1](#ref-source-eaa3beeed4368f46) [R2](#ref-source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4)

An original two-channel example illustrates the inverse problem. For orthonormal real vectors $v,w$, define the dimensionless kernel

$$
\mathcal K_\mu=0.6\,vv^{\mathsf T}+\mu\,ww^{\mathsf T},\qquad -1\leq\mu\leq0.5.
$$

Every member has the same leading eigenvector $v$ and eigenvalue 0.6, yet its response to a source in the $w$ direction is $(I-\mathcal K_\mu)^{-1}w=w/(1-\mu)$. That response varies from 0.5 to 2 in the stated normalization. Seventy-two independently diagonalized examples verify the construction. The lesson is limited: a leading gap pattern alone need not uniquely identify a kernel. These matrices are not assigned to real materials or claimed to be realizable by distinct microscopic mechanisms; no transition temperature is inferred. [R1](#ref-source-eaa3beeed4368f46)

## A shared interaction can give different gaps

Maier and Scalapino studied a bilayer Hubbard model with $U/t=6$, filling 0.95 and a $2\times4\times4$ dynamic-cluster approximation. Increasing interlayer hopping changes the leading response from $d_{x^2-y^2}$ to sign-changing $s$ pairing. Their selected author text connects this change to intra- versus interlayer spin fluctuations. This is a concrete model example of related interactions producing different gap structures, not a material-by-material demonstration of one universal mechanism. [R2](#ref-source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4)

The same paper explicitly lacks the finite-size scaling needed to determine a thermodynamic transition temperature. Its quoted temperature estimates come from a cluster susceptibility divergence. Moreover, a larger pairing-interaction measure does not alone give the largest estimated transition: quasiparticle renormalization also changes. A unification claim must therefore compare both the interaction and the electronic response, not simply rank the strength of a proposed fluctuation. [R2](#ref-source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4)

## Model results depend on the question asked

Qin and colleagues' 2020 study concerns nearest-neighbor hopping only, moderate-to-strong interactions around $U/t=6$–8, and hole doping approximately 0.1–0.2. Its nonsuperconducting conclusion is restricted to that regime; the paper explicitly does not rule out superconductivity everywhere in the Hubbard model. Constrained-path auxiliary-field Monte Carlo introduces a trial-state-dependent systematic error, checked against narrow-cylinder DMRG. The comparison is valuable but does not turn the approximation into an exact solution of all sizes. [R3](#ref-source-74cc3f39d62d38b0)

Xu and colleagues instead include next-neighbor hopping, using $U/t=8$ and $t'/t=-0.2$ on the hole-doped side; a particle–hole mapping gives the positive-sign comparison for electron doping. The checked author manuscript combines twist averaging with a thermodynamic extrapolation followed by removal of the applied pairing field. It reports ground-state pairing coexisting with partially filled stripes and explicitly states that it has not predicted transition temperatures. A dome in a zero-temperature order parameter is not a calculated or measured $T_c$ dome. These studies ask different parameter-dependent questions, so their headlines should not be treated as direct contradictions. [R4](#ref-source-e7b3ac50f76789ac)

## Recent numerical evidence and its limits

Gu and colleagues' June 2026 neural-state paper reports stripe configurations and variational-energy improvements for specified Hubbard systems. Its final accuracy discussion says that $d$-wave correlations strengthen as the calculation improves and that further controlled calculations are needed for superconductivity conclusions. It should not be cited as a definitive absence-of-superconductivity proof. Periodic boundaries remove open edges, but they do not eliminate finite-size or variational errors. [R5](#ref-source-b417dbe2d449c0bb)

An August 2026 preprint by Rende and colleagues uses a translationally symmetric variational ansatz at $U/t=8$, $t'/t=-0.2$ and one-eighth hole doping. It reports long-distance pairing correlations and a finite extrapolated order parameter. Its discussion leaves thermodynamic coexistence with long-range stripe order unresolved. This is a dated preprint result with explicit ansatz and scaling assumptions, not an exact solution or a universal theory. Uniform one-body density in a symmetric state also does not preclude stripe signatures in correlation functions. [R6](#ref-source-095247a10e506437)

## Experimental criteria

Phase-sensitive observations constrain the order parameter, while identifying the dominant microscopic pairing interaction requires additional evidence. The original tricrystal-ring work provides a symmetry test in YBa₂Cu₃O₇−δ; that observation alone does not uniquely invert the pairing vertex. A stronger mechanism test compares momentum, frequency, orbital and temperature dependence across independent probes, together with changes induced by a controlled tuning parameter. Agreement should include observations not used to fit the proposed explanation. [R1](#ref-source-eaa3beeed4368f46) [R9](#ref-source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7)

Several interactions can cooperate or compete. The checked nematic-fluctuation theory predicts enhancement under specified weak-coupling assumptions, rather than a universal pairing symmetry. The FeSe/SrTiO₃ interfacial-mode study considers enhancement on top of a magnetic pairing baseline. Those examples caution against treating magnetic, charge, orbital and lattice effects as mutually exclusive labels. Their presence or proximity in a phase diagram is not by itself a causal measurement of their contribution to pairing. [R7](#ref-source-24dd77640a555a0f) [R8](#ref-source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc)

## Limits and disputes

A convincing unification should state its range of materials, independently constrained Hamiltonian, treatment of correlations and competing orders, and measurable predictions with errors. Cross-method agreement at one parameter point supports that point, not every lattice or composition. Numerical energy accuracy also does not automatically guarantee accurate long-distance response. The cited Hubbard studies are examples for evaluating this logic; they are not an exhaustive survey or a final settlement of all model phase diagrams. [R3](#ref-source-74cc3f39d62d38b0) [R4](#ref-source-e7b3ac50f76789ac) [R5](#ref-source-b417dbe2d449c0bb) [R10](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

## Discovery implications

Compare proposed mechanisms through discriminating predictions: which changes in structure, filling, pressure or disorder alter the gap, collective response and competing phases together? Preserve failures and alternative explanations, and distinguish a broadly useful organizing principle from a quantitatively validated material theory. This research program can guide discovery even while a universal microscopic account remains unestablished within the reviewed evidence. [R1](#ref-source-eaa3beeed4368f46) [R7](#ref-source-24dd77640a555a0f) [R10](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472)

## Related topics

Continue with [spin-fluctuation pairing](/scwiki/spin-fluctuation-pairing), [nematic fluctuations](/scwiki/nematic-fluctuation-pairing), [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), [iron-based superconductors](/scwiki/iron-based-superconductors), and [theoretical tools](/scwiki/theoretical-tools).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-n2-claim-scope-1

A shared mathematical language is available, but it is not yet a demonstrated, quantitatively predictive microscopic explanation of every unconventional superconductor in the sources reviewed here. Three goals should be distinguished: classifying order parameters, identifying a common dominant interaction, and predicting material-specific observables from independently constrained inputs. Success at one level does not establish the others. Scalapino's spin-fluctuation framework is an influential proposed connection across several families, not a proof that every family has an identical mechanism.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-eaa3beeed4368f46, source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4, source-51a15c56a9ac1472.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and inherited named review scopes; independent inverse-kernel example only. No many-body solver or material mechanism reproduced.

### scwiki-n2-claim-scope-2

This question asks what would count as unification and what current examples actually test. It does not assume that cuprates, iron compounds, heavy-fermion materials and every newer platform must reduce to the same minimal Hamiltonian. Conversely, different gap symmetries do not by themselves require unrelated interactions: the same bilayer model can favor different pairing channels when its electronic structure changes.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-eaa3beeed4368f46, source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and inherited named review scopes; independent inverse-kernel example only. No many-body solver or material mechanism reproduced.

### scwiki-n2-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

Here $K$ combines momentum and fermionic Matsubara frequency, $G$ is the normal-state dressed propagator, and $\Gamma^{pp}$ is the irreducible particle–particle vertex in a consistent normalization. Units use $k_B=1$; $N$ denotes the momentum-mesh normalization. Within the specified approximation, a leading eigenvalue reaching one signals a pairing instability. The eigenfunction describes a pairing structure, whereas the vertex and propagators encode more of the microscopic physics. Writing this equation does not solve for those inputs or establish the actual phase-ordering temperature.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-eaa3beeed4368f46, source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and inherited named review scopes; independent inverse-kernel example only. No many-body solver or material mechanism reproduced.

### scwiki-n2-claim-mathematical-assumptions-6

Every member has the same leading eigenvector $v$ and eigenvalue 0.6, yet its response to a source in the $w$ direction is $(I-\mathcal K_\mu)^{-1}w=w/(1-\mu)$. That response varies from 0.5 to 2 in the stated normalization. Seventy-two independently diagonalized examples verify the construction. The lesson is limited: a leading gap pattern alone need not uniquely identify a kernel. These matrices are not assigned to real materials or claimed to be realizable by distinct microscopic mechanisms; no transition temperature is inferred.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-eaa3beeed4368f46.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and inherited named review scopes; independent inverse-kernel example only. No many-body solver or material mechanism reproduced.

### scwiki-n2-claim-a-shared-interaction-can-give-different-gaps-1

Maier and Scalapino studied a bilayer Hubbard model with $U/t=6$, filling 0.95 and a $2\times4\times4$ dynamic-cluster approximation. Increasing interlayer hopping changes the leading response from $d_{x^2-y^2}$ to sign-changing $s$ pairing. Their selected author text connects this change to intra- versus interlayer spin fluctuations. This is a concrete model example of related interactions producing different gap structures, not a material-by-material demonstration of one universal mechanism.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and inherited named review scopes; independent inverse-kernel example only. No many-body solver or material mechanism reproduced.

### scwiki-n2-claim-a-shared-interaction-can-give-different-gaps-2

The same paper explicitly lacks the finite-size scaling needed to determine a thermodynamic transition temperature. Its quoted temperature estimates come from a cluster susceptibility divergence. Moreover, a larger pairing-interaction measure does not alone give the largest estimated transition: quasiparticle renormalization also changes. A unification claim must therefore compare both the interaction and the electronic response, not simply rank the strength of a proposed fluctuation.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-1fe5a46dbbba61a4.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

### scwiki-n2-claim-model-results-depend-on-the-question-asked-1

Qin and colleagues' 2020 study concerns nearest-neighbor hopping only, moderate-to-strong interactions around $U/t=6$–8, and hole doping approximately 0.1–0.2. Its nonsuperconducting conclusion is restricted to that regime; the paper explicitly does not rule out superconductivity everywhere in the Hubbard model. Constrained-path auxiliary-field Monte Carlo introduces a trial-state-dependent systematic error, checked against narrow-cylinder DMRG. The comparison is valuable but does not turn the approximation into an exact solution of all sizes.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-74cc3f39d62d38b0.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and inherited named review scopes; independent inverse-kernel example only. No many-body solver or material mechanism reproduced.

### scwiki-n2-claim-model-results-depend-on-the-question-asked-2

Xu and colleagues instead include next-neighbor hopping, using $U/t=8$ and $t'/t=-0.2$ on the hole-doped side; a particle–hole mapping gives the positive-sign comparison for electron doping. The checked author manuscript combines twist averaging with a thermodynamic extrapolation followed by removal of the applied pairing field. It reports ground-state pairing coexisting with partially filled stripes and explicitly states that it has not predicted transition temperatures. A dome in a zero-temperature order parameter is not a calculated or measured $T_c$ dome. These studies ask different parameter-dependent questions, so their headlines should not be treated as direct contradictions.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

### scwiki-n2-claim-recent-numerical-evidence-and-its-limits-1

Gu and colleagues' June 2026 neural-state paper reports stripe configurations and variational-energy improvements for specified Hubbard systems. Its final accuracy discussion says that $d$-wave correlations strengthen as the calculation improves and that further controlled calculations are needed for superconductivity conclusions. It should not be cited as a definitive absence-of-superconductivity proof. Periodic boundaries remove open edges, but they do not eliminate finite-size or variational errors.

### scwiki-n2-claim-recent-numerical-evidence-and-its-limits-2

An August 2026 preprint by Rende and colleagues uses a translationally symmetric variational ansatz at $U/t=8$, $t'/t=-0.2$ and one-eighth hole doping. It reports long-distance pairing correlations and a finite extrapolated order parameter. Its discussion leaves thermodynamic coexistence with long-range stripe order unresolved. This is a dated preprint result with explicit ansatz and scaling assumptions, not an exact solution or a universal theory. Uniform one-body density in a symmetric state also does not preclude stripe signatures in correlation functions.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

### scwiki-n2-claim-experimental-criteria-1

Phase-sensitive observations constrain the order parameter, while identifying the dominant microscopic pairing interaction requires additional evidence. The original tricrystal-ring work provides a symmetry test in YBa₂Cu₃O₇−δ; that observation alone does not uniquely invert the pairing vertex. A stronger mechanism test compares momentum, frequency, orbital and temperature dependence across independent probes, together with changes induced by a controlled tuning parameter. Agreement should include observations not used to fit the proposed explanation.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-eaa3beeed4368f46, source-2e4d7fdb6c1797b7.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and inherited named review scopes; independent inverse-kernel example only. No many-body solver or material mechanism reproduced.

### scwiki-n2-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Several interactions can cooperate or compete. The checked nematic-fluctuation theory predicts enhancement under specified weak-coupling assumptions, rather than a universal pairing symmetry. The FeSe/SrTiO₃ interfacial-mode study considers enhancement on top of a magnetic pairing baseline. Those examples caution against treating magnetic, charge, orbital and lattice effects as mutually exclusive labels. Their presence or proximity in a phase diagram is not by itself a causal measurement of their contribution to pairing.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-24dd77640a555a0f, source-f9fe6e9bc3792dcc.

Conditions: Retain model parameters, finite-size and trial-state limits, source version and publication status. Ground-state pairing and symmetry are not material Tc or unique mechanism measurements.

Verification scope: Selected primary text/figures and inherited named review scopes; independent inverse-kernel example only. No many-body solver or material mechanism reproduced.

### scwiki-n2-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

A convincing unification should state its range of materials, independently constrained Hamiltonian, treatment of correlations and competing orders, and measurable predictions with errors. Cross-method agreement at one parameter point supports that point, not every lattice or composition. Numerical energy accuracy also does not automatically guarantee accurate long-distance response. The cited Hubbard studies are examples for evaluating this logic; they are not an exhaustive survey or a final settlement of all model phase diagrams.

### scwiki-n2-claim-discovery-implications-1

Compare proposed mechanisms through discriminating predictions: which changes in structure, filling, pressure or disorder alter the gap, collective response and competing phases together? Preserve failures and alternative explanations, and distinguish a broadly useful organizing principle from a quantitatively validated material theory. This research program can guide discovery even while a universal microscopic account remains unestablished within the reviewed evidence.

articles.body:
## Scope

Material-specific first-principles calculations have made substantial progress, but the reviewed studies do not establish a generally reliable, uncertainty-calibrated prediction of $T_c$ across strongly correlated superconductors. A useful answer must identify the predicted observable: a pairing tendency, zero-temperature order, excitation gap, mean-field instability, or thermodynamic transition. These are different targets. Predicting a trend can be valuable without already predicting an absolute transition temperature. [R4](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472) [R5](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194) [R7](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

Here, **ab initio** concerns how the Hamiltonian and interactions are constructed; it does not remove approximations from their solution. A calculation should disclose fitted inputs, the correlated orbital space, screened interactions, treatment of double counting, solver limitations and convergence. A declared absence of material-by-material fitting is distinct from a proof that the chosen functional or embedding is exact. [R5](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194) [R6](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c)

## What conventional calculations demonstrate

Sanna, Pellegrini and Gross developed a superconducting density-functional approximation informed by an Einstein-phonon Eliashberg reference system. Their final paper compares transition temperatures and gaps with measurements for selected conventional superconductors. The calculation uses phonons from density-functional perturbation theory and static-RPA Coulomb screening. Its constants are calibrated to the reference model, rather than fitted separately to each compound. This is a concrete computational achievement within stated approximations, not a universal benchmark for strongly correlated pairing. [R1](#ref-source-f9aa25c4ae4f8b5d)

The same paper distinguishes the auxiliary Kohn–Sham pairing potential from a physical excitation gap. Agreement of an approximate gap equation with a reference calculation must therefore be tied to the quantity actually compared. A plotted auxiliary gap should not silently become an experimental gap or a measured $T_c$ in a database. [R1](#ref-source-f9aa25c4ae4f8b5d)

## Two cuprate advances and their boundaries

Cui and colleagues calculate ground-state pairing using ab initio density-matrix embedding, with a finite $2\times2$ impurity and primarily a coupled-cluster solver. They recover selected pressure and layer trends. Phonons and temperature effects are omitted; the reported auxiliary bulk gap is not the interacting bulk excitation gap. Their conversion to a temperature invokes a weak-coupling relationship whose applicability is explicitly qualified. Incomplete charge self-consistency, implicit doping and omitted long-wavelength orders remain limitations. This work supports progress in material-specific pairing calculations, rather than an independently established finite-temperature prediction protocol. [R2](#ref-source-809aa49ee911889b)

Bacq-Labreuil and colleagues combine charge-self-consistent DFT with cluster DMFT. Their selected author manuscript uses zero-temperature exact diagonalization with a discrete bath; a fictitious temperature sets a Matsubara mesh. Superconductivity is then evaluated in a post-processing step with other orbitals frozen in their normal state. The authors explicitly distinguish zero-temperature order from $T_c$ and leave calculation of the actual transition, including phase fluctuations, for further work. Thus the mesh temperature is not a computed transition. The local solver's name also does not make the finite-bath embedding exact for the entire material. [R3](#ref-source-0fac414ae312f585)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a noninteracting block Hamiltonian, eliminating auxiliary orbitals gives the exact retained-orbital Green's function

$$
G_{dd}(z)=\left[z-\epsilon_d-V^\dagger(z-H_p)^{-1}V\right]^{-1}.
$$

Here $z$ is complex energy, $\epsilon_d$ a scalar energy, $H_p$ a Hermitian auxiliary block and $V$ a coupling column. The term $V^\dagger(z-H_p)^{-1}V$ retains frequency dependence. This algebraic identity explains one reason a static reduced Hamiltonian needs justification; it is not a derivation of an interacting pairing vertex. Choices of orbital space and retained energy window matter when constructing practical effective descriptions. [R6](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c)

An original three-orbital illustration compares direct matrix inversion with this elimination for 60 parameter/frequency choices. They agree to numerical precision. Replacing the eliminated term by its zero-frequency value changes the selected Green's functions, with a largest relative difference of about 46% in this deliberately chosen set. That percentage is an illustrative error, not an error bar for either cuprate paper. All energies use arbitrary common units; no material, interaction or superconducting transition is simulated.

Even a correctly computed magnetic scale is not itself $T_c$. In a half-filled, one-orbital, two-site repulsive Hubbard example, the singlet–triplet separation is

$$
J_{\rm dimer}=\frac{\sqrt{U^2+16t^2}-U}{2}
=\frac{4t^2}{U}+O(t^4/U^3),\qquad U\gg |t|.
$$

The previously checked finite-dimer calculation gives about 21% and 6% overestimation by the leading term at $U/t=4$ and $8$, respectively. Neither the exact finite-system splitting nor its asymptotic approximation establishes superconductivity. The example illustrates why a descriptor, its approximation and a bulk ordering temperature require separate validation. [R8](#ref-source-2f6a1c773323226a)

## Experimental criteria

A useful validation chain connects specified crystal structure and composition to electronic inputs, an adequately controlled many-body calculation and the intended experimental observable. Report convergence with orbital basis, cluster size, bath discretization or sampling where applicable; separate numerical convergence from errors in the physical model. Cross-method agreement on a matched Hamiltonian is evidence about that Hamiltonian, not automatic validation of its correspondence to a compound. [R4](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472) [R5](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194) [R6](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c)

The temperature question adds another layer. A nonzero pairing amplitude or a mean-field instability can occur without the phase coherence required for a thermodynamic superconducting transition. Dimensionality, superfluid stiffness and long-distance fluctuations must be addressed in the applicable regime. A two-dimensional phase-stiffness bound is neither a three-dimensional universal formula nor a procedure that turns any calculated gap into $T_c$. [R7](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

## Limits and disputes

This selected review does not rank every available method, exclude successful calculations in particular correlated families, or independently reproduce the quoted ab initio studies. Final-version comparison of the cluster-DMFT author manuscript, complete supplements and broad material benchmarks remain open. The underlying methodological question is quantitative: how much do plausible changes in input structure, screening, correlated subspace and solver treatment move the predicted observable? A single successful comparison cannot answer this for an entire material class. [R4](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472) [R5](#ref-source-12f2513b257d7194) [R6](#ref-source-2b331df83384bc5c)

## Discovery implications

Use calculations to generate testable candidates with an explicit evidence level. Store the structure, conditions, method and predicted quantity together; compare against measurements on the corresponding sample and distinguish onset, bulk magnetic and zero-resistance criteria. Favor prospective checks on withheld materials and preserve failed predictions. This is a proposed validation standard: the aim is increasingly reliable material prediction, while retaining the difference between a promising pairing trend and a demonstrated transition temperature. [R4](#ref-source-51a15c56a9ac1472) [R7](#ref-source-a57ef549f45fe74c)

## Related topics

Continue with [theoretical tools](/scwiki/theoretical-tools), [cuprates](/scwiki/cuprates), [unifying pairing mechanisms](/scwiki/open-questions/n2), and [flat-band temperature bounds](/scwiki/open-questions/n10).

articles.body:
## Scope

A convincing Majorana claim needs an explicit target. A zero-energy spectral feature, a measurable fermion parity, coherent control of a small device and a protected non-Abelian operation are different achievements. This selected review connects model expectations to measurements without treating one observable as proof of every later step. It is not an exhaustive census of all platforms or a claim that no future experiment could resolve the question. [R1](#ref-source-ade538b429fdd847) [R2](#ref-source-8ffaca56901553f5) [R3](#ref-source-dca781066e96eecc)

In superconductors, the relevant objects are emergent quasiparticle modes, not demonstrations of an elementary Majorana particle. A self-adjoint operator can be constructed algebraically from any fermionic operator; experimentally establishing spatially separated, sufficiently isolated zero modes requires more than that change of basis. The ideal chain's boundary states and its bulk phase provide a theoretical benchmark with specified assumptions. [R1](#ref-source-ade538b429fdd847)

## Mathematical assumptions

Adopt $\{\gamma_i,\gamma_j\}=2\delta_{ij}$. For $c=(\gamma_1+i\gamma_2)/2$, physical pair parity is $P_{12}=1-2c^\dagger c=-i\gamma_1\gamma_2$. A chosen orientation of an ideal adjacent exchange gives

$$
U_i=\exp\left(\frac{\pi}{4}\gamma_{i+1}\gamma_i\right)
=\frac{1+\gamma_{i+1}\gamma_i}{\sqrt2},
\qquad U_i\gamma_iU_i^\dagger=\gamma_{i+1},
\quad U_i\gamma_{i+1}U_i^\dagger=-\gamma_i.
$$

Reversing orientation reverses the exchange. Ivanov derives a projective braid representation for separated half-quantum vortices in a specified chiral p-wave setting, with adiabatic motion relative to excited core states. Overall phases are disregarded. Fixing total parity leaves $2^{n-1}$ states for $2n$ Majoranas; adjacent exchanges can remain noncommuting within that space. This result does not itself identify a material or verify an experimental control sequence. [R2](#ref-source-8ffaca56901553f5)

An original occupation-basis calculation checks four Majoranas, both two-dimensional fixed-parity sectors, unitarity, operator transformations and the braid relations. Two exchange orders give distinct states, with squared overlap $1/2$ for the selected initial vacuum, yet identical occupation probabilities in that readout basis. An appropriate analysis basis is needed to distinguish them. The same example gives equal probabilities for a cross-pair parity measurement in both a coherent preparation and a mixed state. Thus a 50/50 histogram alone is not a unique fusion signature. These are ideal algebraic examples, with no spatial device, noise or experimental data simulated.

## Experimental criteria

Spectroscopy must be assessed against alternatives. Pan and Das Sarma's model study compares topological, inhomogeneity-induced and disorder-induced zero-bias structures. It motivates testing dependence on barriers, fields and gates rather than classifying a device from a single favorable trace. The selected evidence does not supply a universal numerical classifier that uniquely identifies topology from conductance alone. [R3](#ref-source-dca781066e96eecc)

A practical review should retain the entire inference chain: calibrated observables, a device model, controls against competing states, and sensitivity to analysis choices. Bulk and end measurements, controlled perturbations, parity readout and operation tests supply complementary evidence. This is an editorial validation framework, not a theorem that a particular checklist is sufficient. Models and measurements must refer to the same device regime. [R1](#ref-source-ade538b429fdd847) [R3](#ref-source-dca781066e96eecc)

## What recent devices establish

Aghaee and colleagues' 2025 InAs–Al experiment demonstrates interferometric single-shot parity measurement. The authors explicitly retain a finely tuned low-energy Andreev-state alternative, alongside constraints imposed by coupling to both ends. Optimized readout assignment error does not equal the error of a quantum gate. The result establishes a readout capability within the paper's stated limits. [R4](#ref-source-e3824a8727c3ec54)

Van Loo and colleagues' paper, published online on 11 February 2026, measures parity through quantum capacitance in a minimal InSb–Al chain and reports lifetimes exceeding a millisecond. The selected author version describes limited protection in a two-site device. That lifetime characterizes parity stability; it is not automatically a coherence time or a demonstrated braiding operation. [R5](#ref-source-a3c2dc153700478a)

Ten Haaf and colleagues probe all three sites of an InSbAs quantum-dot chain. Their selected post-review manuscript connects outer-site zero-bias peaks with a middle-site excitation gap, controlled by superconducting phase. Detuning responses differ between gapped and gap-closed settings, supporting the finite-chain model. The measured couplings are not independently tunable in every sweep. Three sites allow a useful end–middle comparison, but do not establish asymptotic protection of a long chain. [R6](#ref-source-8adab3c663ccc329)

Luethi and colleagues supply a complementary theoretical caution. In their microscopic dot–superconductor model, some short-chain states resembling poor man's Majoranas evolve into trivial states under uniform extension. Robustness to chemical-potential perturbations or a large excitation gap alone does not remove this ambiguity. Uniform extension is a theoretical diagnostic; real devices may have nonuniform parameters. This does not independently reclassify the experimental device above. [R7](#ref-source-7b9053083c48946f)

## A dated coherent-control advance

The **10 July 2026 preprint** by Zatelli and colleagues reports coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains. Comparing even and odd manifolds helps test residual splitting that could cancel in only one manifold. A selected trace has frequency $106.7\pm0.4$ MHz and exponential Rabi decay $26\pm2$ ns. The authors interpret the sweet-spot behavior as partial protection; no journal acceptance was verified for this review. [R8](#ref-source-818818441532a8ec)

The preprint explicitly separates these operations from topologically protected gates: lifting the degeneracy to perform the rotation is not protected independently of chain length. Reported population leakage is not a measured gate fidelity. Longer-chain protection scaling, fusion tests and braiding are further objectives. Coherent rotation is meaningful progress, while a claim about exchange statistics requires evidence about the implemented operation. [R8](#ref-source-818818441532a8ec)

## Limits and disputes

Nature published a transport-gap critique and an associated reply online on 24 June 2026. Their identities and dates were checked, but the final full texts were not accessible in this review. Both are linked without deciding which analysis is correct. Their existence must not be presented as a retraction of the 2025 parity paper. [R9](#ref-source-9188260c182b771d) [R10](#ref-source-4316d225730f11b8)

Retraction status requires a separate, specific record. The 2018 quantized-conductance article discussed in the Majorana overview has a 2021 retraction notice; that is a different publication from the 2025 readout experiment. Keep notices attached to the exact article. Full supplements, raw-data checks, broad platform comparisons and independent experimental replication remain outside this selected review. [R11](#ref-source-f127bb2d99183698) [R4](#ref-source-e3824a8727c3ec54)

## Discovery implications

For candidate selection, retain promising signals together with their alternatives and operating conditions. For quantum operations, ask which preparation, control and measurement distinguish the proposed transformation from ordinary dynamics, readout bias or an incoherent mixture. Increasing device length or showing a favorable oscillation is useful only with an explicit error and protection analysis. These are proposed review priorities; neither this article nor its ideal algebra constitutes certification of a topological qubit. [R1](#ref-source-ade538b429fdd847) [R3](#ref-source-dca781066e96eecc)

## Related topics

Continue with [Majorana models and readout](/scwiki/majorana-zero-modes), [topological material candidates](/scwiki/topological-superconductor-candidates), and [experimental methods](/scwiki/experimental-methods).

## Experimental criteria

Spectroscopy must be assessed against alternatives. Pan and Das Sarma's model study compares topological, inhomogeneity-induced and disorder-induced zero-bias structures. It motivates testing dependence on barriers, fields and gates rather than classifying a device from a single favorable trace. The selected evidence does not supply a universal numerical classifier that uniquely identifies topology from conductance alone. [R3](#ref-source-dca781066e96eecc)

A practical review should retain the entire inference chain: calibrated observables, a device model, controls against competing states, and sensitivity to analysis choices. Bulk and end measurements, controlled perturbations, parity readout and operation tests supply complementary evidence. This is an editorial validation framework, not a theorem that a particular checklist is sufficient. Models and measurements must refer to the same device regime. [R1](#ref-source-ade538b429fdd847) [R3](#ref-source-dca781066e96eecc)

sections.title: What recent devices establish
sections.markdown:
## What recent devices establish

Aghaee and colleagues' 2025 InAs–Al experiment demonstrates interferometric single-shot parity measurement. The authors explicitly retain a finely tuned low-energy Andreev-state alternative, alongside constraints imposed by coupling to both ends. Optimized readout assignment error does not equal the error of a quantum gate. The result establishes a readout capability within the paper's stated limits. [R4](#ref-source-e3824a8727c3ec54)

Van Loo and colleagues' paper, published online on 11 February 2026, measures parity through quantum capacitance in a minimal InSb–Al chain and reports lifetimes exceeding a millisecond. The selected author version describes limited protection in a two-site device. That lifetime characterizes parity stability; it is not automatically a coherence time or a demonstrated braiding operation. [R5](#ref-source-a3c2dc153700478a)

Ten Haaf and colleagues probe all three sites of an InSbAs quantum-dot chain. Their selected post-review manuscript connects outer-site zero-bias peaks with a middle-site excitation gap, controlled by superconducting phase. Detuning responses differ between gapped and gap-closed settings, supporting the finite-chain model. The measured couplings are not independently tunable in every sweep. Three sites allow a useful end–middle comparison, but do not establish asymptotic protection of a long chain. [R6](#ref-source-8adab3c663ccc329)

Luethi and colleagues supply a complementary theoretical caution. In their microscopic dot–superconductor model, some short-chain states resembling poor man's Majoranas evolve into trivial states under uniform extension. Robustness to chemical-potential perturbations or a large excitation gap alone does not remove this ambiguity. Uniform extension is a theoretical diagnostic; real devices may have nonuniform parameters. This does not independently reclassify the experimental device above. [R7](#ref-source-7b9053083c48946f)

sections.title: A dated coherent-control advance
sections.markdown:
## A dated coherent-control advance

The **10 July 2026 preprint** by Zatelli and colleagues reports coherent parity oscillations in coupled minimal Kitaev chains. Comparing even and odd manifolds helps test residual splitting that could cancel in only one manifold. A selected trace has frequency $106.7\pm0.4$ MHz and exponential Rabi decay $26\pm2$ ns. The authors interpret the sweet-spot behavior as partial protection; no journal acceptance was verified for this review. [R8](#ref-source-818818441532a8ec)

The preprint explicitly separates these operations from topologically protected gates: lifting the degeneracy to perform the rotation is not protected independently of chain length. Reported population leakage is not a measured gate fidelity. Longer-chain protection scaling, fusion tests and braiding are further objectives. Coherent rotation is meaningful progress, while a claim about exchange statistics requires evidence about the implemented operation. [R8](#ref-source-818818441532a8ec)

sections.markdown:
## Limits and disputes

Nature published a transport-gap critique and an associated reply online on 24 June 2026. Their identities and dates were checked, but the final full texts were not accessible in this review. Both are linked without deciding which analysis is correct. Their existence must not be presented as a retraction of the 2025 parity paper. [R9](#ref-source-9188260c182b771d) [R10](#ref-source-4316d225730f11b8)

Retraction status requires a separate, specific record. The 2018 quantized-conductance article discussed in the Majorana overview has a 2021 retraction notice; that is a different publication from the 2025 readout experiment. Keep notices attached to the exact article. Full supplements, raw-data checks, broad platform comparisons and independent experimental replication remain outside this selected review. [R11](#ref-source-f127bb2d99183698) [R4](#ref-source-e3824a8727c3ec54)

sections.markdown:
## Discovery implications

For candidate selection, retain promising signals together with their alternatives and operating conditions. For quantum operations, ask which preparation, control and measurement distinguish the proposed transformation from ordinary dynamics, readout bias or an incoherent mixture. Increasing device length or showing a favorable oscillation is useful only with an explicit error and protection analysis. These are proposed review priorities; neither this article nor its ideal algebra constitutes certification of a topological qubit. [R1](#ref-source-ade538b429fdd847) [R3](#ref-source-dca781066e96eecc)
