articles.body:
## Scope

The microscopic origin of strange-metal behavior remains an open question across material families. Approximately linear low-temperature resistivity is an important observation, but it does not uniquely specify a scattering mechanism, establish the absence of quasiparticles, or identify the interaction responsible for superconductivity. A useful explanation must reproduce several observables in a defined regime and survive comparison with alternatives. This is a selected evidence map, not an exhaustive ranking of all proposed theories. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

Three questions should remain separate: what relaxes electrical current, what broadens a single-particle excitation, and what produces the measured response function? Their answers can differ. An apparent rate inferred using carrier density and effective mass is model dependent. A coefficient near $k_BT/\hbar$ is not, by itself, a microscopic derivation or a universal transport bound. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029) [R4](#ref-source-14387c003c0b024d)

## Experimental criteria

Grissonnanche and colleagues use angle-dependent magnetoresistance in Nd-LSCO to separate an anisotropic residual contribution from an approximately isotropic temperature-dependent rate. Their extraction depends on the band model, energy scale and geometry. At the lower measurement temperatures, some field orientations remain superconducting; these cannot silently enter an all-normal-state fit. This is a stronger constraint than a straight resistivity curve alone, while still being an inference tied to its experimental conditions. [R2](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Optical measurements add frequency dependence and spectral-weight information. Romero and colleagues resolve a narrower channel and a broad background in FeTe1−xSex films. The selected author analysis has a finite frequency resolution and a restricted fitting interval. Such a decomposition should be compared with competing response models, rather than assumed to prove that every apparent optical component represents a distinct microscopic carrier population. [R3](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R6](#ref-source-dea2ebb88fe95936)

Campbell and colleagues report a connection between fluctuating magnetic moments and strange-metal transport in LSCO at high fields, with changes when moments freeze. The checked publisher abstract supports this material-specific association. It does not alone establish the mechanism in every cuprate or distinguish all theories of magnetic fluctuations. Full measurement details remain outside this source check. [R9](#ref-source-62781c6eb802b997)

## Two constructive model routes

Patel, Guo, Esterlis and Sachdev's 2023 theory couples two-dimensional fermions to critical scalar modes, with spatially random Yukawa interactions about a nonzero mean. In a large-$N$ ensemble, interaction disorder produces linear resistivity while a different coupling can dominate the single-particle self-energy. This offers a mechanism for separating current relaxation from spectral broadening. Its proposed generality is a theoretical claim with stated approximations, not a material-by-material experimental identification. [R4](#ref-source-14387c003c0b024d)

Patel, Lunts and Albergo subsequently simulate a different, specified spin–fermion construction. The selected published-version text uses two bands, two auxiliary flavors, zero mean Yukawa coupling and typically a $40\times40$ lattice averaged over ten disorder realizations. An extended region with localized, gapless magnetic fluctuations supports strange-metal transport. The transport rate is inferred from Matsubara conductivity and a zero-frequency spline extrapolation; its coupling comparison uses two disorder strengths at matched rescaled tuning parameters. Avoid turning that comparison into independence from every Hamiltonian parameter. [R5](#ref-source-f7ac8e7f2cfae198)

Fratini and colleagues' paper, published on **24 September 2026**, develops another route through the two-dimensional t–J model. The checked author version and final supplement use finite-temperature and low-temperature Lanczos calculations, including twisted-boundary averaging. Single-hole clusters reach 24 sites and finite-density clusters 20 sites. Selected results connect broad current spectra to an apparent thermal optical width. Gaussian broadening and d.c. extrapolation remain part of the calculation; noninteracting boundary-average benchmarks do not prove exact interacting thermodynamic-limit transport. [R6](#ref-source-dea2ebb88fe95936)

## Mathematical assumptions

For the regular dissipative conductivity at positive frequency, choose a current-spectrum normalization that absorbs charge and volume constants, and set $k_B=\hbar=1$. The thermal relation reads

$$
\sigma_1(\omega)=\frac{1-e^{-\omega/T}}{\omega}C(\omega),
\qquad C(-\omega)=e^{-\omega/T}C(\omega).
$$

It concerns the response and its unsymmetrized spectrum; it is not a declaration that every metal has a finite regular d.c. limit. A separate zero-frequency delta function, if present, requires separate treatment. For finite $C(0)$, the regular limit is $\sigma_1(0)=C(0)/T$. [R6](#ref-source-dea2ebb88fe95936)

An original four-level example verifies detailed balance and the corresponding transition weights in 24 thermal cases. A separate illustrative positive-frequency envelope, $C(\omega)=2\exp[-(\omega/100)^2]$, gives $\rho=T/2$ and a half-width close to $1.59T$ for four temperatures between 0.1 and 1. The envelope is broad and temperature independent; its negative-frequency branch follows detailed balance. This is a bounded response example, not a microscopic Hamiltonian construction or a validation of the optical sum rule across temperatures. It demonstrates why a thermal response width alone need not identify a carrier collision time.

A second independent illustration assumes elastic scattering on a circular Fermi surface. If $W(\theta)$ is an angular transition-rate density, the departure rate weights $W$, whereas the current mode weights $W(1-\cos\theta)$. Eight discretized collision operators verify that forward-peaked scattering can leave a large departure rate but a much smaller current-relaxation rate. Particle conservation is checked independently. These quasiparticle examples explain an inference problem; they do not establish quasiparticles in a strange metal. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

## Noise and the interpretation of carriers

Chen and colleagues measure suppressed noise in YbRh2Si2 nanowires compared with a gold control and specified diffusive Fermi-liquid expectations. Their selected author text uses long-wire measurements to constrain electron–phonon cooling, and interprets the short-wire result as evidence against well-defined quasiparticle carriers in the examined regime. Effective Fano factors come from a finite-temperature, bias-dependent analysis; they are not direct measurements of a fractional elementary charge. [R7](#ref-source-96657a33251c13ee)

Polyak, Khrapai and Tikhonov question that interpretation through contact resistance and energy relaxation. Their model allows current redistribution between the film and its gold covering, includes an added contact contribution fitted to resistance, and omits some contact and amplifier noise terms. These qualifications matter when comparing their alternative with the original controls. This review has not independently refitted either analysis and does not adjudicate the dispute. A low noise level should therefore be reported with its device and thermal assumptions. [R8](#ref-source-be020ff1e20fbae5) [R7](#ref-source-96657a33251c13ee)

## Limits and disputes

The reviewed models explain overlapping features without yet establishing one microscopic origin across all strange metals. Large-$N$ control, finite-system numerical convergence and experimental agreement answer different questions. Keep extrapolation, disorder averaging, response normalization and temperature windows visible. In particular, a model producing narrow and broad optical features from one carrier type does not by itself overturn a two-channel interpretation in a different material. [R4](#ref-source-14387c003c0b024d) [R5](#ref-source-f7ac8e7f2cfae198) [R6](#ref-source-dea2ebb88fe95936) [R3](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Discovery implications

A discriminating program should jointly compare transport, optical response, magnetic fluctuations, thermodynamics and, where feasible, noise. Test how controlled disorder, filling or field changes both the candidate mechanism and its predicted observables. The random-interaction model's proposed spatial magnetic probes offer one concrete direction; independent contact and thermal calibration offer another. These are proposed validation priorities. Reproducing a resistivity exponent or fitting a thermal rate does not certify a pairing mechanism or predict a new material's $T_c$. [R5](#ref-source-f7ac8e7f2cfae198) [R7](#ref-source-96657a33251c13ee) [R8](#ref-source-be020ff1e20fbae5)

## Related topics

Continue with [strange-metal observations](/scwiki/strange-metals), [Planckian dissipation](/scwiki/planckian-dissipation), [parallel conducting channels](/scwiki/parallel-conduction-channels), and [the question of a unified pairing mechanism](/scwiki/open-questions/n2).

# What is the microscopic origin of strange metals?

Compare current relaxation, response-function scaling and carrier evidence across selected experiments and competing microscopic models.

## Scope

The microscopic origin of strange-metal behavior remains an open question across material families. Approximately linear low-temperature resistivity is an important observation, but it does not uniquely specify a scattering mechanism, establish the absence of quasiparticles, or identify the interaction responsible for superconductivity. A useful explanation must reproduce several observables in a defined regime and survive comparison with alternatives. This is a selected evidence map, not an exhaustive ranking of all proposed theories. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

Three questions should remain separate: what relaxes electrical current, what broadens a single-particle excitation, and what produces the measured response function? Their answers can differ. An apparent rate inferred using carrier density and effective mass is model dependent. A coefficient near $k_BT/\hbar$ is not, by itself, a microscopic derivation or a universal transport bound. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029) [R4](#ref-source-14387c003c0b024d)

## Experimental criteria

Grissonnanche and colleagues use angle-dependent magnetoresistance in Nd-LSCO to separate an anisotropic residual contribution from an approximately isotropic temperature-dependent rate. Their extraction depends on the band model, energy scale and geometry. At the lower measurement temperatures, some field orientations remain superconducting; these cannot silently enter an all-normal-state fit. This is a stronger constraint than a straight resistivity curve alone, while still being an inference tied to its experimental conditions. [R2](#ref-source-374c8bc13ced83e8)

Optical measurements add frequency dependence and spectral-weight information. Romero and colleagues resolve a narrower channel and a broad background in FeTe1−xSex films. The selected author analysis has a finite frequency resolution and a restricted fitting interval. Such a decomposition should be compared with competing response models, rather than assumed to prove that every apparent optical component represents a distinct microscopic carrier population. [R3](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb) [R6](#ref-source-dea2ebb88fe95936)

Campbell and colleagues report a connection between fluctuating magnetic moments and strange-metal transport in LSCO at high fields, with changes when moments freeze. The checked publisher abstract supports this material-specific association. It does not alone establish the mechanism in every cuprate or distinguish all theories of magnetic fluctuations. Full measurement details remain outside this source check. [R9](#ref-source-62781c6eb802b997)

## Two constructive model routes

Patel, Guo, Esterlis and Sachdev's 2023 theory couples two-dimensional fermions to critical scalar modes, with spatially random Yukawa interactions about a nonzero mean. In a large-$N$ ensemble, interaction disorder produces linear resistivity while a different coupling can dominate the single-particle self-energy. This offers a mechanism for separating current relaxation from spectral broadening. Its proposed generality is a theoretical claim with stated approximations, not a material-by-material experimental identification. [R4](#ref-source-14387c003c0b024d)

Patel, Lunts and Albergo subsequently simulate a different, specified spin–fermion construction. The selected published-version text uses two bands, two auxiliary flavors, zero mean Yukawa coupling and typically a $40\times40$ lattice averaged over ten disorder realizations. An extended region with localized, gapless magnetic fluctuations supports strange-metal transport. The transport rate is inferred from Matsubara conductivity and a zero-frequency spline extrapolation; its coupling comparison uses two disorder strengths at matched rescaled tuning parameters. Avoid turning that comparison into independence from every Hamiltonian parameter. [R5](#ref-source-f7ac8e7f2cfae198)

Fratini and colleagues' paper, published on **24 September 2026**, develops another route through the two-dimensional t–J model. The checked author version and final supplement use finite-temperature and low-temperature Lanczos calculations, including twisted-boundary averaging. Single-hole clusters reach 24 sites and finite-density clusters 20 sites. Selected results connect broad current spectra to an apparent thermal optical width. Gaussian broadening and d.c. extrapolation remain part of the calculation; noninteracting boundary-average benchmarks do not prove exact interacting thermodynamic-limit transport. [R6](#ref-source-dea2ebb88fe95936)

## Mathematical assumptions

For the regular dissipative conductivity at positive frequency, choose a current-spectrum normalization that absorbs charge and volume constants, and set $k_B=\hbar=1$. The thermal relation reads

$$
\sigma_1(\omega)=\frac{1-e^{-\omega/T}}{\omega}C(\omega),
\qquad C(-\omega)=e^{-\omega/T}C(\omega).
$$

It concerns the response and its unsymmetrized spectrum; it is not a declaration that every metal has a finite regular d.c. limit. A separate zero-frequency delta function, if present, requires separate treatment. For finite $C(0)$, the regular limit is $\sigma_1(0)=C(0)/T$. [R6](#ref-source-dea2ebb88fe95936)

An original four-level example verifies detailed balance and the corresponding transition weights in 24 thermal cases. A separate illustrative positive-frequency envelope, $C(\omega)=2\exp[-(\omega/100)^2]$, gives $\rho=T/2$ and a half-width close to $1.59T$ for four temperatures between 0.1 and 1. The envelope is broad and temperature independent; its negative-frequency branch follows detailed balance. This is a bounded response example, not a microscopic Hamiltonian construction or a validation of the optical sum rule across temperatures. It demonstrates why a thermal response width alone need not identify a carrier collision time.

A second independent illustration assumes elastic scattering on a circular Fermi surface. If $W(\theta)$ is an angular transition-rate density, the departure rate weights $W$, whereas the current mode weights $W(1-\cos\theta)$. Eight discretized collision operators verify that forward-peaked scattering can leave a large departure rate but a much smaller current-relaxation rate. Particle conservation is checked independently. These quasiparticle examples explain an inference problem; they do not establish quasiparticles in a strange metal. [R1](#ref-source-67da95cac5481029)

## Noise and the interpretation of carriers

Chen and colleagues measure suppressed noise in YbRh2Si2 nanowires compared with a gold control and specified diffusive Fermi-liquid expectations. Their selected author text uses long-wire measurements to constrain electron–phonon cooling, and interprets the short-wire result as evidence against well-defined quasiparticle carriers in the examined regime. Effective Fano factors come from a finite-temperature, bias-dependent analysis; they are not direct measurements of a fractional elementary charge. [R7](#ref-source-96657a33251c13ee)

Polyak, Khrapai and Tikhonov question that interpretation through contact resistance and energy relaxation. Their model allows current redistribution between the film and its gold covering, includes an added contact contribution fitted to resistance, and omits some contact and amplifier noise terms. These qualifications matter when comparing their alternative with the original controls. This review has not independently refitted either analysis and does not adjudicate the dispute. A low noise level should therefore be reported with its device and thermal assumptions. [R8](#ref-source-be020ff1e20fbae5) [R7](#ref-source-96657a33251c13ee)

## Limits and disputes

The reviewed models explain overlapping features without yet establishing one microscopic origin across all strange metals. Large-$N$ control, finite-system numerical convergence and experimental agreement answer different questions. Keep extrapolation, disorder averaging, response normalization and temperature windows visible. In particular, a model producing narrow and broad optical features from one carrier type does not by itself overturn a two-channel interpretation in a different material. [R4](#ref-source-14387c003c0b024d) [R5](#ref-source-f7ac8e7f2cfae198) [R6](#ref-source-dea2ebb88fe95936) [R3](#ref-source-05b2d5ff6757b5eb)

## Discovery implications

A discriminating program should jointly compare transport, optical response, magnetic fluctuations, thermodynamics and, where feasible, noise. Test how controlled disorder, filling or field changes both the candidate mechanism and its predicted observables. The random-interaction model's proposed spatial magnetic probes offer one concrete direction; independent contact and thermal calibration offer another. These are proposed validation priorities. Reproducing a resistivity exponent or fitting a thermal rate does not certify a pairing mechanism or predict a new material's $T_c$. [R5](#ref-source-f7ac8e7f2cfae198) [R7](#ref-source-96657a33251c13ee) [R8](#ref-source-be020ff1e20fbae5)

articles.body:
## Scope

UTe2 has substantial evidence supporting odd-parity, triplet-related superconductivity, but its complete order parameter is not fixed by a single experiment. The question must specify the sample, pressure, field magnitude and direction, and superconducting phase. Spin structure, inversion parity, the number of order-parameter components, time-reversal symmetry and topology are distinct properties. This page compares selected evidence rather than declaring all of them settled together. [R2](#ref-source-ca6322be2694e430) [R3](#ref-source-e879550ecef8c596) [R7](#ref-source-dd4e897d833ce69c)

In a suitable intraband description of a centrosymmetric, time-reversal-invariant normal state, an even-frequency odd-parity gap has a symmetric band-doublet pairing component. With strong spin–orbit coupling, that label is not automatically a pair of freely rotating bare electron spins. The doublet's actual crystal transformation rules matter; exceptional bands need not transform as ordinary spin-1/2 pseudospins. Multiorbital and frequency-exchange assumptions must remain explicit. [R1](#ref-source-f2133d67ac862ff4)

## Experimental criteria

The discovery study reported a large, anisotropic upper critical field and triplet-related interpretations. Its b-axis estimate near 40 T extrapolated beyond measurements reaching 20 T. Large critical fields motivate a triplet hypothesis, but the comparison must include orbital limiting, strong coupling, multiband structure and spin–orbit response. UTe2's paramagnetic ambient-pressure normal state also distinguishes it from uranium superconductors with established ferromagnetic order. [R2](#ref-source-ca6322be2694e430)

Li and colleagues' 2025 In/UTe2 junction study probes orbital symmetry through orientation-dependent Josephson coupling. Coupling appeared on the (001) and (0−11) faces, whereas two junctions on a (1−10) surface had no resolved supercurrent at a stated sensitivity of roughly 1 microampere. The authors identify this pattern with B1u among their considered representations. Their argument requires sufficiently smooth interfaces and first-order coupling; interface barriers, geometry and surface reconstruction remain part of the inference. A null signal is resolution bounded, not an exact measurement of zero. [R3](#ref-source-e879550ecef8c596)

Junction temperatures also need careful attribution. In that study, sample E's junction zero-resistance temperature is about 1.2 K, while the UTe2 electrode onset is about 2.0 K. These are different criteria, not two interchangeable bulk transition temperatures. This question page does not create a new material record from either value. [R3](#ref-source-e879550ecef8c596)

## What Knight shifts establish

Kitagawa and colleagues re-examined an early sample using a small field tilt to infer the difficult a-axis response. They found a reduction and attributed the earlier nearly unchanged signal to a remaining nonsuperconducting fraction. The method uses an angular projection and a diamagnetic estimate; the proposed recovery near a 1.5 T a-axis component is an extrapolation interpreted as spin rotation. It should not be presented as a directly mapped universal rotation boundary. [R5](#ref-source-87044bef0f921b4c)

Matsumura and colleagues measured two Te sites at approximately 0.8 T along b and 0.75 T along c, down to about 70 mK. Subtracting their shifts removes an assumed common diamagnetic contribution. The c-axis peaks overlap, and its quantitative subtraction is particularly sensitive to fitting and nearly equal hyperfine slopes. Together with earlier a-axis measurements, the work constrains a three-component d-vector description. The authors nevertheless allow higher-order momentum terms and do not uniquely distinguish a full gap from every point-node model. [R4](#ref-source-b4ce2816b340bde0)

## Mathematical assumptions

In a specified spin-1/2 basis, a pure triplet example has $\Delta=(\mathbf d\cdot\boldsymbol\sigma)i\sigma_y$. Real odd $\mathbf d(\mathbf k)$ gives a symmetric spin matrix and satisfies $\Delta(\mathbf k)=-\Delta^{\mathsf T}(-\mathbf k)$. This algebra must not replace the actual symmetry matrices of a spin–orbit-coupled material. [R1](#ref-source-f2133d67ac862ff4)

For an original illustrative single-band, real-unitary, fixed-d model with isotropic spin coupling, constant density of states and zero temperature, the normalized weak-field response is

$$
\frac{\chi_{ii}}{\chi_N}=1-\left\langle\frac{d_i^2}{|\mathbf d|^2}\right\rangle_{\rm FS}.
$$

Direct Bogoliubov-matrix energy curvatures verify 12 directional cases using two small field steps and a finite energy cutoff. Four separate spherical averages illustrate the distinction: $\mathbf d=\mathbf k$ gives $2/3$ on all axes, whereas $(k_y,k_x,3k_xk_yk_z)$ gives approximately $(0.558,0.558,0.885)$. Both reduce all three responses, although their symmetry and nodal structures differ. These examples do not calculate UTe2's multiband susceptibility, spin–orbit matrix elements, finite-temperature response or field-induced rotation.

For the two-site extraction, write $K_j=A_j\chi+K_j^{\rm orb}+K^{\rm dia}$. Subtraction cancels only the common term. Solving for the diamagnetic contribution introduces a denominator $\Gamma-1$, where $\Gamma$ relates hyperfine slopes. The selected experiment reports ratios near 1.32 and 0.91 for different directions. Four independent synthetic examples recover the imposed common shift and verify amplification of measurement errors as the slopes approach equality; they are not a refit of the spectra. [R4](#ref-source-b4ce2816b340bde0)

## Gap structure and other symmetries

Hosoi and colleagues' July 2026 thermal-transport study adds a bulk directional constraint. Its b-axis heat-current measurements reached roughly 50 mK in two clean crystals. Small residual transport and a low-field kink support a deep but finite gap minimum in the authors' interpretation. However, the zero-temperature term is extrapolated, and the zero-field temperature dependence alone explicitly leaves a restricted true-node scenario open. The finite-field model uses a semiclassical Doppler picture and does not capture all subthreshold conduction. Gap anisotropy is not a direct spin measurement. [R6](#ref-source-4d23ccd63057d066)

Theuss and colleagues measured compression and shear moduli in single- and double-transition samples. Their absence of resolved shear discontinuities constrains a multicomponent interpretation within the elastic-coupling analysis. The paper explicitly states that this result also permits single-component even-parity states. Its additional B2u proposal is therefore distinct from the component-count constraint. Ambient-pressure findings cannot automatically settle the pressure-induced phases. [R8](#ref-source-496eda2b229c9047)

The reviewed Kerr study found no spontaneous signal in its tested single-transition samples. This constrains time-reversal breaking under those conditions; it does not exclude every possible triplet state. Conversely, the high-field halo experiment maps transport boundaries in a very different field regime, with a multicomponent triplet interpretation remaining a model conclusion. Neither observation alone determines the low-field bulk invariant or establishes usable Majorana modes. [R7](#ref-source-dd4e897d833ce69c) [R9](#ref-source-0c4d7cebb12a0d5b)

## Limits and disputes

The evidence supports taking triplet-related states seriously while retaining competing representations and measurement-specific assumptions. A gap minimum, an absent shear jump, a Knight-shift change and a Josephson selection rule do not answer identical questions. Agreement should be assessed on compatible samples and phases, including surface-versus-bulk sensitivity. No independent global fit of these experiments has been performed here, and full scientific acceptance remains open. [R3](#ref-source-e879550ecef8c596) [R4](#ref-source-b4ce2816b340bde0) [R6](#ref-source-4d23ccd63057d066) [R8](#ref-source-496eda2b229c9047)

## Discovery implications

Useful next tests would compare orientation-resolved junctions with bulk spin response and thermodynamic probes on well-characterized crystals, carrying uncertainties and sample fractions through the analysis. Candidate models should predict several observables under the same conditions and identify where their predictions differ. Keep claimed topology separate until the relevant gap, symmetry and electronic structure are established. This is a proposed validation program, not a certification of one microscopic pairing mechanism. [R1](#ref-source-f2133d67ac862ff4) [R3](#ref-source-e879550ecef8c596) [R4](#ref-source-b4ce2816b340bde0)

## Related topics

Continue with [singlet and triplet pairing](/scwiki/singlet-and-triplet-pairing), [p-wave candidates](/scwiki/p-wave), [heavy-fermion superconductors](/scwiki/heavy-fermion-superconductors), and [Majorana evidence](/scwiki/open-questions/n4).

Real odd $\mathbf d(\mathbf k)$ gives a symmetric spin matrix and satisfies $\Delta(\mathbf k)=-\Delta^{\mathsf T}(-\mathbf k)$. This algebra must not replace the actual symmetry matrices of a spin–orbit-coupled material. [R1](#ref-source-f2133d67ac862ff4)

For an original illustrative single-band, real-unitary, fixed-d model with isotropic spin coupling, constant density of states and zero temperature, the normalized weak-field response is

$$
\frac{\chi_{ii}}{\chi_N}=1-\left\langle\frac{d_i^2}{|\mathbf d|^2}\right\rangle_{\rm FS}.
$$

Direct Bogoliubov-matrix energy curvatures verify 12 directional cases using two small field steps and a finite energy cutoff. Four separate spherical averages illustrate the distinction: $\mathbf d=\mathbf k$ gives $2/3$ on all axes, whereas $(k_y,k_x,3k_xk_yk_z)$ gives approximately $(0.558,0.558,0.885)$. Both reduce all three responses, although their symmetry and nodal structures differ. These examples do not calculate UTe2's multiband susceptibility, spin–orbit matrix elements, finite-temperature response or field-induced rotation.

For the two-site extraction, write $K_j=A_j\chi+K_j^{\rm orb}+K^{\rm dia}$. Subtraction cancels only the common term. Solving for the diamagnetic contribution introduces a denominator $\Gamma-1$, where $\Gamma$ relates hyperfine slopes. The selected experiment reports ratios near 1.32 and 0.91 for different directions. Four independent synthetic examples recover the imposed common shift and verify amplification of measurement errors as the slopes approach equality; they are not a refit of the spectra. [R4](#ref-source-b4ce2816b340bde0)

## Gap structure and other symmetries

Hosoi and colleagues' July 2026 thermal-transport study adds a bulk directional constraint. Its b-axis heat-current measurements reached roughly 50 mK in two clean crystals. Small residual transport and a low-field kink support a deep but finite gap minimum in the authors' interpretation. However, the zero-temperature term is extrapolated, and the zero-field temperature dependence alone explicitly leaves a restricted true-node scenario open. The finite-field model uses a semiclassical Doppler picture and does not capture all subthreshold conduction. Gap anisotropy is not a direct spin measurement. [R6](#ref-source-4d23ccd63057d066)

Theuss and colleagues measured compression and shear moduli in single- and double-transition samples. Their absence of resolved shear discontinuities constrains a multicomponent interpretation within the elastic-coupling analysis. The paper explicitly states that this result also permits single-component even-parity states. Its additional B2u proposal is therefore distinct from the component-count constraint. Ambient-pressure findings cannot automatically settle the pressure-induced phases. [R8](#ref-source-496eda2b229c9047)

The reviewed Kerr study found no spontaneous signal in its tested single-transition samples. This constrains time-reversal breaking under those conditions; it does not exclude every possible triplet state. Conversely, the high-field halo experiment maps transport boundaries in a very different field regime, with a multicomponent triplet interpretation remaining a model conclusion. Neither observation alone determines the low-field bulk invariant or establishes usable Majorana modes. [R7](#ref-source-dd4e897d833ce69c) [R9](#ref-source-0c4d7cebb12a0d5b)

## Limits and disputes

The evidence supports taking triplet-related states seriously while retaining competing representations and measurement-specific assumptions. A gap minimum, an absent shear jump, a Knight-shift change and a Josephson selection rule do not answer identical questions. Agreement should be assessed on compatible samples and phases, including surface-versus-bulk sensitivity. No independent global fit of these experiments has been performed here, and full scientific acceptance remains open. [R3](#ref-source-e879550ecef8c596) [R4](#ref-source-b4ce2816b340bde0) [R6](#ref-source-4d23ccd63057d066) [R8](#ref-source-496eda2b229c9047)

## Discovery implications

Useful next tests would compare orientation-resolved junctions with bulk spin response and thermodynamic probes on well-characterized crystals, carrying uncertainties and sample fractions through the analysis. Candidate models should predict several observables under the same conditions and identify where their predictions differ. Keep claimed topology separate until the relevant gap, symmetry and electronic structure are established. This is a proposed validation program, not a certification of one microscopic pairing mechanism. ## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-n6-claim-scope-1

UTe2 has substantial evidence supporting odd-parity, triplet-related superconductivity, but its complete order parameter is not fixed by a single experiment. The question must specify the sample, pressure, field magnitude and direction, and superconducting phase. Spin structure, inversion parity, the number of order-parameter components, time-reversal symmetry and topology are distinct properties. This page compares selected evidence rather than declaring all of them settled together.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-ca6322be2694e430, source-e879550ecef8c596, source-dd4e897d833ce69c.

### scwiki-n6-claim-scope-2

In a suitable intraband description of a centrosymmetric, time-reversal-invariant normal state, an even-frequency odd-parity gap has a symmetric band-doublet pairing component. With strong spin–orbit coupling, that label is not automatically a pair of freely rotating bare electron spins. The doublet's actual crystal transformation rules matter; exceptional bands need not transform as ordinary spin-1/2 pseudospins. Multiorbital and frequency-exchange assumptions must remain explicit.

### scwiki-n6-claim-experimental-criteria-1

The discovery study reported a large, anisotropic upper critical field and triplet-related interpretations. Its b-axis estimate near 40 T extrapolated beyond measurements reaching 20 T. Large critical fields motivate a triplet hypothesis, but the comparison must include orbital limiting, strong coupling, multiband structure and spin–orbit response. UTe2's paramagnetic ambient-pressure normal state also distinguishes it from uranium superconductors with established ferromagnetic order.

### scwiki-n6-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Li and colleagues' 2025 In/UTe2 junction study probes orbital symmetry through orientation-dependent Josephson coupling. Coupling appeared on the (001) and (0−11) faces, whereas two junctions on a (1−10) surface had no resolved supercurrent at a stated sensitivity of roughly 1 microampere. The authors identify this pattern with B1u among their considered representations. Their argument requires sufficiently smooth interfaces and first-order coupling; interface barriers, geometry and surface reconstruction remain part of the inference. A null signal is resolution bounded, not an exact measurement of zero.

claims.statement: There is no justified single pairing assignment for every nickelate. Infinite-layer nickelates and Ruddlesden–Popper bilayers have different structures and electronic settings; pressurized bulk crystals and ambient-pressure strained films also require separate treatment. The approved question about s± versus d-wave pairing therefore needs a material, composition, strain or pressure, temperature range and experimental criterion. A superconducting transition establishes neither the order-parameter symmetry nor its microscopic cause by itself.

articles.body:
## Scope

There is no justified single pairing assignment for every nickelate. Infinite-layer nickelates and Ruddlesden–Popper bilayers have different structures and electronic settings; pressurized bulk crystals and ambient-pressure strained films also require separate treatment. The approved question about s± versus d-wave pairing therefore needs a material, composition, strain or pressure, temperature range and experimental criterion. A superconducting transition establishes neither the order-parameter symmetry nor its microscopic cause by itself. [R1](#ref-source-35fd62b7cb3c490c) [R2](#ref-source-df0c15d62982f853)

In a tetragonal single-band illustration, a d-wave gap changes sign under a quarter turn, whereas an s± state can preserve that rotation while changing sign between Fermi sheets. The two d-wave forms d(x²−y²) and dxy have different nodal directions. Real multiorbital states additionally require orbital and band transformation rules. A nodal or nodeless measurement must be compared with the actual Fermi surface and measured momentum range. [R4](#ref-source-14703288422dbd4c) [R5](#ref-source-ae28d4e3baad051f)

## Experimental criteria

For infinite-layer La- and Pr-based films, Harvey and colleagues report low-temperature quadratic superfluid-density behavior consistent with disorder and a nodal gap. Their Nd samples have magnetic contributions that prevent a direct inference of the intrinsic nodal structure. This is evidence concerning specific infinite-layer films, not a measurement of the bilayer sign pattern. The present check covers the final abstract and selected indexed methods and conclusions; it is not a complete independent penetration-depth analysis. [R3](#ref-source-7b6e19919552090c)

Guo and colleagues' final high-pressure Andreev study fits selected 23 GPa spectra with gaps near 23 and 6 meV. A dominant anisotropic s-like gap with either an s-like or a smaller d-like component describes their selected data better than the tested dominant-d alternatives. It does not measure an interband sign reversal directly. Their estimated contact radius is about 7.3 nm, versus a mean free path near 1.6 nm, and the paper discusses fragmented conducting paths. A broad resistive transition, background normalization and contact assumptions limit interpretation. Its 19 meV passage refers to a different cited film experiment, not this high-pressure gap. [R6](#ref-source-ce76c4830c64c3c7)

Cao and colleagues instead interpret directional spectra in 20–22 GPa crystals as d-wave evidence. Their September 2025 preprint compares V-shaped spectra and zero-bias peaks with an anisotropic tunnelling model; it remains labelled as a preprint here. Different orientations use separate cells, and the authors describe visually aligned contacts, mechanical instability and local suppression by excessive tip pressure. These conditions need validation before treating the contrast with other spectra as a universal symmetry verdict. A zero-bias peak alone is insufficient. [R7](#ref-source-f9976c21a60be0b8)

## What film spectroscopy establishes

Shen and colleagues' 2026 Science paper reports a nodeless gap and electron–boson coupling in (La,Pr,Sm) bilayer films. The checked author version finds a roughly 18 meV gap near the zone diagonal and uses synchrotron measurements to extend momentum coverage. It also reports spectral suppression above the resistive onset and separates that pseudogap behavior from the sharper transition-related change. Its approximately 70 meV dispersion kink does not identify the pairing mediator uniquely. The final abstract is verified, while full author-to-final and supplementary comparisons remain open. [R8](#ref-source-a5e400bcce2d5544)

Sun and colleagues studied Sr-doped bilayer films. Their checked author version finds leading-edge shifts of about 1–2 meV at selected momenta, including the diagonal, with an instrumental energy resolution near 5 meV. Temperature cycling and normalization checks support the reported shift, but a leading-edge displacement is not automatically the full superconducting gap. The July 2026 final publication identity is verified; its complete text has not been compared here. These different observables and film compositions must not be combined into one gap value. [R9](#ref-source-e78a5a3cef51e9fe)

## Mathematical assumptions

An original clean, decoupled two-band Bogoliubov example has

$$
E_{n,\pm}(\mathbf k)=\pm\sqrt{\xi_n(\mathbf k)^2+|\Delta_n(\mathbf k)|^2}.
$$

Changing only the relative gap sign leaves these energies unchanged. Eighteen independent matrix cases also compare the electron spectral functions and recover the same result. This demonstrates a restricted ambiguity of magnitude measurements; it is not a statement that every spectroscopic response is insensitive to phase. A separate fixed-hybridization counterexample changes the spectrum when one gap sign flips. Real matrix elements, interband processes, disorder and interface scattering must be specified. [R4](#ref-source-14703288422dbd4c) [R6](#ref-source-ce76c4830c64c3c7)

For identical layers, a pure symmetric interlayer pairing matrix illustrates how opposite band signs can arise:

$$
U^{\mathsf T}\begin{pmatrix}0&\Delta_\perp\\\Delta_\perp&0\end{pmatrix}U
=\begin{pmatrix}\Delta_\perp&0\\0&-\Delta_\perp\end{pmatrix},\qquad
U=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}\begin{pmatrix}1&1\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}.
$$

The basis change is explicitly checked. It is conditional on equivalent layers and the assumed pairing matrix; it does not establish that real films realize this state. An independent separable angular-kernel example likewise changes its leading s± or d(x²−y²) channel when imposed channel weights change. Twelve grid-and-weight cases verify the eigenvalues, including a degeneracy. These examples calculate neither a material transition temperature nor a microscopic interaction. [R5](#ref-source-ae28d4e3baad051f)

## Why theoretical predictions differ

Xia and colleagues show that two apparently similar bilayer band models can favor different channels in random-phase-approximation calculations. In their selected 30 GPa setting, changing the Ni-eg crystal-field splitting changes orbital weights and pairing competition even when Fermi-surface shapes remain similar. One Wannier model crosses from dxy to s± near 0.37 eV, while their other model crosses near 0.30 eV. These are model-specific boundaries, not experimentally measured universal thresholds. Neither dxy nor d(x²−y²) should be shortened to an interchangeable d label when comparing predictions. [R4](#ref-source-14703288422dbd4c)

Xiong and colleagues use a constrained-path Monte Carlo treatment of a two-orbital bilayer model. In the checked author version, increasing Hund coupling or crystal-field splitting favors interlayer s± correlations over the selected intralayer d channel. The calculation retains density-density interactions while omitting spin-flip, pair-hopping and next-nearest hopping terms. Its ground-state correlations and finite-size comparisons remain conditional on that Hamiltonian and trial-state constraint. They are not an unbiased experimental determination or a finite-temperature Tc calculation; the final-version comparison remains open. [R5](#ref-source-ae28d4e3baad051f)

## Limits and disputes

Nodeless spectra can constrain specified d-wave models without proving s± rather than a sign-preserving s state. Conversely, a contact spectrum interpreted through one d-wave model cannot settle every film and pressure regime. Distinguish gap symmetry, intersheet phase, nodal topology and microscopic pairing interaction. Compare raw conditions, competing fit quality and uncertainties before combining evidence. Complete scientific acceptance, supplementary checks and independent experimental reanalysis remain open. [R6](#ref-source-ce76c4830c64c3c7) [R7](#ref-source-f9976c21a60be0b8) [R8](#ref-source-a5e400bcce2d5544)

## Discovery implications

A useful next program combines controlled disorder, phase-sensitive junctions and momentum-resolved spectroscopy on compositionally and structurally matched samples. Models should predict distinguishable observables using the same orbital parameters and conditions, and report their sensitivity to missing interactions. Preserve oxygen content, strain, thickness, pressure medium and contact geometry alongside each claim. These are proposed discriminating tests, not confirmation of one universal nickelate mechanism. [R4](#ref-source-14703288422dbd4c) [R5](#ref-source-ae28d4e3baad051f) [R6](#ref-source-ce76c4830c64c3c7)

## Related topics

Continue with [nickelate families](/scwiki/nickelates), [d-wave pairing](/scwiki/d-wave), [dxy pairing](/scwiki/dxy-pairing), and [the unified-mechanism question](/scwiki/open-questions/n2).

## Claim evidence and conditions

### scwiki-n7-claim-scope-1

There is no justified single pairing assignment for every nickelate. Infinite-layer nickelates and Ruddlesden–Popper bilayers have different structures and electronic settings; pressurized bulk crystals and ambient-pressure strained films also require separate treatment. The approved question about s± versus d-wave pairing therefore needs a material, composition, strain or pressure, temperature range and experimental criterion. A superconducting transition establishes neither the order-parameter symmetry nor its microscopic cause by itself.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-35fd62b7cb3c490c, source-df0c15d62982f853.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-scope-2

In a tetragonal single-band illustration, a d-wave gap changes sign under a quarter turn, whereas an s± state can preserve that rotation while changing sign between Fermi sheets. The two d-wave forms d(x²−y²) and dxy have different nodal directions. Real multiorbital states additionally require orbital and band transformation rules. A nodal or nodeless measurement must be compared with the actual Fermi surface and measured momentum range.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-14703288422dbd4c, source-ae28d4e3baad051f.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-experimental-criteria-1

For infinite-layer La- and Pr-based films, Harvey and colleagues report low-temperature quadratic superfluid-density behavior consistent with disorder and a nodal gap. Their Nd samples have magnetic contributions that prevent a direct inference of the intrinsic nodal structure. This is evidence concerning specific infinite-layer films, not a measurement of the bilayer sign pattern. The present check covers the final abstract and selected indexed methods and conclusions; it is not a complete independent penetration-depth analysis.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-7b6e19919552090c.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-experimental-criteria-2

Guo and colleagues' final high-pressure Andreev study fits selected 23 GPa spectra with gaps near 23 and 6 meV. A dominant anisotropic s-like gap with either an s-like or a smaller d-like component describes their selected data better than the tested dominant-d alternatives. It does not measure an interband sign reversal directly. Their estimated contact radius is about 7.3 nm, versus a mean free path near 1.6 nm, and the paper discusses fragmented conducting paths. A broad resistive transition, background normalization and contact assumptions limit interpretation. Its 19 meV passage refers to a different cited film experiment, not this high-pressure gap.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-ce76c4830c64c3c7.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-experimental-criteria-3

Cao and colleagues instead interpret directional spectra in 20–22 GPa crystals as d-wave evidence. Their September 2025 preprint compares V-shaped spectra and zero-bias peaks with an anisotropic tunnelling model; it remains labelled as a preprint here. Different orientations use separate cells, and the authors describe visually aligned contacts, mechanical instability and local suppression by excessive tip pressure. These conditions need validation before treating the contrast with other spectra as a universal symmetry verdict. A zero-bias peak alone is insufficient.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-f9976c21a60be0b8.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-what-film-spectroscopy-establishes-1

Shen and colleagues' 2026 Science paper reports a nodeless gap and electron–boson coupling in (La,Pr,Sm) bilayer films. The checked author version finds a roughly 18 meV gap near the zone diagonal and uses synchrotron measurements to extend momentum coverage. It also reports spectral suppression above the resistive onset and separates that pseudogap behavior from the sharper transition-related change. Its approximately 70 meV dispersion kink does not identify the pairing mediator uniquely. The final abstract is verified, while full author-to-final and supplementary comparisons remain open.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-a5e400bcce2d5544.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-what-film-spectroscopy-establishes-2

Sun and colleagues studied Sr-doped bilayer films. Their checked author version finds leading-edge shifts of about 1–2 meV at selected momenta, including the diagonal, with an instrumental energy resolution near 5 meV. Temperature cycling and normalization checks support the reported shift, but a leading-edge displacement is not automatically the full superconducting gap. The July 2026 final publication identity is verified; its complete text has not been compared here. These different observables and film compositions must not be combined into one gap value.

Evidence: experiment. Sources: source-e78a5a3cef51e9fe.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-mathematical-assumptions-3

Changing only the relative gap sign leaves these energies unchanged. Eighteen independent matrix cases also compare the electron spectral functions and recover the same result. This demonstrates a restricted ambiguity of magnitude measurements; it is not a statement that every spectroscopic response is insensitive to phase. A separate fixed-hybridization counterexample changes the spectrum when one gap sign flips. Real matrix elements, interband processes, disorder and interface scattering must be specified.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-14703288422dbd4c, source-ce76c4830c64c3c7.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-mathematical-assumptions-6

The basis change is explicitly checked. It is conditional on equivalent layers and the assumed pairing matrix; it does not establish that real films realize this state. An independent separable angular-kernel example likewise changes its leading s± or d(x²−y²) channel when imposed channel weights change. Twelve grid-and-weight cases verify the eigenvalues, including a degeneracy. These examples calculate neither a material transition temperature nor a microscopic interaction.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-ae28d4e3baad051f.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-why-theoretical-predictions-differ-1

Xia and colleagues show that two apparently similar bilayer band models can favor different channels in random-phase-approximation calculations. In their selected 30 GPa setting, changing the Ni-eg crystal-field splitting changes orbital weights and pairing competition even when Fermi-surface shapes remain similar. One Wannier model crosses from dxy to s± near 0.37 eV, while their other model crosses near 0.30 eV. These are model-specific boundaries, not experimentally measured universal thresholds. Neither dxy nor d(x²−y²) should be shortened to an interchangeable d label when comparing predictions.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-14703288422dbd4c.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-why-theoretical-predictions-differ-2

Xiong and colleagues use a constrained-path Monte Carlo treatment of a two-orbital bilayer model. In the checked author version, increasing Hund coupling or crystal-field splitting favors interlayer s± correlations over the selected intralayer d channel. The calculation retains density-density interactions while omitting spin-flip, pair-hopping and next-nearest hopping terms. Its ground-state correlations and finite-size comparisons remain conditional on that Hamiltonian and trial-state constraint. They are not an unbiased experimental determination or a finite-temperature Tc calculation; the final-version comparison remains open.

Evidence: theory. Sources: source-ae28d4e3baad051f.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-limits-and-disputes-1

Nodeless spectra can constrain specified d-wave models without proving s± rather than a sign-preserving s state. Conversely, a contact spectrum interpreted through one d-wave model cannot settle every film and pressure regime. Distinguish gap symmetry, intersheet phase, nodal topology and microscopic pairing interaction. Compare raw conditions, competing fit quality and uncertainties before combining evidence. Complete scientific acceptance, supplementary checks and independent experimental reanalysis remain open.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-ce76c4830c64c3c7, source-f9976c21a60be0b8, source-a5e400bcce2d5544.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

### scwiki-n7-claim-discovery-implications-1

A useful next program combines controlled disorder, phase-sensitive junctions and momentum-resolved spectroscopy on compositionally and structurally matched samples. Models should predict distinguishable observables using the same orbital parameters and conditions, and report their sensitivity to missing interactions. Preserve oxygen content, strain, thickness, pressure medium and contact geometry alongside each claim. These are proposed discriminating tests, not confirmation of one universal nickelate mechanism.

Evidence: hypothesis. Sources: source-14703288422dbd4c, source-ae28d4e3baad051f, source-ce76c4830c64c3c7.

Conditions: Preserve nickelate family, sample, pressure/strain, momentum coverage, gap estimator, model basis and publication version.

Verification scope: Selected primary evidence and independent restricted examples; no complete raw-data refit or settled material-wide mechanism.

claims.statement: A credible claim of a new superconducting material needs convergent, reproducible evidence tied to a documented sample and conditions. A resistance drop, diamagnetic background or partly levitating fragment is a candidate observation, not a unique identification. This page uses LK-99 as a measurement-control case study. Lee and colleagues' July 2023 preprint claimed ambient-pressure superconductivity above 400 K; that claim is not accepted as a measured material Tc here. Selected independent studies instead found alternative explanations or non-superconducting samples. Those results apply to their investigated specimens and do not constitute a test of every possible composition.

claims.statement: Preserve synthesis records, composition, phase analysis, specimen identifiers, dimensions and contact positions. Connect transport, magnetic and thermodynamic observations to the same specimen where practicable, or to traceably matched pieces with documented differences. Diffraction and microscopy have detection limits; nominal chemical formulas do not guarantee homogeneous doping or exclude minority phases. Puphal and colleagues found spatially inhomogeneous Cu concentrations in their crystals even while their structural analysis identified the lead-apatite phase.

claims.statement: Report raw voltages, excitation current, polarity, temperature calibration, field, sweep direction, stability and uncertainty. Four-terminal wiring reduces ordinary contact-voltage contamination but does not make every contact configuration diagnostic. Change current and voltage contacts, reverse current, check heating and inspect reproducibility across cycles. State a resistance bound at the instrument's sensitivity rather than claiming an exact measured zero. Constant thermoelectric offsets and current-dependent thermal effects need different controls.

claims.statement: A magnetic assessment should distinguish a diamagnetic background, zero-field-cooled shielding and field-cooled flux expulsion. Record holder subtraction, volume or mass normalization, sample shape and ferromagnetic contributions. Geometry, pinning and granularity complicate any conversion to a superconducting volume fraction. Combine these observations with appropriate thermodynamic measurements where sensitivity and sample size permit; a missing resolvable anomaly constrains a claim only in relation to those limits. This is an evidence plan, not a demand that every experimental platform deliver identical signals.

claims.statement: Zhu and colleagues measured Cu2S controls and mixtures containing different Cu2S fractions. In the checked in-press article, pure Cu2S changes from about 13.7 Ω cm at 385.6 K to 0.006 Ω cm at 381.5 K, with a heating–cooling hysteresis of 13.1 K. The lower resistivity is finite. Their Cu2S-rich mixture also shows a sharp resistivity change and a magnetic anomaly. These observations provide an alternative explanation for selected transition-like features; they do not establish superconductivity or explain every magnetic signal in every synthesis. The order of this structural transition is not a universal rule for excluding all possible superconducting transitions.

claims.statement: Preserve unsuccessful batches and negative controls alongside successful-looking traces. Independent groups should document composition, measurement sensitivity and protocol differences before calling results a replication or contradiction. ## Scope

A credible claim of a new superconducting material needs convergent, reproducible evidence tied to a documented sample and conditions. A resistance drop, diamagnetic background or partly levitating fragment is a candidate observation, not a unique identification. This page uses LK-99 as a measurement-control case study. Lee and colleagues' July 2023 preprint claimed ambient-pressure superconductivity above 400 K; that claim is not accepted as a measured material Tc here. Selected independent studies instead found alternative explanations or non-superconducting samples. Those results apply to their investigated specimens and do not constitute a test of every possible composition. [R1](#ref-source-cd8f3ac578e82497) [R2](#ref-source-0d5220e22a764bd4) [R3](#ref-source-a2986ca87572851e) [R4](#ref-source-4065b69b701c07cd)

## Experimental criteria

Preserve synthesis records, composition, phase analysis, specimen identifiers, dimensions and contact positions. Connect transport, magnetic and thermodynamic observations to the same specimen where practicable, or to traceably matched pieces with documented differences. Diffraction and microscopy have detection limits; nominal chemical formulas do not guarantee homogeneous doping or exclude minority phases. Puphal and colleagues found spatially inhomogeneous Cu concentrations in their crystals even while their structural analysis identified the lead-apatite phase. [R3](#ref-source-a2986ca87572851e)

Report raw voltages, excitation current, polarity, temperature calibration, field, sweep direction, stability and uncertainty. Four-terminal wiring reduces ordinary contact-voltage contamination but does not make every contact configuration diagnostic. Change current and voltage contacts, reverse current, check heating and inspect reproducibility across cycles. State a resistance bound at the instrument's sensitivity rather than claiming an exact measured zero. Constant thermoelectric offsets and current-dependent thermal effects need different controls. [R5](#ref-source-c8143afdf96ce96f) [R6](#ref-source-0c63f38b6789c792)

A magnetic assessment should distinguish a diamagnetic background, zero-field-cooled shielding and field-cooled flux expulsion. Record holder subtraction, volume or mass normalization, sample shape and ferromagnetic contributions. Geometry, pinning and granularity complicate any conversion to a superconducting volume fraction. Combine these observations with appropriate thermodynamic measurements where sensitivity and sample size permit; a missing resolvable anomaly constrains a claim only in relation to those limits. This is an evidence plan, not a demand that every experimental platform deliver identical signals. [R2](#ref-source-0d5220e22a764bd4) [R3](#ref-source-a2986ca87572851e) [R7](#ref-source-37f27e50dbdcf3a5)

## What the LK-99 controls show

Zhu and colleagues measured Cu2S controls and mixtures containing different Cu2S fractions. In the checked in-press article, pure Cu2S changes from about 13.7 Ω cm at 385.6 K to 0.006 Ω cm at 381.5 K, with a heating–cooling hysteresis of 13.1 K. The lower resistivity is finite. Their Cu2S-rich mixture also shows a sharp resistivity change and a magnetic anomaly. These observations provide an alternative explanation for selected transition-like features; they do not establish superconductivity or explain every magnetic signal in every synthesis. The order of this structural transition is not a universal rule for excluding all possible superconducting transitions. [R2](#ref-source-0d5220e22a764bd4)

Puphal and colleagues' sulfur-free crystal study attempted four-point room-temperature transport and found resistance above several megaohms. Their magnetic measurements cover 2–800 K and identify weak ferromagnetic contributions alongside diamagnetism. Optical transparency alone is not their decisive transport test. Some displayed magnetization data retain holder offsets, while a separate large-sample calibration explicitly subtracts the holder contribution. Keep those protocols distinct. Merging of cooling histories at the start of a measurement range is not by itself a critical temperature. [R3](#ref-source-a2986ca87572851e)

Wang and colleagues compared half-levitating and non-levitating fragments. Both groups were insulating in the investigated 165–300 K interval. Their magnetic results and shape-dependent torque analysis show how soft ferromagnetism can accompany half levitation without the claimed superconductivity. The fitted activation scale is not a superconducting gap. A levitation video therefore cannot replace transport and magnetic controls, and a ferromagnetic contribution must not automatically be assigned to Cu2S. [R4](#ref-source-4065b69b701c07cd)

## Mathematical assumptions

For a linear resistor with a constant voltage offset, an original current-reversal example gives

$$
V_+=IR+V_0,\qquad V_-=-IR+V_0,\qquad
\widehat R=\frac{V_+-V_-}{2I}.
$$

Nine independent cases recover the imposed resistance and constant offset. With each voltage error bounded by 10 nV at an exact 1 mA current, the worst-case resistance error is 10 μΩ. This is a deterministic bound, not a statistical confidence interval. Current uncertainty, changing thermal offsets, nonlinearity and moving contacts require additional analysis; some thermoelectric effects reverse with current and survive this subtraction. [R5](#ref-source-c8143afdf96ce96f) [R6](#ref-source-0c63f38b6789c792)

A separate four-node resistor network has two conducting branches and voltage probes at their midpoints. Equal branch resistance ratios give a zero midpoint voltage even though the input resistance and dissipated power remain positive. Twenty-seven cases verify Kirchhoff's equations and energy balance, including imbalanced branches. This constructed transfer-resistance counterexample demonstrates why geometry and alternative paths matter. It is not a reconstruction of any LK-99 experiment. [R5](#ref-source-c8143afdf96ce96f)

For a homogeneous ellipsoid with linear intrinsic SI volume susceptibility χ and demagnetizing factor N,

$$
H_{\rm int}=H_{\rm a}-NM,\qquad
\chi_{\rm app}=\frac{M}{H_{\rm a}}=\frac{\chi}{1+N\chi}.
$$

Twelve independent cases check this relation and its inverse. In the idealized χ = −1, N = 0.5 case, χapp = −2; its magnitude does not imply a 200% superconducting volume fraction. The assumed uniform ellipsoid does not model a granular irregular fragment, hysteretic ferromagnet or pinned vortex distribution. Mass susceptibilities and cgs values cannot be inserted without conversion. [R7](#ref-source-37f27e50dbdcf3a5)

## Standards and reporting

The original preprint invokes electric-field or resistivity criteria and cites application-oriented books. Its references 16 and 17 are Wang's electrical-engineering book and Ekin's low-temperature measurement book, not the text of an IEC standard. Separately, the official public scope of IEC 61788-1:2006 concerns critical-current measurement in specified Nb-Ti composite conductors in a liquid-helium bath. An engineering threshold for a known conductor is not a universal certification that an unfamiliar material hosts a new superconducting phase. The paid standard's full clauses have not been checked here. [R1](#ref-source-cd8f3ac578e82497) [R8](#ref-source-183e82eda528f417)

Preserve unsuccessful batches and negative controls alongside successful-looking traces. Independent groups should document composition, measurement sensitivity and protocol differences before calling results a replication or contradiction. A provisional editorial progression can separate a candidate anomaly, reproducible transport evidence and convergent bulk evidence. These are proposed reporting categories, not an official certification scheme. Share data, calibrations, analysis code and versioned corrections sufficiently to test competing explanations. [R2](#ref-source-0d5220e22a764bd4) [R3](#ref-source-a2986ca87572851e) [R4](#ref-source-4065b69b701c07cd) [R6](#ref-source-0c63f38b6789c792)

## Limits and disputes

This review checks selected primary passages and a limited set of figures. It does not reproduce raw experimental measurements, compare every manuscript version or establish the properties of every claimed LK-99 preparation. The original claim is explicitly a preprint; the independent examples above are synthetic controls with stated assumptions. Apparent agreement among several measurements is strongest when they share a traceable phase, specimen history and temperature or field scale. Unresolved differences should remain visible rather than being replaced by a single categorical label. [R1](#ref-source-cd8f3ac578e82497) [R2](#ref-source-0d5220e22a764bd4) [R3](#ref-source-a2986ca87572851e) [R4](#ref-source-4065b69b701c07cd)

## Discovery implications

Allocate effort to observations that discriminate among superconductivity, structural transitions, current-path artifacts and magnetic torque. For a candidate, prioritize reproducible synthesis, contact permutations, phase-resolved characterization and quantitative magnetic controls before advertising an exceptional Tc. State precisely which alternative each new test excludes, which remain possible and what independent work would change the conclusion. ## Related topics

Continue with [zero resistance](/scwiki/zero-resistance), [the Meissner effect](/scwiki/meissner-effect), [room-temperature superconductivity](/scwiki/open-questions/n1), and [measurement methods](/scwiki/experimental-methods).
